Timing of Climate Science Reports Ignites a Hot Fight at U.N. Talks
Several countries that rely heavily on fossil fuels want to delay the next round of scientific assessments that governments use to inform their climate policies.
A squabble over the publication timetable for several climate reports has turned into one of the burning issues of this year’s United Nations climate conference, as some warn that fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization.
The U.N.-backed Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change produces landmark reports that generally come out every five to seven years. The next round of reports would take on topics like physical changes to the earth and greenhouse gas emissions.
Timing is critical because in 2028 nations are supposed to assess their progress and then ramp up their efforts to do more, based on the best science. That process, known as a stocktake and occurring every five years, is the engine of the Paris Agreement.
Saudi Arabia, India and Russia are among those pushing to delay the reports so that at least two of them come out after 2028.
The fact that those nations rank among the largest fossil fuel exporters or importers has led to accusations that coal, oil and gas interests might be interfering with science.
“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the I.P.C.C. in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” said former Vice President Al Gore, who is in Turkey for the talks.

Akshay Kumar is stepping into the world of science fiction with Samuk, his upcoming collaboration with filmmaker Vipul Amrutlal Shah. After the reunion between the actor and producer-director was officially announced, the makers have now released an atmospheric motion poster, offering the first glimpse into the film’s extraterrestrial premise. The visual reveal also confirms the film’s theatrical release date, setting the stage for what appears to be a survival-driven action thriller.
Akshay Kumar starrer Samuk motion poster unveils alien threat; sci-fi thriller to release in cinemas on May 28, 2027
The motion poster features Akshay Kumar in a rugged, military-style avatar, holding a rifle as he faces the ominous silhouette of what appears to be an extraterrestrial creature’s hand. The contrast between the human figure and the unidentified presence establishes the central conflict suggested by the film’s first promotional material. Accompanying the visual is the tagline, ‘The Mission is Human but The Enemy Isn’t’, hinting at a mission in which human survival and tactical resilience will be tested against an unknown threat.
The makers have confirmed that Samuk will arrive in cinemas worldwide on May 28, 2027. They have also announced that another major update about the film will be unveiled today at 2:00 PM. While the nature of the announcement has not yet been disclosed, it has added another element of anticipation around the project. Further details about the cast, characters and story are awaited, with the upcoming reveal potentially offering a clearer picture of the film’s scale and narrative.
One predator. One mission.
A fight that has no rules.
#SAMUK unveils at 2:07 PM. Stay Tuned! https://t.co/xNhr9qAVp8
— Akshay Kumar (@akshaykumar) November 16, 2026
Samuk also brings Akshay Kumar and Vipul Amrutlal Shah together again after a series of successful collaborations across different genres. The duo has previously worked on films such as Aankhen, Waqt: The Race Against Time, Namastey London, Singh Is Kinng and Action Replayy. Their association has covered comedy, drama, romance and action, while their latest project takes them into the science-fiction space.
The motion poster suggests that the film will combine military action with a creature-based premise, marking a different genre outing for the actor. Akshay’s rugged appearance and the suggestion of an alien adversary point towards a narrative built around a confrontation between humans and an unfamiliar force.
With its release date now locked and another announcement scheduled for the afternoon, Samuk has begun revealing details of its cinematic world. Audiences will have to wait for the next update to learn more about the film’s cast and the story behind its human-versus-extraterrestrial conflict.

Respect? Exposure? Why England's star names are going abroad
- Published
Bayern Munich's Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane, Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham, Barcelona's Anthony Gordon - three of England's star players, all of whom are playing their club football abroad.
The Premier League is widely regarded as the most competitive league in the world with the greatest financial muscle, but that does not always translate to the biggest individual profiles and, increasingly, star names are looking elsewhere.
Since Cristiano Ronaldo won the Ballon d'Or in 2008, for example, only Rodri in 2024 was playing in England at the time of being crowned the best player in the world. Michael Owen, in 2001, was the last Englishman to do so while in England.
The trend of English players going abroad has gathered pace since a teenage Jadon Sancho signed for Borussia Dortmund in 2017 and that is reflected in this current Three Lions squad - seven of the initial 25 play outside England.
"Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane were decisive for us in the World Cup and I see no reason they won't be in the future," said England boss Thomas Tuchel when talking about his big stars playing outside of their home country.
"It's good that Anthony has stepped up now. He is the third one. There is obviously a relevance to them playing abroad but I don't see that a player who plays in the Premier League cannot step up and be decisive for us."
At the World Cup in the summer and during the last international break, however, it was those three players' goals and assists that proved decisive.
What could the impact be?
Currently there are 43 English players on the Football Association's radar playing their club football in Europe.
The FA's technical director John McDermott believes it is a "huge positive" to have so many players playing across Europe.
"I spoke to a couple of the boys that are playing abroad at the moment," he told BBC Sport. "The exposure they get in those leagues, playing Champions League or European football, where you're not necessarily having to bang out 55 games, but you still have got time to do your weight training and your gym work.
"Often if you're playing in the English competition or in the EFL, where it's 46 games - you know it's game, game, game, which is fantastic - but for some players that opportunity to get the training in-between and to practise developing on technique or other areas, there's benefits to that."
McDermott was previously at Tottenham Hotspur and says that even when he was in club football, he was a "big believer" in players going abroad to "develop character" and "independence".
"I think being in another changing room and learning another language just puts you under the pressure to adapt," he added.
"And I think for any young person that ability not only to become technically, tactically more adept, but also culturally have to pick up something else - it's huge and prevents people from becoming complacent or just getting used to the same old, same old."
Gordon said in the recent international break he feels he gets more respect now he plays for one of Europe's elite sides, compared with when he was at Newcastle.
"I think he's always been respected," McDermott said.
"I remember when Trips (Kieran Trippier) came back, and Trips was a good player, but when he came back from Atletico (Madrid) I noticed he was just maybe tighter technically and noticed there was a change that Kieran came back with.
"So I'm not sure if he's respected more ... but I think you want all of the players - whether they stay in England [or not] - every six months you see this sort of incremental step where they've added something, another dimension to the game.
"That can sometimes come in this country, obviously, playing with different players, being in new competitions, but I think going abroad definitely helps that.
"And I've seen that with Anthony already and some of the other boys. They come back, it's four months since you've seen them and there's another dimension there."
McDermott is keen to make clear that developing in England can still be of a huge benefit and that Jarell Quansah and Jobe Bellingham, two of England's squad who are now playing in Germany, also played in the EFL.
"There's all different ways, I don't think there's this elixir, I don't think there's this magic formula, 'this is the way'," McDermott said.
England reached the semi-finals of the World Cup for just the third time in their history in the summer.
McDermott was asked if he thought now the Three Lions had more players abroad, it could help develop England's style or performance in major tournaments.
"Yeah, possibly. Again don't underestimate if you're playing now in the Champions League at an English club," he said.
"We would like more players in the pipeline. I think at the moment we're on about 26% or 27% English-qualified players playing the Premier League.
"We've got 40 to 50 players playing at Champions League quality and playing in European football, top Premier League clubs, so let's not underestimate our own product."
McDermott says it is clear the impact having players in different countries is having on the squad, but it is then down to the manager to blend the style.
"I think the different cultural experiences they get, the different exposure they get to play in different types of football is fantastic.
"But still, the England manager has got to try and find that singular blend when they come back of the English players, the Spanish players, the German players, the Italian players, it's all sort of an eclectic mix that they're bringing."
People did not respect 'quality and IQ' in England
Gordon has impressed since making his move to Barcelona in the summer with three goals and five assists in 15 appearances in all competitions.
The 25-year-old is regularly lining up with some of the best players in the world, in a front line alongside Lamine Yamal and Raphinha.
The lure of European giants like Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich is hard for any player to turn down.
Arsenal's approach for Vinicius Jr this summer was always going to be hard to complete as the famous white shirt and lifestyle in Madrid is, for most players, the pinnacle.
But does moving abroad to one of Europe's top clubs also alter people's perceptions of English players?
"I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed, but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon said in a recent interview with ITV.
"Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick."
Gordon produced some standout moments in the World Cup, assisting both of Kane's goals in the last-32 win over DR Congo, winning a penalty in England's last-16 win over Mexico and scoring the goal to put England ahead in the semi-final against Argentina.
Captain Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England" and that Gordon is "relishing" being one of England's "main men".
"I think it's great," added England and Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin. "The fact that we've got top-level English players playing abroad now at top European clubs, I think it's only good for English football and us as a national team.
"You see they bring different experiences that they're learning from overseas and they bring it into this group and I think as you can see they're only growing in confidence and as players and I think it's only a positive thing."

Autlook Filmsales, a leading sales agent for feature documentaries and doc series, has boarded Peter Alsted’s “Dr. Hedgehog” ahead of the film’s pitch at Forum, IDFA‘s prestigious industry program. The Danish project is among the films selected for this year’s Forum Pitch Presentations.
“Dr. Hedgehog” is a deep dive into the chaotic life of researcher Sophie Lund Rasmussen, the self-appointed Dr. Hedgehog. Rasmussen is the only Danish zoologist with a PhD in the small nocturnal animal and is on a mission to save the endangered creature while also battling 23 chronic illnesses. The film will portray a “career-minded woman striving to save a species and get recognition while also fighting to stay alive long enough for it all to happen.”
The project is produced by Denmark’s Elk Film through producers Birgitte Keseler and Katrine Dolmer and executive producer Andreas Dalsgaard. Alsted’s first documentary was 2015’s award-winning “Standing on Water,” with his films playing major festivals such as CPH:Dox.
Speaking with Variety ahead of the Forum, Autlook Filmsales’s Stephanie Fuchs says the project “won us over right away.” “It’s tender, funny and surprising, and through this small creature, Peter says something big about care and our bond with the living world. We’re thrilled to partner again with Elk Film and bring it to audiences worldwide.”
Alsted recalls meeting Rasmussen three years ago: “I read an article about her in the newspaper, and there was something about her that just caught my attention.”
“There was, first of all, the little spiky animal that is endangered, but there were also her arms, which were tattooed with a list of her autoimmune diseases,” he adds. “I contacted her and immediately kind of fell in love with her story, her character, her clumsy, nerdy, driven, passionate way of approaching life and her science. Also, at a time when there is so much fake news, she is dedicated to facts; she is data-driven.”
The director then went to one of her talks, where he saw her speak about her research on stage. He felt there was a creative “chemistry,” and proposed the idea of the film right away. Rasmussen was not only open but greatly enthusiastic about sharing her research and life on screen, with the two spending the first year of their collaboration getting to know each other better and filming kicking off last year.
Alsted believes “Dr. Hedgehog” has great potential to “resonate with the everyday person.” He mentions how Rasmussen defines the hedgehog as “the perfect bridge between wildlife and modern society, because they live in our backyards.” “They are right outside our door, and they’re the easiest wild animal to get close to because they just curl up.”
There is also the fact that Rasmussen is a personable character, someone with a great life purpose but also open about her daily struggles. “She has 23 diagnosed chronic illnesses and her health has been deteriorating since she was four years old. She has a death stamp on her, and I think this speaks to a lot of people who are in similar situations, struggling with either their physical or mental health, and who can’t relate to people like Elon Musk or a big, rich celebrity.”
Keseler was immediately drawn to the project upon first hearing about Rasmussen’s story from Alsted. She and the team at Elk Films boarded “Dr. Hedgehog” right away, and first introduced the project to the market at Nordisk Panorama in September.
“We had such great feedback and a lot of interest,” she says of the experience. “We were nervous, of course, but we got feedback that the film is hopeful, that it’s dealing with something people can connect to. The film is coming at a time when the world is shifting into a horrible place, and Sophie brings a little hope because she’s this regular person who has a lot of challenges but still does something to improve her space and therefore all of our spaces.”
The “Dr. Hedgehog” team is hoping to secure the means to start full production in spring of 2027, with expected completion at the end of 2028. When asked if they feel a certain sense of urgency given the scientist’s unpredictable illnesses, Alsted says: “The sense of urgency also comes from her because she wants us to finish the film so she can actually watch it [laughs]. It’s definitely a thing. She calls me, texts me any time she is doing something, so we have a lot of trust, but she also definitely wants me to finish the film [laughs].”
Autlook Filmsales has a strong IDFA lineup this year, including David Greaves and William Greaves’ “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” Barbara Kopple’s “Union Town,” Michał Marczak’s “Closure” and Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller’s “They’re Here.” IDFA runs Nov. 12-22.

Defending champion Jharkhand will look to continue its winning run when it takes on Rajasthan in the second round of the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy on Monday. Jharkhand began its title defence with a commanding six-wicket win over Mizoram, chasing down a target of 77 in just 8.3 overs. Rajasthan, meanwhile, also made a winning start, beating Uttar Pradesh by six wickets.
Two-time former champion Karnataka will aim to build on its 19-run victory over Bengal when it faces Uttar Pradesh, which will be eager to bounce back from its opening-day defeat to Rajasthan. Tamil Nadu, the tournament’s most successful team with three titles, will also look to make it two wins in a row when it takes on Jammu and Kashmir. The former champion edged past Railways by six runs in its opening fixture, while J&K suffered a 103-run defeat against Delhi.
Mumbai and Gujarat will be involved in one of the day’s most anticipated contests after making impressive starts to their campaigns. Mumbai chased down Hyderabad’s 172 in just 13.1 overs, with Suryakumar Yadav smashing an unbeaten 60 off 21 balls. Gujarat, meanwhile, posted 250 for nine against Odisha, the tournament’s highest total on the opening day, before securing a 21-run win. Both sides will look to maintain their momentum in what promises to be an intriguing Group D encounter.
Delhi and Punjab will also face off in a clash between two opening-day winners. Delhi produced one of the most dominant performances of the first round, defeating Jammu and Kashmir by 103 runs after posting 243 for six. Mayank Yadav starred with the ball, claiming five wickets for 14 runs. Punjab, meanwhile, pulled off a four-wicket win over last season’s finalist Haryana, chasing down a target of 191 with five balls to spare.
Haryana will look to get its campaign back on track when it takes on Saurashtra, while Baroda, a two-time former champion, will aim to recover from its narrow three-wicket defeat to Chandigarh against Mizoram. Maharashtra, which lost to Puducherry by 15 runs despite scoring 189 for five in reply to 205, will face Kerala as it seeks its first victory.
Among the other teams looking to build on winning starts, Vidarbha will take on Odisha after registering a seven-wicket win over Goa. Hyderabad, meanwhile, will be keen to bounce back against Chhattisgarh after its defeat to Mumbai. With several former champions already facing contrasting fortunes, the second round offers an early opportunity for the contenders to strengthen their positions in the group standings.

Comeback kid Joseph thrills as England eye All Blacks
- Published
Eddie Jones aired a complaint about Twickenham's in-stadium experience when he appeared on BBC Radio 5 Live this week.
"Being a spectator and being told when to make noise is a bit funny," said the Japan boss, objecting to a big-screen request for an increase in volume.
Jones sat stony-faced in the coaching box as the message appeared again in the midst of his team's 78-15 thrashing at England's hands on Saturday.
There was little for him to enjoy on his return to Twickenham, where he was head coach for seven years.
But, for the rest of a capacity crowd, it was a fun one.
With junior tickets on sale at £15, there was a different atmosphere from usual. The decibels were higher, the demographic was younger, the spirits a little lighter.
And England brought plenty of entertainment to the party. Thirteen tries in total, with Will Joseph's five putting him in the centre of the chorus line.
The 24-year-old won his only previous England cap under Jones. Back in the summer of 2022, he was a teenage apprentice taken on tour to Australia and thrust into the second Test as a last-minute replacement.
His promise has taken some time to be fulfilled. He struggled for game time and fitness at Harlequins after London Irish's bankruptcy forced him to move on from his boyhood club.
An auto-immune condition that cost him the hearing in his left ear was one setback at the Stoop.
But, as part of a rat pack of exciting young English-qualified backs at Gloucester this season, he has been superb: a swerving, offloading, game-breaking threat either on the wing or in midfield.
England deployed him out wide, to bring some of the razzle-dazzle that they lost as Immanuel Feyi-Waboso limped out of their autumn campaign.
Reports from Pennyhill Park during the week had suggested Joseph was doing a fine job of replicating Feyi-Waboso's explosive elusiveness.
He certainly did on Twickenham's main stage, finishing chances with the same pace and power.
"He is pretty similar to Immanuel Feyi-Waboso in the way he plays his game," said former England wing Chris Ashton on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"He is just so fast. He doesn't look too fast in the first two steps and then he is just gone. He gets away from people."
Joseph's cartwheeling plant of the ball over the line for his fourth summed up his exuberance.
In the aftermath of that score, Japan flanker Ben Gunter put a consoling arm around full-back Kazuma Ueda, who had been comprehensively burned in a race to the corner.
Japan couldn't get near Joseph, whose first try came after just 60 seconds and his hat-trick score in the 19th minute.
"It has been a challenging four years, but I have enjoyed the journey to get back here and I am happy all that hard work I have put in has paid off," he said.
"I have had a taste for it now and I can't wait to do it again."
We have been here before though.
There was another teenage apprentice taken on that tour of Australia alongside Joseph.
Henry Arundell was Joseph's Irish team-mate. His impact on the trip was greater, scoring a try in the first Test and winning his second and third caps in the series.
The following year, while Joseph returned to the club scene, Arundell made his first England start in the Six Nations.
He earned a place in the Rugby World Cup squad and, in a foregone conclusion of a pool match, cantered in for five tries against Chile in Lille.
Arundell was electric against limited opposition. He has yet to convince in sterner Tests.
Joseph still has those to come. A shade slower, but a smidge smarter, he may be better suited to the Test scene.
New Zealand next Saturday, stung by defeat by Wales, would definitely be a step up if Steve Borthwick decides to find out.
There was plenty elsewhere to please the head coach.
George Martin was at his abrasive best. The Saracens second row led England's carry and tackle standings in the comeback performance we have been waiting for since his 14-month injury lay-off ended in May.
Ellis Genge was snorting fire and bruising ribs and Maro Itoje's rejuvenation after a summer off continues.
In the backline, Max Ojomoh was too clever and quick for the Japanese midfield, spotting space either for himself or others.
Henry Pollock, the other point of interest in a much-changed line-up, found it harder to get into the game with ball in hand, but did the dirty work in defence and at the breakdown that some have questioned.
Borthwick will be waiting nervously on news from his medical room this week, with Ollie Chessum, Seb Atkinson and George Furbank hoping to return in time for the All Blacks.
But a fourth win in a row, after five successive defeats, has further buoyed up his regime.
"The team is really starting to play well," he told BBC 5 Live. "The speed and positioning in attack was very good which gave us options to be able to move the ball.
"There was intent to play fast, with all the strengths of English rugby. We've got some really great attacking talent and I think we are seeing that.
"The balance of pass-kick decisions was really good. Ultimately I think one of the main things is the supporters really enjoyed it. The atmosphere was excellent."
Even Jones, who had Borthwick as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and his time with England, managed a smile by the end.
"It kills me that Will Joseph, I gave him his first cap, he scores five tries against me. Now that's not being very loyal, is it?," he joked.
"He's a great kid. He always was going to be a good player."
England will hope he might turn out even better than that.

An analysis of more than 180 epidemiological studies examining the health impacts of air pollution across India has found that over 91% of them reported at least one adverse health association with air pollution exposure.
These studies, published between 1975 and 2025, also noted that health impacts extend beyond respiratory diseases to cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, pregnancy complications, impaired child growth, tumours, blood disorders, mental and neurocognitive disorders, among others.
The analysis, released on Friday, was done by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), an independent research organisation focused on revealing the trends, causes, and health impacts, as well as the solutions, to air pollution.
Notably, out of 180 studies, only 40 examined air pollution's impact on rural populations, of which 38 reported at least one adverse health association, indicating that air pollution's health impacts are not confined to urban areas.
Further, most studies were conducted on Delhi (26) to examine the link between health and air pollution. The national capital was followed by Punjab with 13 studies, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh with 11 each, West Bengal with 10, Tamil Nadu with nine, Karnataka with eight and Telangana with seven, the report said.
In a statement, CREA analyst Manoj Kumar said, "The findings highlight the need to move beyond a city-centric approach and explicitly include rural areas through a regional, airshed-based approach in the next phase of National Clean Air Programme (NCAP 2.0)."
Studies examined a range of air pollutants, with 45 investigating both particulate matter and gaseous pollutants. PM2.5 was examined in 32 studies, PM10 alone in four, and both PM10 and PM2.5 in 16.
Among studies examining gaseous pollutants, statistically significant adverse health associations were reported for increased mortality, acute respiratory hospital and emergency visits, asthma-related hospital admissions, and impaired lung function.
Beyond their direct health effects, gaseous pollutants such as SOx and NOx also contribute to secondary PM2.5 formation by undergoing atmospheric chemical reactions to form sulphate and nitrate particles, respectively.
Kumar said, "Air pollution mitigation must adopt a multipollutant approach, addressing gaseous precursors that contribute to secondary PM2.5 and ground-level ozone formation. This requires emission reductions at major sources, including industries, power plants, residential cooking, and other combustion activities."

Chennai breathes far cleaner air than Delhi. A study that followed 12,064 adults in the two cities put the typical yearly level of fine particles around Chennai homes between 2010 and 2016 at 40.2 micrograms per cubic metre, just above the national standard of 40, against 101.5 in Delhi. In both cities, the dirtier a person’s air, the likelier they were to develop type 2 diabetes.
The World Health Organization’s theme for World Diabetes Day, on November 14 this year, is early action. The sixth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6), carried out in 2023-24, found 17.8% of women and 20.9% of men aged 15 and above had high blood sugar or were on medicine for it, up from 13.5% and 15.6% per cent in NFHS-5, conducted in 2019-21. In Chennai district, nearly 3 in 10 women fall in the group.
That said, there are limitations to this data: NFHS teams prick a finger at whatever hour they visit, so people may or may not have eaten, and a reading above 140 milligrams per decilitre counts as high. One such reading cannot diagnose diabetes. However, what is most routinely blamed for the rising burden of diabetes in the country -- and it is rising -- are weight and diet. And while these are significant factors, dirty air is rarely blamed. Perhaps it’s time it is.
The outdoor evidence
Siddhartha Mandal of the Centre for Chronic Disease Control in New Delhi and his colleagues used satellite and weather data to estimate daily levels of fine particles, called PM2.5, near each participant’s home.
Over a median of almost five years, 743 people developed type 2 diabetes. Each extra 10 micrograms in a person’s yearly average accounted for a 22% higher risk, after the researchers allowed for age, socio-economic status, tobacco and alcohol use, diet and exercise. Studies in richer, cleaner countries have put the rise at 7 to 11%.
A 2024 global review of 46 studies also linked PM2.5 and the coarser PM10 to type 2 diabetes. Its authors point mainly to inflammation and oxidative stress (damage from reactive oxygen), which blunt the body’s response to insulin, the hormone that moves sugar into cells. The Global Burden of Disease project puts about a fifth of the healthy years lost worldwide to type 2 diabetes in 2019 down to PM2.5, about 14% from outdoor air and 6% from household smoke.
Smoke in the kitchen
Between 2018 and 2021, researchers from the Madras Diabetes Research Foundation tested adults in 30 villages of Cheyyur taluk in Chengalpattu district as part of a project called TREND.
All but 208 of the 13,877 adults lived in homes cooking on traditional fuels such as firewood or kerosene. Diabetes was more common among them, 14.2% against 12%, and more common still, 16.5%, in homes without a separate kitchen. Among women, traditional fuel use was linked with 80% higher odds of diabetes of diabetes, after the researchers allowed for age, weight, family history, education and income.
One round of testing, however, cannot prove what causes diabetes, and the group using clean fuel was small. Even so, a 2022 review of nine studies with 45,620 people found that those who cooked with solid fuels had 46% higher odds of diabetes. However, in homes that burned only biomass like wood or dung, the link was too weak to be certain.
Short of gas, short of data
The NFHS used to report cooking fuel and blood sugar from the same homes. Clean fuel, mostly LPG, reached 58.6% of homes in 2019-21, up from 43.8% in 2015-16, as the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana distributed connections. Even at that pace, about 3 homes in 10, mostly in villages, would still have cooked on fuels such as wood, dung and kerosene by 2023-24. The NFHS-6 fact sheets, released on May 29, leave this figure out. The Health Ministry has said this, and other missing statistics are being monitored through dedicated national surveys and administrative databases; however these other surveys do not take blood samples, leaving possible connections unable to be made.
Much of India’s LPG comes from abroad. About 90% of those imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which the West Asia war choked in early March, leading to shortfalls across the country. Poor homes, though, used little gas even before the war. The average Ujjwala household bought 4.71 cylinders in 2025-26, and about one in seven in Bihar bought none, the Petroleum Ministry told the Lok Sabha. The ministry has since cut subsidised refills from nine a year to four, about half of what a family cooking only on gas needs, as per figures cited by think tank, the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW).
Every return to the wood stove brings back smoke tied to diabetes, and even a month of dirtier air nudged up blood sugar in the Delhi and Chennai study, a worry for anyone already living with the disease. As long as India’s kitchens depend on imported gas, the next war or blockade can push them back to wood, and more people towards diabetes.
The Kerala puzzle
If dirty air alone drove the numbers, the least polluted States would sit at the bottom of the survey’s tables. A satellite study of 2024 pollution by independent research organisation, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), put Kerala among the seven States and Union Territories with the cleanest air. Yet Kerala has the highest share of women with high blood sugar of any State or Union Territory, 28.9%, according to NFHS-6. Meghalaya, where CREA found every district above the national pollution standard outside the monsoon, has the lowest of any State, 7.1%. Kerala also has the oldest population of any State, and diabetes grows more common with age. This complicates the picture.
What could help, would be more data, and long-term studies that could tease apart the effects of air, with those of age, weight, diet and access to doctors, of the same people.
The NFHS, though, could provide answers sooner than any new study. The Health Ministry has said that a more detailed NFHS-6 national report will be released, though it is not clear if this will include cooking fuel numbers. If the report and household data include cooking fuel, researchers could compare blood sugar in homes using wood and gas, taking age and weight into account, and use data from before the shortage as a baseline. The Petroleum Ministry already tracks Ujjwala refills by State, and could publish this information monthly for every district.
It remains to be seen, however, if the data will materialise. Until then, India remains the country with the highest burden of diabetes, and one of the highest levels of air pollution.
(Dr Margubur Rahaman is a public health researcher at MAMTA Health Institute for Mother and Child, New Delhi. margubur48@gmail.com; Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Doctoral Fellow at the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Prayagraj. ankitmishrakoraon@gmail.com)

US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
- Published
A professional American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.
The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".
In statement on Sunday, the agency he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.
The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.
A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.
The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.
Nigeria, once regarded primarily as a transit hub for drug trafficking, has increasingly become a producer, consumer, and distributor of illegal drugs, according to the UN.
Recent NDLEA operations have uncovered several industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratories, raising concerns about links between Nigerian drug producers and Mexican cartels seeking to manufacture and export the drug.
In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos.
Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a highly addictive synthetic drug that can cause severe psychosis, heart attacks or stroke.
In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after the authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28m (£21m), which was destined for the UK.

Cloud storage certainly has a lot going for it. For a start, if you drop your laptop into the sink, it's likely that a lot of your important work will be backed up somewhere in the cloud, as long as you’re using services such as Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud.
Then there's file sharing: Not too many years ago, swapping large amounts of data with other people meant dragging and dropping and running around with USB drives (and perhaps even mailing them). Now, via a couple of clicks and a link, you can share just about anything with just about anyone, anywhere in the world.
However, this comes with security risks attached. You don't want those links making their way to anyone they weren't intended for, otherwise they've got access to your files and folders. They could potentially see what's in them, and maybe even make changes or delete files, depending on the permissions you've set.
It's worth emphasizing that sharing files through these cloud storage services isn't inherently insecure—these shared links are actually very well protected, by default. However, the longer they stick around, the bigger the risk gets. Your links could get mistakenly forwarded in an email, or one of your contacts could have their email account hacked.
With that in mind it's prudent to run a regular audit on the cloud sharing links you've got active. It shouldn't take long: The apps involved usually make this pretty straightforward. Once you've closed a link down, no one else can get to it.
Microsoft OneDrive
If you head to the Microsoft OneDrive portal on the web, you'll see a Shared link in the navigation pane on the left: Click this, then select By you up at the top of the file list to see everything you've shared with other people. Use the Modified header if you want to sort the files and folders by the oldest or most recent.
Click the three dots next to any file or folder, then Manage access to control who can get to it. If you've shared the file with specific people, you can remove some or all of them; if the file or folder is shared more widely with just a link, clicking the trash can gets rid of it. You can also open up Office files to manage access there.
It's worth knowing that when you opt to share a file in OneDrive on the web (via the three dots and Share), if you click the cog icon on the Share panel you can set an expiration date for the sharing—which saves you the trouble of having to tidy it up afterwards.
Apple iCloud
If iCloud Drive is your cloud storage service of choice, once you've got the main interface up on the web, you can click Shared on the navigation pane on the left to go straight to the files and folders you're sharing with other people. There's no easy way to sort them, but you can use the search box up in the top right corner.
Click the three dots next to a file and folder, then Managed Shared File, to make changes. The next screen lets you block access for specific contacts, and to change permissions (from editing to just viewing, for example). If you want to cancel the sharing altogether, click Stop sharing.
Unlike OneDrive, iCloud doesn't give you any way of putting expiration periods on shared links, so you have to clear them up manually.
Dropbox
Dropbox is one of the more aggressive services when it comes to tidying up shared links, and if you use the Dropbox apps you might see reminders to review the files and folders you've shared with others. From Dropbox on the web, click Shared in the left-hand navigation pane to see files and folders you're currently sharing.
You can get quite a detailed breakdown here, including by Files or by Folders. Click the three dots next to any entry, then Share, to see the current sharing options: You can remove access for contacts one by one, or click the cog icon (top left) to find the Unshare button that ends all sharing completely.
Dropbox does have link expiry features built in: If you open up the share settings whenever you're sharing a file or folder, you'll see Link expiry is one of the options. It's an easy way to tidy up after yourself, provided the people you're sharing the file or folder with get around to viewing it in time.
Google Drive
Google Drive, surprisingly, isn't quite as on top of shared links as other cloud storage services. If you open up the web portal, there's no easy to access list of everything you've shared: The closest thing to it is clicking the People filter, and then choosing contacts to see files and folders you've shared with them specifically. If you pick Anyone with the link from the drop-down list, you'll see everything shared with a simple link.
To change the sharing settings for a file or folder, click on the three dots, then Share. Click the cog icon on the panel that pops up, then you can remove contacts as needed and turn the visible link off.
As with iCloud, there's no link expiry feature you can rely on here, so shared files and folders can't be set to become unshared after a certain time has elapsed. It has to be done manually, so it's a shame Google doesn't make it as easy as it could be.

'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.
"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.
The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:27 local time (21:27 GMT) on Saturday and was successfuly caught.

Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
- Published
A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

The housing market hasn't been inspiring for prospective homebuyers lately.
With many potential buyers waiting on the sidelines as interest rates rise, home sales are taking a hit.
In 2024 and 2025, existing home sales were identical, at 4.06 million. However, that number fell to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October 2026, according to the National Association of Realtors. It's the lowest number in over a decade.
"Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said. "As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010."
So who's still buying homes?
NAR released its annual Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. This year's report covers home sales between July 2025 and June 2026, offering a snapshot of the economic climate and housing market over the past year.
Since the previous report, the median homebuyer age has dropped slightly, while their income has grown considerably. Buyers also resoundingly favor the suburbs.
Here's what the typical homebuyer looked like in the past year, according to NAR.
The median age of a homebuyer dropped to 58, down from its peak of 59 last year.
The steady increase in the median age of homebuyers has been a talking point for years.
When NAR published its first report in 1981, the median age of all homebuyers was 31 — now it's up to 58.
For first-time homebuyers, that number stayed put at 40, while the age of repeat homebuyers also stayed flat at 62. While the age of first-time buyers is usually the report's main talking point, the median age of repeat buyers has increased at a faster rate since 1981.
Even though the median homebuyer age was 58, the most common homebuyer was in the range of 65 to 74 years old — that age group made up 26% of all homebuyers.
More married couples bought homes than single buyers.
Homebuyers figured it was easier to go in on a house with another person than alone.
Married couples accounted for the largest share of homebuyers by a wide margin. Sixty-three percent of all homebuyers were married.
The amount of single women homebuyers slightly decreased to 20% — after doubling since 1985 — but they are still more common than than single men, who accounted for 8% of all homebuyers.
The gap between single women and single men homebuyers was only a 2% difference in 1985 — 11% and 9%, respectively.
The typical homebuyer's household income is well above the nationwide median.
According to the US Census, the median household income reached its peak in 2025 at $87,460. Homebuyers this year make well above that, with a median household income of $120,000. For first-time buyers specifically, that number is $100,000.
Most homebuyers are empty nesters.
The typical buyer bought a house with three bedrooms, two bathrooms, and 1,900 square feet of space; enough room for children or extra guests. Most buyers, however, were without kids.
Homebuyers with no children under 18 living in the home accounted for 74% of buyers.
Buyers with one or two children made up 10% of buyers, and those with three or more children made up 6%.
Most buyers have at least one college degree.
Today's homebuyers are highly educated. NAR's survey found that 30% of buyers have a bachelor's degree, followed by 27% with a master's degree, MBA, or law degree. Just 16% are high-school graduates.
College graduates tend to have higher incomes than people without degrees, which may help explain their higher homeownership rates.
The suburbs are the place to be.
The suburbs are the "It" place for the typical buyer.
This year, 48% of all buyers purchased homes in suburban neighborhoods, compared with 21% in small towns and 14% in rural areas.
It's a reversal from recent years. In 2022, the share of buyers purchasing homes in the suburbs fell below 40%. Small towns and rural areas attracted an influx of buyers that year, narrowing the gap between suburban and small-town buyers.
As more Americans gravitate toward suburban areas, the shift suggests the pandemic-era rush for more land and space in smaller towns and rural communities is easing.
The typical buyer doesn't want to share walls.
The typical homebuyer would rather not share walls with neighbors.
This year, 80% of homebuyers chose detached homes. By comparison, townhouses accounted for 7% of purchases, while duplexes and condos made up 4%.
With buyers continuing to favor the suburbs, it's not surprising that condos, often concentrated in urban areas, are getting less love.
Repeat buyers are dominating homebuying.
The real estate market is increasingly a tale of the haves and have-nots. NAR's survey shows that first-time homebuyers are struggling to keep up.
In 2026, the typical buyer had already purchased one or more properties. Repeat buyers, whether purchasing a new primary residence or a vacation home, accounted for 78% of all home purchases.
Repeat buyers are also much older than they were in the past. In 2026, their median age is 62, compared with 36 in 1981.
"Repeat buyers are driving the housing market," said Jessica Lautz, NAR's deputy chief economist and vice president of research. "Unlike first-time home buyers, repeat buyers have seen their housing equity grow rapidly over the past decade, enabling them to trade up for larger homes or move into more desirable locations. These are often moves by choice rather than necessity."

Japan’s Akane Yamaguchi beat China’s Wang Zhiyi to win the Kumamoto Masters title on home soil on Sunday, with all-conquering world number one An Se-young not competing at the tournament.
World number two Yamaguchi downed third-ranked Wang 21-14, 22-20 to claim her fourth title of a women’s badminton season dominated by An.
The South Korean has won an incredible 11 titles, including the world and Asian Games crowns, and has lost only one match all year.
Of the titles An did not win in 2026, she finished runner-up at the All England Open and pulled out injured from the Japan Open.
Yamaguchi was happy to give the fans in western Japan something to cheer about.
“There aren’t so many tournaments held in Japan, especially in Kumamoto, which is my training base,” said the 29-year-old.
“I was able to win in front of my supporters, and that gave me a different happiness than the other stops on the tour.”
Yamaguchi has lost the last 11 matches she has played against An.
The pair could meet again at the season-ending World Tour Finals in China next month.
“I’m a little bit tired at the moment, so I think getting into good condition will be the most important thing,” said Yamaguchi.

IIHF confirms Russia not competing at world juniors next month in Alberta
2027 World Juniors will take place in Edmonton, Red Deer from Dec. 26 - Jan. 5
The International Ice Hockey Federation confirms in a statement that Russia will not have a team at the world junior hockey championship next month in Alberta.
The IIHF says Russia will not be able to play at the tournament starting Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer, despite a mandate for the country's reinstatement from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, due to restrictions put in place by the federal government.
The organization says Canada will remain as host despite going against the CAS's ruling.
Russia and Belarus have been banned from competing in international hockey tournaments since 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The CAS mandated Russia's reinstatement in an Oct. 30 ruling, but days later Prime Minister Mark Carney said Russians and Belarusians would be barred from competing regardless of that decision.
The impasse left the tournament in limbo, with Norway's federation saying it would be bumped from the competition in favour of a Russian team, while hockey officials from Russia suggested the tournament should be moved elsewhere.
The CAS's decision was met with immediate pushback, with hockey federations from Sweden, Finland, Czechia and other nations refusing to play against a reinstated Russian team.

In the weeks since Jane Doe alleged she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity party in 2024, the plague of campus sexual assault has once again become the topic of a heated national debate.
Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten
The Cornell case shows that something’s missing in how young people learn about sex. Fixing it could change a lot.
Those discussions inevitably land on familiar solutions. Experts, pundits, and parents argue for stricter criminal laws and a more transparent and punitive Title IX campus adjudicatory process. But these solutions have been tried in the past and not proven effective: Campus climate surveys show persistently high rates of assault, and Cornell’s own data show that reported incidents rose from 23 percent to 35 percent between 2023 and 2025.
It’s increasingly clear that to make meaningful progress requires a focus on prevention — not just punishment. Anyone horrified by the Cornell fraternity text thread published by the New York Times would agree that enforcement is only part of the story, and a fuller solution would begin with raising young people who don’t think it is remotely okay to treat each other’s bodies and emotions this way. There is a group of scholars and advocates across the country who are working on one surprisingly effective policy that might get us closer to that goal: comprehensive sex education.
Yes, you read that right: sex ed. But not sex ed as it’s currently taught in most American public schools — a haphazard set of state programs, often deeply political, which often stress abstinence over how to be in healthy sexual relationships with other people. This other version, known as comprehensive sex ed and currently required in just seven states, takes a holistic approach with focus on how to refuse unwanted sexual advances, establish clear boundaries, and have intimate relationships based on open communication and mutual desire, not force, coercion, or extreme intoxication.
An important step in the prevention of sexual assault is making comprehensive sex ed more common in American schools, and, in the states that do, making that education start earlier and comply with the National Sex Education Standards. Evidence suggests that this kind of instruction can reduce sexual violence.
Giving young people information about contraception and how to avoid STIs is an essential part of sex ed, but it isn’t enough. Far too many of our children head off to college without the interpersonal skills required to have healthy relationships involving physical intimacy, which are critical to their psychological development into caring and fulfilled adults.
The consequences can be devastating, and I see them firsthand. I am a law professor who runs a clinical program at the University of San Francisco that trains second- and third-year law students by having them litigate real cases under close supervision. Since 2018, we have been representing Title IX clients — the accusers and those they accuse — at colleges and universities all over the United States. In every case, every time, the end result is the same: pain, heartbreak, and ruined lives. The legal “resolution” is almost beside the point.
The allegations in the Cornell case are at the extreme end of the spectrum. In nearly all of the cases we handle, there is no malicious intent or casual cruelty. Instead, there are two young people who are inexperienced, hesitant to convey their real feelings, and bad at reading nonverbal cues. They drink excessively and use drugs to overcome their awkwardness and insecurity, which only makes the poor communication worse. My colleague and I joke bleakly that we are in the wrong business. What we really need to be doing is going to secondary schools and preaching the value of comprehensive sex ed to tweens and teens to stop these assaults from happening in the first place.
Recently, I interviewed Jennifer Hirsch, who is a professor at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and the co-author with Princeton sociologist Shamus Khan of the book Sexual Citizens, which synthesizes the findings of a five-year study of campus sexual assault that surveyed 2,000 students attending Columbia and Barnard.
“Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”
— Jennifer Hirsch, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health
Sex education needs to start in kindergarten, she said, by teaching children to respect the bodies of their classmates by keeping their hands to themselves and refraining from playground activities like chasing down a classmate trying to kiss them. In higher grades, she explained, the instruction should change to become more age-appropriate, gradually adding topics relating to sexual health for tweens and teens “to teach the things you need to know, to grow into being a person who can have sex without hurting other people or yourself.” Currently, only Washington and Oregon start this early. (A few other states begin in first grade.)
While it is true that many colleges and universities have mandatory trainings for students that involve learning about consent, bystander intervention, and how intoxication is a risk factor for sexual assault, it is too little, too late. By then, Hirsch said, “there is a non-trivial possibility that they’ve already experienced sexual violence or perpetrated sexual violence.” She compared it to “starting with calculus when they’ve never done arithmetic.”
The need for such education is even more urgent today when kids snap and text instead of talk face-to-face as they are fed a diet of toxic social media messages and violent pornography that tells them what women want is to be dominated, degraded, and objectified.
Gen Z in particular is in desperate need of a sexual education that is designed to dispel the fear, shame, and ignorance most young people feel around this topic and replace it with candid instruction on how to set boundaries, read cues, and treat intimate partners — whether it is a long-term relationship or a casual hook-up — with a basic modicum of respect and care.
Study after study has shown that there is widespread bipartisan support for having sex ed incorporated into secondary school instruction that teaches students the skills they need to have safe and healthy sexual relationships. Comprehensive sex education holds promise in combatting sexual assault, although the data is limited. A 2016 survey of more than 1,600 college students led by John Santelli, who is also a professor at Columbia’s Mailman School (and Hirsch’s spouse) found that when high schoolers received comprehensive sex education, it lowered their risk of sexual assault in college. Instruction stressing abstinence or how to avoid unwanted pregnancies and STIs did not.
This makes intuitive sense. If a young person learns early on how to extricate themselves from a sexual encounter that has turned uncomfortable or scary, they will be more likely to leave before an assault happens. If he or she is taught that other people’s bodies are not theirs for the taking, they will be less likely to violate them and instead ask for clarity whenever there is ambiguity about consent.
Still most schools shy away from such instruction. “It is better to tell kids that rape is bad than to say nothing,” but to stop there and hope for the best is not effective, Hirsch told me. “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”
But comprehensive sex ed, despite its popularity, has for decades been blocked by a minority of loud opposition, often motivated by religious beliefs, in states that consider adopting it. Since 2017, New York state lawmakers have advocated for a law mandating comprehensive sex ed for students in grades K-12. Every year, Hirsch told me, it dies in committee. At the federal level, the Trump administration has eliminated most of the federal grant money for sex ed that isn’t abstinence-only even though the research has shown that telling kids to “just say no” to sex has no impact on their behavior.
Suspension, expulsion, even criminal prosecution are not the solutions. They are the inadequate answers on offer by the adults in the room, who are trained only to react once the problem has become too big and ugly to ignore in any particular case before bracing for the next one. Reducing the accused to monsters and the accuser to a pitiable victim reinfects the wound, it does nothing to heal it. Wringing one’s hands and asking why, a generation later nothing has changed, virtually guarantees that nothing ever will.
If we really want to combat the plague of sexual assault on campus, we need to vaccinate our children in the same way we would against a lethal virus. Comprehensive sex ed is the best place to start.

Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, continues to attract advance bookings as it enters its thirteenth day in cinemas, Tuesday, November 17. The Nitesh Tiwari-directed mythological epic has registered advance ticket sales worth Rs. 4.57 crores nett, with 1,71,256 tickets sold across 18,001 shows. The figures indicate continued audience interest as the film moves through its second full working week. Interestingly, the latest advance-booking tally represents a significant increase over the earlier snapshot, when Ramayana had generated Rs. 2.83 crores nett from 1,09,981 tickets across 10,152 shows. Since then, advance collections have increased by Rs. 1.74 crores, or 61.5%, while ticket sales have jumped by 61,275, registering growth of approximately 55.7%. The number of shows has also increased by 7,849.
The Hindi version has generated Rs. 3.18 crores nett, accounting for approximately 69.45% of Tuesday's advance revenue. However, the biggest surprise comes from Malayalam, which has emerged as the second-highest-grossing language with Rs. 40.98 lakh nett. Tamil follows closely with Rs. 38.42 lakh, while Telugu has collected Rs. 31.86 lakh and Kannada Rs. 28.53 lakh. Together, the four South Indian versions have generated approximately Rs. 1.40 crores nett, accounting for 30.55% of Tuesday's advance revenue.
All 3D formats have collectively generated Rs. 3.31 crores nett, accounting for approximately 72.42% of Tuesday's total advance-booking revenue. In comparison, non-3D formats have contributed Rs. 1.26 crores, representing 27.58%.
With Rs. 4.57 crores nett already registered in Tuesday advances, the film has established a stronger booking base than indicated by the earlier snapshot.
The eventual Day 13 collection will depend on spot bookings, occupancy and audience turnout throughout the day.

'One of the greatest wins' - Wales stun All Blacks to go from no-hopers to heroes
- Published
One of the greatest Wales wins of all time.
That is how former captain Sam Warburton described the monumental result against New Zealand in Cardiff on Saturday.
At the time of the kick-off, the All Blacks were effectively the top-ranked side in the world following South Africa's tension-filled loss to France on Friday night.
So no-one gave Welsh hope - even Warburton - with some bookmakers offering odds of 30-1 during the week.
The question, not of when but can, Wales beat the All Blacks again has beset them since 1953.
That wait 73-year wait has been marred by cheating, national scandal and pure sporting drama.
Little wonder then that few wanted to leave the Principality Stadium long after the final whistle had sparked unprecedented scenes of utter joy - and relief - to the strains of Yma O Hyd.
That losing run - stretching across 34 matches - has hung like a millstone around the necks of generations of Wales players.
Warburton himself was part of the one of the most successful teams of all time during the Warren Gatland era - but lost all five meetings with New Zealand.
Even the legendary team of the 1970s fell short, although Sir Gareth Edwards was among the Principality Stadium crowd on Saturday to witness history.
How many more will claim in years to come they were there as well?
Warburton said: "When you think what the fans and this team has been through, from the highs of a Grand Slam seven years ago, down to 12th in the world rankings and a record losing run of any tier one nation, we've been down in the pits.
"No-one gave Wales a chance, that's why this is one of the greatest Welsh wins of all time.
"Yes, New Zealand had made changes but that was one of the most heroic defensive performances I have ever seen."
Dan Biggar, sat alongside Warburton for host broadcaster ITV, put the result into wider perspective.
"This is not a day for analysis, it's just to celebrate being Welsh," he added.
"That was probably the biggest shock in world rugby since Japan beat South Africa in the 2015 World Cup."
Winston Churchill was prime minister and Queen Elizabeth II had not long had her coronation when Wales last beat the All Blacks in 1953.
Respected rugby commentator Huw Llywelyn Davies attended the game as an eight-year-old with his father, who was writing for the weekly Welsh language newspaper Baner ac Amserau Cymru.
"I never thought I would see it happen again, not unless I lived to 100," said an emotional Davies, now 81, as he stepped away from the media seats inside the Principality Stadium.
"With everything that has been going in Welsh rugby recently, I didn't think we would beat them this decade but the way we matched them physically was incredible."
Wales had only come close on a handful of occasions with one-point defeats in 1978, when New Zealand lock Andy Haden infamously dived out of a lineout to gain a match-winning penalty, and then in 2004.
Wales even turned to four New Zealand coaches in Sir Graham Henry, Steve Hansen, Gatland and Wayne Pivac to help break the hoodoo, but none of the quartet could inspire a Test victory over the land of their birth.
So there will be added satisfaction that it was a Welshman who masterminded the long-awaited win.
Steve Tandy's side may not have the household names of teams gone by, nor the winning pedigree, but they had courage when it mattered.
Three times they held up black shirts over the try-line during a second-half defensive efforts that at times beggared belief.
Initial statistics had second-row Dafydd Jenkins equalling Thierry Dusautoir's world record of 38 tackles in a single match - also set against New Zealand in 2007.
Jac Morgan and man of the match James Botham also topped 30 tackles, while centre Eddie James and captain Dewi Lake were not far behind.
It earned high praise from former New Zealand captain Sean Fitzpatrick.
A winner in all six meetings with Wales, the ex-hooker has ties to that day seven decades ago when his father Brian made his New Zealand debut.
Observers say he was unlucky not to be awarded a try after he was adjudged to have been tackled just short of the line. How different history might have been.
"New Zealand played well in patches and terrible in others but this is all about Wales," said Fitzpatrick, now a board member of Welsh region Scarlets.
"They way they started the game and took their tries showed the amazing belief they had. But the defensive effort was out of this world."

The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States’ measles-elimination status after 26 years, because the country did not halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The international health body did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the report, which cited people familiar with the matter.
The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the U.S. battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades.
Some 7,500 people in the U.S. have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.
As part of its evaluation, PAHO reviewed epidemiological and laboratory evidence to determine whether the same strain of measles had been circulating in the United States uninterrupted for 12 months or longer, a sign of local transmission rather than imported cases.
As of Thursday (November 12, 2026), 5,182 confirmed cases of measles had been reported in 2026 to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 45 States, New York City and the District of Columbia, surpassing last year’s total of 2,289, making it one of the country’s worst measles resurgences in decades.
The U.S. achieved its measles-elimination status in 2000. A country can halt transmission when 95% of its population is vaccinated, creating so-called herd immunity that also protects those unable to receive the vaccine.
Two doses of the measles vaccine — by far the best way to prevent infection and transmission — provide 97% protection against the virus, which can cause blindness, deafness, brain damage or death.

Burnham urges caution on scrapping 3pm TV blackout
- Published
Andy Burnham has urged caution on lifting the Saturday 3pm TV blackout in the UK, saying the health of the football pyramid should come first.
The rule was introduced in the 1960s to encourage fans to attend lower league games and prevents matches from being shown on UK television between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on Saturdays.
The blackout, which is enforced by Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes and is imposed by the English and Scottish football associations, comes into effect when 50% of fixtures in the top two divisions are scheduled to kick off at 3pm.
The Premier League is in the middle of a record £6.7bn domestic TV deal for Sky and TNT to show up to 270 live games a season.
But there could be room for change with the 3pm rule in the upcoming broadcast cycle, as the rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and SPFL all end in 2028-29.
The prime minister said any decision to remove the ban would require careful thought about the consequences.
"I would urge a bit of caution [on the blackout], because it does protect the income of lower-league clubs," Burnham said.
- Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end

  - Published15 August 2025
"If you have effectively wall-to-wall Premier League football at any time, it takes away perhaps the incentive to go and watch the football league or non-league.
"So I think it has to be considered carefully. I'm not going to take the pure consumer view here. I'll take the health-of-football approach to this particular issue."
Only the FA Cup final, which traditionally kicks off at 3pm, is allowed to be broadcast during the blackout window.
In October, the SPFL said it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the TV new deal, which BBC Sport understands includes matches shown on a Saturday afternoon.
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters has previously said a decision about whether the blackout stays in place would need to be made in the future.
But Burnham added: "I would first of all want to protect the football pyramid before I agree to saying 'let's have even more live football'".
"I think it's about protecting the experience with the paying supporter, protecting the football pyramid. Those issues matter to me, first of all."

I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date. That’s not the case with YouTube Music’s “Beyond the Beat,” an AI-generated DJ that explains songs to you.
YouTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice. And since I’m a software reporter, I always enable the beta features available through YouTube Labs, which include Beyond the Beat. YouTube’s AI DJ randomly interjects for about 30 seconds between songs, teeing up the vibe shift and providing context about the next track.
More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps. While YouTube launched this experimental AI DJ in 2025, Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023. It doubled down on its AI DJ efforts in November, expanding the different personalities available to users and adding more controls over the commentary.
These AI DJs aren’t just annoying. Their attempts to provide helpful context and mimic human candor ultimately fall flat. Lucky for me, both features are optional and avoidable.
After months of leaving it enabled, a bad experience with Beyond the Beat this week pushed me to swear off AI DJs altogether. I was listening to a pop divas playlist as part of my morning workout and got slapped with 30 seconds of exposition after a Slayyyter track:
“Hey Boy delivers that high-energy surge perfectly, but we're shifting our focus to a sharper, more visceral reality. In Rock Music, Charli XXC [sic] weaves in a biting, dark sense of humor regarding the physical toll of her relentless 2024 and 2025 touring. She turns the genuine nerve damage she sustained on the road into a strange sort of battle scar, reclaiming the exhaustion of a weary party girl as a badge of honor. It's an unflinching look at the cost behind the spectacle, where the grind of the industry becomes the actual subject matter. Here is Rock Music by Charli XXC [sic].”
What a lengthy paragraph of platitudes with little substance. That’s not even mentioning how the AI DJ butchered the pronunciation of a little-known, indie act called Charli XCX. This flub reflected my overall experience with YouTube Music’s AI DJ. It took me out of the groove and didn’t feel additive.
In another example, it went in-depth on the meaning of Olivia Rodrigo’s Expectations remix featuring Chappell Roan, calling it a "structural interpretation” that unpacks the “nuances of queer dating.” Then YouTube Music played the original track, sans Roan; so much for the queer yearning.
Curious how Spotify’s AI DJ experience would compare, I upgraded my account to the premium tier for access to that beta software. One of the biggest recent changes to Spotify’s AI DJ was adding new voices to the lineup, so I went into my settings and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices.
Maybe I was already a bit miffed from my YouTube Music experience because these voices immediately started to frustrate me. Multiple voices leaned into filler words such as “you know” and “like,” as the AI described the next songs it would play. Knowing an AI voice is being trained to use filler words to sound more human gave me the uncanny-valley ick.
Spotify’s AI DJ was fairly different from YouTube Music’s version. On Spotify, the AI DJ is also an algorithmically guided experience that picks songs for you based on past listening habits and song requests. Overall, Spotify’s synthetic commentary felt tighter and more tolerable than YouTube’s blabbering DJ. That said, neither software experience was enjoyable enough for me to return.
Although Spotify claims it has “80 percent of listeners coming back to DJ week after week,” according to the company’s launch blog, I won’t be one of them. My rejection of AI DJs isn’t based on how they audibly sound. The voices, from both companies, are decent and sound convincingly human. The content of their commentary is what truly turns me off. Whether it’s empty platitudes or mimicking human mistakes, I’ve heard enough.
