AO3 is back online but with limited features
The outage lasted two weeks but full functionality is expected to resume soon.
After two weeks in the dark, popular fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back online. However, Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit organization that runs AO3, said that some features have been temporarily disabled as a compromise to bring the site back earlier than the four-week mark, according to an update post on the website. OTW said that features like icons and external work importing are currently disabled, while works can only be downloaded in HTML format. The organization clarified that these features will be restored and that no icons have been deleted.
AO3 was taken offline at the end of October due to "evidence of a security incident" that OTW said would result in two to four weeks of downtime. Now that the open-source fan fiction repository is back online, its users may still run into some issues, according to OTW. The organization said it implemented an "intentional measure to help manage traffic," so users may experience delays with the website loading but can refresh to continue trying.
As for the site's data, OTW said that none of it was deleted, adding that user "works, bookmarks, kudos, etc. are still safe." OTW also managed to pause AO3's draft deletion feature so that no drafts were deleted during the downtime. Users should log back in and check on their drafts, though, since the feature will turn back on starting November 29 so that drafts longer than 30 days old will be deleted.
It's still unclear what the cause was, but OTW confirmed it was a "security incident" and that it would "not be sharing specifics about what mitigating changes are being made at this time." OTW added that it partnered with a security firm to review the incident and analyze the site to prevent future incidents. The update post said that OTW has "no reason to believe that the user database was compromised, though we cannot rule out that possibility," recommending that users change passwords, update linked emails and change passwords of any other sites that share a password with AO3 accounts.

African Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
- Published
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.
Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.
"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.
Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.
Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.
"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.
Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.
The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.
In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.
"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.
Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.
The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.
Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.
"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.
Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."
In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.
She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"
The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology-Kanpur have identified a molecular pathway through which immune cells in the pancreas can rapidly suppress insulin release, opening up a potential new avenue for developing therapies to protect insulin production in people with obesity and Type-2 diabetes.
The findings, published in ‘Journal of Clinical Investigation’, show that immune cells called macrophages can switch off insulin secretion by neighbouring beta cells within minutes, rather than gradually damaging them through inflammation over months or years, according to a note issued by IIT-Kanpur on Thursday.
Simran Singh and Ashish Kumar led the study as co-first authors under the supervision of Sai Prasad Pydi, assistant professor, department of biological sciences and bioengineering, IIT-Kanpur.
“We discovered that immune cells that are present next to beta cells can switch off insulin release within minutes,” Pydi said.
The researchers found that the process involves sphingolipids, a class of fats released by macrophages, rather than the inflammatory proteins traditionally associated with obesity-related pancreatic damage.
The team traced the trigger to GPR18, a receptor on macrophages. Once activated, it prompts the immune cells to release sphingolipids, which are taken up by neighbouring beta cells through a surface transporter, and interfere with their insulin-producing machinery.
Using a precision genetic technique, the researchers found that activating this pathway reduced insulin secretion in mouse models, while switching it off improved insulin release. Blocking GPR18 or other steps in the pathway also restored insulin secretion.
The team, working with the Indiana Biosciences Research Institute in the US, confirmed that the same pathway was present and active in human pancreatic tissue.
Activating it in donated human tissue also suppressed insulin secretion, according to the communique.
While the study does not offer an immediate treatment for diabetes, the findings establish a potential target for developing drugs to preserve insulin production in people with obesity and Type-2 diabetes, it said.

Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
- Published
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.
Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.
The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.
Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.
Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.
Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.
However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.
Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."
He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.
Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.
What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."
While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."
In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF. However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.
"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."
Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.
Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.
In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.
"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.
Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.
Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government.
However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.
In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace.
"Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.

12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న 4వ జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను తగ్గించడం/మాఫీ చేయనున్నారని చెబుతూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో విస్తృతంగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న 4వ జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను తగ్గించడం/మాఫీ చేయబడతాయి.
ఫాక్ట్: ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను మాఫీ చేస్తున్నట్లు జాతీయ లేదా రాష్ట్ర లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీలు ఎక్కడా ప్రకటించలేదు. అయితే, 2026లో కర్ణాటక, బీహార్, ఒడిశా వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాలు పెండింగ్ చలాన్ల చెల్లింపులో రాయితీని కల్పించాయి. తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాలు గతంలో ఇలాంటి రాయితీలు ఇచ్చినప్పటికీ, డిసెంబర్ 2026లో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లో మాత్రం ఎలాంటి రాయితీని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా ఈ విషయం గురించి జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించే నేషనల్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (NALSA) అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్ను పరిశీలించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న దేశవ్యాప్తంగా పలు రాష్ట్రాలలో లోక్ అదాలత్లు నిర్వహిస్తున్నట్లు తెలిసింది. దీనిలో భాగంగా విచారణలో ఉన్న సివిల్, క్రిమినల్, చెక్బౌన్స్ కేసులు, కాంపౌండబుల్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్ కేసులు, మోటారు వాహన ప్రమాదాలు, కుటుంబ తగాదాలు మొదలైనవాటిని రాజీ మార్గం ద్వారా పరిష్కరించుకునే అవకాశాన్ని ఈ లోక్ అదాలత్లు కల్పిస్తాయి. అయితే, పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను 100% మాఫీ చేయనున్నట్లు ఇందులో ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు.
ఇదే విషయమై తెలంగాణ స్టేట్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (TSLSA) వర్గాలను సంప్రదించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న తెలంగాణలో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు మాఫీ/ డిస్కౌంట్ ఇస్తున్నట్లు తాము ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా పేర్కొనలేదని స్పష్టం చేశారు.
అంతేకాకుండా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ వ్యాప్తంగా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను రాయితీపై చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించడం లేదని తెలంగాణ పోలీసులు కూడా మాకు ధృవీకరించారు. మార్చి 2026లో కూడా ఇటువంటి వార్తలే వచ్చినప్పుడు వారు దీన్ని ఖండించారు. మరోవైపు, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీని, పోలీసులను సంప్రదించగా వారి స్పందించలేదు. అయితే, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ పోలీసులు కూడా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీ కల్పించే విషయం గురించి ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
అయితే కర్ణాటక, ఒడిశా, బీహార్ వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాల్లో 2026లో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు రాయితీ కల్పిస్తూ సెటిల్మెంట్ చేసుకునేందుకు వీలుగా ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించిన సందర్భాలు ఉన్నాయి. గతంలో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు కూడా ఇలాంటి లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించారు. 2016, 2017 సంవత్సరాల్లో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు గోషామహల్లో లోక్ అదాలత్ నిర్వహించి, 50% రాయితీతో పెండింగ్ చలాన్లను చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించారు. అయితే, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాల పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్ ద్వారా ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీని కల్పించే పథకాన్ని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
చివరిగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరిగే జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లు 100% మాఫీ అవుతాయని సోషల్ మీడియాలో జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారంలో నిజం లేదు.

PM Modi, Trump to join ASEAN Summit in Manila; global conflicts, maritime, economic ties on agenda
Modi will travel to Manila on November 16 to participate in the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit the following day.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Manila on Monday for a three-day trip to attend the annual India-ASEAN Summit, which is expected to focus on strengthening maritime security ties and expanding economic and commercial partnerships.
US President Donald Trump, Brazil’s Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney are also expected to attend the summit.
What's on PM Modi's agenda
Modi will travel to Manila on November 16 to participate in the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit the following day, on the margins of the ASEAN Summit being hosted by the Philippines.
He is also expected to join the leaders of Australia, Japan and the US for a Quad Leaders’ Summit and hold several bilateral meetings.
Throughout the India-ASEAN and East Asia summits, New Delhi is looking to boost naval and maritime coordination among like-minded Indo-Pacific states.
What is ASEAN
ASEAN or the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is one of the most significant geopolitical blocs in the region. The group primarily comprises Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand, Vietnam, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and East Timor.
New Delhi will be joining major global powers, including Washington, Beijing, Tokyo and Canberra, as an official dialogue partner.
Prominent world leaders to gather in Manila
Global delegations have steadily arrived in the country ahead of the main event, with representatives from ASEAN member states, dialogue partners and international organisations preparing for a packed itinerary of high-level meetings from November 15 to November 17, according to Philippine News Agency.
The three-day summit, which includes scheduled talks with world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, will focus on conflicts, including the war in Myanmar, The Associated Press reported citing drafts of post-summit communiques.
Trump, Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Canada’s Carney and Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov also feature on the roster for November 17.
What's on agenda for ASEAN
ASEAN has emerged as a central pillar of India’s Act East policy and vision for the Indo-Pacific, and Rudrendra Tandon, secretary (East) in the external affairs ministry, told a media briefing that the 11-member bloc serves as a “locomotive for peace, stability and economic prosperity”.
Annual trade between India and ASEAN member states is worth about $122 billion.
“India strongly believes that as an Indian Ocean country that abuts this very important Southeast Asian maritime zone, a strong strategic relationship with ASEAN member states, as a collective as well as individually, is good for both of us,” Tandon said.
“It will make us more resilient to handle the very rapid geopolitical changes that are taking place around us. It will also contribute to peace and stability in Asia as a whole.”
According to the senior official, strengthening maritime defence mechanisms and commercial exchanges will be among the key agendas during the deliberations.
Serving as the premier diplomatic platform across the Asia-Pacific for addressing defence and security challenges, the East Asia Forum has fundamentally shaped regional strategic evolution since its launch in 2005.
Alongside the core Southeast Asian member countries, the wider regional dialogue framework encompasses New Delhi, Beijing, Tokyo, Seoul, Canberra, Wellington, Washington and Moscow, bringing together all ASEAN member states.
In the context of trade with the Southeast Asian block, Tandon said New Delhi wants the review of the ASEAN India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA) to be completed “as soon as possible”. India is also engaged in discussions with individual ASEAN member states for trade facilitation and trade agreements to open up new opportunities, he said.
Tandon acknowledged that the review of AITIGA is a “difficult” process as it involves developing consensus with all ASEAN member states. AITIGA entered into force in 2010 and the review began six years ago, largely because of India’s concerns about trade imbalance due to imports of more than $80 billion from ASEAN member states.
Asked about India’s position on dealing with the situation in Myanmar, Tandon said: “We have always said that isolating Myanmar is not the right approach because if we do, someone else will fill that vacuum. There is no alternative to engagement.”
India strongly supports ASEAN initiatives to engage the Myanmar government, while taking into account the country’s complex history and society. “Patience and consistency in engagement is very important,” Tandon said.

The U.S. economy hitched its wagon to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Now that he has stepped down, the company faces deep uncertainty.
A week ago, we learned the news that Jensen Huang, the rock star C.E.O. of the chip-making company Nvidia, had acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. It turns out that may have been just the beginning. Shortly after revelations of a second affair, this time with a subordinate, Huang resigned.
Nvidia’s stock has tumbled in the days since, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in value, and analysts have begun trying to process just how the downfall of one of the most important figures in the A.I. industry is going to play out. One Silicon Valley venture capitalist recently called him “irreplaceable.”
But why are Huang and Nvidia so irreplaceable — and is anything that cannot be replaced automatically vulnerable? Today I’m writing about power, vulnerability and choke points.
Why there’s only one Nvidia
Last week, as it became clear that Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia might be in jeopardy, a meme began making the rounds on the internet. It showed a complicated, multitiered structure, delicately balanced on a tiny block. The structure was labeled “entire global economy”; the block was labeled “Jensen Huang’s wife.”
The meme is already outdated: Huang has resigned from his role as Nvidia’s C.E.O. (and it never made sense to put any of this on his wife). But the image still captured the idea that so much of the business world somehow came to depend on one man and his — now, it seems, questionable — judgment.

Welcome to Edition 9.19 of the Rocket Report! Will something historic happen this weekend? No orbital rocket has ever been fully recovered with the intent of reusing all of its components. Electron set for milestone launch. The next launch of Rocket Lab’s Electron vehicle is due to lift off from the Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand on November 14 at 5:30 UTC. This mission will serve as Electron’s 100th overall mission—a notable milestone for the small rocket that first flew in 2017, NASASpaceflight.com reports.
A true commercial success … This flight of Electron, named “The Mountain God Rises,” will deliver another iQPS satellite into LEO for iQPS’s synthetic aperture radar constellation. The anniversary rocket features a special gold-and-black livery which looks fantastic. Rocket Lab truly does deserve recognition as the world’s second purely commercial launch business to make a successful go at it. We are all celebrating with them.
Is the Vega rocket a dead end? Last month, Italian rocket builder Avio presented a market update that outlined the additional investment required to increase the annual launch cadence of its Vega C rocket to six and eventually nine flights per year, European Spaceflight reports. The need for this additional funding raises an interesting question about the future of Italy’s Vega launch vehicle family. Is investing in the infrastructure needed to secure just three more Vega C flights per year by the end of the decade the best use of resources, particularly when several emerging European launch companies appear poised to offer comparable capacity?
Boosters may be better used by Ariane 6 … Vega C isn’t going anywhere. But it’s an inescapable reality that a single Ariane 64 launch requires the equivalent of an entire year’s worth of solid rocket boosters for Vega C at its baseline annual launch cadence of four flights. Does it make sense to continue investing in expanding Vega C’s launch cadence and later introducing Vega E when the future of both vehicles depends on production capacity that is increasingly demanded by Ariane 6?

Synspective inks 10 Alpha rockets. Firefly Aerospace announced on Tuesday a multi-launch agreement with Synspective, a Japanese synthetic aperture radar satellite data and solutions provider, for up to 10 launches on Firefly’s Alpha rocket through 2030. With the ability to launch 1,000 kg to low Earth orbit, Alpha will deliver two of Synspective’s SAR satellites to orbit per mission, deploying up to 20 total satellites.
Getting it done with one ton … Under the agreement, Firefly will launch Synspective’s SAR satellites from both Pad-0A at Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia and Space Launch Complex 2 at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. “This landmark agreement reflects growing customer confidence in our Alpha Block II vehicle,” said Jason Kim, CEO of Firefly Aerospace. “With 1-ton payload capacity and responsive launch capabilities, Alpha is a natural fit for customers like Synspective seeking direct access to orbit to get their operations up and running sooner.”
Stoke and Planet sign multi-launch agreement. Stoke Space on Monday announced a multi-launch agreement with Planet Labs PBC. The companies did not announce the terms of the agreement, including the total number of launches under contract, nor the cost of the launches. “We need launch partners who move as quickly as we do,” said Will Marshall, Co-Founder & CEO of Planet.
An open-ended agreement? … The announcement suggests this could be an open-ended agreement, however. “Planet builds and operates the largest fleet of Earth-imaging satellites in orbit and captures imagery of Earth’s landmass every day,” a related release says. “Operators like Planet launch on a regular basis to expand and replenish their fleets, and that steady demand is what our Nova fleet is designed to serve.”
The launch crunch comes to national security. The US military is taking a new approach to prop up commercial launch companies as SpaceX looks to wind down its Falcon rocket program, suggesting defense officials see the workhorse rocket’s retirement as a potential national security risk, Ars reports. More pads and rockets … First, on October 26, the office announced a $150 million conditional loan commitment to Stoke Space. Military officials revealed a second $150 million Pentagon loan Tuesday for Rocket Lab. Stoke Space’s loan is tailored to support the buildout of the company’s second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The loan to Rocket Lab will support the company’s efforts to increase the flight rate of its partially reusable Neutron rocket.
Rocket Lab raises Neutron price. Citing strong customer demand and a constrained market for launch, Rocket Lab announced this week it had increased the cost of a dedicated Neutron rocket from $55 million to $70 million, Payload reports. In recent months, the coming shortage of launch capacity in the US—mainly due to SpaceX sunsetting its Transporter rideshare program—has sparked a flurry of interest in new medium-lift rocket entrants.
Positive on Neutron … “Neutron is rapidly establishing itself as the backbone of next-generation constellation deployment and government missions in the medium-lift launch class,” CEO Peter Beck said in a statement. “Strong international demand and a growing launch manifest, at a new price point, is proof that Neutron is the launch vehicle the market has been waiting for.” The price hike for Neutron isn’t keeping customers away as new bookings continue, the company said. Customers’ next options to fly on Neutron are now in the 2030s and beyond.
Rockets are not hard? During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit, Ars reports. Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a “simple” rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, “the best part is no part.”
This sounds a little naive … “Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines,” he said of the rocket. “So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite.” The Blacklift rocket will be “simple,” he said, because it will be solely tailored to lift five Bluebird satellites into low-Earth orbit at a time. It will have 20 metric tons of lift capacity, a reusable first stage, and launch twice a month from a pad at Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia that formerly served the Antares rocket. (submitted by thegooglemonster)
When will the Eclipse rocket be ready? During an earnings call this week (see transcript), Firefly CEO Kim spoke about the company’s ongoing work to develop the Eclipse rocket. “We’re heads down on Eclipse,” he said. “We’re laser-focused on delivering the first stage to our co-developer Northrop Grumman. And we’re over 175 hot fires on Miranda, counting the one from today. And we’re looking at all the data, verifying the capability. It’s a very mature engine, and we’re very confident in its capabilities.”
Probably not launching soon … However, when an analyst pressed on Firefly getting a launch in 2027, Kim did not offer a direct answer. “Everything is just laser-focused on all the milestones in terms of qualifying Miranda and qualifying our composite tanks and fluid systems as well,” he said. “So we’re really, really just excited about the future of Eclipse, especially with this injection of capital that will help accelerate our production line.” Bottom line: Don’t expect to see Eclipse on a launch pad any time soon.
Starship set for 15th test flight on Friday. Flight 15 of Starship is preparing to launch as soon as Friday, November 13, pending regulatory approval, SpaceX said. The 75-minute launch window will open at 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC). The upcoming flight is planned to be the first to return both Starship and Super Heavy to the launch site for catch. If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system.
All eyes on the ship … Starship’s initial return-to-launch-site mission is expected to orbit the Earth at an altitude of about 275 km and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet over the course of a more than 22-hour flight. Starship’s primary mission will be to deliver 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit. But really, this mission is all about the landings, first of the booster and then, more dramatically, of the upper stage Starship on Saturday.
SpaceX is now an ‘infrastructure’ company. For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with developing newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets, Ars reports. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week’s UP.Summit conference in Florida, SpaceX’s vice president of launch, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company’s changing focus.
From AI to Mars? … “In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point,” Dontchev said. “We’re building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars.” However, Dontchev insisted that human settlement and Mars remain part of the core of SpaceX’s aspirations. “We have come to understand that this tool is critical to us accelerating our pace of innovation,” he said of artificial intelligence. “Without AI, I think we still would have gotten to the Moon. Palestinians in the southern region of Masafer Yatta, in the occupied West Bank, have faced growing settler attacks and arbitrary arrests in recent years. Mohammed Hesham tells Alex Croft that he feared for his life while being abused by soldiers

A Palestinian journalist has said he was beaten, blindfolded and handcuffed with zip ties after being taken from his village by a group of Israeli soldiers in a horrific six hour ordeal - before being released without charge.
Mohammad Hesham, 23, was seized from his village of at-Tuwani and ordered onto his knees before being driven to Susya military base in Masafer Yatta, in the southern part of the occupied West Bank.
Over a six-hour period, Mr Hesham told The Independent he was spat on, abused, and told he would die in custody. He says his treatment worsened after the troops took his phone and discovered he was a journalist and activist.
“It was terrifying,” he says ten days on from the incident. “It was crazy. It was really tough for me, especially after they knew that I was a journalist. That was a nightmare.”
The Israeli military said Hesham was arrested “after approaching an Israeli community in the southern Hebron Hills in a suspicious manner”. It said he was “held for several hours and subsequently released”, adding: “IDF soldiers are authorized to detain suspects for six hours.”
But Mr Hesham says he was seized while at home with his family. Security footage seen and published by The Independent, shows no evidence of the military’s version of events. Instead, the troops are seen approaching Mr Hesham’s village and summoning him out before detaining him.
It is the latest example of incidents across the occupied territories in which Palestinians are arbitrarily detained for hours by Israeli forces without being formally charged or accused of any crime.
According to Israeli human rights group B’tselem, the Israel Prison Service (IPS) was holding 3,198 Palestinians, including 94 children, in ‘administrative detention’ - the arrest and imprisonment of individuals without a formal criminal charge, trial or conviction - as of June 2026.
This is one of several manifestations of Israel’s decades-long occupation of Palestinian land, deemed by the UN’s top court as illegal under international law.
Mr Hesham was not added to Israel’s long list of administrative detainees - but arrests such as his are common in Masafer Yatta, an area facing a steep increase in forced evictions, home demolitions and settler attacks in recent years.
“Whatever you do, you are just a Palestinian, you have to suffer,” he says. “And this was actually our crime. They took me from my house with no reason for the arrest, just lies. We knew that our only crime was being Palestinians.”
The journalist and activist, who among others has written for The New Arab, +972 Magazine, and documents life in Masafer Yatta on social media, says he was with his family in at-Tuwani at around 4.30pm in the afternoon when the troops approached and ordered him to leave.
The footage of Mr Hesham’s detention shows him being taken away with his hands behind his back, before another video shows him on his knees, surrounded by the armed soldiers.
He is afterwards seen with his hands on a car, as the troops tie a blindfold round his head - that Mr Hesham says was fashioned from a used rubbish bag with a “really bad smell”.
Mr Hesham was taken to a military base, where he says his hands were zip tied and he was thrown to the ground, before being ordered to unlock his phone. When he refused, he says, he was beaten and told by one of the soldiers: “When I tell you to open the phone, you open the phone.”
He relented: “For how long can I resist? I was in a military base. So I cannot really fight for so long because if I do, it will not be [just] one soldier beating me. Everyone will come and they will enjoy beating me.”
Once they discovered he was a journalist and activist with an online following, the situation worsened, Mr Hesham says.
He was told he is “not allowed to take whatever, no water, no food, no bathroom, nothing”, he says, adding that he “had to stay on the ground” with his blindfold on for the full six hours.
“When I said I want to go to a bathroom they said: ‘We will let you die here. Whatever you ask, we will not give you here. You are here just to die,’” Mr Hesham adds.
The military said detention at a military post is “carried out in accordance with established procedures”, adding that it “works tirelessly to investigate suspicions of violations of the law within the IDF”
“The allegations of abuse of the detainee are not known to the IDF,” it added. “It should be emphasized that any instance of violence or degrading treatment toward detainees is contrary to IDF orders and values and is inconsistent with the conduct expected of its soldiers.
“The IDF examines every suspicion of unlawful conduct thoroughly and professionally, in accordance with the circumstances of each case.”
But the incident has highlighted the increasingly blurred lines between Israeli soldiers and armed settlers, with Mr Hesham saying those that initially detained him were a well-recognised group from the nearby settlement of Havat Ma’on - an unofficial outpost considered illegal under both Israeli and international law.
Known as Hagmar, these settler-only IDF units were set up as regional security forces in the West Bank following the October 7 attacks. But their creation has been followed by an sharp uptick in violence against Palestinians.
According to one former reservist speaking to the Guardian earlier this year, they are “armed militias doing what they want” who are “given a free hand” on the ground.
Havat Ma’on, in particular, is infamous in Masafer Yatta as the home of a group of settlers that have allegedly been behind several violent attacks - including one in which homes were set on fire with children still inside.
Mr Hesham says the car in which he was detained - and the group that detained him - are notorious in the area for seizing Palestinians without basis.
“It's not my story personally, it's the story of every Palestinian in Masafer Yatta,” he says. “There are people I know have been arrested three, four, five times by the same car, by the same settler-soldiers.
“Every day they arrest someone from Masafer Yatta. They take you to make you feel that you are nothing.”
He issues a plea for help: “This situation is really crazy. I hope it’s going to be changed, there will be serious actions and sanctions against these settlers and soldiers themselves.”

Republicans weren’t the only big losers in last week’s midterms: Across the country, voters also backed restrictions on data centers and elected candidates promising tougher oversight of AI companies. Out of 41 local ballot initiatives limiting the data center buildout, 40 of them passed, according to the New York Times.
OpenAI is betting a data center rebrand will make you hate them less
They’d really like you to call them “compute campuses” now.
The AI industry knows it was a tough cycle: Chris Lehane, the chief global affairs officer for OpenAI, told Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram that “I could take my shirt off and show you my [metaphorical] bruises if you want.”
Now, OpenAI is figuring out how to move forward. Lehane talked with Sean from rural Texas, where he said he was on a “listening and learning” tour of communities around the site of a massive OpenAI data center. They discussed the lessons of the midterm election, why OpenAI would prefer that we call data centers “compute campuses,” and why Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election will largely revolve around AI — just not in the same way that 2026 did.
“I just don’t think it’s going to be good enough for a candidate from either party to emerge from their primary by simply being the person who’s against things,” Lehane said.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
You guys at OpenAI, in the wake of this shellacking, put out this big document saying that you’re going to be listening, you’re going to be learning, you’re going to be empowering local people and bringing jobs.
You’re also, in this document, rebranding data centers to “compute campuses,” which when I say it, I have trouble not laughing because it sounds like a bit of a joke to meet everyone’s concerns with a rebrand. Please tell us why you think this could work or why it’s a good idea.
We were very intentional in actually using that phrase. And we did it with the full knowledge that people would potentially be skeptical of it. But I do think there’s an intent behind provoking this conversation.
Data centers have existed for 20-odd years and at some level they’re the proverbial empty box in a pasture. And they’re called data centers because that’s in fact what they were. When people talked about the cloud, this is actually where the cloud was housed, where you would load data if you were streaming a video, if you were ordering something from a delivery service. These AI facilities are really fundamentally different.
What is being generated at these facilities is something called compute. And compute is just the raw computing power that it takes to train AI systems and then run AI tools and products when you’re using them.
Second of all, they’re different because [of] the amount of jobs that do get created directly. This is not half a dozen people in that empty box. These are real jobs, these are six-figure jobs. They are also huge opportunities for economic transformation if a community approaches it in a really strategic way and companies like ours do our part to work with those communities. We’re not just building in the communities, we’re building with the communities.
You’re out there in Texas because essentially, data centers and artificial intelligence have a PR problem. Seventy percent of the country, maybe more than that, says that they’re against data centers, or “compute campuses,” as you’re now calling them.
Why do you think it is that data centers have such a public relations issue in this country right now?
There’s a variety of factors, but before even jumping into those, I do think it’s worth noting and worth emphasizing that we have roughly six of these projects up and running in the country. They’re in different stages of being built out and developed, but each and every one of them is moving forward. I do think that there is a right way to build these and perhaps a wrong way and we can get into that.
Do you think that you guys were doing it the wrong way before?
This goes to why I think we’ve actually been able to get approvals for each of the projects that we are doing.
I think each of the individual projects themselves have been some version of a laboratory of democracy, where you actually learn from each project and apply those learnings to the next project. But I do think we got the fundamental insight right at the beginning, which is to actually go on the ground, listen, learn, hold yourself accountable and take the feedback and build your facility with the community.
I think that for a lot of communities, folks were coming in, they were building data centers, they were then transferring the electricity costs to the public, they were potentially impacting their water, they weren’t necessarily doing the type of community investments that you should do if you’re going to be building with a community.
Where we’ve really tried to differ ourselves — and again, we’re not perfect, we’re learning every step of the way — but I do think that we have successfully applied the baseline as we’ve gone through this, which is, we make sure we’re paying for our own electricity, our own energy.
Point two is that we make sure we’re preserving water. We have something called closed water loops. I know this is getting a little bit technical, but think of these as sort of large radiators. You fill it up once and therefore you’re able to preserve the water.
One thing that seems clear from the election results is that there’s just not a lot of trust. Now there’s going to be a new Congress, and various components of said Congress are pledging to do more to regulate AI and tech.
It wasn’t so long ago that the head of your company, Sam Altman, was calling for Congress to get more involved. Does that call still stand now that it’s a different Congress that might be more inclined to come down hard on AI?
When it comes to data centers, these are typically state or local issues. We envisioned that as state legislation that would actually make these requirements for folks who are building data centers to help give the public confidence that there’s going to be a real material benefit for them.
I think what you’re referring to was our call as OpenAI for there to be national-level mandatory safety requirements for the frontier labs who are building AI. We thought about that and called for it before the election. We think it’s more important than ever.
Back in early September, I had a blog post out there that talked about this idea that the policy window was opening up to create a real opportunity to pass those mandatory safety requirements. And the reason I talked about the policy window being opened up is that you could clearly see where the politics were going, what was likely to happen with the election.
You’re in Washington, DC. At some level, you have to be a romanticist to believe that you can actually get legislation passed. But what is happening is the politics are coming into alignment with the policy. I actually think both parties do recognize the importance of having mandatory national safety standards that would be good for the country. It would also put us in a position to be able to create international standards, which we also think is very important.
It’s funny, because we just had New York [state] assemblyman Alex Bores on the show. He was trying to be a congressperson, but a super PAC partly funded by OpenAI co-founders and some other Silicon Valley tech types spent a lot of money — millions — to defeat him.
We asked him, if Democrats in Congress could do one thing to regulate AI, what would it be? And he said banning full recursive self-improvement, ban the practice of letting AIs build the next AIs without any human in the loop. Would OpenAI be open to that kind of regulation immediately?
The version that we have talked about is some version of broadly defined speed limits. I’ll use an analogy: As we were building out the automobile, ultimately we built out speed limits. Now, those speed limits changed over time, but the idea was to make sure that humans could actually have both hands on the wheel and be able to control the car and the car should not be able to go at a speed where a human would not be able to control it.
Our north star in everything when it comes to AI is that people should be in control of this technology. The technology itself is accelerating, the capabilities are becoming stronger. And so I think there is a world here where we do need to build out a framework, potentially a regulatory framework, through legislation that effectively imposes some version of a speed limit.
If you think of speed limits being applied in the context of your question about recursive self-improvement, that’s a place where you could see the speed of the technology getting so strong that actually humans do lose control over it.
I’m not sure it’s quite as binary as saying you do or do not do RSI. But I think spiritually, a similar concept, which is making sure that at the end of the day we have a lot of confidence that humans are actually in control of this, able to monitor it, able to make sure that it is not getting out of their control.
Before you worked with companies like OpenAI or Coinbase or Airbnb, you worked in government and you worked specifically in [the] Clinton White House.
I wonder, in the wake of this election — which people are calling the first big American AI election, and are saying that AI is going to be an even bigger issue for the presidential election in 2028 — what do you think companies like yours and all the other big-frontier AI companies need to be doing to flip the script in the United States, maybe around the world?
I think of 2026 as the trailer to 2028. AI was an issue. It wasn’t a top issue, but it was certainly an issue and an issue that was moving up the charts as we got closer and closer to the election. I think there is a decent chance, maybe even a strong chance, that AI is the issue in 2028.
First and foremost, how do we make sure that people are actually in control of this technology? Who’s actually putting out an idea and a vision and approach to give people confidence that they’re going to actually be able to control this?
I do think the 2026 election now sets up 2028, frankly for both parties, to have a conversation that I just don’t think we’ve had in this country for a long, long, long time. And that is, what does this social contract look like? Who actually has a big idea about how we’re going to make sure that the American dream actually exists in this country? And as part of that big idea, what is the role of AI going to be in that?
I just don’t think it’s going to be good enough for a candidate from either party to emerge from their primary by simply being the person who’s against things. I think they’re actually going to have to have some real ideas of what they are for. And at the core of that is, how are they going to address this anxiety that the American people have? And at the center of that anxiety is their ability to control their lives and make decisions about their lives.

Black Friday, the deal-drenched marketing blitz that kicks off the holiday shopping spree, might feel more muted this year.
That’s because just about everything is getting more expensive. As the global economy reckons with challenges from the AI industry’s memory crisis and the ongoing war in Iran, prices for many products have risen, especially consumer electronics like smartphones and gaming consoles.
While many sales have already begun, the prices on offer may feel less like a deal than in years past. Weaker deals will likely revolve around products that use a lot of memory (RAM). Gadgets like robot vacuums, headphones, and other products that don’t rely as much on memory may see better prices.
“Things are getting more expensive, and they'll probably continue to get more expensive well into 2027, maybe even 2028,” says Jitesh Ubrani, director of Consumer Devices Research at IDC. “When it comes to PCs, tablets, those kinds of devices, that's where everyone's going to struggle.”
Case in point: Amazon, the absolute behemoth of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, has hiked the prices of its latest Kindles, tablets, and Echo speakers, meaning its next sale on those devices likely won’t impress compared to years past.
Black Friday and Cyber Monday remain the best shopping days of the year, says Edgar Dworsky, a consumer advocate who has long used his website Consumer World to call out companies that stealthily raise product prices.
“However, just because an item is advertised with significant savings claimed, doesn't mean it is a good deal or the best price,” Dworsky wrote in a message to WIRED.
Dworsky recommends tracking Amazon’s prices by monitoring price-history websites like CamelCamelCamel. Google has a built-in price-tracking tool in the Chrome browser, but many other third-party extensions do the job as well.
“Because of high memory prices, laptops, desktops, and SSDs will still be on sale,” Dworsky predicts. “But not nearly as low-priced as previously offered.”
It might be a good move to buy a used or refurbished gadget. Sean Cleland, vice president of Mobility Tech at the product resale company BStock Solutions, says some manufacturers are leaning into selling refurbished units more than ever, even buying them from resellers like BStock. They're filling gaps in the budget phone market by offering up refurbished products.
“The new trend that we're seeing is the [manufacturers] buying back their own stuff in the secondary market so that they can refurbish it and sell it as authorized refurbished or certified renewed,” Cleland says. “They're trying to get anything and everything back.”
What Black Friday will be good for, it seems, is the companies selling all this stuff. They get to set the costs, after all. With all the economic turmoil in the market, companies have been adept at passing additional costs to consumers.
“There's no good news right now for consumers,” Ubrani says. “It's unfortunate that the consumers are the ones who are going to struggle because of all this.”
So maybe the deals won’t be great. But they might be the best you can get for a while. The memory crisis isn’t ending anytime soon, so now might be the time to get something you need. If you do that, Ubrani recommends making sure it’s something you actually need. And something that will keep working for a long time.
“They should be purchasing the most amount of performance that they can afford today,” Ubrani says. “We're going to face elevated pricing for years. You want that device to last you for a while.”

Nationwide flight grounding unlikely in Canada, says aviation expert
Canada's air traffic control system 'the envy of the world,' says John Gradek
An aviation management expert says Canada is less likely than the United States to ground flights nationwide as that country did on Friday afternoon, calling the Canadian system a model its southern neighbours should look to.
John Gradek, a faculty lecturer in supply networks and aviation management at McGill University, says the Canadian system is more robust and modernized than the one the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration operates with.
"They should look north — they should look to Canada," Gradek said.
"You have to take it out of the hands of the politicians to finance your air traffic control system … If the system can go down the way it did Friday night [because] some guy supposedly clipped a wire on a router … and it brings down the whole of the U.S. aviation system, something is wrong."
The FAA issued a so-called ground stop order on Friday, citing communications issues affecting the nearly two-dozen air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports across the country.

Duffy blames underinvestment
The FAA on Sunday described a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Ark., as potential sources for the problem, which involved excess data flooding the air-traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said after a contractor replaced old copper wire with new fibre wire at the Arkansas site and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up in Texas, cascading into the ground stop.

Canada 'envy of the world'

"We're the envy of the world in Canada in terms of how we have our air traffic control systems in place, and the management of those systems by Nav Canada," Gradek said.
"I've never seen this type of fragility in an air traffic control system where one wire brings down everybody."
In an emailed statement, Nav Canada said its systems were not affected by Friday's outage in the United States, and air traffic services in Canadian airspace continue to operate normally.
The statement pointed to $3.5 billion it invested in the air-traffic management system and associated infrastructure.

A tiny, $900 wearable device being developed by an Indian billionaire entrepreneur and showcased by some of the country’s top sportspersons has sparked criticism from doctors who say its claims of tracking blood flow to the brain are exaggerated.
The Temple device is less than 1 inch (2.54 cm) wide and weighs under 2 grams (0.07 oz). It sticks to the side of the head between the forehead and the ear, or the temple area.
Promotional materials for the device, developed by Deepinder Goyal, say that its BrainFlow feature shows how well the brain is being supplied with blood in real time and its Entropy feature can detect how hard the body works to shed heat.
It can also measure thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive and emotional readings that help to transform how a person regulates their health, they say.
Priced at 85,000 rupees ($907), the device comes in six colours. India’s cricket captain Shubman Gill and Olympic medal-winning badminton player P.V. Sindhu have worn it.
Some well-known doctors in the country, however, are sceptical of the claims, saying the device’s capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research. In prime-time shows and on social media, they are calling for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators.
Prominent Indian hepatologist Cyriac Philips, known as “TheLiverDoc”, has been criticising the device on his X account with 328,000 followers, calling Temple “the biggest health scam”.
“People must be aware of wellness hacks such as wearables also, even though they are not marketed as health devices,” he told Reuters.
On one prime-time TV discussion, paediatrician and nephrologist Sanjeev Bagai called Temple a “gimmick”, saying it had “no formal approval or clearance”.
Goyal has hit back at the criticism from doctors, saying Temple is a “fitness tracker, and wellness device”, not a medical one.
Indian doctor Jason Philip wrote on X that assessing blood flow to the brain was not easy, and optical signals placed over the temple skin would only give data on the “superficial temporal artery” that supplies blood to the face and skin.
In a statement to Reuters, Temple said BrainFlow and Entropy were new metrics “with emerging science”, and that more research would follow, adding that some metrics would eventually need regulatory approval.
India’s health ministry did not respond to Reuters queries, and the government has so far not reacted to the public debate.
The debate on Temple comes as wearable makers overseas also face questions on when a fitness feature becomes a medical one.
Some Apple Watch features, such as hypertension notifications, have received US Food and Drug Administration clearance as software-based medical features. Last year, the US FDA warned Whoop, saying its wrist-worn fitness tracker’s blood-pressure feature looked like a medical one — a view the company disputes.
Goyal is best known for co-founding Eternal, which houses India’s biggest listed food-delivery company Zomato and has a market value of about $35 billion. The 43-year-old stepped down as chief executive of Eternal this year to focus on Temple.
Temple, which has professors from the University of Ottawa and Harvard on its advisory board, raised $54 million in February at a valuation of about $190 million.
Goyal said Temple has received orders from more than 62 countries since November 1.
On its website, Temple says it is also working on detecting conditions including snoring and jaw clenching.

Quick Answer
You can run AI models locally on Android and iPhone using Google AI Edge Gallery or PocketPal AI, and on Mac and Windows using LM Studio or Ollama. Simply install the app, download a compatible AI model, and start using it offline. Your data stays on your device, with no cloud access required after setup.
While many think AI is a bubble that is going to burst one day, it might be true, or it might not be at all. Only time will tell. But we should all accept that AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with our devices and do work.
For me, my life revolves around AI: I hand off some of my work to it and do things that once weren’t possible.
AI models are rapidly evolving. If you don’t know what an AI model is, it powers the apps and interfaces you interact with. For instance, the ChatGPT app uses GPT models, and the Claude app is powered by Claude models, which run behind the scenes.
While AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with devices and making work easier, handing your sensitive data to it has remained a major privacy concern.But thanks to rapid AI model development, many capable, powerful AI models enough to run locally on your device, without your data leaving your device
Companies like Google and Meta offer free AI models that can run locally on most consumer devices, including your mobile phone. Apps like Google’s AI Edge Gallery and PocketPal AI also make it easy to discover and run AI models locally without technical expertise.
If you have a capable computer with decent RAM, you can also run AI models locally to use them for writing your email, summarising PDFs, data analysis, coding, using their vision capabilities, and much more.
However, setting up an AI model locally involves downloading the app, choosing the model yourself, and understanding its capabilities first.
To help you out, I have created this detailed, comprehensive guide to set up and run local AI models on your device on Android, iPhone, Mac, or even on Windows.
I wrote this guide with beginners in mind, so every step is comprehensive and easy to follow. If you have questions, comment below. I am happy to help you. Most of these models can run locally on many consumer applications, but before that, don’t forget to check our prerequisites because that’s where your journey starts.
Table of Contents
Pre-Requirements To Run AI Models Locally on Device
Your device’s RAM determines whether it can run AI models.
Technically, a model loads into your RAM to run. As a general rule of thumb, a model needs about as much free RAM as its download size.
So, more RAM leaves room to run large AI models. A minimum of 6 GB of RAM is required to run decent, capable AI models locally on your device
Similarly, you need enough storage to download and store models locally. A model can generally range from 2 GB to 20 GB or even more, depending on its size and capabilities.
Finally, you need an internet connection and enough data to download the model so you can run it offline.
As I said before, these models can range from 2 GB to 20 GB. So it requires an internet connection to download the model and store it locally on your device.
Of course, Other minimum specifications, such as a capable Processor, Operating system, and platform, also matter but not as much as RAM does.
How to check how much RAM your device has
On Android:
Go to About Device to see how much RAM your smartphone has. To do that: Open Settings on your device, tap on the search bar at the top, and search for “About Device”. On some phones, scroll down and tap “About Device”. Look at the RAM specifications.
On some phones, you will see extra visible RAM after the plus sign, for example, 16GB + 12GB. However, only the first number is the real memory.
iPhone:
Apple generally doesn’t disclose the RAM used in iPhones. However, iPhone 15 Pro and newer devices generally have at least 8GB, while older iPhones have less than 6GB, which can run 1 billion to 2 billion models. You can check how much RAM your iPhone has from here.
Mac:
To check how much RAM on your MacBook: From the home screen, click on the Apple icon in the top left corner screen and tap on About This Mac. From here, you can check chip and memory options. Apple MacBooks running on Apple Silicon are especially good for running local AI models since the graphics chip shares all the memory.
Windows:
On Windows, you can go to Settings > System > About. From there, check the installed RAM, graphics card, and system type (x86 or ARM-based), which determines which applications you can download to run AI models locally.
Once your device meets the minimum RAM requirement, follow these steps to set it up to run AI models locally. Use the table of contents above to go to the device you want to set up. This guide covers Android, iPhone, Mac, and Windows.
How to Run AI Models Locally on Any Device
Android:
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on Android with Google AI Edge Gallery
You can run Google’s family of Open-weight AI models locally for free on your Android device using Google’s own AI Edge Gallery app (Free).
Gemma 4 is Google’s latest open-weight model. It comes in five model sizes. Gemma 4 E2B and Gemma 4 E4B are suitable for running on Android devices. 2B requires at least 8GB of RAM, and 4B requires at least 12GB of RAM.
Gemma 4 also supports vision capabilities, so it is not just text; you can also use it to understand images.
How to install and run the latest Google Gemma 4 models locally on your Android phone
Step 1: Download Google AI Edge Gallery from the Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI Chat.
Step 3: Under the recommended models, tap Download below. To download the model you want. Gemma 4 E2B is 2.6 GB and best for starters, while Gemma 4 E4B is 3.7 GB and smarter, but your phone needs at least 8 GB of RAM to run it locally.
Step 3: Once the model is downloaded, tap Try it.
Step 4: Type your prompt in the Type prompt box and tap the send button.
Step 5: Like the other AI apps, the model replies to your prompt. You can also see how fast the model runs, measured in tokens per second, and how much RAM it uses. On my Android phone, the Gemma 4 E2B model ran at about 30 tokens per second, and my model comes with 16 GB of RAM.
Method 2: Run any open model on Android with PocketPal AI
PocketPal is a popular free and open-source app for running AI models locally on Android.
Unlike Google’s AI Edge Gallery, it supports a wide variety of third-party models, including Google’s Gemma, Meta’s Llama, Microsoft’s Phi, Qwen, and more. It also supports GGUF models, including compressed versions.
How do I use the PocketPal app to run AI models locally on my device?
Step 1: Download and install the PocketPal app from the Google Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and, during onboarding, tap Download Model.
Step 3: Pick any available model to download and tap Download,
or tap the plus option to find more. To get a new model, tap the plus icon, select Hugging Face, then tap Choose and add from Hugging Face.
Step 4: From here, you can search for any model. In this case, I searched for the Qwen3 1.7B parameter model and tapped the download icon to download it locally.
Step 5: Once done, open the Models tab and select the model to load it. Now go to the chat interface and enter the prompt, and the model uses the model that you have loaded, in this case, the Qwen3 1.7 billion parameter model, to answer your queries. You can also see how much time it takes to run this model on your device.
iPhone
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on iPhone with Google AI Edge Gallery
Google’s AI Edge Gallery is also available on iPhone and supports the latest Gemma 4 family of open-weight models, similar to Android. You can download and use E2B (around 2.6 GB) and the E4B model (around 3.7 GB).
Apple doesn’t disclose the RAM used on iPhones. However, the latest iPhone models, including the iPhone 15 Pro and later, support up to 8 GB of RAM, which can run these models faster and more reliably. However, older iPhones may struggle with slow responses, battery drain, and overheating, so keep that in mind.
Step 1: Download the Google AI Edge Gallery app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI chat
Step 3: Now download the compatible AI model. In this case, I’m downloading Gemma 4 E2B, which is about 2.59 GB. Click on the download icon under the model.
Step 4: Wait for the model to download, then tap Try It, enter the prompt, and wait for a reply. If you want to use the vision capabilities, tap on the plus icon and upload an image
Method 2: Run open models on iPhone with PocketPal AI
Similar to Google’s AI Edge Gallery app, the PocketPal app is also available on iPhone. It also gives access to some of the popular Hugging Face model library and other third-party models, including models from Meta, Cohere, and more. It also supports Google Gemma 4 models.
Step 1: Install the PocketPal AI app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app, tap Download Model, select a model, and tap Download. In this case, I am downloading the Qwen3 1.7B model.
Step 3: Once downloaded, tap the Load option at the top, enter the prompt, and wait for the reply
Mac
Method 1: Run AI models on a Mac with LM Studio
You can use LM Studio on Mac to run AI models locally.
It supports a wide range of models, including models from Google Gemma, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, and more. Like the mobile app, you can install LM Studio on your Mac, download a model, and start chatting. It also supports GGUF and Apple-optimized MLX models.
Depending on the model, you can have text conversations, image analysis, and more. You can also use it as a local API for other apps.
However, LM Studio is only available on Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
How to install and run AI models locally using LM Studio on Mac
Step 1: First, go to lmstudio.ai/download and download the LM Studio app for Mac. Select the compatible version and drag and drop LM Studio into Applications to install it.
Step 2: Open LM Studio on the Mac, click on the model search in the sidebar, and search for the model; for example, in this case, I searched for the Gemma 4 E4B model
Step 3: You can also pick a different model, select it, and click Download. A likely fit badge here means that it is suitable to run locally on your Mac using your Mac’s available memory. Once the model is downloaded, tap on Use in the new chat instead.
Step 4: On the home screen, click Load Model in the dialog and select the model. You can also raise the context length here if you are planning for long conversations.
Step 5: Now enter the prompt and press Enter. The model returns with an option. You can also click the model server in the sidebar and turn on the status to use the model for other apps via an OpenAI-compatible API at http://localhost:1234.
Method 2: Run AI models on a Mac with Ollama
You can also run AI models on your Mac using Ollama. It is a free, lightweight tool by Meta that lets you run local AI models in the terminal with one command. It also works with many local apps that support local AI.
Step 1: To run Ollama locally on your device, go to ollama.com/download and click on the Download manually option. You can also directly paste the command into the terminal if you are a developer.
Step 2: Next, open the Ollama.dmg, drag it into Applications, and open it
Step 3: On the onboarding screen, while setting up an account, Ollama asks you to sign up for an account; however, you can tap on No thanks, I will use Ollama locally’
Step 4: Next, to run ollama run llama3, copy the ollama run llama3 command, open Terminal, and paste it. Wait for the model to download completely. Ollama can run Qwen3 4B parameters and other models. In this case, I am going to run the Ollama run Qwen3 4B model. So, wait for the model to download completely.
Step 5: Finally, you can start using the Ollama model right there. You can enter the prompt directly, and it will reply in the same terminal.
Windows
Method 1: Run AI models on Windows with LM Studio
You can use the same LM Studio on Windows as well to run AI models locally on your device
Step 1: Download and install LM Studio for Windows. Here is the download page link.
Step 2: Open the LM Studio app and, in the left sidebar, tap Model Search and search for the model you want to run locally. In this case, Iam using Qwen3 1.7 billion parameters; on the model details page, click the download option.
Step 3: Wait for it to download, and once it has downloaded, tap on Use in new chat
Step 4: Now, on the home screen, in the model box, select the downloaded model. You can tap on the model to select and enable it, then enter the prompt and press enter.
Method 2: Run AI models on Windows with Ollama
Ollama is also available on Mac. It supports NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards, as well as the latest ARM-based Snapdragon PCs. You can download models and use them directly from the terminal. Here is how.
Step 1: First, download Ollama on Windows. Go to ollama.com/download/windows and click Manual download. If you are a developer, you can install it directly in PowerShell using the PowerShell command.
Step 2: Now install the Ollama app on Windows. While setting up, click Continue, and then tap on No thanks, I will use Ollama locally, so you can skip creating an account.
Step 3: Next, copy the command shown in the app, open Terminal, and run this command: ollama run qwen3:1.7b, and press Enter. It downloads the model. Wait for the download to complete.
Step 4: Now enter your question and press Enter.
This is how you can set up and run AI models locally on Android, iPhone, Windows, and Mac. Choosing the right model is important to get high-quality output. Bigger models don’t always mean better outputs, as their capabilities can vary. Our guide to the best AI models to run locally should help you choose the right model for your needs. If you have any issues setting them up, feel free to comment below, and I’ll be happy to help.
