Russia is allowing men in Moscow to skip their standard one-year military conscription by signing a contract with the country's drone force, which the Kremlin seeks to expand quickly.
State media outlet TASS cited the capital's military commissar, Maj. Gen. Maxim Loktev, saying that Moscow was piloting the alternative program.
Russia requires male citizens aged 18 to 30 to serve a year of military service, which can be deferred or exempted in some cases. Most draftees are sent to the Russian armed forces, though some go to alternatives such as the emergencies ministry or national guard.
Loktev said the new program would count a special one-year contract with Russia's Unmanned Systems Forces as fulfillment of compulsory service.
Fully established in November 2025, the service branch is Russia's dedicated force for air, land, and sea drone warfare.
"Selection is underway for positions as drone operators, engineers, and technicians, with priority given to candidates with experience in IT, electronics, radio engineering, and aeromodelling," Loktev told TASS.
There have been concerns in the country, however, about one-year military contracts being renewed indefinitely while the war in Ukraine lasts.
Russia's defense ministry did not immediately respond to a comment request sent outside regular business hours.
Such contracts might not be what they seem
The Kremlin drafts roughly 250,000 to 300,000 conscripts a year, and has pledged that these men would not be sent to the front lines of Ukraine. But some conscripts have been posted to Russian regions close to Ukraine, subject to drone attacks or sabotage.
Similar conditions are promised to those who sign up for the Unmanned Systems Forces. Russia has tried recruiting for this branch from universities and colleges, telling students that they would only be posted to rear areas of the war.
Opposition media in Russia, however, has repeatedly raised concerns that the country's special one-year military contracts are subject to involuntary renewal.
One anti-war lawyer, Artem Klyga, in April posted what he described as a letter from a top military official in the branch, which said that once a soldier's contract was up, his commander was legally given the right, but was not obligated, to discharge him.
The letter posted by Klyga has been cited frequently by Russian opposition media. Russia's defense ministry publicly issued instructions in April for commanders to abide by contract terms, but the framework for discharge remains murky since federal law still gives them discretion over a soldier's release.
There have also been reports that some who signed such contracts were sent to infantry assault units. The BBC's Russian service reported in June that three students were killed in frontline combat after signing up for the Unmanned Systems Forces.
Despite all of this, Russia's Unmanned Systems Forces appears to be recruiting steadily.
Ukrainian officials have estimated that it grew from about 10,000 to 20,000 members in November 2025 to over 100,000 troops by April 2026. Russia plans to expand the branch to 210,000 servicemen by 2030, they said.
Kyiv has its own Unmanned Systems Forces, established in 2024, comprising elite drone units that work alongside the drone squads of Ukraine's regular armed forces. Led by Maj. Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, it's been credited with about a third of Ukraine's verified drone hits.

Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies age 80
- Published
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.
Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.
He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.
In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena.
Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.
His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.
In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.
In the 1980s, Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.
From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.
In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.
Félix Gallardo's life has been portrayed in a number of television programmes including the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. The show depicted his rise to power as well as his relationship with Guzmán.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

“There is no established playbook for making wearables in India. If you have the capital, you can set up a team, hire a bunch of researchers and scientists and come up with a product and even start selling it,” a California-based Indian founder of a wearable startup told us this week. The heated and contentious battle on X over Temple has brought out a lot into the open. A lot has been said and written about Temple this month, and who’s right and who’s wrong. What has gone unanswered in the cacophony is what it takes to actually launch a health or fitness tracking wearable that’s made in India. Where do founders turn when they need their hypothesis tested? Which agencies are the most approachable and how much red tape can one expect? These questions are not just about Temple. It’s about any new device that’s being launched in India, whether it is looking to track blood flow to the brain or it is just a heart rate or fitness monitor. The distinction matters in a market where wearable manufacturers can build and sell products that track physiological parameters without necessarily undergoing the clinical validation expected of medical devices. For India’s wearable industry, the debate has exposed gaps in how companies develop, validate and market products that make health-related claims or even basic activity tracking. But first, let’s see where Temple stands before diving deeper into the ecosystem of health wearables. Temple’s Bet On Something New Deepinder Goyal launched Temple with a core proposition of tracking blood flow to the brain and entropy. The company set out to create two new metrics that give users something their smartwatches could never. Firstly, BrainFlow is said to track relative changes in the blood flow to the brain during everyday activity. On the other hand, Goyal has described Entropy as a measure of how hard the body works to shed heat. The company’s website says the metric captures the body’s load across thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive, emotional, pharmacological, postural, reproductive and recovery systems. However, research papers uploaded on its website clearly state that Temple cannot directly measure cerebral blood flow. In response to Inc42’s questions about how these are measured, Temple said the Brain Flow Index is a relative index derived from optical signals collected at the temple. The company said the index rose and fell alongside blood-flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery, a major artery in the brain, as measured through transcranial Doppler ultrasound. Temple said the metric currently has two applications in its fitness app. It helps users compare the intensity of their cardio sessions and sends prompts to move when their Brain Flow Index drops during long periods of sitting. Unlike heart rate or sleep tracking, which have been part of consumer wearables for years, Entropy is being positioned as a new physiological metric. Its scientific validity will depend on whether the underlying signals can reliably measure what the company claims. The fact that Temple is broaching new territory with these metrics is what has set alarm bells ringing. Founders we spoke to say most wearables already have algorithms available for the heart rate and sleep tracking that have been improved and enhanced over the years since the first such devices came about. “The real work comes when you develop a new tracker or establish a new biomarker or a new benchmark for measuring something new,” the founder quoted at the beginning said, adding that specialised algorithms need research papers and validation. This is why there’s so much scepticism around Temple in the medical fraternity, with many doctors accusing the company of pushing a product without adequate backing. Temple’s research page lists multiple studies examining its BrainFlow technology, including a study involving 23 healthy adults that compared its reading with transcranial Doppler (TCD), a clinical technique used to measure blood-flow velocity in major brain arteries. Another study compared Temple’s BrainFlow readings with near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), a technique that can distinguish blood volume changes in the brain from those in the scalp. The company says it has partnered with academic institutions across the world to study additional and more diverse groups of people, with further validation studies underway. Both studies are listed as being under peer review. A Temple spokesperson told Inc42 that validation work on Entropy is in its final stages and that it plans to publish the findings soon. Of Preprints And Peer Reviews After much criticism, on November 8, Goyal acknowledged the gap between the peer reviews, the studies and the launch of the devices, adding that the research on Entropy would be published soon. He also said BrainFlow was not the primary proposition behind Temple, but the starting point for its research. In an earlier November 5 post, Goyal said preprints would precede peer-reviewed publication and that further validation would continue as the product reached users. The distinction between publishing a white paper, uploading a preprint and completing peer review matters. But what do these words mean for founders who are entering the space fresh? Simply put, a white paper and a preprint make research available for public scrutiny, while peer review brings an independent assessment of the methodology, findings and conclusions. A second founder, an early stage entrepreneur building neuro-centric wearables, said credible validation requires controlled trials. “Generally, you need a double-blind test, a control group and a placebo group. The bare minimum that is respectable enough is 90 people.” However, there is no fixed requirement on the number of participants, they said when we asked whether 23 people is a large enough sample size for Temple’s study. “You can do it for 10 people. Nothing is a mandate. But is it respectable to have a big test group? Maybe,” the founder added. We were also told that publishing research papers is not compulsory either, but it helps establish credibility. At the moment, no regulations govern the release of such papers along with a product. “It’s not necessary to put out your research papers, but it is something that people demand for credibility,” the second founder added. Plus, getting a study peer-reviewed is not easy. Founders need to find the right testing bodies to conduct reviews. This comes along with a growing demand for independent validation from investors and others who want to partner with the startup. “Third-party trials are what most wearables get asked for, by investors and consumers. Even doctors are asking for them,” the founder added. For early stage startups, the cost of conducting larger studies can be a huge constraint. In their case, a study comprising just 100 subjects cost the startup around ₹15 Lakh, which the company claims is a lot at the early stage especially when the product has already been built. Most of the funds raised are depleted by the time the startup reaches the testing stage. Is Temple A Medical Device? The debate also raises questions about how India’s regulatory framework applies to wearable devices. Under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, a product’s classification depends on its intended purpose and the function it is designed to perform. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) regulates devices intended for purposes such as diagnosing, preventing, monitoring or treating diseases, as well as investigating or modifying physiological processes. Simply calling a product a fitness or wellness tracker does not settle its regulatory classification. Its intended use, advertised claims and actual functionality matter when it comes to clearances. Some well-known doctors in the country, who are sceptical of Temple claims, said the device's capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research. Hence, they have called for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators. However, Goyal has repeatedly maintained that Temple is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose or prevent any diseases. He has also said that the company will obtain regulatory clearance wherever required before making claims that need it. Responding to Inc42, a Temple spokesperson said the device does not diagnose, treat, cure, mitigate or prevent any disease, and makes no claims about any medical condition. The company argued that under Indian law, a product is classified as a medical device based on its manufacturer's intended purpose. It also cited CDSCO's 2026 guidance on medical-device software, which says software intended for general wellness, without any reference to disease, does not fall under the purview of the Medical Devices Rules, 2017. Temple said that if it ever intends to introduce a feature for a medical purpose, it will seek CDSCO approval before making it available to users. The Regulatory Road Uncertainty extends beyond how companies position their products into what regulatory clearances are needed. The second founder, who had earlier spoken about the importance of clinical trials and third-party validation, said their company obtained CDSCO approval despite not making any medical claims. The founder said the company pursued approval because it was developing a brain-focused wearable device. “In India, any brain wearable device needs CDSCO approval. Whether it is tracking blood flow or not,” the second founder claimed, adding that wearables targeting the brain face additional requirements compared with other wearable devices. “Even though I am not making a medical device, I have a CDSCO clearance. Because it is mandatory in India.” The approval process in this case stretched around 16 months from November 2024 to March 2026. We were told that before receiving approval, companies can test only a limited number of units in India, with CDSCO determining the permitted number. This also makes it harder for companies to continuously iterate and test. The founder was describing their company’s regulatory experience. However, CDSCO’s 2026 guidance on medical device software does not establish a blanket approval requirement for all brain wearables. The founder acknowledged that rules remain unclear for products positioned as wellness devices. They also pointed to gaps in enforcement, saying regulatory scrutiny is not always consistent. “The CDSCO is not very active in looking into such companies, unfortunately. This is a loophole in India that many exploit,” the founder said. A third founder said navigating regulatory requirements can be difficult for early stage startups, leading some companies to be over-cautious. “Here you need to play around with the regulatory parts. Because in India the regulations are very hard. The only reason we never say that it is a medical device is that compliance becomes very hard. Especially for a new startup.” The founder said companies need to be particularly careful about making claims related to detecting or predicting medical conditions. “So if we say we can detect, then it would be a medical device. So you have to play very carefully with the words.” The question, therefore, is whether wearable manufacturers are making claims that bring their products within the scope of medical-device regulation, regardless of how they choose to market them. Beyond medical device approvals, the founder also highlighted other certifications such as Wireless Planning and Coordination (WPC) approval for relevant equipment that allows wireless connectivity, and Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification that are mandatory for electronic devices. Similarly, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) framework applies to relevant products marketed in the US and should not be confused with Indian regulatory clearance. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) certification, meanwhile, relates to an ultra-low-power short-range data transmission over Bluetooth. The Temple spokesperson told Inc42 that it holds all the certifications required to sell the device in the countries where it is currently available. However, the company did not specify the individual certifications. Does The Wearable Industry Trust Temple? Temple’s development also needs to be viewed in the context of Goyal’s earlier work through Continue research and the Gravity Aging Hypothesis. The hypothesis explores whether gravity’s long term influence on blood circulation could contribute to aging, particularly through changes in cerebral blood flow. Goyal has previously argued that understanding brain circulation could help researchers investigate longevity and aging. Temple emerged from this broader research effort. The device was developed to monitor brain-flow-related signals continuously, giving researchers a way to study physiological changes outside conventional laboratory settings. However, a hypothesis, a measurable physiological signal and a validated biomarker are all different things. Establishing a relationship between a wearable’s readings and an existing clinical measurement does not automatically demonstrate that the device can predict aging or provide meaningful insights into longevity. One of the founders we spoke to said Temple’s placement near the temporal artery was a considered engineering decision, as the location offers a relatively accessible site for optical sensing. However, the founder cautioned that measuring blood flow at the temple does not necessarily establish that a device can measure blood flow within the brain. The second founder suggested the strength of Temple’s existing athlete study as a basis for broader performance claims arguing that larger studies involving control groups and independent validation would provide greater confidence. For Goyal, the next task is to establish that Temple’s proprietary measurements offer meaningful information beyond existing wearable metrics. In his November 8 post, he said consumers were free to wait for peer-reviewed evidence before purchasing the device. He also promised a detailed explanation of how BrainFlow is calculated, its potential application and its limitations. The wearable industry does not necessarily need every product to become a medical device; some can remain lifestyle devices. But as manufacturers move beyond counting steps, measuring sleep and tracking heart rates to developing new physiological benchmarks, they will have to show what those numbers actually mean, and how they actually derived it. Breakthrough products often begin with a hypothesis. Innovation lies in testing it, learning from the evidence and iterating, while being clear about the outcomes achieved and what remains under study. Many senior founders and investors have shown faith in Goyal’s ability to build Temple, pointing to his record of building and scaling Zomato and Blinkit (Eternal). Temple is an opportunity for him to bring that experience to a far less proven field: establishing a new category of wearable technology. Most importantly, Goyal has shown conviction by committing substantial personal capital to Temple. However, its scientific claims will need to withstand independent scrutiny before consumers can judge what the device can deliver. If Temple can successfully demonstrate that, through continued testing and iteration, it could help create the wearable playbook India lacks. Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam Creatives: Abhyam Gusai

Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.
Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
Following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy Congress wants to crack down.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.
Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

Washington, Nov 16: India, the US and eight other countries have signed a declaration to treat safeguarding artificial intelligence supply chains as a “shared endeavour” amid growing competition with China in emerging technology.
The San Francisco Declaration was signed at a meeting of the founders of the US-led Pax Silica initiative convened by US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg on Sunday.
The declaration was released by the Governments of the US, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom.
The Pax Silica initiative was announced by the US in December last year to secure supply chains for silicon and other minerals essential to semiconductor production and, by extension, to artificial intelligence and other advanced technological industries.
The declaration on Sunday affirms that economic security is fundamental to national security, sets out the participants’ common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin Super Intelligence supply chains, and declares that safeguarding them is a shared endeavour, a State Department statement said.
The US government refers to Artificial Intelligence (AI) as Super Intelligence (SI) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename it.
The Declaration on Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity also resolves to establish working groups to carry common purpose into common practice.
It proposed to set up five groups covering pro-innovation policy frameworks, SI adoption in key sectors, supply chain cooperation across the SI stack, safe harbours and supply chain security hubs, and SI security and resilience.
“No nation can secure the foundations of the SI era alone, and the prosperity SI makes possible will only be as durable as the supply chains and infrastructure beneath it,” the statement said.
The declaration said that by agreeing on what must be protected and committing to protect it together, participants are laying the secure foundations on which partner nations can innovate, invest, and grow.
“Less than a year after its launch, Pax Silica is entering a new phase. With the San Francisco Declaration, the coalition cements its shared principles into a working partnership with a common baseline and a path to act on it, the statement said.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.
Iran has targeted an airbase inBahrainin the latest resumption of strikes since September, prompting public warnings and sirens to ring out in the Gulf kingdom this morning.
According to Iranian media, the IRGC said it had sent six drones to attack a US radar system hosted in the US-allied island state.
Explosions were heard around the capital, Manama, but Bahrain authorities say their air defences intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets.
Bahrain, which lies directly across the Persian Gulf from Iran, is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, and has been repeatedly attacked by Tehran during the course of the war, which has seen flare-ups in strikes amid long bouts of inaction.
There are fears Iran’s attacks this morning might signal a resumption of the war while US President Donald Trump has threatened but refrained from returning to major combat. Negotiations to end the war remain at a stalemate, with the US maintaining its naval blockade and Iran its stranglehold over the strait of Hormuz.
Developments in the Red Sea this morning will add to further concerns for Gulf oil flows.
The Yemeni government forces supported by Saudi Arabia, fighting the Houthis, have retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb area, giving the Iran-aligned rebels even greater control over the critical shipping lane, which Saudi Arabia and other Gulf oil producers had been relying on to get their supplies out.
Elsewhere, Hamas has confirmed that a senior commander involved in planning the 7 October attacks was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday.
Here’s a recap of what the various sides have said this morning regarding the latest Iranian strikes targeting a US air base in Bahrain.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards:
The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force.
The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry
Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain.
[Bahrain] rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks.
I’m yet to see a response from the US, but can expect Centcomm (which oversees all American military operations in the Middle East) to comment at some stage, like it did for Friday’s attack. Those strikes also targeted a radar site.
Bahrain locals: 'I was hoping this period was behind us'
After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.
Locals reported hearing blasts about 4am local time, and then a second round at 6.30am.
It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them”, Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP news agency.
Another resident, Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital Manama, which is just north of the air base targeted said:
I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry posted public warnings on X, telling “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.
Iran had last launched strikes in the first week of September, when the regime targeted US military assets in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base on Sunday morning, reported Iranian media.
They said they had attacked the air base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. The base is about a 30-minute drive south of Manama.
US forces have been quietly carrying out a series of strikes on Iranian sites in recent weeks, including on the key Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where there’s a major IRGC presence. Trump has called them minor strikes.
Bahrain officials this morning have accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” to the kingdom.
The drone flurry this morning comes just 48 hours after Iran launched drones on Friday, the first escalations targeting Bahrain in two months.
That attack targeted an American radar facility. US Central Command said it had shot down the two drones without any injury or damage.
Bahrain officials hadn’t issued any warnings for that attack, but were forced to send out public alerts this morning telling residents to seek shelter. The Interior Ministry told locals to remain calm but proceed to to the nearest safe location.

Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
- Published
For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.
In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.
Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.
On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.
Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.
But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force.
Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.
The ministry has defended , externalAgnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.
But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.
When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.
But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.
"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.
These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.
The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.
This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.
Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.
The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.
"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says.
The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported, external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.
But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.
Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued, external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.
Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.
"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.
"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight."
Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.
Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI, external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.
But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.
Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.
Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.
There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget, external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.
By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.
"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.
He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.
Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.
"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.
Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says.
"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that."
The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment.
The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.
For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.
But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

Briana Middleton has something to show me. “Wait!” she says just as we’re about to end our Zoom call, reaching for something just beyond her screen.
“When I found out we were going to be doing this,” she says, “I was at the thrift shop in my neighborhood and I found this.” Then she points it at the camera: an issue of WIRED from 1995 featuring Keanu Reeves on the cover alongside the line “William Gibson on the making of Johnny Mnemonic.”
Very apropos. The 1995 film Johnny Mnemonic was based on a short story by Gibson, who also wrote the screenplay. Molly, the “razorgirl” Middleton plays in Apple TV’s forthcoming Neuromancer adaptation, made her first appearance in that short story. Her relationship with the protagonist Case, played in the series by Callum Turner, mirrors the one Reeves’ Neo had with Trinity in The Matrix, which is steeped in Gibsoneque lore.
For Middleton, to be giving an interview to WIRED about Neuromancer’s epic journey to the screen not long after finding a 1995 issue of the magazine in a secondhand store is so uncanny it almost feels like a glitch. “Dude, it was eight bucks,” she says, agreeing that eight dollars is a steal for a vintage WIRED. “I was like, ‘This is crazy.’”
Maybe all things happen exactly when they’re supposed to. Gibson originally released Neuromancer in 1984, back before hackers were cool. Back before hackers were CEOs. It focused on Case, a young computer jockey who can get online through a jack in his head. He teams up with Molly and a former military man named Armitage to break into the offworld home of the Tessier-Ashpool family, who became astoundingly rich thanks to the tech company they founded.
The book’s novel ideas—cyberspace, brain-computer interfaces, all-powerful AIs—were years away from being mainstream, let alone possible. In the years since, there’s been much talk of turning Neuromancer into a movie or TV show, but it never took off, even as Hollywood mined sci-fi for hits.
On January 22, all of that will change when Apple TV releases its long-anticipated adaptation. Ahead of its release, WIRED got in touch with Middleton, Turner, and creators Graham Roland and JD Dillard to find out how they became the first to bring the book to screens—and the burden of taking on one of sci-fi’s classics.
On adapting an iconic sci-fi novel:
Graham Roland: It's a huge seminal book. I had not read it until the summer of 2020, but I was aware it was one of those white whales. It inspired a lot of things, and people had been trying to adapt it for years.
Callum Turner: The world will be taken on a wild ride. It’s an epic. It’s Blade Runner; it’s 2001: A Space Odyssey; it’s The Fifth Element. This is the first time it comes onto our screens, and that's a big moment for us and fans of sci-fi.
Briana Middleton: When we were shooting it and in the thick of it, it was easier to not get freaked out by the expectations. It felt nice to be in a little bubble with the world that we had created. I tried to look at the expectations that people clearly have and the love that people have for this book and what these characters mean. I definitely get freaked out sometimes and I just have to shut my computer and not think about it.
On getting the rights:
Roland: I had a meeting at Skydance, and they had given me the book and said, “Hey, the rights of this book are going to come available again. We’re going to try to adapt it as a TV show as opposed to a movie or several movies." It made so much sense. So I read the book, and really responded to it right away. JD and I had been friends for years prior to that, and were looking for a way to work together. He had also had a meeting at Skydance, and they had also given him the book.
JD Dillard: Yeah, there was a wonderful kismet of this moment, and we were like, “Wait, we’re both talking to people about this. Why don’t we do it together?”
On how Drake became a producer:
Dillard: Drake has always been a fan of Neuromancer and as a storyteller has great taste, but that's only part of it. The real magic is that he’s built an incredible team at [his production company] DreamCrew that he trusts to bring things to life once he identifies something he loves or believes in. Jason Shrier, who leads film and TV for DreamCrew, is one of the folks in our little brain trust on this show, and someone we pride as always having his finger on the pulse. But he has a relationship with [entertainment company] Anonymous Content, and Skydance, so it was kind of serendipitous that as Drake and DreamCrew had identified the books, all of these parties were starting to form and realize that they could work together to go get the rights. Drake, individually and by way of DreamCrew, is part of the mix and remains an important part of our process.
On working with William Gibson:
Roland: The way it was set up was that William Gibson was going to be the decider of who was going to get the rights when they came available. So we went to work on a pitch and with the hope that we would be the people he would choose.
We had heard that there were some bigger names, much bigger than JD and I. I just felt like there was a counterculture vibe about him and I was like, I don't think it matters that we're nobodies. I think if we can somehow communicate our passion for his book, and not just go and say, “Oh, obviously we’ll take care of your book, you can trust us,” but actually go in and do the work and come up with a thoughtful presentation and a thoughtful pitch, then I think we've got as good a shot as any.
Dillard: I'm sure Bill would not mind us sharing this part of it, but it's very easy to look at these big pieces of literature or movies that have stood the test of time and just think that they were immaculately conceived. Just to hear him talk about where he struggled and what he was self-conscious about and then what he was surprised worked and what he wished he could have done, what he wished he had time to do—it was the first time Graham and I both looked at Neuromancer as a living text.
On making Neuromancer their own:
Dillard: One of the first questions we asked ourselves was “How do you make this feel new in spite of inspiring so many things that have now already come out ahead of this?” It was never going to be our ambition to out-Cyberpunk 2077 Cyberpunk 2077. But what we could do is talk to Gibson and find out where, for him, some of those big tonal touchpoints are. An interesting one that came up really early in talking to him was that he had never perceived the world of Neuromancer as a dystopia. Even that was a nice thing to just remember as we found our way through it.
The best we could do is bring people to the experience of what it felt like reading it for the first time in 1984. Because anything beyond that, your reference points are already going to be derivative. If you put up Blade Runner reference art, you're already behind it. The joke that we were even making when hiring [production designer] Luke [Hull] was like: Here's someone who's done Chernobyl and Andor, and in our minds Neuromancer is Chernobyl plus Andor. It's old-school and hi-fi and colliding those things together.
Roland: We didn't want the world of Neuromancer to feel like X amount of years after the world that we were living in. In the teaser that opens the show, you see this piece of technology in the late '60s, early '70s that we know did not exist back then in our world. We wanted to announce right out of the gate: Don't be looking for the iteration of whatever phone you have in your pocket 50 years from now. We want this to be its own world.
Dillard: Watching someone hack will only be exciting for so long. But what is stakes-driven is the danger to Case in doing it and the toll it takes on his body. Is he going to get the thing they need for the larger story for himself? Can he prove to himself that he can still do it? All of those things were immediately stickier than just watching him do it.
A thing Bill [Gibson] said really early on is, he had always sort of imagined Case as a neurological athlete. We took that and ran with it, in that it should take a toll. There's an expenditure to do this work.
On adapting a book beloved by fans:
Turner: I try not to think about how important it is and focus on my job of playing the scenes in front of me. JD and Graham had William Gibson’s approval, the scripts were brilliant, and the world so detailed and real. You can smell this world, which feels unique.
Roland: I'm so glad that one of the first things we did was go see Bill Gibson up in Vancouver. He took the burden off of us and let us know that he wasn't expecting a literal translation of his text. He's the one that we're really beholden to.
Even in those early conversations with him, he mentioned, “Oh, I always wanted to do a bigger Tessier-Ashpool story, the story of the family [behind the powerful AI called Wintermute]. I had a book deadline, and I never really got to expand on that story. But if you find yourself looking for other things, other liberties or places to go into and make your own, that would be one.” So that's why we came up with that storyline.
On the set design:
Roland: Before we ever got to hiring the heads of any departments, JD planted a flag and said, “As much as we can, we want an in-camera aesthetic. We want to be practical.” That really drove the decision to go to Japan, because trying to recreate Chiba City, we already have set extensions, obviously, because it takes place in the future, but the textures of Japan [are there], and we wanted it to feel like you were actually there.
The other thing we did, the thing I had never done on any other show, was we hired our production designer first, before any other head of a department. We knew that while we were still writing we needed that person to help us realize the world. What they were going to do practically—from a props perspective, from a concept art perspective—was going to inform our writing as well.
Dillard: It is a very bespoke version of the future; everything had to be machined and built and designed. We didn’t have all of these things that you could normally just go to the prop shop and get. But that is what drives the feeling of Neuromancer, feeling textured and grounded and real and a place you could go to, and it is both familiar to the past but aspirational to the future.
On the design of Case’s deck, the terminal he uses to access the virtual world of the matrix:
Dillard: We saw a lot of decks. If I remember correctly, I feel like we were on the way to being like, "OK, this is the deck." Then Luke was like, "Sorry, before we make that, here's another one." That is the one we went with. But we were all resistant to it just feeling like a laptop. We wanted something that was a little bit like a station.
On getting the synth-rock band Son Lux for the score:
Dillard: Graham and I knew from the beginning we wanted Neuromancer to feel different, not feel cyberpunk. In the same way that every other department had to honor retro-futurism in their own way, we wanted to charge our composer with doing the same.
They're the best, and a band we've been fans of for a long time. I don't know how many Son Lux concerts I've gone to, and it was really cool in the last few years to see their turn into scores. Obviously, Everything Everywhere All at Once was a big one for them. Ryan [Lott] and the gang just really found Neuromancer's own sonic signature.
On casting Case:
Roland: We had finished two or three scripts, and we started having conversations about casting. Apple had had a great experience with Callum on Masters of the Air and they encouraged us to meet with him. It was the first and only meeting we had. He was in LA for something else and he came to meet JD and I, and within five minutes of hearing his voice it was like, “This is the guy.”
Turner: My vision was aligned with theirs, and luckily they asked me to join. I hadn’t read the book, but I was in a sci-fi mode. I’d read I Am Legend and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? when this came through. I remember we had [Neuromancer] in our house when I was a kid, but I’d never picked it up. Graham and JD had written a wonderful character, and he felt so nuanced and detailed on the page—I jumped off from their starting point.
Case has the right mix of dangerous, courageous, and naive. Joe Strummer was a big influence. Thom Yorke. Iggy Pop. There’s an incredible documentary called Streetwise that I used as a base. There are always many, many things that go into a pot.
On maybe casting the actor who will be the next James Bond:
Dillard: We're crossing our fingers and toes.
On casting Molly:
Dillard: We had Case, so it was about “What completes the duo?” It’s a vibe thing; it’s a physicality thing. Callum's quite tall. And not that our shorter friends can't kick ass too, but you just wanted it to make sense on screen. Callum was shooting in Vancouver, and we brought a few people to read across from him. It was Briana for sure. They just had such a fun chemistry, and she just had the kind of no-nonsense grit to her. She could find these neat moments of warmth, but also not have that break her hard shell. I know everybody says this in their interviews about their show, but we really lucked out.
Middleton: I was not familiar with the book, and I had a meeting with David Levine at Anonymous Content. When he initially told me about the character and the fact that she's got lenses over her eyes, I was like, “I don't think I want to do that. That doesn't sound fun at all.” Then I met with JD and Graham months later, and they just sold me on it.
I feel like Molly is very funny in our show, and in the book, Molly is very cool, and there's a lot that we don't see that is very clearly there. Molly is a guarded character, but there is so much going on, and we do get to see some more of the very human part of her outside of the “razorgirl” badass trope.
On Molly’s razorgirl lenses:
Middleton: They were stuck on my face. It was double-sided sticky tape basically, but they held on. I think they fell off maybe once or twice throughout the entire shoot, and that includes fight scenes, so they held up. Steps were always a daunting thing. I couldn't really tell when I was going to step off something or be fine.
Whenever I took them off, it would feel weird. I would feel kind of exposed. I think at some point in the shoot, they started to feel probably how Molly feels, that they are very comforting and very much like, I can hide a little bit.
On having the jack—a brain-computer interface—attached to the back of your neck:
Turner: Actually, it was fine.
On William Gibson’s cameo as a patron at the Chatsubo dive bar:
Roland: We invited him to the set in London. I knew we had a lot of fans of his book working on our crew, but it wasn’t until he arrived that I saw the number of people that had brought their personal copy of Neuromancer hoping to get it signed. I was like, “Oh wow, I guess they're not here for the scripts.” [Laughs]
Dillard: I think we were like, “We want him to get out here, and we know it's a long slog from Vancouver, but if we can get him out here, we got to put him in. We have to just immortalize his presence in the show.” So part of it was timing, but it actually worked out for what we wanted because Chatsubo is such an iconic location in the book, and to see him there as a barfly just was like, “This will be so fun.”
On whether the other books in William Gibson’s Sprawl Trilogy—Count Zero and Mona Lisa Overdrive—could find their way onto the small screen:
Roland: It's too early to say at this point. I think we're still kind of focused on getting this one out into the world, but we'll see. I hope so.
On tech entrepreneurs being inspired by Neuromancer:
Dillard: There's some great tweet that went viral last year that is sort of like, "New tech CEO says they're launching a product called Skynet.” It's like you're missing the point if you're naming the thing after the bad thing.
Middleton: Our show is asking what happens whenever corporations have unchecked power and when a technology is unchecked and there's no regulations, and our relationship with that technology goes unchecked. Our show is asking what we lose without oversight. I think life gets much, much worse. It's scary. I'm scared.

England are favourites against All Blacks, and fearless Wales are an inspiration
- Published
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's emphatic 78-15 thrashing of Japan and looks ahead to the match against New Zealand next weekend.
I would love to see the England players absolutely bombarded with the favourites tag before their meeting with New Zealand next week.
Perhaps even over-egg it a little bit - I want to see how this side handles it.
At the end of the day, beating New Zealand or South Africa will likely be a requirement if you want to win a Rugby World Cup.
Are England really favourites? Yes, I genuinely believe they are.
While victories over Australia and Japan have been encouraging, it was Wales' epic win over the All Blacks on Saturday that has given me real faith that this England side is good enough to compete at the highest level.
The key question is whether they can play as they have done over the last two weeks while carrying the favourites tag.
England are playing a better style of rugby than New Zealand. I thought the All Blacks' attack, particularly in the second half in Cardiff, was incredibly one-dimensional.
That is nothing for England to be afraid of as their own attack has been very slick this campaign.
New Zealand aren't going to fix those issues in a week, and England should be capable of soaking up that style of attack defensively.
Of course, the All Blacks were missing some frontline players, including Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie, Will Jordan and Jordie Barrett.
However, what I saw during the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series was the Springboks beginning to work out that style of play after losing the first Test.
They went on to win the next three Tests in a row.
Two Tests to turn England into World Cup contenders
Having beaten the All Blacks last year, I don't want England to approach this home fixture with an underdog mentality. This side needs to get used to being a contender.
The next few weeks could prove crucial in determining whether they are genuine challengers at next year's World Cup.
An undefeated autumn, regardless of whether they finish top of the northern hemisphere standings in the Nations Championship, would elevate England to contenders for the Six Nations.
Two weeks ago, England would have been delighted to find themselves in this position. Now, the reward could be two massive Tests against the very best.
They are not at the level of France or South Africa yet. I think those two sides, particularly after Friday's Test match, are still a little bit ahead of everybody else.
However, England have a good chance of facing New Zealand back-to-back over the next two weeks. What an unbelievable opportunity that would be and what a feather in the cap it would represent for this team.
It would not only give the players belief in what they are capable of achieving, but also send a message to the rest of the world that they can beat New Zealand and potentially follow that up with another victory over the All Blacks or South Africa.
They are not there yet, and I'm not suggesting that beating Australia and Japan alone puts them at that level.
These next two weeks present a huge opportunity to show just how far they have come.
- Joseph scores record-equalling five tries as England rout Japan 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Comeback kid Joseph thrills as England eye All Blacks

Joseph, Ojomoh and Fisilau impress
Immanuel Feyi-Waboso's unfortunate injury against Australia leaves a spot open on the left wing.
Five tries against Japan certainly puts Will Joseph in contention. Although he played on the right wing, his experience at centre means he should be comfortable on either side of the pitch.
He is a clever defender who understands the game well and looks a real threat that can offer something different with his balanced running game.
Seb Atkinson keeps the number 12 shirt if he is fit, but Max Ojomoh's performance against Japan means I would have no concerns if he is unavailable.
Ojomoh looks like a Test-level 12. He brought a toughness to his game on Saturday that head coach Steve Borthwick has been asking for.
The bench is also an interesting area, I thought Greg Fisilau was excellent against Japan.
I think England have the ability to step things up when they find their perfect number eight.
Fisilau brought a huge level of physicality in defence and was technically very good. The way he got around the field and controlled things at the base of the scrum was also excellent.
Offensively, England have been playing sevens at eight, with Ben Earl and Henry Pollock filling that role for a while.
It would be a bold call to bring Fisilau into the starting side next week, but he has certainly put himself in the equation over the coming months.
The context is that he was playing against Japan with England miles ahead, but I thought he looked like a natural international number eight.
Wales shine to provide inspiration
Wales being in England's World Cup pool next year was never going to be an easy prospect.
That statement performance against the All Blacks reminded everyone why it is so important for the northern hemisphere to have a strong Welsh side.
You won't hear many Englishmen say they want to see them being successful, but I do.
Having Wales competing in that atmosphere, and seeing that narrative of success, is hugely important for northern hemisphere rugby.
I have nothing but admiration for the way that squad played and what they have been through over the last couple of years.
It is important we recognise just how big a win that was. It wasn't simply a case of New Zealand having a shocker. Wales stepped up and delivered a fantastic performance.
To achieve something that hasn't been done for 73 years must bring an incredible feeling of relief and disbelief.
There was talk of the death of Welsh rugby, the struggles of the provinces and whether the game would ever recover. It is a perfect example of how quickly narratives can change in Test rugby.
Wales were excellent in the way they fearlessly attacked New Zealand, and England should take plenty of inspiration from that.
A wounded All Blacks side is a scary proposition. England must go into the game expecting them to be back to their very best.
That is the mentality they need to adopt, while also embracing they are favourites for a reason.
