- Microsoft confirms Project Helix will be a console that plays PC games, not a gaming PC.
- Xbox wants instant access to games, customizable settings, and backward compatibility.
- Project Helix will focus on neural rendering, improved graphics, and cross-device gaming.
Microsoft has clarified that its next-generation Xbox, codenamed Project Helix, will be a traditional gaming console capable of running PC games rather than a gaming PC that also supports console games. The company also shared more details about its plans for the new hardware, which will use a custom AMD processor, including backward compatibility, graphics technology, and a unified Xbox experience across devices.
In the official Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, Xbox Vice President of Next Generation, Jason Ronald, explained Microsoft’s vision for Project Helix. “Helix is designed to be a console capable of playing games from your PC,” Ronald said, adding, “It is not a PC that can also play console games.”
Xbox Project Helix Console Details Reveal PC Flexibility with New Tech
Ronald explained that Microsoft wants players to enjoy the convenience of a traditional console without dealing with operating system updates, drivers, or complicated settings. Players should be able to launch their games instantly, while those looking for more control will still have options to customize settings and performance.
This unified approach builds on Microsoft’s experience with the ROG Xbox Ally handheld. Ronald revealed that feedback from players using the handheld, particularly its Xbox Mode and unified gaming library, has helped shape Project Helix’s development.
Microsoft wants to create a familiar Xbox interface that works across consoles, PCs, handhelds, TVs, and other screens. Backward compatibility is another crucial part of that vision. Xbox wants players to retain access to their existing game libraries and progression across four generations of Xbox consoles. The company has also expanded Xbox backward compatibility on PC as part of its 25th anniversary celebrations.
To achieve these goals, Microsoft has been working closely with its first-party studios since the early stages of development. Developers were asked about their creative ambitions and the technical limitations they wanted future hardware to overcome.
The company is also using its Human Factors Lab to study controller ergonomics and accessibility, while its Advanced Prototyping Center tests hardware designs using CNC machines and industrial 3D printers.
Beyond the hardware design, Microsoft is exploring neural rendering to deliver higher visual fidelity more efficiently. Ronald explained that the next generation should focus on deeper immersion and new gameplay experiences rather than simply chasing specifications such as 8K resolution or 240Hz refresh rates.
However, rising component costs like RAM prices remain a challenge. Ronald acknowledged that the ongoing component crisis is making gaming hardware more expensive, forcing Microsoft to balance technological improvements with affordability. These decisions also reflect how gaming habits are changing.
Players now expect to switch between consoles, PCs, handhelds, and other devices without losing access to their games or progress. Project Helix aims to reduce those traditional platform barriers while retaining the familiar Xbox experience.
While alpha hardware is expected to reach developers in 2027, its official release date, pricing, and final launch lineup remain unannounced.

The pros and cons of using your phone as a mobile hotspot
Skip the questionable coffee shop Wi-Fi and bring your own internet.
Whenever you're out and about with your laptop and you don't have a Wi-Fi network to connect to, a mobile hotspot can save the day. Thankfully, your phone can be used to share its cellular data connection with other devices, from your laptop to your tablet to your friend's phone. On iPhones, this feature is called Personal Hotspot; on Android devices, it's usually found under Hotspot & Tethering, depending on brand.
As remote work and travel keep more and more people away from traditional office spaces and your comfy home desk, it makes sense that more people need to connect to portable internet options. Of course, hotspot devices are available to buy, but more often than not flipping a simple switch on your phone's settings makes a lot more sense. Still, as appealing as this option is, there are some trade-offs that you should consider about using your phone, from battery drain to the cost of your data plan. It's not the end of the world by any means, but it's something that comes with both pros and cons, much like anything else in the world.
What are the benefits of using your phone as a mobile hotspot?
There are quite a few benefits to using your phone as a mobile hotspot. First of all, it's so convenient to set up your laptop on the table of your go-to coffee shop, grab your phone and turn on the hotspot feature before quickly connecting to it. Your phone now handles your internet sharing, as well as all the other things you use it for, like calls, texts and the endless list of apps without worrying about a second gadget to charge, update or remember to pack.
Using your phone as a mobile hotspot is also extremely useful because you can do this anywhere you go, whether you're connecting your own laptop or you're making it easy for your kids to play Roblox on your trip. This can also be cost-efficient because you skip the expense of a dedicated hotspot device and a potential extra data plan.
There's also another fact that should most definitely be mentioned here, and that's tied to online security. Using a mobile hotspot is a safer option because you control who connects to it. That's preferable to joining potentially unsafe open Wi-Fi networks any day of the week (and twice on Sunday). It's important, however, that you set up a strong password so random people can't join, and to make sure your hotspot uses WPA2 or WPA3 encryption. For someone who only needs a backup connection a few times a month, these benefits often outweigh the drawbacks of a dedicated device sitting unused in that tech drawer filled with cables and random gadgets.
What are the downsides of using a mobile hotspot?
The convenience of using your phone as a mobile hotspot does come with some downsides that matter the more you rely on it. One of the most obvious ones is that running a hotspot is quite power-intensive, so your battery will drop noticeably faster while it's active. This can be solved by quickly refilling that battery with the help of a power bank or your laptop's charger.
Besides battery drain, it's also worth considering your data plan limitations. If your plan has a hotspot data cap, exceeding it can dramatically slow your internet speed or cost you a lot more money at the end of the month. Of course, it all depends on what you'll be using your hotspot for because video calls and streaming will burn through that data cap quickly.
You should also be aware that sharing a mobile hotspot with multiple people may mean slower speeds for everyone. Every connected device shares that same cellular connection, so performance drops as more devices join. Just be sure to remember the risks of leaving it password-free. An unsecured hotspot is very much an open door for anyone nearby, and you never really know who poses a risk. So tighten that security with a strong password.
How to turn on mobile hotspot – and should you rely on your phone for it?
In order to activate the mobile hotspot on your Android device, pull down the quick settings panel and tap on the Mobile Hotspot icon. On most phones, long-pressing on the icon will take you directly to the configuration menu where you can name the network, set up a strong password and choose the frequency band (2.4GHz or 5GHz, or 6GHz on some new phones). Depending on your phone, you may also find options for the MAC address type and an automatic shut-off timer for when no one is connected to the network. The procedure is similar on iPhones. Open Settings, then Personal Hotspot (or Cellular, then Personal Hotspot). You'll need to turn on Allow Others to Join and set a strong Wi-Fi password.
For occasional use, using your phone as a hotspot is a practical option that often costs nothing extra as long as your plan includes hotspot data. It usually saves you money, doesn't require any extra purchases and gets the job done without issue. But if you're tethering daily, streaming video or connecting multiple devices for hours at a time, the downsides pile up fast. For such situations, a dedicated hotspot device may be the best option and worth the investment. You should review your data plan and your usage patterns before deciding on the best way for you.

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.
The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.
“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”
Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

NEW DELHI: Ahead of the Quad leaders' summit in Manila, a senior US official dismissed as fake news a media report that said the informal strategic and diplomatic partnership involving Australia, India, Japan and the US was withering under the Donald Trump administration.
Quad leaders will meet in the Philippines capital on Tuesday after a gap of two years, looking to boost cooperation in maritime security, critical and emerging technologies, climate, health and economic security, along with infrastructure and connectivity.
Assistant secretary of state Dylan Johnson described as an utterly ridiculous take a report by Politico that quoted an anonymous Washington-based Asian diplomat to say that Quad was on life support.
Working to formalise Quad summit at Asean: Johnson
"Secretary Rubio has formally met with the Quad foreign ministers five times in the past two years - with three meetings in the past six months. The Secretary's first official call in office was to the Quad. We have regular monthly Quad sherpa calls and meetings. And we are working to formalise a Quad Leaders Summit at Asean next week. Fake News!" said Johnson, responding to the article.
The leaders' summit in Manila will also reaffirm commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific that is governed by the rule of law, UN Charter, sovereignty and territorial integrity, while strongly opposing unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion in the East and South China Sea. 
The meeting takes place on the margins of the Asean summit, amid renewed China-Philippines hostilities because of overlapping claims in the South China Sea.
Also read: Hundreds clash with police in Manila ahead of Trump's Asean visit
With India unable to host the summit for the past two years, the Politico article though touched upon concerns in not just India but also Japan and Australia that Quad may have become a casualty of the India-US trade dispute and also Trump's China outreach.
While the foreign ministers' meeting has taken place 5 times since the return of Trump, it's the leaders' summit that was thought to have been derailed with Trump apparently reluctant to travel to India for Quad. The summit is finally happening but in a non-Quad country and on the margins of a multilateral event. Quad had been upgraded to the summit level in 2021.

As an intermittent Tyler Perry fan, I was eager to see what a Tyler Perry Christmas movie would look like. That’s partly because I love Christmas movies, but also because it seemed a natural for his wheelhouse. Did I want to hear Madea, in her sinfully irreverent but pious way, go off on Christmas? Hell, yes. I also wanted to see Tyler Perry’s idea of making merry.
But Perry’s “The Gospel of Christmas” turns out to be as earnest and generically reverential as its title. There is no Madea in it; there is no Tyler Perry performance as any other nasty relative; and there is very little of his shameless but diverting soap-opera extravagance. “The Gospel of Christmas” is a straight-up drama of faith (losing it, testing it, regaining it), which would be fine if the film weren’t wrapped around a family saga so rickety and threadbare it’s like watching a Sunday sermon padded out to movie form.
One reason “The Gospel of Christmas” has such a weirdly abstract flavor is that it’s a musical, filled with churchy soul and gospel numbers designed to carry the action along. Some of the songs are quite lovely, and a couple of them are pop-gospel rousers, yet their mood is so at odds with the rest of the film that they almost seem part of another movie. The songs don’t make “The Gospel of Christmas” any less sodden — they just break up the soddenness like commercials.
The film’s star, Durrell “Tank” Babbs, is a good actor, but the role Perry has written for him calls on him to mope, wallow in self-pity, get angry and irritated, and then mope some more. It’s as if we were watching George Bailey from “It’s a Wonderful Life” at his most hopeless moment, only stretched out to 90 minutes. Babbs’ Isaac Jefferson is a former bad-boy pop singer who was once famous (his biggest hit: “Gimme Them Panties”), but his career hit the skids 20 years ago. How did that happen? We’re not sure. Nothing in “The Gospel of Christmas” is filled in in a convincing way. The film plays like a Christmas “parable” because it’s so stripped of detail.
On his deathbed, Isaac’s clergyman father asks Isaac to take over the Baptist church of his great-grandfather, which is located in New York City. Isaac, the prodigal son, has no desire to become a pastor. But he feels like he can’t turn his father down. So he and his wife, Rebecca (Fantasia Barrino), and their two sons — Jacob (Mason Douglas), surly and tall, and Esau (Eric Wiltz), who’s about 10 and does not speak — move from Georgia to Perry’s studio-set version of the big bad city, which looks even stagier than the New York of “Eyes Wide Shut.” The church, a stone edifice, is an impressive chunk of real estate, but when Isaac gets into the office he sees a pile of foreclosure letters. The church is five months behind on rent, and with penalties and taxes they’ll need to come up with $58,000 to keep it going.
That’s quite a demand, but Isaac’s real burden is that he’s forgotten how to pray; he’s forgotten how to believe. The movie is all about his coming to see the light, but you wish it happened in a more flowing, less contrived way. “The Gospel of Christmas” has a chorus of angels, who give the movie its only hint of levity. It’s got a villain, Mr. Ehtami Lived, a pawn-shop purveyor who represents Temptation — though Ricco Ross, who plays him, is a subtle enough actor to give him more dimension than anyone else in the movie. There’s a plot twist that’s a real whopper, as Isaac, out of nowhere, gets offered $3 million to do a concert tour — an offer, his whole family realizes, that’s coming straight from the devil, though the audience for his kick-off concert is so pumped that all I could think was, “Why did his career jump the track?” Isaac, of course, gets his faith groove back, and I suppose you could say that “The Gospel of Christmas” is more of a Christmas movie than most Christmas movies, since it’s really about…believing in Jesus. If only it were easier to believe the story it’s telling.

In French Election, Centrists Eye a Judo Star and a Central Banker
Centrists want alternatives to a matchup between the far right and far left in the 2027 presidential election. Teddy Riner, the judo champion, is in, while Christine Lagarde is less likely.
When Teddy Riner, a judo champion and one of France’s most popular athletes, announced this week that he would run for president, it was less a game changer than a welcome diversion. For all of his appeal, Mr. Riner, 37, is unlikely to win the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron next spring.
Yet his quixotic candidacy reveals a hard truth about France’s presidential campaign. Five months before voters go to the polls, many are eager, even desperate, for a fresh face to upend a race that looks increasingly as if it’s on a glide path to the election of France’s first far-right government since World War II.
The main far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has held a commanding lead over all her rivals for months — a lead that has only been reinforced by weeks of protests, marred by violence, that have shaken France. The most prominent center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, has faded in the polls as the unrest has sharpened the appeal of far-right calls for law and order and left-wing calls for social justice.
Another beneficiary of the upheaval is a far-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who now appears to be the likeliest candidate to advance into a second round against Ms. Le Pen in France’s two-round system. As things currently stand, French voters would be confronted with a choice between two poles of the political spectrum.
Centrist voters are “afraid of being confronted with a duel between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said Jean-Daniel Lévy, deputy director of Toluna France, a polling firm. These voters, he said, are an “orphan electorate,” lacking an inspiring candidate, and are “still looking for someone.”
Raphaël LLorca, an analyst at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning research group in Paris, said the search for a white knight showed “the panic of the centrist bloc.” He added, “It is clear that the election is slipping away from them.”

WASHINGTON — Two senators are introducing a bill Friday to rein in conflicts of interest on an influential federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services.
The bill, from Sens. Angus King (I-Maine) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), follows reports that a number of members picked by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. could profit from the decisions they make on the panel, known as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. It would codify standards for membership on the panel and for avoiding conflicts of interest.
The bill comes after STAT reported that members of the panel hold stock in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and that two of them own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care. The New York Times reported on the financial investments as well. Federal officials granted all members blanket waivers, allowing them to remain on the panel, though they could still be required to recuse themselves from particular matters. The panel has not met in more than a year.

The Keralam government will take steps to implement ‘Family Sustainability Mapping’ across the State to identify, at an early stage, children living in high-risk environments, Minister for Women and Child Development Bindhu Krishna has said.
Speaking at a press conference to announce the Ujjwala Balyam Awards on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), she said a decision regarding the mapping was reached during a meeting convened following the death of a two-year-old child in Alappuzha recently due to suspected malnutrition.
The circumstances of families and children will be assessed with the cooperation of schools, Anganwadis, local self-government institutions, District Child Protection Units, healthcare workers and the police. Children facing risks such as malnutrition, neglect, domestic abuse, child labour, begging, school dropouts, substance abuse-related issues or various forms of exploitation will be identified and necessary protection and rehabilitation will be ensured.
“Child protection efforts should not be limited to intervening only after abuse or exploitation has already occurred. The government’s objective is to proactively identify high risk situations and ensure timely protection for children. Coordinated action among various departments and institutions will be strengthened to prevent issues such as sexual abuse, physical and mental abuse, neglect, child labour, child begging, human trafficking and online exploitation,” she said.
Activities will be jointly coordinated by departments including the Department of Women and Child Development, the Health Department, the Police, and the Local Self Government Department. This will enable the strengthening of existing child protection systems as well as the proactive identification of risks and the implementation of preventive measures. The Minister stated that the active participation of society is essential to ensure a safe childhood and equal opportunities for every child and to create an environment in which they can grow up with self confidence.
Ms .Krishna said that a total of 52 children from 14 districts have been chosen for the Ujjwala Balyam Awards for showcasing exemplary talent in arts, sports, literature, science, social work, environmental protection, information technology, agriculture, waste management, humanitarian activities, crafts, sculpture and acts involving extraordinary courage.
The winners were selected by a committee chaired by the District Collector in each district. The award consists of a cash prize of ₹25,000, a citation and a plaque. The awards will be presented at the State-level Children’s Day celebration to be held in Thiruvananthapuram on November 14.
The award recipients are children who have demonstrated excellence in various fields, including social work, environmental protection, information technology, agriculture, waste management, humanitarian activities, crafts, sculpture, and acts involving extraordinary courage.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket lifts off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm local time Sunday. The rocket later suffered a failure.
Credit:
Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto via Getty Images
A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket lifts off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm local time Sunday. The rocket later suffered a failure.
Credit:
Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto via Getty Images
United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.
The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.
Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.
Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).
In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”
“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”
Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.
“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”
ULA’s Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 main engines made by Blue Origin.
Credit:
United Launch Alliance
ULA’s Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 main engines made by Blue Origin.
Credit:
United Launch Alliance
Something amiss
The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.
Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.
Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.
Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.
A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.
ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.
Amazon Leo’s launcher fleet. The Atlas V is no longer available.
Credit:
Amazon
Amazon Leo’s launcher fleet. The Atlas V is no longer available.
Credit:
Amazon
Wider impacts
Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.
First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.
The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.
Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers.
Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.
“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”
Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.
Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.
What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.
That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, its chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.
It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.
Previous Vulcan delays forced Space Force officials to swap move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.
A US Space Force GPS navigation satellite is seen during encapsulation inside a Falcon 9 payload fairing. The eight newest GPS satellites all launched on SpaceX rockets.
Credit:
SpaceX
A US Space Force GPS navigation satellite is seen during encapsulation inside a Falcon 9 payload fairing. The eight newest GPS satellites all launched on SpaceX rockets.
Credit:
SpaceX
Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.
But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.
Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.
NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.
“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.
Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.
The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.
“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.
The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.
“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.
Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.
During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.
“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.
It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.
Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.
Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.
The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.
Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.
“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

Japanese animated phenomenon “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” retained the top spot at the South Korean box office over the weekend of Nov. 13–15, securing a fifth consecutive frame at No. 1.
According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Toho-distributed fantasy feature generated $875,745 from 116,176 admissions across 859 screens, claiming 18% of the weekend market. Directed by Kei Oikawa and adapted from the manga by Nagano, the animated hit has accumulated $22.6 million from 2,949,096 total admissions since its Sept. 30 rollout.
Survival thriller sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” opened in second place, pulling in $822,633 from 107,532 admissions across 797 screens to capture 17% of theatrical revenue. Since launching on Nov. 11, the film has grossed $1 million from 140,037 admissions.
Next Entertainment World’s corporate mystery thriller “Final Interview” placed third in its sophomore frame, earning $543,822 from 69,506 admissions across 747 screens for 11.2% of the market. Directed by Kim Jung-hoon and adapted from Akinari Asakura’s novel, the ensemble thriller stars Cho Yi-hyun, Kim Jae-won, Shin Seung-ho, Kang You-seok, Kwak Dong-yeon, and Bae Gang-hee. It has collected $2.1 million from 283,290 admissions since its Nov. 4 bow.
Sony Pictures and TriStar’s wilderness survival drama “Heart of the Beast” took fourth place in its third weekend, generating $286,045 from 37,589 admissions across 684 screens to represent 5.9% of receipts. Directed by David Ayer and starring Brad Pitt alongside J.K. Simmons, the Alaskan survival adventure has amassed $3.3 million from 452,535 viewers since its Oct. 28 debut.
Toho’s anime mystery special “Detective Conan: The Counterfeit Case of Ultra 30” finished fifth in its second weekend, collecting $282,456 from 36,600 admissions across 301 screens for 5.8% of the frame, pushing its cume to $1.3 million from 173,355 admissions.
Damien Chazelle’s 2016 musical romance “La La Land” returned to the chart in sixth place via a theatrical re-release, taking $296,650 from 36,435 admissions across 633 screens for a 6.1% market share. The re-issue pushed the film’s total South Korean tally to $24 million from 3,860,803 cumulative admissions.
Local animated comedy “Maca and Roni The Movie: The Great Memory Exploration Adventure!” debuted in seventh place, earning $174,614 from 25,277 admissions across 243 screens for 3.6% of the market. Counting early previews ahead of its Nov. 14 release, the animated title has grossed $175,837 from 25,481 viewers.
Denis Villeneuve’s 2021 sci-fi epic “Dune” placed eighth on the admissions chart through re-release, drawing 17,874 viewers across 26 screens while generating $256,287 (5.3% market share). The re-issue brought its cumulative South Korean gross to $14.3 millionfrom 1,691,805 admissions.
Aniplex’s anime fantasy “Puella Magi Madoka Magica the Movie -Walpurgisnacht: Rising-” took ninth place, pulling in $127,785 from 14,725 admissions across 163 screens for a cumulative total of $579,023 from 68,042 admissions.
Rounding out the top 10, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s family feature “The Cat in the Hat” earned $101,191 from 14,714 admissions across 412 screens, lifting its cumulative haul to $361,113 from 52,675 admissions.
The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $4.8 million, down from last week’s $5.3 million.

London City's 'bravery' paying off in top three pursuit
- Published
After 10 games in the Women's Super League season, London City Lionesses have shown they are capable of finishing inside the top three.
Their narrow 2-1 defeat by Manchester City two weeks ago provided snippets of their potential but a 1-1 draw at the Emirates against an improved Arsenal on Sunday confirmed their credentials.
Eder Maestre's side sit third in the table - the last qualification spot for next season's Women's Champions League - and are six points above Arsenal.
It is a strong position to be in just shy of the halfway stage having already faced big hitters Arsenal, Manchester City and Manchester United.
Current leaders Chelsea await in December but, for now, London City's progress is moving at a pace that looks set to challenge the usual suspects.
Showing 'bravery' at the Emirates
A sold-out away end helped fill out the 32,000-strong crowd at the Emirates on Sunday as many hoped for an end-to-end encounter.
They were not disappointed as fearless London City showed bravery against an Arsenal side who played with a spark following their 1-1 draw with Barcelona.
The visitors were helped out by Arsenal's wastefulness - the Gunners had 17 shots and only converted one - but London City caused plenty of problems of their own.
Maestre said after their defeat by Manchester City that their opponents showed more experience and know-how but against Arsenal, his side matured.
They were under pressure early on and fell a goal down thanks to Frida Maanum's opener but it took just 98 seconds for Izzy Goodwin to equalise for London City.
That killed Arsenal's momentum and when the pressure increased again from the hosts in the second half, goalkeeper and player of the match Mary Earps stepped up to make crucial saves.
"The performance was there. We had the chances to score and get a better result but Arsenal had chances too. The game was very open," said Maestre.
"The way we faced and challenged every circumstance in the game shows we are here, and able to play with that mentality in these big games.
"We came here to take risks. Our energy was good. We were brave and weren't scared about the context or the opponent.
"We tried to play as if we were at home. I always want to feel that my teams are brave and go for the win."
That bravery showed as Alexia Putellas came close twice with long-range efforts, Goodwin could have been onside when she was played in behind later on.
London City hit the crossbar through substitute Delphine Cascarino and had 14 shots compared to Arsenal's 17, including four inside the box.
Arsenal are still yet to win at home this season in the WSL but this was still an impressive showing from London City, who came to the Emirates to play.
But while they were willing to take risks, they were smarter than they were against Manchester City, choosing when to press aggressively and when to hold off.
"We tried to match the pace of the ball and not expose ourselves as much to the players that Arsenal have," added Maestre.
"We were trying to mix the moments we were more clinical in our press. We made some adjustments at half-time and were much better at recognising those."
Earps and Goodwin shine on big stage
London City are backed by US billionaire Michele Kang and that has made a big difference in the transfer market.
They recruited superstars Alexia Putellas, Mary Earps, Mapi Leon and Kadidiatou Diani in the summer.
Such is their depth that high-flying Spaniard Lucia Corrales, the dangerous Cascarino and England international Freya Godfrey came off the bench.
Those individual talents have made a difference and on Sunday it was goalkeeper Earps who took the plaudits, claiming the player of the match award.
She made crucial saves late on as Arsenal pushed ferociously for a winner, tipping Maanum's effort onto the crossbar and blocking her shot from close range.
Earps had to bide her time for the number one shirt after making the switch from Paris St-Germain this summer but has started the past three WSL games.
"Mary is a very strong character and is much more than the things we see in terms of the performance," said Maestre.
"She has experience, and energy that you can bring to every part in the process and not just the things we see in the matches.
"I think the energy that she brings to the position is massive and has a massive impact. I'm very pleased with her."
Watching on in the stands was England boss Sarina Wiegman who will have been pleased with the display from goalscorer Goodwin.
The 23-year-old got the better of England captain Leah Williamson when she fooled her with quick feet and fired the ball into the back of the net, making it 1-1.
She is proof that competition for places in the London City starting XI is pushing players on and that their depth is improving each week.
"I think Izzy is becoming a more mature player. She has the inner competition and the signings sometimes push you to bring 100% every time," added Maestre.
"She is committed to keep pushing and, with the performances she is having, why not [earn an England call-up]?
"Izzy is moving forward in the ways she can take advantage and that commitment is the way she is reaching those performances. I'm very proud of her."

The Centre is testing 3D concrete printing under the Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G). A ₹14-crore pilot project covering 177 houses is underway in the villages of Burripalem and Obulanaidupalem in Guntur District, Andhra Pradesh, to assess the feasibility of scaling up 3D concrete printing technology for rural housing. Mint take a look:
How does 3D concrete printing differ from conventional construction?
Conventional rural houses are largely built using bricks, cement mortar and manual labour. The 3D concrete printing (3DCP) technology replaces conventional brick masonry with digitally designed, machine-produced hollow interlocking concrete blocks. These blocks are manufactured using a mix of cement, sand, fly ash and bagasse ash, and assembled at the construction site.
The technology, developed by CSIR-Central Building Research Institute (CSIR-CBRI) for the pilot, uses a 3D printer to produce precision-engineered, modular hollow blocks of different shapes at a production yard. These blocks are then assembled at the construction site, using mortar and Murfor reinforcement to form the walls of the house. The technology reduces cement consumption, incorporates agro-industrial waste, requires fewer workers and shortens construction time.
What advantages does 3D printing offer in terms of construction speed, cost, quality, labour requirements, and durability?
The technology is expected to support the goal of housing for all by reducing construction time, lifecycle cost, material wastage and carbon emissions, while enhancing quality, durability, and inclusivity. 3D concrete printing could make rural housing construction faster, cheaper and less labour-intensive under the PMAY-G.
According to the government, the technology can reduce construction time by around 40% and manual labour requirements by 50%. The cost of walling using 3D-printed blocks is estimated to be around 40% lower than conventional brick masonry, at ₹48,496 compared with ₹79,920 for the prototype house.
The use of fly ash and bagasse ash also reduces cement consumption and the environmental footprint. For beneficiaries, the technology promises earlier possession, better thermal insulation, noise reduction and greater resistance to earthquakes, fire and moisture. The houses will also include accessible features and individual household toilets, without any additional financial burden on beneficiaries.
What is the next phase after Guntur, where will the technology be expanded, and how many more houses are planned?
The Guntur pilot project is to be completed in six phases over 80 weeks. The pilot shall demonstrate construction of the PMAY-G rural houses using 3DCP through structured technology transfer. It shall also establish standardized yet replicable housing designs and construction protocols. The technical learnings, standard operating procedures, construction protocols and performance outcomes generated under the pilot shall be utilized by the ministry of rural development for replication and scaling of 3DCP technology in any state or Union territory.
Decisions on additional locations and coverage shall be based on the outcomes and evidence generated by the Guntur pilot.
If successful, how will the government develop technical guidelines and a framework to scale up 3D-printed construction?
The pilot shall serve as a national reference project for future policy decisions on integrating 3DCP into the PMAY-G and other public housing programmes.
The standardized designs, documented construction protocols, validated mix designs and performance data generated under the pilot shall form the technical basis for a framework that states can adopt.
The ministry of rural development shall have perpetual, royalty-free rights to use, adapt and scale the technology and project learnings across all states and Union territories.
CSIR-CBRI shall prepare SOPs, construction manuals, safety checklists and inspection formats, and shall extend technical support for replication and scaling. "The learnings from this initiative will help develop standardized construction protocols and inform future decisions on scaling up this technology across states and Union territories, with the ultimate objective of ensuring safe, dignified and inclusive housing for rural families," said Rohit Kansal, secretary, ministry of rural development
What are the key challenges in taking 3D-printed housing beyond the pilot?
The wider adoption of 3D concrete printing faces challenges, including the availability of printing equipment and its operation at scale, a shortage of trained manpower and the need to develop concrete mixes suited to local materials and climatic conditions. Site preparation and soil stabilization are also key considerations.
The pilot will address these challenges through measures such as pile foundations for black cotton and clay soils, flood-resilient plinths and climate-specific insulated walls. Pile foundations use long, slender columns driven, drilled or screwed deep into the ground to provide structural support. The project is designed to generate evidence on the technology’s operational and technical feasibility.

Last week, President Donald Trump named Stephen Miller, his longtime adviser and architect of the administration’s widely unpopular immigration agenda, his new chief of staff. With the midterm elections delivering a Democratic majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, Miller, whose titles until now were deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, will likely play a critical role in shaping the White House’s agenda over the next two years.
There is probably no one who understands Miller better than journalist Jean Guerrero. During Trump’s first administration, Guerrero became fascinated by Miller, who, like her, had grown up in Southern California, surrounded by immigrants, in largely liberal (or at least not hard-line conservative) communities. How, she wondered, did this man, whose family came to the US fleeing antisemitic pogroms, who grew up in close proximity to immigrants, come to align himself with white supremacist and anti-immigrant views?
Her research culminated in Hatemonger, her 2020 biography of Miller, in which she charted his rapid ascent to power in the first Trump administration and dove into the ideas, mentors, and experiences that formed the foundations of Miller’s beliefs.
“Stephen Miller has been a key player in delivering on President Trump’s America First agenda including spearheading the administration’s crime crackdown including in DC and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashing American energy, dismantling drug cartels, and securing our border. In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people,” says White House spokesperson Lauren Bis.
WIRED spoke to Guerrero about where Miller goes from here in his new role, and the ways in which her understanding of Miller has evolved during Trump’s second term.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
WIRED: Miller has now ascended to the most powerful role he has ever occupied. Is this something he has always been aiming for?
Jean Guerrero: Stephen Miller has had a disproportionate amount of power for a very long time. He's been so instrumental in so much of what Trump has done, starting from the first campaign to today. So regardless of the role that Stephen Miller's had, he always somehow turns that role into something more than it has been historically.
While I haven’t been necessarily talking to people in this administration, I suspected that this was coming, and when I heard the news I wasn't at all surprised. I remember thinking that Stephen Miller was going to, if not immediately then at some point, be named chief of staff because of the fact that he has been the most effective sycophant in Trump's orbit, and has been his longest-lasting and most trusted adviser.
Miller’s appointment happened only a few days after a midterm election that some called an “extinction-level” event for Republicans. Why right now?
I think Trump is hoping that Stephen Miller is going to somehow get him out of this mess. In the past, when he has been in trouble, he has turned to Stephen Miller and his expertise on anti-immigrant scapegoating to distract people and rally his base, and it has worked. But I suspect that this time it's not going to work, because the American people are so horrified by where Stephen Miller has already taken this war on immigrants.
I think many people on the right are realizing that the violence we saw in ICE’s conduct—particularly the shooting of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis earlier this year—is actually very unpopular. Do you think this will push Miller to change tack or to double down?
I see it as an impetus for him to double down, absolutely. He's always been driven by a desire to inflame and antagonize and horrify, from the time that he was a teenager to today. If there's any restraint at all, it'll be on the performative nature of the cruelty and maybe shifting towards a more performative nature on the war on the allies of immigrants and trying to characterize anyone who fights for social justice, not just for immigrants, as domestic terrorists. I think that is the war that Stephen Miller has been dying to fight for a very long time.
I think Miller is going to do this in collaboration with surveillance companies and the tech billionaires that he and Trump have decided to align themselves with. They're going to continue to attack the right to privacy and the right to free speech. He's always trying to find the most creative ways to target and terrorize and torture the communities that he despises. And among them are not only immigrants, but the allies, the citizen allies of immigrants and people who are marginalized.
Stephen Miller was very influenced by the book The Camp of the Saints, the white supremacist, dystopian French novel. Reading that book was very illuminating for me, because the heroes are the characters who advocate for wiping out brown immigrants who are approaching by boat, who are cast as a threat to white civilization or Western civilization. In the book, the villains, in addition to the immigrants themselves, are the citizen allies of the immigrants.
You wrote your book during the first Trump administration. Has your understanding of Stephen Miller evolved since then?
My understanding of him has really changed. I used to see him fundamentally as a white nationalist, but now I see him more as a class supremacist and as a case study in oligarchic capture.
I came to this conclusion because when I first saw what the administration was doing on the foreign policy front, I was confused. Why would they be interfering in Venezuela or the elections in Honduras, when we know those are the exact types of actions that cause instability and migration? But when he told Jake Tapper, “You can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else. But we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” I pulled out my book, and I read back through the sections where he's demanding that the custodial staff at his high school pick up his trash.
This is something he did in college too, where he would leave out his trash and protest any requests that he clean up after himself. When he was a teenager, he was really motivated by a desire to keep everybody in what he saw as their place. He didn't mind having immigrants around so long as they stayed “in their place,” where they were quietly serving him and picking up the trash that he was throwing on the floor or leaving on the cafeteria tables.
I realized that before Stephen Miller was a white nationalist, he was a class supremacist.
He hated poor people. He hated people who were less well-off than him, because he thought they were inferior to him.
Has this understanding changed the way you think about Miller’s focus on immigration now?
By focusing all the attention on the war on immigrants, it distracts us from understanding that when you have one sector of the population that is being criminalized and forced to stay in the shadows, then they cannot link arms with other workers to demand to live with dignity. Under this new administration, he has reverted to his most authentic self. Stephen Miller wants a servant class, not a working class.

His start featured a perfectly placed sideline strike between two defenders to a reception-starved Justin Jefferson on third-and-second in the first quarter, and so too a high-level tight-window bullet to Myles Price for a 38-yard touchdown catch-and-run on third-and-23.
It would become Jefferson's best game of the season as he made eight catches from nine targets for 92 yards and two touchdowns, Cousins' reconnecting with one of the stars of the league having seen him suffer for the first half of the season.
Much of the debate and, at times, criticism around Cousins throughout his career has been the shortage of point guard ability as a needle-moving creator. The Patrick Mahomes' and Josh Allens and Joe Burrows and Lamar Jacksons of the world have unfortunately heightened that bar for all quarterbacks across the league. But what has never been in doubt with Cousins is the efficiency at which he feeds his best players, and at which he moves the ball and at which he can accentuate an offense's strengths without being spectacular. Spectacular isn't exactly needed when there is a Brian Flores defense foaming at the mouth in wait of their chance to go hunting on the sideline.
In one game the Vikings looked a more polished, more accomplished operation behind Cousins, and alongside that came another rampant defensive play that saw Minnesota sack Jordan Love eight times.
In the first half alone they produced five sacks, 12 pressures, one interception and one fumble recovery, including sacks on back-to-back plays at the end of the second quarter. Their sixth sack then arrived on the very first play from scrimmage after the break, followed by the third of their four turnovers when Dallas Turner recover a wayward snap.
They were frightening, and the perfect complement once Cousins had helped the Vikings get on top early. The impact was evidenced through the time of possession, Cousins' offense holding the ball for 17.55 minutes in the first half and 35.16 a week on since the Vikings mustered just 17 minutes and 28 seconds of possession against the Bills. What a difference some respite for one of the league's most potent defenses makes.
There was a nice moment in the second half when former New Orleans Saints quarterback Drew Brees paid tribute to Cousins' communication at the line of scrimmage, where he shifted personnel and changed the play like an orchestra conductor. It was long-lost control and assurance under center.
Cousins later executed a trick play that saw him pump fake left and the swivel to pump fake to his right before tossing to Gavin Bartholomew over the middle of the field for a touchdown. For Kevin O'Connell to dial up a play like that just days after Cousins' arrival is testament to the footballing brain now leading Minnesota's offense.
"It was emotional coming to this stadium three years ago, tearing my Achilles here. It's been a tough three years, just grateful for the opportunity to play here, grateful for my teammates and what they did to make this outcome possible.
"It's been a tough three years. There's more of the story to be written," said Cousins post-game, his voice cracking several times."
Cousins won just one playoff game in six seasons during his first stint with the Vikings, before signing a four-year $180m contract with the Atlanta Falcons in 2024, only to be bench for Michael Penix Jr in his first season. He was then released in March earlier this year before landing in Las Vegas as something of a bridge towards their new era under Mendoza.
What looked like a declining career hurtling towards its end is instead flirting with one final twist.
What we learned
Patrick Mahomes' new friends are alright. The Kansas City Chiefs were without their best player this season in Kenneth Walker III on Sunday; it did not matter. The absence of last season's Super Bowl MVP paved the way for an increased role for fifth-round rookie running back Emmett Johnson, who capitalised emphatically with 22 carries for 101 yards and six catches for 70 yards and two scores through the air as Kansas City beat the Atlanta Falcons 35-13 in a five-touchdown day for Patrick Mahomes. Johnson showcased his menu of evasive manoeuvres in the open field with a clinic in tackle-missing jukes and the yards-after-catch threat primed to see him become one of Andy Reid's favourite weapons over the second half of the season.
There was also a debut for wide receiver Josh Downs, who had four catches for 53 yards and a touchdown in his first game since arriving via a trade from the Indianapolis Colts. It's been a long time since Mahomes and the Chiefs posed a consistent vertical threat but Downs could prove an answer to as much. Mahomes completed seven of 12 attempts on passes of 10-plus air yards for 206 yards and three touchdowns, while going three of six on attempts of 20-plus yards for 132 yards and two scores. The Chiefs offense is clicking.
Denzel Ward is playing at an All-Pro level. It is hard to be one of the best players on the league for so long on a team that has been bad for so long; Myles Garrett did it in Cleveland, and Denzel Ward is still doing it. He stepped up when the Browns needed him most on Sunday with a stunning diving pass break-up against Xavier Hutchinson to deny the Houston Texans with 30 seconds left in Cleveland's 27-24 victory. Ward allowed just four receptions for 16 yards from nine targets on Sunday while lining up against Nico Collins in man coverage on 10 of 11 routes, according to Next Gen Stats. Pat Surtain II may still hold the honour of top dog in the eyes of many, but Ward will feel he holds a strong argument as being the best corner in football.
There are encouraging signs for Fernando Mendoza. The Raiders ushered in a new chapter this weekend as No 1 overall Draft pick Mendoza led his side out against the Seattle Seahawks in his first regular season start following Cousins' trade to the Vikings. It started strongly with a touchdown run on his opening possession before Mike Macdonald dialled the pressure up a notch on defense in the second half as the Raiders offense suffered without star weapon Brock Bowers. He went 11 of 13 for 90 yards through the air in the first half, before managing just six of 16 for 53 yards following the interval. Mendoza finished the game 17 of 29 passing for 143 yards, zero touchdowns and zero turnovers while being sacked six times. Facing the league's best defense always beckoned as a baptism of fire, so the shortage of interceptions or apparent ball security issues was a plus point.
Overreaction or reality?
Brock Purdy is a top five quarterback in the NFL. For somebody so often pigeonholed as a 'system quarterback', he sure does do a lot of good outside of the system. Purdy continues to showcase an elite ability to extend plays and create outside of the pocket, perhaps best epitomised by the 74-yard McCaffrey touchdown catch-and-run that saw him side-step a near-certain sack, slide to his left, cut back inside and fire a dart to his open running back. Poise in the face of chaos and a ground threat that makes him dangerous off-script. Purdy finished the game 22 of 28 for 389 yards and three touchdowns with a 154.5 passer rating. He is in the MVP hunt and playing at a level among the premier play-callers in football. By now, though, he knows his true judgement comes around playoff time.
Winners and losers
Winners:
Christian McCaffrey: If you thought injury setbacks had zapped the juice in the 49ers running back, think again. McCaffrey went off for 223 scrimmage yards and three touchdowns to tear apart of hobbling Cowboys defense, which surrendered a franchise-worst 584 yards at home. McCaffrey's 161 receiving yards were the most by a running back in a game since Jamaal Charles' 195 in 2013, while he is the first 49ers player with 200 scrimmage yards and three scores in a regular season game since Jerry Rice in 1995.
Parker Washington: Jacksonville Jaguars head coach Liam Coen called him the best player on the field, and a man possessed. The Tennessee Titans could not live with Parker Washington as the Jags receiver took another major step closer towards a bumper new contract with a career-best seven catches for 152 yards and a touchdown in his side's 40-23 win. One play saw him put Alontae Taylor in a blender with another clinic in route-running, another play saw him levitate to haul in Trevor Lawrence's pass at the sideline, and another saw him race free for a 50-yard catch-and-run. His outstanding season continues.
Losers:
Mike Vrabel: On more than one occasion on Sunday, the camera captured Mike Vrabel closing his eyes in excruciating thought at the sight of another setback for his Patriots, be it an injury or a pre-snap penalty. The game was over before it ever really began for last year's beaten Super Bowl finalists, Drake Maye departing after the opening drive through injury and a sputtering offense later losing AJ Brown in the latest disruption to what is threatening to become a nightmare maiden season in New England. They are 5-5 with the Buffalo Bills, Minnesota Vikings and Kansas City Chiefs coming up over the next month; their season is teetering on the edge.
Aidan Hutchinson: Perhaps it is unfair to kick a man when he is down, but it is hard to overlook a game-ending, potentially season-ending injury caused by a celebration. Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson is feared to have suffered a serious knee injury after landing awkwardly during a post-sack celebration on the opening drive of New England's defeat to the Lions in Munich. It was the same play that saw Maye suffer his own game-halting injury, with neither returning to the field. His absence would leave Detroit without their star edge rusher heading into the second half of their playoff charge
Player of the Weekend - Jahmyr Gibbs, RB, Detroit Lions
Jahmyr Gibbs is a familiar resident in this slot, but he is impossible to ignore as the clear frontrunner for Offensive Player of the Year through 10 weeks. The Lions running back was at his scintillating best in Munich as he put up 252 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns to torch the Patriots defense, his 62 career touchdowns breaking Terrell Davis' record for most by a player through his first four seasons in NFL history. He is not only the perfect cocktail of speed and shiftiness, but one of the smartest crease detectors in football. He runs hard, he runs fast, he runs with high-powered intelligence as the focal point of Drew Petzing's Lions offense. Another clinic, this time on European soil, to extend his lead as the NFL leader in scrimmage yards.
Game of the Weekend
The 49ers and the Cowboys go way back as one of the NFL's most storied rivalries between two of football's most prestigious franchises. They renewed their dislike to the sight of record numbers as they combined for a series-high 86 points, with San Francisco beating Dallas 46-40 to improve to 8-1 on the season. While the 49ers flexed their offensive power, in doing so there were more glaring concerns over the Cowboys and a defense ranked third worst in yards allowed. Dak Prescott threw five touchdown passes, three to George Pickens, as the Cowboys put up 439 yards of offense, only to come out second best. Purdy produced two scoring strikes to McCaffrey and one to Deebo Samuel.
"The second half was unacceptable; tackling was atrocious, you can't give up three explosive plays of over 65 yards for touchdowns and expect to win. Totally unacceptable defense in the second half," said Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer.

Depression over Bay of Bengal likely to intensify into severe cyclonic storm by Nov 17, move towards Andhra Pradesh coast: IMD
The weather system is likely to become a Severe Cyclonic Storm over the westcentral Bay of Bengal by the evening of November 17, the IMD said.
A depression over the Bay of Bengal is likely to strengthen into a cyclonic storm by the evening of November 16 and further intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by November 17, before moving towards the Andhra Pradesh coast over the following two days, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Sunday.
The weather system is expected to move north-northwestwards as it gains strength over the central parts of the south and adjoining west central Bay of Bengal. It is likely to become a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by the evening of November 17, the IMD said.
"The Depression over Southeast & adjoining Southwest Bay of Bengal moved north-northwestwards with the speed of 07 kmph during past06 hours and lay centered at 1730 hours IST of today, the 15thNovember, 2026 over the same region, near Latitude 10.2°N and Longitude 86.8°E,about 630 km east-northeast of Trincomalee (Sri Lanka), 670km west-southwest of Sri Vijaya Puram (Andaman & Nicobar Islands), 780 km east-southeast of Chennai(Tamil Nadu), 920 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and 1030km south-southeast of Gopalpur (Odisha)," the IMD said.
"It is very likely to move north-northwestwards, intensify further into a Cyclonic Storm over the central parts of south & adjoining west central Bay of Bengal on evening of 16th November and into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over west central Bay of Bengal on evening of 17th November, 2026. Thereafter, it is likely to intensify further and move northwestwards towards Andhra Pradesh coast during subsequent2 days," the IMD further added.
Naidu seeks financial assistance
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Sunday sought urgent financial assistance from the Centre for relief and rehabilitation work after Cyclone Murasu caused estimated damage of ₹2,484.43 crore in the state, news agency PTI reported.
A seven-member Central team, led by Chittaranjan Das, Joint Secretary in the Union Home Ministry, held a virtual meeting with the Chief Minister after inspecting nearly 60 locations across Bapatla, Palnadu, Eluru and East Godavari districts.
The Central team inspected damaged agricultural fields, canals, roads and houses. It also interacted with farmers at Surappagudem and visited paddy fields at Ravulapalem, the Kommu canal, irrigation works at Kunakalamarri and fishing boats at Chirala.
The team assessed damage to houses, horticultural crops, farms and duck-rearing units at Boppudi. It also inspected roads crossing the Jaladi stream between Yedlapadu and Turlapadu.
Naidu said El Nino conditions and two cyclones hitting the state within a short period had contributed to the widespread damage.
He said the state government had taken precautionary measures in advance and started restoration work immediately after the cyclone.
Road connectivity, electricity supply and mobile networks were restored within 24 hours, the Chief Minister said. He added that the government was also arranging crop insurance assistance and additional ration supplies for families affected by the cyclone.

India’s tuberculosis (TB) burden remains substantial despite progress. The country has the largest TB burden in the world, accounting for approximately one-quarter of all TB cases globally. The number of new cases fell 21% between 2015 and 2024, while treatment coverage rose to 92%, according to World Health Organization data cited by the government. The Central government recently started the JOSH campaign -- launched in 11 States and 55 districts to promote screening, early diagnosis and treatment adherence. JOSH stands for Joint Squad for Health. It is a youth-led community mobilisation initiative to strengthen India’s campaign to eliminate TB.
Dhun Davar, deputy CEO & chief of programmes, Asian Venture Philanthropy Network (AVPN) spoke to The Hindu about the challenges in the TB elimination programme. AVPN is a pan-Asian network of social investors, philanthropists, foundations, corporations and other organisations that work to direct funding and expertise towards social and environmental challenges. Its work includes health equity, gender equality, climate action and economic inclusion.
