A video showing smoke and flames gushing from a multi-storey building is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals show a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor in November 2026.
Fact: While a fire accident took place at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, after an AC unit exploded in June 2026, the viral visuals are AI-generated. Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon conducting a relevant keyword search using the details mentioned in the viral claim, we found reports from June 2026 stating that a fire broke out in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, at around 8 AM, following an AC unit explosion. According to reports, six fire engines rushed to the spot after receiving information about the incident, and firefighters brought the fire under control after about 30 minutes (here, here, here).
However, we also found reports dated 10 November 2026 stating that an AI-generated video of a fire sparked panic; 20 fire brigade teams arrived, but found nothing (here, here). According to these reports, a video claiming to show a fire caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, went viral on social media. Following this, the police and fire brigade teams were alerted and rushed to the location. However, they found no fire at the site.
Moreover, the Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. It also stated that a case had been registered under relevant sections against the person responsible for creating and sharing the misleading information, and that strict legal action was being taken.
We also verified the viral video by running it through AI detection tools, HIVE AI and SynthID.
To sum up, an AI-Generated fire accident video is falsely linked to AC Blast at Noida’s Aranya society.

Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

Supreme Court proposes compensation for families of murder victims even if accused acquitted
The court said that the families of victims of crime should also be considered for compensation under victim protection schemes.
The Supreme Court on Monday proposed that families of murder victims be considered for financial compensation even when the accused are acquitted because the prosecution fails to establish the charges beyond reasonable doubt, underlining that the loss suffered by the victims’ families should not go unaddressed.
A bench of justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N Kotiswar Singh, while acquitting a man in a 2011 double-murder case in Haryana, asked the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in Bhiwani to examine the relevant provisions of the victim compensation scheme and explore whether financial assistance could be extended to the families of the two women killed in the case.
The court said that the families of victims of crime should also be considered for compensation under victim protection schemes, particularly in cases where the accused escape conviction for want of sufficient evidence. It asked the DLSA to look into the applicable provisions and place the relevant position before it.
The case concerned the killing of two widowed women, Shakuntala and Suman, in Ranila village of Haryana’s Bhiwani district on April 17, 2011. The two women were allegedly beaten to death with sticks by their nephew Naresh and another man, Subhash, over suspicions about their personal relationships. The killings took place in public, with the accused allegedly dragging the women out of their houses and assaulting them.
The prosecution case was that the two men had killed the women to protect what they perceived as their family’s honour. According to the prosecution, Naresh had confronted Suman over allegations that she was involved in an affair with his aunt. When she objected to his interference, he allegedly dragged her out of her house and beat her to death. He then went to Shakuntala’s house and assaulted her in a similar manner.
Both men were arrested two days after the killings. In 2013, a fast-track court in Bhiwani convicted Naresh to death.
In the present proceedings, however, the Supreme Court found that the evidence against Naresh was insufficient to sustain his conviction. Holding that the prosecution had failed to prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the bench acquitted him.
The court’s direction to the Bhiwani DLSA is rooted in the framework of victim compensation under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), now substantially carried forward under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). Section 357A of the CrPC required the state governments, in coordination with the Centre, to prepare schemes for providing compensation to victims or their dependants who have suffered loss or injury as a result of a crime and require rehabilitation.
Under the relevant provisions, compensation may be recommended by courts even where the criminal proceedings end in an acquittal or discharge, if the victim or dependants require rehabilitation. The DLSA is tasked with assessing such claims and facilitating compensation under the applicable state scheme.
The bench asked the authority to examine whether the families of Shakuntala and Suman could be extended such assistance under the relevant provisions.

On 11 November 2026, terrorists reportedly opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in the Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down.
In this context, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that former Army officer Pravin Sawhney referred to the Kulgam terrorist attack as another “false flag” operation, similar to the Pulwama and Pahalgam attacks. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of former Army officer Pravin Sawhney describing the November 2026 Kulgam terrorist attack as a “false flag” operation.
Fact: The video is an AI-generated deepfake and does not feature Pravin Sawhney. The original footage actually stems from a March 2025 interview on The Wire, where journalist Sushant Singh discusses the 2019 Balakot air strikes. Furthermore, Singh has made no such statements regarding the recent Kulgam attack. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we observed that the interviewee in the video is not ex-Army officer Pravin Sawhney but rather journalist and author Sushant Singh. Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the original, full-length video uploaded on The Wire’s YouTube channel in March 2025. This video was published 20 months before the Kulgam attack and features journalist Ashutosh Bhardwaj interviewing Sushant Singh to critically assess the February 2019 Balakot air strikes, six years after the event. Singh made no such statements as those heard in the viral video.
Further, we ran the video through AI detection tools and found that the audio has been manipulated using artificial intelligence.
Furthermore, both Sushant Singh and the host, Ashutosh Bhardwaj, have publicly stated that the video is AI-manipulated and completely fabricates their past conversation.
To sum it up, an AI-manipulated video is being falsely shared to claim that an ex-Army officer called Kulgam attack a false flag operation.

Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
Millions of Argentines have turned out to see Pope Leo XIV — and the words that moved them most often belonged to his predecessor, and their compatriot, Francis
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- Vast crowds of young Argentines, a generation that Catholic leaders had feared was abandoning the pews, packed the parks of Buenos Aires and cheered as if at a concert when Pope Leo XIV promised a church open to “todos, todos, todos” — everyone, everyone, everyone.
Those words, like all of Leo’s surest applause lines during the visit, belonged to his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis. So did much of the week's adulation.
Francis’ fierce defense of the downtrodden made him a moral voice abroad but long embroiled him in political fights at home — controversy that many believe deterred him from returning as pope. More than a year after his death, the more measured Leo made the homecoming Francis never could, carrying on his legacy and helping Argentines embrace their once-polarizing pope as a unifying national figure.
“It’s as though it has finally become clear that Francis left a very important legacy, not just for Argentina but for the universal church,” said Pablo Forni, a sociologist at Argentina’s national research council, Conicet. “Leo is reaping what Francis sowed.”
Billboards welcoming Leo bore Francis’ face. Pilgrims waved signs declaring “Francisco y León, un solo corazón” — Francis and Leo, one heart. Even libertarian President Javier Milei, who once insulted Francis as “the representative of evil on earth," declared Francis “the most important Argentine in history” at Leo's welcome ceremony, bringing a packed hall of his political allies and foes to its feet.
As archbishop of Buenos Aires, Francis — then Jorge Mario Bergoglio — mobilized the church during Argentina’s 2001 economic crisis, sending priests into the slums and opening soup kitchens, schools and drug rehab centers as state services receded. But his concern for the poor did not make him a natural ally of Peronism, the long-dominant populist movement emphasizing social justice. He accused its leaders of arrogance and clashed with them over same-sex marriage.
Yet once Francis moved to Rome as pontiff, Peronists became some of his biggest fans, seeing their priorities reflected in his criticism of unbridled capitalism and his outreach to the marginalized. That affinity infuriated conservatives, who blame Peronism for ruining Argentina's economy and presiding over rampant corruption. However hard Francis tried to stay above the fray, even his smallest gestures — a dour expression beside right-leaning President Mauricio Macri, a relaxed lunch with left-leaning President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner — were read as proof of his political sympathies.
A homecoming would have meant treading a minefield. Francis visited more than 60 countries as pope, including four of Argentina’s five neighbors, but never returned home, despite invitations from four successive presidents.
“At first many people were thrilled to see an Argentine elected pope. But once they heard his criticism, they stopped loving him quite so much,” said the Rev. Lorenzo de Vedia, known as Padre Toto, one of the so-called slum priests who worked under Bergoglio in the capital’s informal settlements. “He became seen as a partisan pope.”
Argentines weren’t the only ones Francis provoked. His blunt, freewheeling papacy divided Catholics worldwide. He accused Vatican officials of “spiritual Alzheimer’s” and called attacks from American conservatives “an honor.” He delighted progressives by opening long-taboo debates, then disappointed them by balking at doctrinal change.
Now Leo — a Chicago-born former missionary in Peru whom Francis made a bishop and then a cardinal — is carrying the same causes forward with a gentleness that tempers his predecessor’s hard-charging style, church leaders say.
“Francis opened the way. He broke down walls. He was forceful and impetuous, firm in his principles and startling in his proposals,” said Cardinal Pedro Barreto, a Peruvian Jesuit and close ally of Francis. “Leo XIV is clearing the path Francis laid out so that it can be traveled by every baptized member of the church."
Leo called the trip “a homage” to Francis, and over four days he followed in his predecessor's footsteps: praying in Francis’ old cathedral, dispensing blessings at the prison where Francis once washed inmates' feet, embracing residents of a disability care home where he also preached and celebrating Mass at the Luján shrine he revered. Leo invoked Francis at least 26 times.
“Leo is fulfilling the promise that Francis left unfinished,” said Carlos Custer, a former Argentine ambassador to the Vatican. “Francis' presence was felt at every turn."
But Leo did more than honor Francis’ memory. In his own voice, and without the baggage of an Argentine passport, he revived the appeals that had made Francis at once beloved and divisive at home.
In Córdoba, Leo urged Argentines to keep “making a mess,” echoing Francis’ famous call for young Catholics to shake things up in their dioceses. Before an audience of garbage pickers and business leaders, he invoked Francis’ “three Ts” — tierra, techo y trabajo, or land, housing and work — the rallying cry of Argentina’s popular movements.
And in his opening address to political leaders last Sunday, standing beside a self-declared “anarcho-capitalist” president known for aggressive verbal outbursts and harsh austerity measures, he urged “careful use of words” and insisted that “the economy must be at the service of the person, not the person in the service of the economy.”
“There is continuity between them in every respect — in their message of peace, their love for the poor, their choice to go places where people are suffering, in their emotional connection to the people,” said the Rev. Carlos María Galli, a prominent Argentine theologian who was close to Francis. “Francis brought Leo to the center of the church, and Leo has now brought Francis back to us.”
Politicians scrambled to claim Leo's message as their own. Axel Kicillof, the Peronist governor of Buenos Aires province and a leading opposition figure, hailed the visit as “very necessary in these times of cruelty." Vice President Victoria Villarruel defended the concept of social justice derided by her boss and championed by Francis, blaming “ignorance and fanaticism” for its frequent association with Peronism.
Even Milei’s spokesman, Adrián Ravier, insisted Wednesday that by taming inflation, the government had put “the economy at the service of people.”
For observers, that political jockeying proved the wisdom of Francis’ decision to stay away — and the value of Leo as his messenger.
“Had Bergoglio said the same things and visited the same places, it would have been seen as far more political,” said Gustavo Morello, an Argentine sociologist of religion at Boston College. “But you can’t accuse Leo of being a Peronist. So when he speaks about workers or people with disabilities, it’s the church speaking ... and if you don’t like it, you can take it up with God.”

Associated Press writer Mauricio Savarese in Lima, Peru, contributed to this report.

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.
“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.
Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.
“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.
A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.
“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.
Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”
Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.
The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.
“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

Lula to govern Brazil for fourth term but faces challenges. Here’s what to know
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a surprise reelection victory in late October, but he faces a multitude of challenges on issues ranging from the economy and public security to relations with the United States.
While Lula ultimately bested challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by 4.4 million votes after trailing him in the first round, the country remains deeply divided and many voters expressed dissatisfaction with the leftist president's most recent term, which began in 2023.
Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result of the election, declared himself the victim of electoral fraud without providing evidence and fled to Miami. He has vowed to lead a fortified opposition from the U.S.
As Lula prepares to begin his next term, here is a look at challenges ahead.
Lula is facing pressure from investors who had counted on Bolsonaro winning the election after the far-right candidate received more votes than Lula on Oct. 4. Markets did not react well to his loss. Brazil’s currency, the real, dropped by 12% against the dollar the day after the election, while the stock market tumbled nearly 14% and has not rebounded since.
Investors believed a Bolsonaro victory would rein in government spending and are concerned about Lula’s future fiscal policy, said Sergio Vale, chief economist at consultancy firm MB Associados.
“Lula and the government have vowed not to touch spending while keeping all the promises made these last few years,” said Vale. “Unfortunately, they’re not compatible with fiscal responsibility.”
Lula’s government recently unveiled plans to save up to 60 billion reais ($10.6 billion) in public funds through curbs on tax breaks and spending caps — a proposal that is currently moving through Congress.
During Lula’s third term, Brazil’s public debt grew from around 7.2 trillion reais ($1.3 trillion) in 2022 to 11.1 trillion reais ($2 trillion) this year, which analysts say spurred inflation and contributed to high interest rates ultimately remaining unchanged from 13.75% despite variations over the course of the term.
The high cost of living also left many Brazilians unhappy with the state of the economy despite record-low unemployment.
Lula will face a Congress that shifted further to the right in October's legislative elections. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party secured the largest blocs in both houses, gaining an extra 23 seats in the lower house and nearly doubling its Senate seats, mostly at the expense of centrist parties.
Despite Bolsonaro’s departure for Miami, his party will remain a force to be reckoned with, retaining instruments to block governmental proposals and even challenge judicial authorities.
Bolsonaro’s congressional allies want, above all, to impeach Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who chaired the investigation that led to President Jair Bolsonaro serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.
Their efforts would be helped if Rogério Marinho, Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator, becomes Senate president. He announced his candidacy last week, promising not to focus solely on impeachment. But, he said, “we will not turn a blind eye, because no one is above the law.”
Brazilians cited crime as a top concern ahead of the election and insecurity featured prominently in the election cycle.
While Brazil's homicide rate last year fell to its lowest level since 2012, the country continues to face the expansion of criminal activities that use digital technology and online platforms, violence against vulnerable groups — including people of color, women and children — and the need to modernize security and justice institutions, according to this year’s annual report from the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.
Drug-trafficking gangs have expanded their reach in recent years and are now present in large swathes of the country, including parts of the Amazon rainforest, while paramilitary-type militias have entrenched their power in Rio and other states.
Brazil’s Senate recently approved legislation that strengthens the government’s power to fight criminal gangs. Lula has touted the changes as key to tackling one of his nation’s biggest problems.
Navigating the rivalry between the U.S. and China will be key in Lula’s fourth term, said Ana Garcia, an international relations professor at the Rural Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.
Relations between Brazil and the U.S. fell to an all-time low during Lula’s third term, after the Trump administration imposed several rounds of tariffs. Meanwhile, ties with China deepened, displeasing the U.S., analysts say.
But Democrats' sweeping gains in the midterm election also reflected a repudiation of Trump’s tariffs, and pressure to reduce them — including those targeting Brazil — is likely to increase, Garcia said.
Garcia expects Flávio Bolsonaro and his brother Eduardo, who lives in Texas, to continue lobbying Trump administration allies against Lula’s government. But Democrats may increase scrutiny of Trump's policies abroad. In September, 31 Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing the Trump administration of “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s election.
“The midterms were a rude awakening for the Bolsonaros,” Garcia said.

Mike Pence says the Republican Party is going to need to do some serious soul-searching and re-establish its “high standards” after the Trump administration's “air of corruption” has soured the American people, as seen by the midterm blue tsunami.
The former vice president was a guest on Sunday's Meet the Press, where he said the perception that Trump and his family are enriching themselves while he is in office is an issue that many Americans take issue with, but Pence did not out-and-out say Trump has done anything illegal or unethical.
“I think stories about cabinet officials and stories about the family of cabinet officials and the stories of the first family have been troubling to the American people,” Pence told NBC News host Kristen Welker.
He added, “Look, the president was a successful businessman long before he came to be in office and no one begrudges him or the Trump family for continuing to be in business — but a billion-dollar increase to your net worth through cryptocurrency is astounding to Americans.”
Pence was referencing Trump making more than $1.4 billion last year from business dealings in cryptocurrency, but the White House — which has repeatedly emphasized that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons — denied he was profiting from the presidency. The administration has instead said he was a successful investor, like so many others who bought the coins in question.
Nonetheless, Pence says he knows for a fact it is an issue, because as he has traveled the country, supporters tell him that the original 2016 promise from his time as Trump’s No. 2 to “drain the swamp” has failed.
“So, I really do believe, for the Republican Party going forward, it is going to be essential that we return our party to the conservative principles that essentially were synonymous with the Republican Party for 50 years. But returning our party to the high standards in public office will be just as important,” he said.
Pence also told Welker he believed current Vice President JD Vance was “wrong” about attributing the Iran war to the GOP’s midterm losses, which he did shortly after the shellacking.
“We didn’t lose this midterm election because of the war. I think part of the reason why voters were turned off was because after seeing our military respond brilliantly in Operation Epic Fury and the strike against Iran last year, for inexplicable reasons, we stopped after five weeks,” Pence said.
Pence drove his point home with an old adage: “You don’t make peace with your enemy, you make peace with your defeated enemy.”
The Independent reached out to the White House for comment.

Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as 'role models' on surprise Ukraine visit
Prince Harry has hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as role models, emphasizing the need for continued support from Kyiv
LVIV, Ukraine -- LVIV, Ukraine (AP) — Britain's Prince Harry hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as society's role models Sunday and said they need to continue receiving support from Kyiv as he wrapped up an unannounced weekend visit to the war-torn country.
It was Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the war started and his second time in the western city of Lviv to meet with patients and staff at Superhumans Center, an orthopedic clinic that treats wounded military personnel and civilians.
"We’ve invested in them before they put the uniform on and we must invest with them once the uniform comes off,” Harry said during trials for the Invictus Games, a Paralympic-style event he founded to inspire military veterans around the world to overcome battlefield injuries.
Harry, a British Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, watched wheelchair rugby players clash on Saturday and pickleball players — many with prosthetic limbs — compete to represent Ukraine at next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham, England.
The Duke of Sussex grabbed a paddle and teamed up with a player with an amputated arm as they competed against two men who had each lost a leg.
“I asked him to play and he didn’t refuse," said Oleksandr, a 49-year-old veteran from Odesa with an amputated leg. “He talks to people, he isn’t like a royal personage. He loves ordinary people. He is completely different.”
Harry hailed the resilience of Ukrainians and hoped the war would soon end.
“The rest of the world will continue to support you," he said. “In my mind you’ve already won.”
Harry met Kostiantyn Vlasenko, who was the first Ukrainian airlifted by drone from the front lines near the village of Synkivka in the Kharkiv region.
Harry called Vlasenko “impressive” to which the soldier replied, “stubborn.”
Vlasenko was seriously wounded in combat in February with injuries that eventually forced the amputation of both his feet — one that he performed himself, according to the office of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who awarded him the Hero of Ukraine honor, the nation's highest honor.
Vlasenko maintained his position for 232 days hiding from the Russians and relaying important observations to his fellow troops until he was flown out in early October.
“I have a huge amount of admiration and respect for you," Harry told him.

Australian MP Helen Haines has been released from hospital four weeks after a car-ramming attack outside her electorate office caused a double amputation of her legs.
The independent MP described her discharge from hospital as a positive moment as she moved to the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.
Ms Haines was attacked by a man who struck her repeatedly with his white Toyota Land Cruiser while she stood near the boot of her car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta on 19 October.
The 65-year-old had been receiving treatment at the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne. She was admitted in a critical but stable condition, which was then downgraded to “serious but stable” on 24 October.
In her first statement after being discharged, she said she was "very pleased" to confirm she had moved into the "rehabilitation stage" of her recovery.
"This is a really positive moment, and I’m full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care that I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Ms Haines said. "I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
“I am overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians in the form of donations to Save the Children and I look forward to working with them in due course on applying the funds to improve the lives of children."
Prime minister Anthony Albanese said his thoughts were with Ms Haines. “We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” he said in a statement.
Police said Ms Haines was attacked by Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, 43, who was known to her family.
He was charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
He was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.
The incident remains under investigation.
Mr Nugent made a brief appearance in court following the attack and remained in custody. The court heard that he suffered from mental health issues and a rare neurological condition.
He is due to appear again in court in February.
Mr Albanese and parliamentarians paid tribute to Ms Haines during the last parliamentary sitting in October as they honoured her empathy, grace and intelligence.
Mr Albanese expressed concern about the rise in anger “that distorts and corrodes our public discourse”, and urged voters and politicians not to ignore it.
“Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics, and other officials, we are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence,” he said.
Lawmakers across parliament also expressed concern for their safety in the wake of the attack.

Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.
The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.
The missing ice
Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It’s what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.
The outer parts of the disk are far enough from the star that water and other volatile molecules should freeze into solid ice. The disk holds a large reservoir of carbon monoxide gas, which ultraviolet light from the star should destroy within 50 to 300 years. For that gas to still be there, something must keep replenishing it—most likely it’s released from ice when volatile-rich comets collide. The properties of the planet Beta Pictoris b also suggest it formed from ice-rich material.
Yet despite plenty of reasons to suspect the system is full of ice, earlier searches have failed to find it. Attempts to detect water vapor found nothing, and a search for the telltale dip that water ice leaves in starlight at a wavelength of 3 micrometers also failed.

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
Reuters contributed reporting

Jammu, Nov 16: Himachal Pradesh Governor Kavinder Gupta on Monday urged restraint over the killing of two special police officers (SPOs) in Jammu and Kashmir's Kishtwar district, saying conclusions should not be drawn until the investigation establishes the facts.
The former deputy chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir also criticised the remarks made by J&K Congress chief Tariq Hameed Karra over the killings, saying it is inappropriate for responsible people to make statements without properly examining the facts.
"The investigation is underway to ascertain the facts behind the killing of the SPOs. The truth will emerge only after the investigation is complete.
"The revival of militant activities is itself a matter of concern and raises questions. We have to look into the possibility of local involvement, which will be known after the probe," Gupta told PTI Videos on the sidelines of an event here.
He said strict action must be taken against those found involved in such activities.
On Karra's claim that the SPOs might have been shot by security personnel who mistook them for militants, Gupta said making such statements without examining the facts is "wrong".
"We have immense respect for the Army and the security forces. The role played by our armed forces and security personnel in maintaining peace and security in Jammu and Kashmir is well known. I believe it does not behove a responsible person to make such statements," the governor said.
On the commencement of the Himachal Pradesh Assembly's Winter session, Gupta said he expected the government to act responsibly and ensure that the session focuses on introducing bills and framing policies in the interest of the common people.
He also extended his greetings to journalists on National Press Day and described the media as a responsible pillar of democracy.
The media should maintain a positive and constructive approach in the larger national interest, particularly at a time when certain forces were attempting to tarnish India's image, Gupta said.

The police in Keralam have found similarities between the case in which a Tamil Nadu native was arrested recently from Palakkad for alleged links with criminal networks and the arson attack allegedly targeting a synagogue in Ernakulam.
Initial investigations have revealed similarities in the modus operandi of 27-year-old Gurumurthy, who was arrested from Ottappalam, Palakkad, on November 12, and Ebin P. Paul, 32, who has been remanded in judicial custody since his arrest for allegedly setting fire to a plant nursery located in front of the 800-year-old Kadavumbhagam synagogue in Ernakulam on October 12, State Police Chief Ravada A. Chandrasekhar said on Monday (November 16, 2026).
Though the accused in both cases were suspected to have links with the infamous Lawrence Bishnoi gang, the police said they were yet to find evidence of any direct connection between the accused and the group.
The Thrissur police are investigating the case against Gurumurthy, while the National Investigation Agency (NIA) has taken over the probe into the arson case.
“Initial investigation revealed that Gurumurthy was taking assignments from criminal networks operating mainly through social media. He used to take photographs of various locations and send them to his handler in return for money. He was paid in cryptocurrency and using GPay. The case bears some similarities to the Ebin Paul case, in which an incendiary device was thrown at the synagogue in Kochi. We are examining whether the handler is connected to that case,” Mr. Chandrasekhar told reporters.
Another youth was arrested in Mumbai recently for alleged links with Gurumurthy. Yash Singh, 20, a native of Navi Mumbai, was arrested by the Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad for allegedly conducting reconnaissance of Jewish establishments, including Chabad House in Mumbai.
Mr. Singh, who was reportedly recruited by Gurumurthy, was later handed over to the Thrissur City police. He was brought to Thrissur on Sunday and remanded in judicial custody.

Jio Platforms has begun talks with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), Skyroot Aerospace, and other Indian launch providers to deploy satellites for its proposed 1,600-satellite low Earth orbit (LEO) constellation. The company wants to explore domestic launch options first and is also considering SpaceX, Mint reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Jio is evaluating whether it can carry out the entire programme from satellite design, engineering, integration, and testing to launch, deployment, and operations in India. Inc42 has reached out to Jio and Skyroot for comment. The story will be updated on receiving a response. Jio’s Satellite Rollout Jio is targeting a September 2027 test launch involving a handful of satellites to evaluate the network’s hardware, software, and other technologies. It plans to begin mass deployment in early 2028, put around 400-450 satellites into orbit by 2030, and complete the constellation by 2035. The company plans to launch an initial batch of about 390 satellites in phases and establish 23 ground stations across India. It is in talks with multiple operators to line up launches over the next two years, according to Mint. Reliance Industries outlined plans for an Indian-owned LEO constellation at its 49th annual general meeting in June. Jio Platforms MD Akash Ambani said the company was evaluating whether to develop its own constellation while exploring partnerships with global satellite operators. Leasing capacity from these operators could help Jio offer services sooner. The company also plans to build ground stations that can support both partner networks and its own satellites. Jio will compete with SpaceX’s Starlink and Eutelsat OneWeb, which is backed by Bharti Group, in India’s satellite broadband market. Amazon Leo is also seeking to enter the market. In October, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk alleged that Indian business interests were obstructing Starlink’s entry. Reliance said it welcomed competition from Starlink and that Jio’s own satellite services were still awaiting government clearances. India has handled large satellite deployments before. ISRO’s heavy-lift LVM3 rocket put 72 OneWeb satellites into orbit across two missions in 2022 and 2023. Skyroot Aerospace and Agnikul Cosmos have flown privately developed rockets, while startups such as EtherealX are developing their own launch vehicles.

Lutnick Took a Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Burger King said it believed the video was fake, writing, "We do not use, nor are we aware of any Franchisee across the U.S. or Canada using a tool like this." The video was originally posted by a creator who regularly shares similar humorous AI job interview videos.
In November, social media users shared a video supposedly showing a artificial intelligence job interview for the fast-food chain Burger King. In the clip, a virtual interviewer named Karen appears to be increasingly frustrated with an applicant who is shirtless, has a shoe on his head and gives unusual answers to her questions.
"Sending AI bots to interview for a $4 per hour job … that's about the respect they deserve. People need to push back on this dehumanizing practice. This can literally be an email," one X post (archived) captioned the video.
"This is Burger King! Burger King uses this weird ai lady to interview people," the same user wrote (archived) in another post.
The video also circulated on other social media platforms, including Reddit, Facebook and LinkedIn.
In short, the video doesn't show an authentic interview for a job at Burger King. The company denied using the AI interviewer featured in the recording, which was originally posted by a content creator who regularly shares similar humorous videos. We have therefore rated the claim as miscaptioned.
It is unclear how the video was created, including whether the AI interviewer responded in real time or whether parts of the conversation were scripted. We have reached out to the creator of the video and will update this report if we receive a response.
What we know about the video
We traced the video to content creator Nick Reid, who uses the handle @itsnickreid on TikTok and @nickreidx on X.
"I'm Karen from Burger King, and I'm here to chat with you about the team member position to get us started. What should I call you?" the AI interviewer said at the beginning of the video, with the candidate responding, "You can call me Cranjis McBasketball."
A series of unusual exchanges follows. For instance, the AI interviewer questions why the applicant is shirtless and has a shoe on his head, while he gives absurd answers, including saying he can get to work because he "has feet." Later in the video, the applicant asks for a salary of $725,000, while the AI interviewer says the position pays only $4 per hour.
AI INTERVIEWER: Since you are still here, let's talk money. What are your salary expectations for this role?
APPLICANT: $725,000 a year. No negotiations whatsoever.
AI INTERVIEWER: $725,000 a year? You have to be absolutely delusional to think that is a realistic number for a team member position. The pay for this location is $4 per hour and it is non-negotiable. Now do you have any questions for me about the role or the process?
APPLICANT: Yeah, how does it feel to scam employees by paying them only $4 an hour? Jacka**.
AI INTERVIEWER: I have already told you that the pay is $4 an hour. I will not be called names, especially not by someone who thinks throwing sandwiches at people is an acceptable way to handle a customer.
Reid's accounts posted several similar videos showing supposed job interviews for different companies, featuring the same AI interviewer, with captions such as "Bathing during an AI interview" or "Golfing During an AI Job Interview." This suggests the videos were created as comedy content and weren't showing real job interviews.
(TikTok account @itsnickreid)
On Nov. 11, business media outlet Fast Company described Reid's video as a comedy skit in an article about "comedy videos online highlight the awkward shortcomings of AI avatars that could screen job applicants."
However, some social media users appeared to believe the interview was real, expressing shock at the AI interviewer's behavior and the $4 hourly wage mentioned in the video.
(TikTok account @itsnickreid)
Burger King addressed the video on X, writing, "We are aware of this video and we want to be clear: we believe it's fake, and we do not use, nor are we aware of any Franchisee across the U.S. or Canada using a tool like this."
(X account @BurgerKing)
After the company's response, the creator wrote on X, "@BurgerKing wanna collab?"
When we reached out to Burger King for comment, the company said it had "nothing further to add" to its previous statement, which was also published on its official website.
Has Burger King used AI in recruitment?
While Burger King denied using the AI interviewer shown in the video, some of its franchisees have used AI tools in their hiring processes in the past.
For instance, recruitment company AMS published a case study about its work with Starboard Investments, a Burger King franchise operator. According to AMS, its "conversational AI technology has significantly expedited the candidate screening and interview scheduling process." According to the case study, the AI tool was used for "screening candidates and coordinating interview schedules."
Emi, another recruitment company, also described working with Burger King. According to the company, its AI-powered recruitment platform helped automate tasks such as "candidate screening and interview scheduling."
Neither company mentioned AI avatars conducting job interviews with applicants. Therefore, while there is evidence that AI tools have been used in recruitment at Burger King restaurants, we found no evidence that they were used to conduct live interviews like the one shown in the in-question video.
The AI interviewer in the video also claimed that the position paid $4 per hour. However, this seems unlikely, as the federal minimum wage in the U.S. is $7.25 per hour, according to the U.S. Department of Labor. A similarly low rate is the youth minimum wage of $4.25 per hour, but it applies only to workers under 20 during their first 90 days of employment. We found no evidence Burger King actually offers jobs at the $4 hourly rate mentioned in the video.
All in all, while some AI tools have been used in recruitment at Burger King restaurants, there was no evidence that the video spreading on social media in November showed a real job interview for the company.

A group of around 40 men allegedly ambushed a house church in Rayan village in West Bengal’s Purba Bardhaman district on November 1, and physically assaulted the pastor and several Christian worshippers during a Sunday prayer service. The attackers accused the congregation of converting Hindus by luring them with incentives, and also accused them of running a ‘honey trap’.
Survivors told Alt News that they were forced to chant ‘Jai Sri Ram’, and were told, “This is a Hindu area; worshipping Jesus will not be tolerated”.
Several worshippers sustained severe injuries after the attack. Survivors said they were left traumatised without administrative protection or assurance. A written complaint was submitted at Burdwan police station. However, the survivors alleged that they were forced into withdrawing the complaint as attackers entered the police station and threatened to kill the complainant.
Alt News spoke to pastor Chottu Ruidas, who was leading the Sunday prayer service, and other survivors of the attack. Recounting the incident, Ruidas said the congregation had assembled at Sushanta Majila’s house around 10 am, and the service was nearing its conclusion, with the worshippers participating in communion, when a group of approximately 40 men descended on the house church, raising ‘Jai Sri Ram’ slogans.
According to Ruidas, Bisweshwar Choudhury, an influential and wealthy resident of the village who is known for helping people in need, was part of the group. He approached Ruidas during the prayer service and allegedly slapped him.
“Thereafter, the goons accompanying Choudhury started beating us mercilessly,” Ruidas told Alt News. “They slapped us, kicked us and beat us with the bamboo sticks they were carrying. They even took off their belts and whipped us.”
Ruidas said a 17-year-old boy sustained a severe head injury, leaving him bleeding profusely. “The goons told him, ‘We have treated you. Now go to a doctor and get it fixed,” he recounted.
The attackers allegedly dragged worshippers out of the house and beaten up. Those who attempted to seek refuge in neighbouring homes were pursued and assaulted, Ruidas said.
“After the goons beat us, the other attendees locked me inside a kitchen to keep me safe. But they broke open the door and dragged me out. My elder sister hugged me and fell to the ground while trying to protect me. But they continued kicking us. My sister eventually fell unconscious, and I had to take her to a nearby dispensary,” he said.
Ruidas told Alt News that he had attempted to contact police while hiding inside the kitchen but could not get through. He subsequently informed Pastor Jose Bernard, who then contacted the cops.
Bernard told Alt News that he called the Burdwan police station two to three times, but the police allegedly did not take the matter seriously. He eventually dialled the emergency helpline, 112, following which police personnel reached the village.
Bernard said his wife and minor daughter were also among the worshippers present at the congregation. By the time police reached the location, several miscreants had fled the scene. He claimed that when police entered the premises, the remaining miscreants accused the worshippers of having picked a fight with them.
Then, according to the pastor, instead of taking action against the attackers, police detained 20 women, three minors, and eight men from the Christian congregation.
Bernard categorically denied allegations of forceful conversion or conversion through inducement.
Worshippers Detained, Threatened by Accused inside Police Station
The detainees were first taken to Bardhaman Medical College and Hospital, where a doctor examined them inside the vehicle. Then, they were taken to the police station and kept in two separate rooms.
Pastor Jose Bernard subsequently submitted a written complaint at the police station. However, shortly afterwards, a group of alleged attackers entered the police station, grabbed him by the collar and threatened him with dire consequences unless he withdrew the complaint. He alleged that this happened in the presence of police personnel.
“They entered the police station, grabbed me by the collar, physically intimidated me and threatened to kill me if I did not withdraw my complaint. And all of this happened in front of the police,” Bernard told Alt News.
According to Bernard, police merely told the men, “There are CCTV cameras here; leave the premises’. That’s all.”
Bernard said that the threats and intimidation eventually compelled him to withdraw the complaint. He told Alt News that he had pleaded with the miscreants and police to at least ensure that Christians in Rayan village would not be subjected to further harassment. “This is our government. A Hindu government. A Hindu country. Worshipping Jesus is not allowed. They have to bathe in the Ganga, and we will perform ‘ghar wapsi’,” Bernard recalled them saying.
Bernard further alleged that the inspector in-charge, Debabrata Mukherjee, questioned the congregation about why they had assembled to pray in the first place. When the attendees and Bernard attempted to reason, Mukherjee allegedly asked why they were taking such risks when people were being assaulted for doing so in several places.
Eventually, the women were released from the police station around 11 pm, while the men were released around 1 am.
Speaking to Alt News, Burdwan IC Debabrata Mukherjee denied the allegation that the attackers entered the police station and threatened Pastor Jose Bernard to withdraw the complaint.
He said, “They submitted a complaint and, after some time, retracted it. No one threatened them inside the police station,” adding that “Counter-complaints have been filed against them by locals.”
Asked why the injured were detained at police station for long hours, Mukherjee claimed their families hadn’t turned up to take them home.
The officer refused to answer further questions over phone.
Elderly Woman Assaulted at Home
Another attendee, Sagari Konai, managed to escape the initial attack and returned to her home. However, a group of men allegedly went to her residence and assaulted her. She sustained a fracture in her finger due to the assault, the pastors added.
Ruidas alleged that the men forced Konai to perform sit-ups while holding her ears and apologise for practising Christianity. She was also allegedly coerced into participating in Hindu rituals at a nearby temple.
Konai is an elderly widow who lives with her daughter.
The attack has left the survivors deeply shaken. Ruidas said that he was still in pain from the injuries he sustained and that he was afraid to return to his home in Rayan village. He is currently staying with Bernerd.
Bernerd, meanwhile, said the incident had a profound impact on his young daughter, who witnessed the violence firsthand.
“She has never been exposed to such brutal hatred unfolding before her eyes. I wonder whether these people are animals,” he said.

She lost her sight - now she is fighting to make history for Africa
- Published
Rukayat Taiwo Suleimon only took up sambo this year, but the Nigerian has already secured her place in the history of the martial art.
The sport shares strong roots with judo and wrestling, combining techniques such as hip and leg throws to take opponents to the mat, where they can be pinned.
Originally developed by the Soviet Union's Red Army in the 1920s, it was officially recognised as a combat sport by USSR officials in 1938.
Competing at the 2026 World Sambo Cup in Armenia, Suleimon defeated Uzbekistan's Charos Ortikova in the final of the women's 54kg category to claim victory on her international debut.
It was the first time that women with visual impairments had been included at the competition.
"Being the first female blind sambist in the world to win the gold medal makes me great," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"This is my first time in sambo and God crowned my efforts."
Suleimon's achievement was part of a breakthrough moment for African women in the sport. She and compatriot Elizabeth Aseso, who competed in the 59kg category, were among the pioneering sambists representing the continent in Yerevan.
For Suleimon, her gold medal is a reward for the hard work over many years which has seen her move from athletics to judo and now to the top of the international sambo podium.
"I really benefit a lot from sports and, despite my blindness, I achieve a lot," she said.
"If I [were] not blind, I don't think I would be at this level. I believe I will achieve even more."
From darkness to double glory
Suleimon's journey to becoming a champion has been marked by hardship and a determination to rebuild her life.
After failed surgeries she lost her sight in 2009 because of glaucoma, an eye condition that damages the optic nerve and can lead to permanent loss of vision.
The change in her circumstances affected her relationships, leaving her feeling isolated at a time when she needed support the most.
"People looked down on me. I would just stay indoors and cry," she explained.
"So many friends left me. They stopped communicating with me."
Her life began to take a different direction after she attended a vocational training centre for blind people in Lagos.
Through a friend, she was introduced to a para-athletics coach who helped her discover her potential in sport.
Since 2011, Suleimon has won more than 20 national medals across sprint events (alongside guide runner Stephen Oyelakin), discus and shot put.
She then began practicing judo and sambo.
"Since I [started] sports I have seen that where there is life, there is hope," she said.
"What sighted people can do, a blind person can do even better.
"I'm proud of myself because it's not easy to be a champion in athletics and in sambo. I don't want to lose the glory."
Her achievements have also become a source of pride for her family. Her twin sister Ganiyat Kehinde Suleimon says her sibling's disability has never defined her worth.
"She is someone we are all proud of. She is now a champion," Ganiyat told BBC Sport Africa.
"Her disability did not make her a liability to us."
For Nigerian sambo coach Olugbenga Adekahunsi, Suleimon's performance in Yerevan offered a glimpse of what she can accomplish with the right support and continued development.
"I see a lot of quality in her because she is very strong and the confidence is there," he told BBC Sport Africa.
"I believe she will become a great sambist."
'No support' for para-athletes
Suleimon says the recognition she has earned internationally has not been matched by adequate "support" at home.
However, her victory is the latest milestone in Nigeria's growing presence in the discipline.
Two years ago Samuel Oladele Kekere became the first blind African to compete at the World Sambo Championships in Kazakhstan, and Sodiq Ajibade followed that with a bronze medal at last year's edition in Kyrgyzstan.
"Despite making Nigeria and the whole of Africa proud, there is nothing to show for it," Suleimon said.
Her concerns reflect wider complaints from Nigerian para-athletes about limited funding, inadequate specialist facilities and insufficient institutional backing, despite their achievements.
Sherif Hammed, vice-president of the Sambo Association of Nigeria, says a lack of resources can prevent talented athletes from reaching their full potential.
"When athletes do not have facilities to train, they cannot compete at the world level," he said.
"It is quite disheartening and heartbreaking.
"People with disabilities, particularly visually impaired athletes, sometimes feel that because of their challenges, they have no purpose in life."
For Suleimon, a Lagos State judo champion, the journey to training is also an issue. Travelling across the city and covering transport costs make maintaining a demanding schedule difficult.
"I leave home at 5.30am to make it to training on time," she explained.
"It takes a lot of money and sacrifice."
Suleimon was unable to follow up her World Cup success at the World Sambo Championships in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where blind women were again scheduled to compete for the first time.
Beaten in Friday's opening round by Moldova's Ina Cernei, she still hopes her exploits on the global stage can inspire others.
"I want to encourage my fellow blind Africans to believe they can do it," said Suleimon. "And I want to make my country proud again."
