Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named Dianjunus rex.
The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” D. rex is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighting nearly five pounds, D. rex’s are huge.
Within the Ascomycetes, the giant fungus constitutes an entirely new biological family (the broader classification of genus and species), meaning that it has no close relatives—at least that we know of. While 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, mycologists believe the province known for its biological diversity could easily harbor 100,000
“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests,” Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Kunming Institute of Botany and the lead author of the paper, said in a press release.
Senanayake and his research team conducted surveys in the Nanban tropical rainforest, where they came across large, whitish fruiting bodies growing in the soil near the roots of dying trees. They documented and collected fungi growing in a wide variety of shapes like cylinders, spindles, and cupped palms. The fruiting bodies appeared to develop finger-like branches upon maturity. They found that the above-ground portions are covered with white, powdery fibers that turn dark yellow as the fungi mature while the portions buried in the soil are black and smooth.
The fruiting bodies dried rapidly when the scientists took samples back to the lab. They found that the interiors were dense and sponge-like, appearing white or yellow with no strong odor or taste. (Don’t try this experiment at home.)
Analyzing the DNA of these fungi, the researchers reconstructed a “molecular clock,” which revealed that D. rex diverged from other species approximately 65 million years ago. This is the end of the Cretaceous period, immediately following the mass extinction that is believed to have wiped out three quarters of all plant and animal species, including the dinosaurs. That means D. rex and T. rex never met, but this era was likely a boon for fungi. Large quantities of dead plant material became available following the die off, which could have provided new ecological opportunities for fungi and other organisms that decompose such matter.
Genomic analyses, however, indicated that D. rex doesn’t have nearly as many decomposition-related genes as the scientists expected. Compared to some of its closest relatives that also feast on plant matter, the huge fungus has only about half the usual number of decomposition-related genes.
Senanayake has a theory about this. Though, so far, they have only found the fruiting bodies around dying plants, the fungus may be leading a “double life”—living inside healthy trees and then feeding on dead plant material when the hosts die. That could perhaps explain how D. rex is able to store enough energy to build the massive fruiting bodies.
This is just a theory for now, but the giant fungi undoubtedly do need a surplus of energy to grow so large. Senanayake hypothesizes that the benefit of these large fruiting bodies is that they tower higher than the surrounding plants and fallen leaves, which could be advantageous for wind-mediated spore dispersal in a dense forest. “However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs.”

Another round of US-brokered Russia-Ukraine talks this week again failed to make significant breakthrough towards a long-awaited peace deal, as differences over territory hinder progress.
The days since have seen the countries continue launching major attacks on each other’s energy and oil infrastructure and on cargo vessels in the Black Sea, after the talks in Abu Dhabi failed to bear fruit.
Eight regions of Ukraine overnight going into Sunday, Mr Zelensky said on Sunday, in attacks he said were made partly possible due to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's Starshield service.
But it comes after a potential positive emerged for Kyiv from the talks. Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday 14 November that the US delegation had proposed Ukrainian membership of Nato in exchange for ceding the entirety of the Donbas region.
It marks an implicit rejection of Russia’s long-term demand that Ukraine must commit to not joining the western military alliance.
While ceding land that it currently controls had been a red line for Kyiv, Mr Zelensky said he would hold a referendum to allow Ukrainians to vote on a peace agreement should the US and Nato support the proposals.
It could mark a welcome shift in the US approach as Kyiv continues to be battered by Russian attacks on energy and railway infrastructure. Russian forces struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk, the defence ministry said on Saturday.
Attacks by Ukraine, meanwhile, killed one and injured several others in Russia's southern Rostov region overnight, the region’s governor said on Sunday.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Nizhnekamskneftekhim petrochemical plant, a major producer of rubbers and plastics, and an oil refining facility in Russia's Tatarstan region overnight, Kyiv's General Staff said on Sunday.
Following the talks earlier this week, Russia’s chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said that mutual understanding had been achieved on some issues and that more talks would be held, adding that the two sides had agreed on a large-scale prisoner swap.
Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said that there was “good momentum” towards reaching a solution by the end of this year, but that Europe should also be represented in future discussions.
The talks marked a restart for diplomacy some nine months after delegations last met in Geneva to discuss peace terms.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky voiced concerns in February that Kyiv was being asked “too often” to make concessions as Moscow stuck to its maximalist demands for land in Ukraine’s mineral-rich east.
The last year has seen Ukraine test Russia’s resilience with expanded strikes on major businesses and energy infrastructure across the border, piling pressure onto the Kremlin to end what has become a costly and gruelling attritional conflict.
But Moscow has largely benefited from concessions from an increasingly favourable United States, which temporarily waived sanctions in October and cut a deal to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.
US president Donald Trump had tried to orchestrate an ‘energy ceasefire’ between the two sides to rein in attacks on oil refineries and keep down global prices lifted by his own war with Iran.
But when Russia apparently ignored the truce last month, Ukraine restarted its attacks on Russian infrastructure and drew Trump’s ire.
Several months ago, Kyiv subsequently reported difficulty with its Starlink communications service and officials said they were no longer receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks.
The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, however Mr Zelensky says restrictions on operating speeds are still affecting defence capabilities.
"The Russians are targeting substations with 'shaheds'," Mr Zelensky said on X on Sunday.
"And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there."
In comments to NBC’s Meet the Press, Zelensky acknowledged that Ukraine would not be able to “prevail” if the United States “officially” takes Russia’s side in the conflict.
President Trump has positioned himself as a key mediator in the conflict since returning to office last year. But he has fairly consistently argued that Ukraine will have to give up land to end the nearly five-year war.
In an interview with 60 Minutes only on November 9, Trump said he expected a peace deal, but that Ukraine was “going to end up with a little bit [of a] different shape”.
“I believe that that war is going to end and it's going to end soon. And the only reason it's going to end is because of me,” he said, assessing that the biggest obstacle to peace was “the hatred between Zelensky and [Russian president, Vladimir] Putin”.
But when negotiators met in Geneva, it was territory that emerged as the major sticking point. Russia held firm on its demand that Ukraine cede the remaining 20 per cent of the eastern region of Donetsk.
The frontlines have moved since those talks in February. Russia then had claimed 43,585 sq miles of land, according to analysis by the Institute for the Study of War. Today, that figure has shrunk marginally to 43,527 sq miles.
Assessed Russian advances - land where Russian forces have operated in or launched attacks but do not control - sat at 1,465 sq miles in February, and are now down to 1,448 sq miles.
And assessed Ukrainian counteroffensives - “territory where Ukrainian forces are reportedly or assessed to be conducting counteroffensives or counterattacks” - has swollen from 23,089 sq miles in February to 27,113 sq miles in November, according to the same source.
Changes on the battlefield are reflected in changes in technology and tactics behind the scenes. Russia went into the war with the range advantage, hosting stockpiles of ballistic missiles and access to long-range Shahed drones as early as summer 2022.
Those Iranian-made drones can travel up to 2,000km with a 50kg warhead.
That advantage gave Moscow the ability to thrash morale in Ukraine’s major cities, destroy warehouses full of munitions, and devastate energy infrastructure deep behind enemy lines.
But Ukraine today says its weapons are destroying targets some 1,750km away - up from 630km in 2022.
Kyiv says its strategy of targeting Russian energy facilities is aimed at sapping a key source of Russia’s war funds and showing Russians the conflict started by Moscow is closer to home than ever. In these objectives, it has been effective.
As of November 10, analysts estimate that around 30 per cent of Russia’s total oil-processing capacity has been knocked offline or disrupted. That figure is a jump from a fifth - 20 per cent - reported only in June.
“This level of disruption is unprecedented in the history of the Russia-Ukraine conflict,” the IEA said over the summer.

The High Court of Karnataka has advised the security and police organisations to prioritise the mental health and well-being of personnel entrusted with firearms while asking the authorities to examine existing policies and take appropriate steps to strengthen the mental health and welfare measures for their personnel.
Justice Suraj Govindaraj passed the order while quashing the criminal proceedings against a 37-year-old CISF Sub-Inspector for attempting to kill herself in 2022 by using her service pistol while on duty in Mangaluru. She had attempted to end her life following years of severe mental distress over her inability to conceive a child due to a blocked fallopian tube.
Allowing her petition, the court set aside the lower court’s order and discharged her from the offence under Section 309 of the IPC (attempt to commit suicide). The court ruled that Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, creates a mandatory presumption of severe stress, placing the burden on the prosecution to prove otherwise. Since no such evidence was produced, the court held that continuing the trial would be an abuse of the judicial process.
‘Grief and anxiety’
“Personnel serving in these forces are also human beings. They have families, relationships, responsibilities and personal problems. They experience grief, anxiety, financial difficulties, marital discord, illness in the family and other difficulties common to human life. Wearing a uniform or undergoing rigorous training does not make them immune to such problems,” the court said.
Further, the court said that “the expectation that they must remain available for duty at all times and discharge their responsibilities, come rain or shine, irrespective of their personal circumstances or mental condition, requires a change in institutional thinking.”
The concerned organisations must ensure that accessible and confidential counselling, professional mental healthcare and timely treatment are available to personnel at all levels, including those posted in remote and difficult locations, the court said.
Signals of distress
Commanding and supervisory officers, the court emphasised, must be sensitised to recognise signs of distress and facilitate appropriate assistance, and personnel who undergo treatment or experience mental health difficulties must also receive suitable support for rehabilitation and return to duty, based on professional assessment.
“The welfare of personnel and the security of the public are not competing considerations. A force which looks after the mental and physical well-being of its personnel is better equipped to maintain discipline, operational readiness and public safety, the court said.

North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
- Published
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.
"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.
Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.
According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.
A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".
"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

U.S. envoys meet with Putin in the Kremlin after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.
The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.
Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.
U.S. envoys want Europe at the negotiating table, too
Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.
The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.
But Moscow doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent.
Many in Europe see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the trans-Atlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.
Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, Kushner said in Moscow.
Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate targets. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," he said.
He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.
Zelenskyy sees a political "window of opportunity"
Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.
Zelenskyy said political changes, including Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following midterm elections and balloting in France next year, could bring "a window of opportunity" for a peace deal.
"The political landscape in Europe could change in 2027. … We also see changes already taking place in the United States," Zelenskyy said in Dublin late Wednesday.
He called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace.
Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement.
Fighting continues as another bitter winter approaches
Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.
Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."
Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.
U.S. Starlink problems return, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.
Military units have recorded "significant disruptions," including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.
Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.
Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.
Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn't be used for offensive strikes against Russia.
Zelenskyy said in Dublin that the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on. "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he said.
Russian colonel reportedly killed by a car bomb
A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's main criminal investigation agency. It didn't identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.
Several senior Russian military officers have been killed by bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
If you want to maintain a healthy weight, you probably know you should watch what you eat and get some exercise, maybe hit the gym. But what about hitting the hay?
There is a lot of evidence linking lack of sleep to overeating and an increased body weight. But does that mean that getting more sleep could also boost efforts to lose weight?
"That's a good question," says Seth Creasy, an associate professor of medicine at the University of Colorado Anschutz who studies the interplay between weight management and lifestyle behaviors like sleep, diet and physical activity. "It's actually still an active area of research."
Creasy says the best evidence so far comes from a randomized clinical trial involving 80 overweight adults who were chronically short on sleep. Researchers randomly assigned half of them to get counseling on how to extend their snooze time.
"They got them to sleep a little over an hour more per night," Creasy says. "And they saw that, without intervening on food, these people started to eat less by about 270 calories per day. So once they were getting adequate sleep, they ate less."
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Other research has found associations between better sleep and weight loss. For example, one study found that people enrolled in a year-long weight loss intervention program who had good sleep health lost more weight and more fat mass compared to poor sleepers.
The poor sleepers in that study were also much more likely to report having trouble sticking to their diet and exercise goals, says Christopher Kline, the study's lead author and an associate professor of health and human development at the University of Pittsburgh.
And good sleep health doesn't just mean how long you sleep, Kline says. He says that factors like sleep timing, regularity and satisfaction also play a role.
"A good analogy I like to make is if you get your eight hours of sleep, but those eight hours are between 4 a.m. and noon, that might not be as healthy as someone who regularly obtains their sleep between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.," says Kline, whose research focuses on how physical activity, sleep and cardiometabolic risks are related.
The links between sleep loss and weight gain
Researchers say right now, the evidence that more sleep can boost weight loss efforts is still scant, but the science is much more consistent when it comes to linking insufficient sleep to weight gain.
When researchers restrict people's sleep, they eat more — by an average of around 300 calories a day if you look across studies, says Creasy, who recently published a review of the research on sleep and weight management.
Most of those studies required participants to severely curtail their sleep, usually to around four or five hours a night. That's much less than the seven to nine hours of sleep that adults are supposed to get.
But Creasy worked on a recent study that found even milder sleep loss can result in weight gain. In that study, people who were assigned to sleep just 90 minutes less than usual gained an average of one pound over six weeks. While that may not sound like much, "over time, it adds up," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, the study's senior author and a sleep and nutrition scientist at Columbia University.
Imaging studies from St-Onge and other researchers have found that, when we're short on sleep, activity ramps up in areas of the brain involved in pleasure and reward. In other words, it becomes harder to make good food choices.
"Our brain is less able to inhibit our desires for those sweet and salty foods" — especially later in the day, Kline says. The result is we end up overeating when short on sleep.
Kline says he experienced this phenomenon first-hand when he was still a doctoral student working the overnight shift in a sleep study lab. Once a week, every week, one of his fellow lab workers would bring in glazed donuts from Krispy Kreme.
"I can tell you there was no chance I was going to end a shift without having at least one or two of those donuts. And I don't even really like glazed donuts," Kline says ruefully.
Skimping on sleep can also disrupt our circadian rhythms and impair our sensitivity to insulin, which may promote fat storage and make it easier to gain weight.
Creasy says early studies suggested poor sleep also affects hormones that regulate appetite, but newer research hasn't always borne that out. "Some studies have shown an effect on them and some have not. So it's just been inconsistent," he says.
Better sleep through food?
St-Onge says the relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. "As we find that how we sleep influences our food intake, we also find that what we eat during the day also influences our sleep at night," she says.
Research from her team and others has linked eating added sugars and saturated fat to more sleep disturbances and less deep slumber. Meanwhile, fruits, vegetables and fiber were associated with better sleep and fewer awakenings at night, she says.
If you want to eat better to sleep better, St-Onge says you can start with small, easy changes. "As a first step, cut out foods that are higher in added sugars and sweetened beverages," she says.
Switching to whole grains instead of refined carbohydrates is also a good idea. Her research has linked added sugars and refined carbs to a greater risk of insomnia.
And she says look for opportunities to eat more fruits and vegetables throughout the day.
"I always put a ton of leafy vegetables in my dishes, like stews and soups and stir fries," St-Onge says.
And of course, don't forget good sleep hygiene, says Philip Cheng, a sleep and circadian rhythms researcher and professor of medicine at Henry Ford Health in Michigan. That means things like keeping your bedroom cool and dark, and sticking to a regular schedule for going to bed and waking up as best as you can.
"That's going to stabilize your sleep in the long run," Cheng says.
But if your poor sleep lasts months or even years, he says it's time to see a medical provider for help.

In November, a claim (archived) circulated online that the U.S. Air Force had held Maj. Jason Watson, an active-duty airman who publicly called for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, in solitary confinement for more than 80 days while he awaited court-martial.
CNN reported that the Air Force ordered Watson into "pre-trial confinement" on Aug. 18. Two days later, on Aug. 20, Watson's lawyer Christopher Mutimer told CNN that Watson was "basically in solitary confinement." He repeated this claim in early October, telling CNN (at 1:46, archived) that Watson was "still in solitary confinement."
One X user who claimed Watson remained in solitary confinement in early November — 84 days after the Air Force first ordered him into pretrial confinement — wrote:
Maj. Jason Watson has been in 24-hour solitary confinement for 80+ days & has reportedly lost 20 pounds, all before any trial. UN experts consider solitary beyond 15 days to be torture. He offered to resign, give up all his benefits, & the Air Force said no. Because he protested.
The claim also circulated on Facebook and Threads (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
Speaking to Snopes on Nov. 10, Mutimer confirmed Watson had been detained at Maryland's Calvert County Detention Center since Aug. 18 and described conditions that he said met generally understood definitions for solitary confinement.
Mutimer said Watson "is in a room by himself 22 to 23 hours a day. No one stays in there with him, he is not allowed to have any interaction. When he's let out it's to shower, make a phone call, get some time in the yard by himself." He described Watson's cell as a "pen" where "the light is on all the time."
Mutimer added, "Because he's an officer, he is in the military, that contract says he is not allowed to be with anybody who is not in the military."
A spokesperson for the Department of the Air Force said in a statement on Nov. 13:
The Department of the Air Force can confirm that Maj Watson is not being held in solitary confinement. Maj Watson is held in administrative protective segregation—not punitive solitary confinement—at the Calvert County Detention Center (CCDC) pursuant to an official Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) between CCDC and the 11th Wing Security Forces Squadron (11 SFS) at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling (JBAB).
Maj Watson is physically separated from CCDC's civilian general inmate population to comply with military policy and statutory segregation mandates. While separated from civilian detainees, Maj Watson does have regular access to standard institutional amenities and programs, including the facility library, religious services/chapel, and physical fitness time. He also retains normal access to defense counsel, military leadership visits, medical care, and personal visitation.
Because of the opposing descriptions of Watson's confinement from his lawyer and the Air Force, we leave this claim unrated. we leave this claim unrated.
By November, the docket of the Air Force's military justice branch showed Watson was due for general court-martial in February. Mutimer said he would argue a petition for Watson's pretrial release on Nov. 17.
Mutimer also confirmed the claim some social media users made that Watson had attempted to resign after his July 1 arrest but said officials had denied his resignation and instead pressed ahead with the court-martial, a move that Mutimer described as "absolutely unheard of."
Tracking Watson's case
Capitol Police arrested Watson on July 1 on after he publicly called for Trump's impeachment while wearing his Air Force uniform. A live stream (at 50:56) of the arrest showed Watson standing on the Capitol steps in uniform while holding a sign that read "Impeach Convict Remove."
Watson said at a news conference earlier that day that he was calling for Trump to be impeached because he thought the president and Vice President JD Vance had governed in an unconstitutional way throughout their administration.
Watson highlighted the war in Iran, Elon Musk's sweeping cuts to federal government and the Department of Homeland Security's immigration crackdown and killings of protesters as "high crimes and misdemeanors" (at 28:28) for which "the president and vice president must be impeached, convicted, and removed."
The Air Force major repeated his call for Trump and Vance's removal while speaking to CNN's Erin Burnett (at 1:52) on Aug. 17. Burnett said (at 2:41) during the interview that the military had placed a "gag order" on Watson after his July 1 protest and that he was "under investigation."
According to a later CNN report, the Air Force took Watson into pretrial confinement days after he spoke to the network.
CNN reported that the Air Force charged Watson with 10 violations of three articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the military's legal framework, on Aug. 20. Mutimer reportedly spoke to Watson on that date and reported that he was "basically in solitary confinement."
On Sept. 29, The New York Times reported that an Air Force investigating officer had recommended Watson's case for general court-martial, the military's highest level of trial court.
According to the Judge Advocate General's Corps Department of the Air Force, which investigated and charged Watson, the major faced charges of four violations of articles 88, 92 and 133 of the UCMJ.
Article 88 (Page 34) of the UCMJ states that any commissioned officer who uses "contemptuous words" against certain public officials, which includes the president and vice president, should face a court-martial. Article 92 (Page 35) states that a person subject to the code that fails to obey an order or regulation can be subject to court-martial. Article 133 (Page 48) states that "Any commissioned officer, cadet, or midshipman who is convicted of conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman shall be punished as a court-martial may direct."
The code does not explicitly define what "conduct unbecoming an officer" means.
An Air Force spokesperson reportedly told Military.com in October that the Air Force had acted in accordance with the Rule for Court-Martial 305 when it took Watson into pretrial confinement in August. That rule says someone can be placed in pretrial confinement if there is probable cause they committed "an offense triable by court-martial."
That rule also says that someone taken into pretrial confinement can ask a military judge to review the "propriety" of the confinement, meaning whether it is appropriate. Mutimer said such a review for Watson would happen on Nov. 17.
According to the UCMJ's Article 13 (Page 5), it is prohibited to punish a service member awaiting trial. Any confinement before trial must not "be any more rigorous than the circumstances require to insure his presence, but he may be subjected to minor punishment during that period for infractions of discipline."
At the time of this writing, Watson had not been convicted or sentenced. Punishments for service members convicted by court-martial range from reprimands and salary reductions to dismissal or discharge.

Bengaluru expands public transport, but poor connectivity keeps residents reliant on cars
The Indian technology hub is adding metro lines and buses to ease traffic congestion, but gaps in coverage and road safety concerns continue to make private vehicles a more convenient option for many residents.
BENGALURU: Despite already owning two cars, finance professional Shireesh Jacobs and his wife Shifrah, a small business owner, are considering buying a third.
For the Bengaluru couple, the decision is driven less by a desire to drive than by the lack of convenient public transport and concerns over road safety for their two teenage children.
"There isn’t really that much good local transport the way you might see overseas where you can walk, (and) within five minutes there is a tube station, you get down and take the metro. That is not the case here," Jacobs told CNA.
His workplace is about 30km from home, yet the drive can take between 90 minutes and two hours during peak traffic.
There is no direct metro connection for his commute, while poor pedestrian infrastructure makes walking along some roads unsafe.
"You can see here that there are no footpaths, completely uneven surface, big ditches,” he said, pointing out the poor road conditions to CNA while driving to work.
“There is at least 25 feet (7.6m) that can be developed as a good walking footpath, but people are forced to avoid the ditches, walk closer to the roads, and that makes it very unsafe,” he added.
His wife Shifrah said the couple are reluctant to let their teenage children cycle or ride motorbikes.
"We have two teenagers now, and we are not even okay with them having cycles and bikes because of the lack of safety. We are talking about (whether) we need to buy a third car,” she added.
The family's dilemma reflects Bengaluru's struggle to reduce reliance on private vehicles.
The Indian technology hub was ranked the world's second most congested city in traffic technology company TomTom's 2025 index, with a 10km journey during the evening rush hour taking more than 45 minutes on average.
The city, home to more than 12 million residents, is also the first in India to have more than 2.5 million registered private cars.
BRIDGING GAPS IN PUBLIC TRANSPORT
Bengaluru's metro network now spans about 103.6km, following the inauguration of a 7.5km stretch of the Pink Line by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Nov 13, but urban planners say expanding rail services alone will not solve the city's transport problems if commuters cannot easily reach them.
"We don’t have the last-mile connectivity to the public transportation, which includes walkability," said Vijay Narnapatti, founding director of architecture and design firm mayaPRAXIS.
He called for improvements to pedestrian infrastructure, non-motorised transport and bus services to be integrated with the metro network.
One initiative aimed at addressing the problem is a covered walkway at International Tech Park Bangalore, which connects the business park directly to a nearby metro station.
Singapore-listed CapitaLand India Trust, which owns the park, worked with Bengaluru's metro operator to build the bridge.
The trust's CEO Gauri Shankar Nagabhushanam said about 12,000 people use the connection daily.
“Public-private partnership is required … this benefits everyone. It is aligned to sustainability goals as well. So I definitely think some of these projects go a long way in easing traffic and making life much better for employees,” he said.
MORE TRAINS AND BUSES PLANNED
The Karnataka state government is also investing in public transport, with its budget targeting the completion of 41km of metro rail in the current financial year.
Bengaluru has been allocated 4,500 additional electric buses under India's PM E-DRIVE programme, a central government initiative aimed at promoting electric vehicle adoption and expanding electric public transport.
The city's transport authority also plans to expand feeder bus services connecting neighbourhoods to metro stations.
Greater Bengaluru Authority Chief Commissioner M Maheshwar Rao said the city is taking a multi-pronged approach to easing congestion.
"The approach is to see that you improve mobility, you invest in public transport, you increase the supply of road space in some way," he said.
He added that reducing on-street parking and providing more off-street parking spaces are also part of the strategy to ease congestion.
Despite these efforts, private vehicle ownership continues to grow.
Government data shows Bengaluru registered more than 116,000 new cars and nearly 330,000 two-wheelers in the first nine months of 2026.
As the city expands its transport options, a key test remains making public transport accessible and convenient enough for more residents to leave their vehicles at home.

Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the world
MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.
The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.
Haines' family asked well-wishers to make donations to the international charity Save the Children instead of sending flowers. The appeal has raised more than 1.4 million Australian dollars ($950,000), Save the Children Australia said Monday.
Haines was “overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians” through their donations and looked forward to working with Save the Children to use the money to “improve the lives of children,” she said.
Her shocking injuries renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers. However, public incitement against officials is growing.
Security at several lawmakers’ electorate offices has been enhanced in response to the alleged attack.
Within hours of Haines being struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser Troop Carrier, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told a news conference her catastrophic injuries were not an accident.
“All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery,” Albanese said in a statement Monday in response to her hospital discharge.
“I have been in regular contact with Helen and her extraordinary family. We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese added.
Police have yet to disclose a motive for the alleged attack. Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old man who lived in the Wangaratta area, has been charged with offenses including intentionally causing serious injury.
Nugent has been in custody since bystanders dragged him from his SUV and rendered first-aid to Haines at the scene.
His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement a day after Haines was hospitalized describing the lawmaker as a “friend for more than 20 years” and the circumstances of her injuries “unfathomable.”

In the Israeli legislative elections held in late October 2026, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority required to govern. The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, alongside other opposition factions, won 48 seats. Notably, Arab-led parties made historic gains, winning 19 seats and becoming potential “kingmakers”. Following the vote, President Isaac Herzog formally accepted the results. He opened a two-day consultation window with party leaders to determine who is best positioned to assemble a stable coalition.
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament building.
Fact: The video does not show the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. It shows a pro-Palestine activist replacing the German national flag with a Palestinian flag on a flagpole outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on 08 November 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring visuals similar to those seen in the viral video. According to these reports, the incident took place outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on Sunday, 08 November 2026.
The reports (here, here) state that a 22-year-old pro-Palestine activist climbed a 30-metre-high flagpole in front of the Reichstag building at around 11:30 am, removed the German national flag, and replaced it with a Palestinian flag.
The group ‘Peacefully Against Genocide‘ claimed responsibility for the incident, stating that the action was a protest against the German government’s pro-Israel policy and its silence on alleged human rights violations in Gaza.
According to a press release issued by Berlin Police on 08 November 2026, two people who allegedly assisted the 22-year-old activist were detained and later released after their identities were established. The Palestinian flag was subsequently removed with the assistance of the Berlin Fire Brigade. Police also launched an investigation into suspected offences, including insulting state symbols, damaging government property, trespassing, and violating Berlin’s assembly law.
To sum up, the viral video shows the Palestinian flag hoisted outside the German Parliament, not the Israeli Parliament.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alex Shi, a 37-year-old freelancer who moved back to Beijing. She worked as a freelance director and stand-up comic. It has been edited for length and clarity.
When I graduated from college in Beijing, I wanted to start work right away. My mom had other plans.
Her views had swung wildly. When I was in high school, my English teacher told me to leave China and study in the US, where she said I'd thrive. My mom said only kids who couldn't get good grades went overseas. A couple of years later, studying abroad became hugely popular, and suddenly my mom thought I needed to go too. We fought for 2 months.
In the end, I went to Boston University and got a master's in broadcast journalism. At 25, I moved to Charlotte, North Carolina, for a boyfriend. We broke up, and I'd wasted most of my OPT year in a city where I knew no one. But I wasn't ready to go home, so I did a second master's in media studies at The New School in New York.
My plan was to stay in New York, but a teaching offer from a film school fell through when they found out I needed visa sponsorship.
I left the US in 2018, on the same day my best friend got married. I'd helped him pick the cake and the menu, but missed the wedding.
A few years in Big Tech
Back in Beijing, I freelanced for a few years, taking on corporate projects and producing for international news outlets. I started dancing salsa as well.
When the pandemic started, the only entertainment left was comedy open mics. I watched for 2 months before trying. My first time on stage, I got laughs. The comics I knew were encouraging.
But freelancing had died down. I wanted a bit more stability, and my family was encouraging me to find a steadier job. In 2021, I was hired by ByteDance as an intercultural communication expert. Two months in, my whole department disappeared, so I moved into product design.
We worked with teams in other time zones, so the day never really ended. It was the most stressful 2 years of my life. I stopped doing comedy and dancing. I was the heaviest I've ever been.
The office was in an old building in Beijing with low ceilings and turnstiles on every floor that made me feel like I was swiping myself into prison.
I went back to freelance, focusing on intercultural communication. I work with corporate clients, including Chinese businesses looking to expand overseas. This time, I drew a line for what projects I'd take on rather than taking on everything I was offered. I knew that I didn't want to be a generic creative. I now have more control.
Finding my creative outlet
I never set out to do comedy. In New York, I was into live storytelling, inspired by the podcast "The Moth." Back in China, I traveled to Shanghai twice to tell stories.
What I like most about doing comedy is that when I bomb, I have to tell myself to get over myself.
For most of my life, I only chose things I was about 90% sure I'd be good at. I don't play sports I'm bad at because I don't want to look stupid. Comedy is the one thing I told myself I wouldn't give up. I can't blame the audience every time, and I can't blame myself every time.
It's still a hobby, but I'd love to tour as a stand-up comedian and turn it into a career.
My days in Beijing are flexible
Unless I have a morning meeting, I get out of bed around 10:30 a.m., spend about two hours making coffee and not cleaning my room, and then start work in the afternoon. Last night, I edited a podcast until 3 a.m. with an in-person meeting the next day.
Plenty of people assume I was more creative abroad. It's true that in New York, I was surrounded by artists. I shot photography and independent films. I'd see a woman at a restaurant and ask if she wanted to take photos. It was free-wheeling and fun.
But in Beijing, I'm a creative professional. I take things more seriously; I don't just do whatever comes to mind.
In New York City, I was living with four other roommates. Now I'm in a different stage of life. I live alone. The city is expensive, and more money- and status-oriented than anywhere else I've lived. I'm Chinese, living in my own country's capital, and I feel I have something to prove.
I don't want to be a struggling artist here. My parents live in Beijing too, and I hate admitting how much pressure that adds. When an idea hits, I ask where it can go and how to carry it to the next step. I'm happier as a creative person in Beijing, because I finish what I start.

A zombie virus has overtaken South Los Angeles. Authorities, hoping to contain the outbreak, have decided to barricade the neighborhood, leaving residents to make do on their own. So begins They Left Us to Die, a new microdrama from media company Mansa that runs 30 episodes and is entirely AI-generated.
“The plague was made here, made on us, on purpose,” says Imani Cross, an emergency room nurse desperate for a cure to help her brother DJ, who’s been infected.
On Instagram, the trailer drew mostly favorable reaction when it was released on October 29. A cascade of fire emoji filled the comments section as anticipation mounted. But the following day, as the first episode was set to go live at midnight, new tensions began to stir. Why had Mansa created a show with zero human roles? Weren’t actors David Oyelowo and Nate Parker, the company’s founders, about uplifting artists of color, not erasing them?
“Mansa was one of the first vertical apps that was supposed to support and cultivate black talent, but here they are … another AI sellout,” said one user on Threads. “Why would any self-respecting casting director, producer, or director ever consider hiring Oleyowo again after this?” posted another. Actress Yvette Nicole Brown responded with a single note of disapproval: “*sigh* Mmkay,” she wrote, adding a gif of Viola Davis expressing irritation.
Parker wasn’t surprised by the backlash. “When we hear the words AI, it immediately drives us to the realities of what we are facing and the real lives it’s impacting,” Parker tells WIRED.
The problem is that while Hollywood is desperate for more expansive Black stories, not everyone agrees on the best way to make them happen.
As part of Mansa’s development strategy, the company says it is using AI as a chess piece rather than a replacement for human-centered content. The power comes in leveraging a show like They Left Us to Die as a way to bring more awareness to what Black audiences will support. He describes the approach as “holding the line on our very existence” in an industry that’s consolidating, and being able to “use all the tools that we have at our disposal to make sure we can staff up around shows that get greenlit.”
In the shrinking Hollywood of today, a series about a Black ER nurse fighting off a zombie virus unleashed on her neighborhood by white people would likely struggle to find the backing of a major studio without first having proved its value 10 times over. Mansa’s strategy is to test the appetite of audiences with its AI shows. Parker believes this will demonstrate to studios that there is a demand for those kinds of stories before committing to a live production.
Parker says studio heads are even more reluctant in this climate. But with microdramas, “you get to test a piece of content, not just test it in a way of proof of concept like a short film, but you get to monetize it,” he says. “You get to track data around engagement and see if this is something the audience wants.”
As attention spans shrink, microdramas have sprung up as a preferred portal of entertainment for both studios and young people. They’re vertically shot, minute-long soaps that are produced at a fraction of the cost of a TV show and mirror back the kind of frenzied consumption that has come to define modern entertainment. As streamers like ReelShort and DramaBox dominate the industry, stories anchored around romance, billionaire fantasies, revenge, and supernatural sagas have become the genres driving a boom largely fueled by women viewers.
An Omdia analysis of mobile usage in the fourth quarter of 2025 found that users spent an average of 10 more minutes per day on ReelShort (36 minutes) compared to Prime Video (26 minutes) and Netflix (20 minutes), with the firm predicting that the microdrama market will reach $14 billion in 2027.
Hoorae Media, Issa Rae’s production company, expanded into the sector this year with two microdramas, including Screen Time, a couples thriller comedy that, as of October, had over 580 million views across TikTok and its in-house microdrama app, PineDrama. There are also upstarts Juccee Shorts and Urban Operas, which is launching with six series later this month, that are angling to offer more diverse stories for audiences.
Among Gen Z, watching short-form video is now more common than watching movies, accounting for 26 percent of weekly media time among young adults aged 18 to 24, according to a recent survey by the entertainment analytics firm Luminate.
Streamers are also investing more into the format and have even started to redesign their own user experience to keep pace with Gen Z’s twitchy consumption habits. Between April and August, Peacock, HBO Max, Prime Video, Paramount+, Netflix, and Disney+ all launched a short-form vertical feed on their respective mobile app.
Maria Rua Aguete, global head of media and entertainment at Omdia, suspects that AI will change the economics of the industry. But more cheaply produced content doesn’t automatically mean more viewers. “Ultimately, audiences will decide what succeeds,” she says, adding that there is a “significant opportunity” to tap into overlooked demos.
The backlash in response to They Left Us to Die is a direct symptom of this rapid evolution. “What Nate is trying to do, no matter how practical and logical it is, he’s not reading the room and understanding that people don’t care about that. They just see technology as stealing their opportunities,” says J. Christopher Hamilton, an associate professor of communications at Syracuse and entertainment lawyer.
The reality of Hollywood is dire. The $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance is projected to eliminate up to 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles, according to the county’s Department of Economic Opportunity and Film Office. That reality can feel doubly crushing for Black artists and industry workers because they’re already vastly underrepresented.
The concern in response to They Left Us to Die highlighted the desperation that so many people are feeling around losing opportunities they were already struggling to land. Despite Black, Indigenous, and people of color moviegoers over-indexing as ticket buyers, representing the majority of opening weekend domestic ticket sales, Black actors accounted for only 6.5 percent of movie leads while Black directors made up 3.3 percent of releases in 2025, according to the 2026 UCLA Hollywood Diversity report.
As a distributor “showcasing diaspora-focused content,” Parker wants to prove that there is value in being able to go from an idea to a script to market in a matter of weeks rather than the years it might take through the Hollywood system. Mansa has produced nine live-action microdramas so far, in addition to two that are fully AI-generated. The company declined to share data on how its AI series were performing.
But what Mansa is attempting is also about trust for viewers, some of whom wonder whether Parker is worthy of it. In 1999, Parker was charged and later acquitted of sexual assault while in college. The case resurfaced following the release of The Birth of a Nation, his 2016 film about a slave rebellion led by Nat Turner; it depicted a fictionalized rape scene as motivation for the uprising. “Nate Parker been a pariah,” one person wrote on Threads under the announcement about Mansa’s AI series, as more people poured on.
Whether Mansa succeeds or fails, Hamilton believes AI microdramas are “too compelling a business proposition” for the industry to ignore.
“Real-life actors and storytellers aren’t going away completely, but I do think we’re going to see a resetting of the table, and some people are in denial about that,” Hamilton says. “When it hits, it’s going to be like a blackout. No one’s going to know which way is up.”

Kevin Pietersen has fired England up ahead of the ODI series decider against Australia in Hobart on Wednesday, according to fast bowler Gus Atkinson.

49ers stun Cowboys, Chiefs and Bengals impress - NFL week 10
- Published
The NFL's brightest stars lit up week 10 of the 2026 season with some astonishing plays on Sunday.
The likes of Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, Patrick Mahomes, Jahmyr Gibbs and Ja'Marr Chase showcased their skills with some explosive action to help their teams to victory.
The San Francisco 49ers produced a historic display in Dallas while there were also big wins for the Kansas City Chiefs, Detroit Lions and Cincinnati Bengals.
It means the 49ers and Buffalo Bills continue to share the league's best record (8-1), while five teams moved to 7-2, including the in-form Jacksonville Jaguars.
Purdy shines for free-scoring 49ers
The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys have a fierce rivalry stretching back to the 1990s and they delivered another classic with a shootout in Texas.
Brock Purdy showed why he is among the leading contenders for the Most Valuable Player award as the 49ers won 46-40, racking up 584 yards of offence - the most Dallas have ever allowed at home.
San Francisco had three touchdowns of more than 65 yards, while Purdy threw for a career-high 389 yards and three touchdowns. The quarterback even blocked for one of the 49ers' other three scores, a 70-yard run by Deebo Samuel on a reverse trick play.
The highlights were two Purdy passes to Christian McCaffrey. The first saw Purdy show remarkable poise as he scrambled out of the pocket before finding McCaffrey for a 74-yard score, while the second was a perfectly-executed play over the middle that saw McCaffrey sprint in untouched from 66 yards.
Dual-threat running back McCaffrey finished with three scores and 223 total yards, including a career-high 161 receiving yards.
Purdy's MVP rival Josh Allen had a relatively quiet game as the Buffalo Bills won 31-12 at the New York Jets, while the Jacksonville Jaguars won 40-23 at the Tennessee Titans.
Including the end of last season, the Jaguars have won 15 of their past 17 regular-season games and must be considered Super Bowl contenders, especially after bringing in three key defensive players before the trade deadline on Tuesday.
Burrow keeps Bengals run going
Joe Burrow became the new MVP favourite last week and continued his superb form as the Cincinnati Bengals romped to a 38-18 win in their divisional match-up against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
New Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino was among the crowd as Burrow was involved in four touchdowns for the fifth straight game, tying an NFL record.
The Bengals quarterback had 300 passing yards before half-time and finished with 409. Most of them were to Ja'Marr Chase, who claimed 231 yards from just 11 catches for the 7-2 Bengals.
Their divisional rivals, the Cleveland Browns, pulled off another comeback as they recovered from 17-0 down to beat the Houston Texans 27-24.
The Browns have won their opening four home games for the first time since 1963 and are now 6-4.
Quarterback Deshaun Watson led the Browns to a game-winning drive in the fourth quarter of all six of those wins and he said this one was "definitely special" as it came against his former team.
Dream international trip for St Brown
Munich staged the penultimate international game of the season and just playing in Germany was a "dream come true" for the Detroit Lions' wide receiver Amon-Ra St Brown.
The 27-year-old's mother is German, and he and his two brothers speak the language fluently and have been regular visitors to their mother's homeland.
St Brown, who arrived wearing lederhosen and waved the German flag as he ran on to the field, scored two touchdowns as the Lions charged to a 35-10 win over the New England Patriots.
Yet St Brown was outshone by team-mate Jahmyr Gibbs, who had 99 receiving yards, 153 rushing yards and two touchdowns, taking him to 62 overall - a new NFL record in a player's first four seasons.
The Patriots lost Drake Maye to an ankle injury when he was sacked on the game's opening drive by Aidan Hutchinson, who injured his knee as he celebrated, and the Lions fear it is a significant injury.
Detroit, the Minnesota Vikings and Chicago Bears are now all 7-2 in the ultra-competitive NFC North, with the Vikings bouncing back after suffering back-to-back defeats.
Kirk Cousins returned to Minnesota before the trade deadline on Tuesday and the veteran quarterback led them to a 30-10 win at their other divisional rival, the 6-4 Green Bay Packers, with their defence claiming eight sacks - the most in a single game this season.
Seahawks spoil Mendoza's first start
The Las Vegas Raiders allowed Cousins to rejoin Minnesota as they felt Fernando Mendoza, this year's first overall draft pick, was ready to become their starting quarterback.
Mendoza's first start came against the Seattle Seahawks, the Super Bowl champions, and he managed to run in a 10-yard touchdown on the Raiders' opening drive.
But the Raiders' offence then struggled and Mendoza was sacked six times as the Seahawks won 21-13.
"It's good to get punched in the face because now it's a great opportunity to grow and learn," said Mendoza.
Seattle quarterback Drew Lock made two big touchdown passes on the run, one to Cooper Kupp and the other a 71-yard score by Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

Another milestone for Mahomes
The Kansas City Chiefs' run game has caught the eye so far this season, in particular new signing Kenneth Walker, but he was out injured on Sunday as Patrick Mahomes reminded everyone he has one of the best arms in the business.
For the first time since 2022, the three-time Super Bowl winner threw for five touchdowns, plus 348 yards, as Kansas City won 35-13 at the Atlanta Falcons.
Running back Emmett Johnson stepped up in the absence of Walker to claim 101 rushing yards, 70 receiving yards and two touchdowns.
Mahomes made explosive plays to Cyrus Allen and Andrew Armstrong for their first NFL scores, while fellow wide receiver Josh Downs scored on his debut after the Chiefs traded for him on deadline day.
That took Mahomes to 332 career touchdown passes, including the play-offs, putting the 31-year-old top of the all-time list for the most in a player's first 10 seasons.
The Chiefs are 7-2 and will need their receiving corps to ease the burden on Walker during a tough five-game stretch after next week.

Pakistan’s former Prime Minister Imran Khan was taken to hospital in Islamabad late on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) for medical treatment and returned to prison, sources said.
Khan, who is imprisoned in Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi, had an eye check-up at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), one of the officials said on Wednesday (November 11).
“He had some blood pressure issues ... and was given required treatment last night. He has been shifted back to his prison cell,” the person said.
The cricketer-turned-politician has faced multiple corruption charges since he lost power in a no-confidence vote in 2022, and has been in prison for more than three years. All of Khan’s convictions bar one have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing and says the charges are politically motivated, a claim the government denies.
Khan’s lawyers say the 74-year-old’s health has deteriorated in prison and that he has lost significant vision in his right eye.
It is the first known instance of Khan being taken to hospital for treatment and returned to jail since August, when his hospital visit was cut short.
A Pakistani court has also ordered jail authorities to allow Khan’s legal team to see him and his wife, his party said.
His party’s deputy chairman, Shah Mehmood Qureshi, was also taken to hospital in the eastern city of Lahore from a jail in the same city on Tuesday (November 10). He remains in hospital.

While this claim spread in 2026, the actual incident happened in 2020.
A claim is spreading online that a bald eagle attacked a $950 "government drone" in midair, sending it crashing into Lake Michigan.
Social media users shared the story on Facebook and Reddit, prompting Snopes readers to search the website to determine whether a bald eagle had, in fact, launched a successful attack against a foreign object in its airspace.
This story is true — although it happened years ago, not in 2026. It is also worth noting that while some posts online appear to show a bald eagle flying at a drone, there is no actual footage of the incident, according to the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy, or EGLE — the agency whose drone lost to the eagle.
Michigan state officials confirmed the eagle's assault in an Aug. 13, 2020, news release titled, "Shoreline-mapping EGLE drone sent to watery Lake Michigan grave by U.P. bald eagle." (U.P. is a reference to Michigan's Upper Peninsula.)
Here's how that release began:
An Upper Peninsula bald eagle launched an airborne attack on a drone operated by a Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) pilot last month, tearing off a propeller and sending the aircraft to the bottom of Lake Michigan.
The brazen eagle vs. EGLE onslaught took place near Escanaba in Michigan's Upper Peninsula on July 21 when EGLE environmental quality analyst and drone pilot Hunter King was mapping shoreline erosion for use in the agency's efforts to document and help communities cope with high water levels.
King had completed about seven minutes of the mapping flight — his fourth of the day in the area — when satellite reception got spotty. He pressed the "Go Home" recall button. The drone dutifully turned, reacquiring a strong satellite feed.
King was watching his video screen as the drone beelined for home, but suddenly it began twirling furiously. "It was like a really bad rollercoaster ride," said King. When he looked up, the drone was gone, and an eagle was flying away. A nearby couple, whose pastimes include watching the local eagles attack seagulls and other birds, later confirmed they saw the eagle strike something but were surprised to learn it was a drone. Both King and the couple said the eagle appeared uninjured as it flew from the scene of the crime.
The release also confirmed that the drone was "a $950 Phantom 4 Pro Advanced" and shared data indicating that the eagle tore off a propeller, as many of the claim posts said (emphasis ours):
Data from the flight records detailed the drone's final moments:
- The eagle strike occurred 7:39.7 into the flight roughly four-tenths of a mile from King and 162 feet above the water
- Its speed instantly dropped from 22 mph to 10. Within a half-second the flight record shows the beginning of downward spiral along with "excessive spinning" warnings
- In the next 3.5 seconds the drone sent 27 warning notifications including one indicating a propeller had been torn off
- Gaining momentum as it fell, its last communication came at 34 feet above the water, falling at 30 feet per second, or 20.4 mph.
Per the release, King and the unidentified couple searched for the drone, "but hours of scouring the shoreline were fruitless." An unmanned aircraft systems coordinator with the state agency, Arthur Ostaszewski, also attempted to find the drone using a kayak, snorkeling gear and "telemetric data from the flight that pinpointed exactly where the drone hit the lake." He, too, was unsuccessful, even after walking a grid pattern for two hours — "like I was playing Battleship and wanted to cover the entire board," he said.
A week later, however, a team of Michigan state employees — which the agency cheekily dubbed in a news release as the Willful Eagle Trauma Team Engaged in Retrieval, or WETTER — managed to uncover the drone in almost the exact same location after "the previously murky water had cleared due to shifting winds and currents." EGLE shared a few pictures of the recovery effort on X, then known as Twitter:
The agency noted that the drone was not recording at the time of the bald eagle's assault, meaning that there would not be any footage of the fight over airspace.
Michigan officials speculated that the attack could have been "a territorial squabble with the electronic foe, or just a hungry eagle."
"Or maybe it did not like its name being misspelled," EGLE said, poking fun at its agency acronym.
At the time, EGLE said it was considering steps to try to prevent a repeat attack, including adding a design to make the drones look less like seagulls. Snopes found no evidence of any bald eagle drone attacks since EGLE's incident in 2020, however, so this may have just been a one-time thing.
EGLE also said the Michigan Department of Natural Resources was unable to issue a citation or violation notice to the "rogue eagle."
"Unfortunately, there's nothing we can do," the agency's spokesman said. "Nature is a cruel and unforgiving mistress."

Paul Barril, French ‘Supergendarme’ Turned Mercenary, Has Died
After years in elite police units, he drew scrutiny from human rights groups for selling arms and providing other services to unsavory governments. He was 80.
Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”
Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).
Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.
His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.
By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.
In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.
