- The claim that a video shows two Muslim New York Police Department officers taking away a woman's dog for disturbing the peace, supposedly in the interests of enforcing the Islamic teachings known as Shariah, is still under investigation.
- We contacted the NYPD to ask questions and request an incident report to independently confirm several details, including to fully verify the woman's purported charge or charges. We also filed a formal request to receive officers' body camera footage and will update this story if we receive further information.
- The person who says he recorded the video told Snopes he knew of "no evidence" regarding the claim the officers were Muslim, or that Shariah or the Islamic faith played any role in the incident at all.
- The video made the social media rounds as a 3-minute clip with dramatic background music, showing NYPD officers questioning and detaining a woman walking her dog. At least one officer grabs hold of the dog's leash and also grabs the woman's arm. The clip's onscreen captions read: "Sharia is starting in NYC" and "Muslim police taking dog for disturbing the peace."
- A viewing of the original 16-minute video revealed that the officers didn't appear to actually take away the dog, and that they apparently charged her with disorderly conduct.
In early November, people shared a video allegedly showing two Muslim New York police officers taking away a woman's dog for disturbing the peace, supposedly as their way of enforcing Shariah (Islamic law).
Shariah serves to guide the moral and religious practices of Muslims, such as prayer, pilgrimages, fasting, charitable donations and personal virtue.
As a prime example of the rumor, on Nov. 8, an X user posted (archived) the 3-minute clip showing an incident that apparently began moments earlier. Two NYPD officers stand on a street corner at night, with one of the officers alleging that the woman, who identifies herself as a nurse who recently had surgery on her foot, was standing or dancing and recording a video "in the middle of the street" and wouldn't move to the sidewalk, blocking the officers' vehicle.
The officer grabs the woman's arm, briefly takes her dog's leash and tells her that if she doesn't identify herself, they will arrest her and take her "to prison," adding, "We'll take the dog, too." He then grabs her arm again.
The clip's soundtrack features dramatic music as the action takes place.
The onscreen caption reads, "Sharia is starting in NYC," and "Muslim police taking dog for disturbing the peace. Oh wait for that dog ban boy oh boy."
Reverse image searches found others sharing the same video and captions on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived), as well as clips with similar (archived) claims (archived).
The video appears authentic in that someone on the scene genuinely recorded it and did not create it with artificial intelligence.
The brief clip shared on social media omits 13 minutes of the original 16-minute video (archived), which shows that while one of the officers did briefly grab the dog's leash, it doesn't appear he actually took away the animal — nor did he or the other officer mention the dog as a problem. The longer, raw video not only lacks the dramatic music heard in the shorter clip but contains no mention of religion or Shariah at all.
TikTok user @nuyoricannomad, who said he recorded and first posted the raw video, told Snopes he knew of "no evidence" regarding the claim of the officers' religion playing a factor in the incident.
Pending more corroboration, Snopes hasn't added a fact-check rating to this article. We contacted the NYPD to ask questions and to request an incident report. We also filed a formal request to receive the police body camera footage. We will update this story if we receive further data.
People reposting the video with mentions of Shariah and a "dog ban" appeared to be playing on the exaggerated notion that Muslims hate dogs and view them as unclean. The stereotype apparently originates from an overgeneralization not from the Quran, but instead from the hadith, a narrative record of the sayings or customs of the Prophet Muhammad and his companions.
Video location and citation
In our interview with @nuyoricannomad — who wished to not be identified by name — he said he recorded the video around 3 a.m. Nov. 8. The incident occurred on the northwest corner of Second Avenue and East 39th Street in Manhattan's Murray Hill neighborhood.
According to @nuyoricannomad, both he and the woman, who he indicated is his friend, were walking north and using the East 39th Street crosswalk on the west side of Second Avenue. "We were walking slowly but she had recent surgery," he said, referencing her foot, which she briefly mentions in the clip (at 8:55).
At about the same time, the officers were traveling by car south on Second Avenue and attempting to make a right over the same crosswalk and onto East 39th Street, similar to the turning white SUV visible in this Google Street View image (archived).
Regarding charges for the woman, @nuyoricannomad said, "The citation was written for disorderly conduct." That charge, which Snopes is attempting to independently verify, would line up with a moment in the video in which one of the officers appears to make a phone call and mention disorderly conduct (at 3:30), possibly referencing New York state law's descriptor of obstructing vehicular or pedestrian traffic.
What the full video shows
The full video appears to begin moments after the incident started. One of the officers grabs the woman's arm and she tells him to stop touching her. He also takes her dog's leash for a brief period of time, tells her she will go to prison if she doesn't identify herself and says he'll take her dog, too. He doesn't clarify whether he's joking about taking the dog to prison or seriously warning he'll take her dog away if they take her into custody.
At least one person standing nearby tells the officers he's calling 911 to ask for a supervisor to come to the scene. One of the officers tells that person to stand back and says, "You can do whatever you want." (A user posting one popular Instagram video (archived) about the incident falsely claimed the officer said not "You" but "We," as in, "We can do whatever we want.")
The woman identifies herself as a nurse and challenges the officers' version of events. For example, one officer says, "You were in the middle of the street taking video." She responds, "I did not make a video." He then tells her she's being detained, saying, "You are not free to leave right now."
The woman says she had the right to walk across the crosswalk with a walk signal (at 6:25 and 8:10). We haven't yet been able to independently confirm the status of the traffic signal.
One of the officers alleges he, with the other officer in his passenger seat, was turning right and that the woman and others were in their way (ar 9:30). In that moment, he doesn't challenge the woman's claim she had the right of way with a walk signal.
Later in the video, an apparent police supervisor arrives and tells one of the officers to place @nuyoricannomad and another pedestrian under arrest if they interrupt the officers' investigation again (at 12:20).
The video ends with one of the officers appearing to hand a citation to the woman, who then appears to be free to leave with her dog and friends.
As to what started the incident, @nuyoricannomad told us that "at no point were we just standing on the crosswalk or 'dancing,'" referencing the officer's allegation that the woman had been dancing (at 8:55).
"The point of the video was to show how the cops mishandled the situation and escalated to a point that was not necessary," he said.

Dolly Vadalia, brought to India from Mozambique as a newborn, received her passport after a 26-year citizenship battle
NEW DELHI: A 26-year-old woman from Gujarat, whose Indian parents brought her to the country as an unregistered newborn while fleeing floods in Mozambique, has finally received an Indian passport after a prolonged citizenship battle. Dolly Vadalia received the passport on November 11, following a Union home ministry memorandum recognising her as an Indian citizen, news agency PTI reported citing her brother-in-law Ronak Vadalia on Monday.Born on February 18, 2000, in Xai-Xai, Mozambique, Dolly was just 18 to 20 days old when her parents evacuated her from the country after a tropical cyclone triggered massive floods. The family returned to India and settled in Rajkot, their hometown.Dolly's citizenship status became a hurdle after she married Khilankumar Vadalia, a Rajkot resident employed in Canada, in 2023. Her inability to obtain an Indian passport kept the couple separated.Her three passport applications, filed in 2023 and 2025, were rejected because she could not establish her Indian citizenship through the required documents. Authorities sought proof of cancellation of her emergency certificate or consular registration of her birth.
The matter was subsequently taken up with Lok Sabha MPs Ramesh Dhaduk and Parshottam Rupala, who forwarded it to the Rajkot collectorate, the Gandhinagar secretariat, the MHA and the MEA, Ronak said as cited by PTI.The MEA sought the MHA's opinion. In October last year, the home ministry reiterated that under Section 4(1)(b) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a child born outside India must have their birth registered at an Indian consulate within one year to claim citizenship by descent. Although Dolly had an Aadhaar card, it was not sufficient to establish her eligibility for an Indian passport, Ronak said.On April 30 this year, a single-judge bench of the Gujarat high court observed that Dolly's parents had not followed the mandatory birth registration procedure. It held that she was neither an Indian citizen by birth nor by descent under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act.
"The court advised us to apply for citizenship; however, we could not file an application initially because we lacked a valid passport — a mandatory requirement for the process," Ronak said, explaining why the family subsequently approached a division bench.Following a background check and verification, the Indian embassy in Mozambique and the MHA issued a memorandum."Based on this, Dolly's birth was registered with the Indian High Commission in Maputo, Mozambique, in November. Using that certificate, we applied for a passport, which we finally received last week," he said.

On Sunday’s Last Week Tonight, John Oliver channeled the anger felt by millions of Americans at last week’s nationwide FAA ground stop.
Oliver noted that official information was fairly scarce during most of the five hours when some 3,500 planes were grounded. He then suggested that, when they finally did appear on TV, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin weren’t quite up to the task of explaining the situation to Americans.
After calling Mullin a “moron,” Oliver had this for Duffy: “Rather than use that press conference to dispense information, which would have been ideal, he instead took it as an opportunity to air grievances and make demands.”
Watch on Deadline
The show then cut to a clip of Duffy.
“What went down was old. It was old, legacy equipment that failed,” said the secretary. “And, listen, it’s going to continue to fail…The president for the last year has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system…The president’s asked for $30B. I want $50B. I can’t build things if i don’t have money…I want &50B. President Trump is a builder. He is going to build this network for the American people.”
Oliver couldn’t contain himself.
“What are you doing going on TV to demand $50B?!” he asked. “You sound less like a secretary of transportation trying to calm people down and more like a Batman villain trying to hold Gotham hostage! ‘I need $50B unless the Batman can solve my riddles in time!'”
Oliver admitted that Duffy is right about one thing: U.S. flight systems are outdated. But the Last Week Tonight host pointed out that Republicans have had both houses of Congress (and the presidency) for the past two years, so if there’s a complaint about underfunding, it should land on their collective doorstep. He also pointed out that the Republican Congress and the administration collaborated to nearly triple ICE’s budget last year to $28B, an amount that surpasses the annual budgets of almost all other major federal law enforcement agencies combined.
Oliver then went in for the kill.
“It is hard to take a panicked shakedown from Duffy, not just because his cost estimate jumped by $20B mid-sentence, but also because he’s part of a flagrantly-corrupt administration who spent a chunk of his time in office shooting a shitty reality show with his family to encourage Americans to take more road trips.” [Duffy, his wife and their nine kids shot The Great American Road Trip over seven months this year and last.]
“To that end,” said Oliver in reference to both the show and the recent flight stoppage, “guess what, Sean? Mission f*cking accomplished!”
Batman villains are more competent and have a plan.

A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
As retirees live longer, governments need to spend more on pensions. That makes it harder to fund other services, spurring protests like those planned this weekend in France.
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.
“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.
But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.
“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”
This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one that is at the heart of mass antigovernment demonstrations planned for Saturday in France, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?
“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.

The IT ministry (MeitY) has opened the registration process for consent managers under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023. The registration framework, which came into effect on November 13, will enable eligible Indian companies to apply for registration. IT secretary S Krishnan also launched an online portal, dpbi.gov.in today to enable the companies to submit their applications to the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI). A consent manager is an entity registered with the DPBI that enables individuals, referred to as data principals (DPs) under the Act, to give, manage, review and withdraw consent for the processing of their personal data through an interoperable platform. The framework seeks to give individuals greater control over how their personal information is used and strengthen accountability in the digital ecosystem. Consent managers will be accountable to data principals. Companies incorporated in India with adequate technical, operational and financial capacity can apply for registration as Consent Managers. They must have a minimum net worth of ₹2 Cr to qualify. "The framework marks an important step towards operationalising a system that enables data principals to exercise greater control over consent relating to their personal data. It forms part of the phased implementation of the DPDP framework and enables eligible entities to seek registration and prepare to offer consent management services," MeitY said. The DPBI will assess the applicants against the prescribed requirements and will approve the companies that meet the eligibility criteria. A list of registered consent managers will be made publicly available on the Board's website. DPDP Act: Key Provisions And Implementation Timeline The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 establishes a legal framework for processing digital personal data in India. It also defines the rights of individuals and obligations of organisations handling their personal information. The legislation was passed by the Parliament in August 2023. It identifies two key entities: data fiduciaries and data principals. A data fiduciary is an organisation that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data. This includes banks collecting customer details, ecommerce platforms storing purchase histories and companies maintaining employee records. A data principal, meanwhile, is the individual to whom the personal data belongs. Under the Act, data fiduciaries must obtain consent before processing personal data, except in specified circumstances permitted under the law. Such consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous. They must also inform individuals about the purpose of collecting their data and how it will be used. The law also grants data principals several rights, including the right to access information about the processing of their personal data, seek correction and erasure, withdraw consent and raise grievances. They can also nominate another person to exercise their rights in certain circumstances. On the compliance front, data fiduciaries are required to implement reasonable security safeguards to protect personal information. They must also notify the DPBI and affected individuals in the event of a data breach, in accordance with the prescribed framework. The Act also provides additional safeguards for children's data. It requires verifiable parental consent before processing the personal data of children below 18 years and restricts tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children, subject to specified exemptions. The implementation framework took shape with MeitY notifying the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, in November last year. The rules lay down a phased timeline for bringing the Act's provisions into effect. According to a Press Information Bureau (PIB) backgrounder published in November 2025, the government received 6,915 inputs during the consultation process from startups, MSMEs, industry bodies, civil society organisations, government departments and citizens. The rollout will continue in phases. The provisions concerning the rights of data principals, obligations of data fiduciaries, and the DPBI’s inquiry and penalty processes are scheduled to come into effect on May 13, 2027.

The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.
Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.
“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”
That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”
Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”
Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.
Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”
Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.
Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”
Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”
Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.
In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.
Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”

STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.
The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.
The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.
When it came time for the first stage to return to the ground, it dropped like a rock. However, due to an unspecified issue, the vehicle was commanded to divert into the Gulf rather than return to the Starbase facility to be caught by the launch tower. It created a fantastically powerful explosion, even for observers more than 10 miles away.
Primary mission, a success
The primary aim of Friday’s launch was the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites from a narrow door at the base of the spacecraft. This occurred about 40 minutes into Starship’s flight, and all 26 satellites—which have solar panels that stretch 60 meters end to end when fully deployed—safely made it into orbit, where they will now use onboard propulsion to raise their altitude.
This means that Starship is now an operational, orbital rocket. It is the largest and most powerful machine humans have ever launched into space. The challenge for the company now is to make Starship reusable and dramatically increase its flight rate.
In that sense, the first part of Friday’s mission was not a success. SpaceX had hoped to return the first-stage booster, refurbish it, and fly it again. The company has previously landed and reflown Starship boosters but has yet to do so with the latest iteration of the vehicle, version 3.

IFS Sanjeev Chaturvedi moves SC seeking framework to protect whistleblowers
New Delhi, Magsaysay Award winner and whistleblower Indian Forest Service officer Sanjeev Chaturvedi has moved the Supreme Court seeking protection of whistleblowers and appropriate guidelines to bridge the constitutional and "statutory vacuum" that has been caused by the non-operationalisation of a 2014 law.
Chaturvedi, who has exposed some corruption cases in the past and is facing several cases by private persons and action by different governments, said in his plea filed in a pending petition that this continuity of institutional persecution in the absence of any protective framework is not an exceptional case; it is the systemic norm.
"The absence of the Whistleblowers Protection Act's operational framework means there is no single institutional mechanism to which a whistleblower in the petitioner's position can turn for protection, and no authority charged with the specific task of preventing and investigating retaliation," he submitted.
"This structural vacuum is the condition that enables the petitioner's persecutors to act with impunity, and it will continue to enable such persecution indefinitely unless this court intervenes," he submitted.
The senior IFS officer said the present application, while filed by an individual petitioner, raises a constitutional/systematic issue of nationwide importance that affects every public servant and citizen who has made, or may make, a public interest disclosure.
The relief sought is not merely personal; it is systemic, he said and sought to enlarge and expand the scope of the present writ petition to convert into redressal of an issue of constitutional importance: the failure on the part of the Centre to operationalise the Whistleblowers Protection Act, 2014, which has remained a "dead letter" for over a decade despite being enacted by Parliament in 2014, resulting in incessant misery of the petitioner and many other similarly placed whistleblowers.
He also sought the court's intervention under Article 142 of the Constitution to frame and issue an appropriate interim Whistleblowers Protection Framework/ guidelines to bridge the constitutional and statutory vacuum that has been allowed to persist, leaving whistleblowers across India entirely without statutory protection.
"The inaction of the executive is not merely a policy failure- it is a constitutionally impermissible abdication of a statutory obligation that strikes at the foundational rights of whistleblowers as well as citizens guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution, creates a nationwide chilling effect on anti-corruption disclosures, undermines the very rule of law, which this court has consistently sought to fortify and continues to keep the lives of whistleblowers under tenterhooks," he said.
Referring to repetitive actions against him, Chaturvedi said it underlines the need for robust institutional protection for whistleblowers in India, as only name and faces of perpetrators of corruption changes and nothing else, and hence urgent need for effective protection mechanism for whistleblowers, which is completely lacking at this moment.
Giving details of the enactment, he said the Whistleblowers Protection Act, 2014 was notified on May 12, 2014, after being passed by Parliament. However, in terms of provision of sub-section of section 1 of the Act, the provisions of the Act had to come into force on such date as the Central government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, may fix.
"No such notification has been made by the Central government on the grounds that the Act requires amendments aimed at safeguarding against disclosures affecting sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, etc., before it is brought into force," his plea said.
It said to make these amendments to the Act, the Centre introduced the Whistle Blowers Protection Bill, 2015 in the Lok Sabha on May 11, 2015, which was passed by the Lok Sabha on May 13, 2015 and transmitted to the Rajya Sabha.
"The Bill has since lapsed upon the dissolution of the 16th Lok Sabha. Since then, the government has taken no legislative initiative whatsoever to re-introduce the Bill or to enact the requisite amendments, nor has the government considered bringing the existing Act into force even without the proposed amendments, and prescribing appropriate rules to address the purported concerns, with the result that the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, is still non-operational/dysfunctional," his plea said.
He said despite the rising tide of corruption, whistleblowers in India face numerous challenges, including retaliation and hostility from the organisations/departments or individuals they expose, including threats to life and livelihood, institutional barriers, and a lack of anonymity in reporting mechanisms.
"As India continues to position itself as a global economic powerhouse, strengthened whistleblower protection mechanisms are imperative and could be a critical step toward combating the malaise of corruption," he submitted.

Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
- Published
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.
But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.
His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," one woman watching the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.
Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.
There's a sense of injustice that Australia can't escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja was telling the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".
Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Cameron Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.
Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.
But he was also frank - using strong words to reject Khawaja's claims and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."
As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioning Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.
"I don't know what the outcome will be."

Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy can lead to severe outcomes, including preterm birth, stillbirth and congenital abnormalities in newborns, prompting experts at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) to highlight maternal health risks and call for targeted adaptation strategies.
The issue comes into focus as countries at COP31 prepare to discuss progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, a framework to help nations develop key adaptation measures, including those needed to address the health impacts of climate change.
However, translating growing recognition of climate-related health risks into action remains a challenge, particularly in the absence of adequate financial support.
According to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), only about one per cent of formal climate finance under its financial mechanism is currently directed towards health.
The broader issue of adaptation finance for developing nations is also expected to feature prominently in discussions in the coming days.
Speaking to PTI on the sidelines of COP31, Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at the Wellcome Trust, said the foundation is seeking to highlight the evidence of heat-related impacts on pregnant women through three key areas -- elevating the issues as a risk for women, developing guidelines and preparing health systems.
“We have three key points: recognising that pregnant women are a particularly vulnerable group when it comes to climate-driven extreme heat, developing guidelines to help nurses, midwives and doctors respond to the challenges pregnant women face during heatwaves, and prepare health systems for a new world shaped by climate change, and identify the most vulnerable people so they are protected,” Dangour said.
He said pregnant women were not always recognised as a particularly vulnerable group and stressed that health systems must specifically account for their needs and risks during heatwaves.
“At the moment they are not recognised as such, and they need to be included in clinical guidelines. When it comes to data, we are keen that countries record the impacts of climate change on pregnant women and then work out how their guidelines and processes can protect them,” he said.
“That evidence is important because we can see what works and what doesn’t in different parts of the world, and share that knowledge,” he said.
Former World Health Organisation (WHO) chief scientist Soumya Swaminathan stressed the importance of highlighting the issue at COP31, saying the health impacts of climate change were already being felt and required immediate action.
“It is good that for the last three COPs or so we have had a day focused on health and climate, because everyone is increasingly recognising that the health impacts of climate change are already happening and need immediate action. They are also hitting certain vulnerable groups disproportionately, and pregnant women are one of them,” Swaminathan told PTI.
Citing studies showing that exposure to extreme heat can affect pregnant women's health, pregnancy outcomes and the health of newborns, she said the WHO had recently released a document identifying pregnant women as a high-risk group and recommending measures countries should take to protect them.
She also stressed the need to integrate climate and health data, saying policymakers must urgently begin linking exposure to extreme heat and air pollutants with their effects on human health.
“When heat and air pollution occur together in the same place, the impacts are three times as high as from either risk factor alone. India has many places with both heat and bad air pollution, so we must start looking at these data and correlating exposure to climatic and weather variables, such as heat and pollutants, with health outcomes,” the former WHO chief scientist told PTI.
Swaminathan said there was an urgent need for a research programme to address the issue, adding that sufficient evidence was already available to warrant action. She also called for the government's and states' Maternal and Child Health Programme to factor in heat exposure and take proactive and preventive measures to minimise its impact on pregnant women.
Youssef Nassef, Director of the Adaptation Programme at UN Climate Change, said the first 1,000 days, from conception until a child turns two, were considered the most critical period, as climate-related harm could begin even before birth.
“A lot of what we're talking about in terms of climate impacts generally, but heat in particular, has a severe impact on maternal health, on newborn babies. Unfortunately, in climate finance, about 1 per cent of formal climate finance under the financial mechanism goes to health. There is an incongruence between the needs, the demand and the supply,” he said.
Bhavreen Kandhari, an environmentalist and the co-founder of the ‘Warrior Moms’ movement, underscored that heatwaves have had a significant impact on pregnant women, particularly those living in more vulnerable areas or working in more vulnerable occupations, such as daily-wage workers, construction workers and farmers.
“Daily-wage workers, for instance, have to earn a living. They have to continue working because they simply cannot afford to stop. There is no looking back for them. Vulnerable mothers and other at-risk groups are not thinking about the future, but simply trying to survive this particular season, or, at most, looking ahead to the next one,” she said.

Instability in a system that allows communications between the Federal Aviation Administration, air traffic controllers, and pilots was responsible for the country’s most disastrous nationwide ground stop in air traffic since September 11. The ground stop lasted five hours.
Several outlets reported that a failure in the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network was linked to the FAA’s decision to declare a ground stop. The FTI is the private communications backbone for the air traffic control system. The system is in the midst of a major, multiyear modernization project, which involves replacing a decades-old network of copper wire with high-speed fiber-optic cables. The FAA has said the update will reduce outages and outage-related delays, and make the system safer. It will also be equipped to more easily handle newer aircraft, including drones, electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOLs), and other “air taxis.”
At the time the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, over 6,300 flights within, into, or out of the US had been canceled, according to the aviation tech company FlightAware; 9,500 had been delayed. Freight and mail flights have also been affected. It will likely take days, if not weeks, for airlines to reposition aircraft and crew and get their schedules back on track.
“It will take us some time to unwind what has happened,” US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said in a Friday evening briefing at the White House. He blamed “old switches, old routers,” and a “data overload” for the communications system failure. He said a “legacy system”—likely referring to FTI—was involved.
The issue was caused by “putting patches into the system” as new equipment was being installed, US Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin said at the White House briefing. “The new technology was overwhelming the older system,” he said.
Mullin said there were no indications that the outage was related to a cyberattack, but “there’s not complete certainty right now.”
The system is managed by the government contractor L3Harris Technologies. On its website, L3Harris says that its “team’s deep knowledge of the US national airspace allows us to upgrade systems without disrupting air traffic operations.” A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment.
In May, L3Harris said it had completed 50 percent of its modernization project. Seventy percent of FAA sites have been upgraded to fiber, the company said earlier this month. The Trump administration has said it aims to overhaul the nation’s air traffic control system by the end of 2028.
In August, the FAA tapped AT&T to upgrade the FTI, the private FAA communication network, to an entirely new system. That contract is worth $73 million, though its worth is likely to climb into the billions over the years. Previously, Verizon had been selected to build and operate this new system. L3Harris is meant to operate the legacy system until the upgrades are in place.
Earlier Friday, before the ground stop, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy sent a letter to congressional leaders asking them to approve his department’s request for $30.1 billion in funding to further upgrade the air traffic control system and to improve airports. On Friday, he upped the ask: “I want $50 billion,” he said during a briefing at the White House.
A September report published by the US Government Accountability Office raised concerns that the FAA’s attempt to accelerate long-delayed modernization plans “could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruption.” It found that the FAA does not have a “well-documented” life-cycle cost estimate for its programs, and that, rather than a master schedule guiding the sprawling project, has 11,389 schedules that are not integrated.
