The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.
The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.
“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”
ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.
“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.
Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.
“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.
For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.
Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.
This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.
A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.
The former general is separately being investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.
For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.
The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.
The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.
However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.
Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.
More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.
A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.
“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
- Published
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.
In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.
"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.
"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.
Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.
"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.
"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

Buongiorno! Today’s stories have me wondering what it must be like to study the human brain: Every new discovery is a breathtaking revelation, and also a reminder of how little we know, and how far the horizon of full understanding still is. It feels a little like looking at the universe, only what is infinite is, in the most literal sense, ourselves.
The homegrown experiments trying to free kids from their phones
For many teenagers, phones are pervasive — and destructive. And the policy proposals and scientific research meant to address the crisis are moving too slowly to help a generation already hooked on screens.
But as STAT’s Isabella Cueto reports, a variety of homegrown initiatives are filling the gap, many of them led by teens. Some programs draw inspiration from Alcoholics Anonymous, helping teens develop tools and strategies to refocus and put their devices away. Others are pushing teens to understand the financial incentives behind holding their attention. The techniques are as varied as they are creative: public interventions, manifestos, and overall a movement that is reclaiming attention, real life connections and, ultimately, freedom. Read all about it here.
The weight of knowing you are at risk of Alzheimer’s
Biomarker-based diagnostics have improved our understanding of who may develop severe dementia, advancing our knowledge of Alzheimer’s disease and the hope of finding effective early treatment.
Yet for the people who become aware of their heightened risk, the knowledge is bittersweet. The information allows them to act by taking drugs that may delay dementia onset, but it also carries a weight. In a new First Opinion, Neurotransmissions columnist Jason Karlawish shares how learning of elevated risk changed people’s outlook on the future, from bucket lists to plans for care, to considerations about assisted suicide. (And in case you missed it, check out the first installment in this miniseries here.)
We finally have a map of the brain’s ‘Grand Central’
The basal ganglia is a gumball-sized region of the brain so central to psychiatric and neurologic conditions that one scientist called it “the Grand Central station of disease.”
Now a massive scientific collaboration has created a map of the area, including a list of which cells are present and how they arranged. This research has led to the discovery of a new type of neuron, and the identification of cells linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Authors consider it a “monumental achievement” that opens the door for understanding the brain in health and disease, but further progress may be at stake amid government funding cuts, Jonathan Wosen reports.
Takeaways from STAT’s investigation into the MRT tourism industry
When STAT’s Megan Molteni started investigating the experimental reproductive procedure known as MRT, or mitochondrial replacement techniques, she didn’t know that she would uncover a sprawling international network of clinics that that market to older women.
Over the course of her reporting, she also found evidence that MRT can effectively treat age-related infertility is lacking. In fact, data obtained by STAT shows MRT doesn’t work for patients of advanced maternal age.
Read more of her takeaways from this eight-month investigation here. And if you haven’t already read Megan’s original investigation, I encourage you to dig in.
Brain implant startup pauses trials
Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation brain-computer interface. The Brooklyn-based startup’s device was a wireless version of its first-generation device, which snakes a catheter through veins to park a stent near the brain’s motor cortex. The aim was to connect users to digital devices using brain activity. The pause is not safety related, leaders said.
It’s the first major hiccup for Synchron, one of the leading companies in a fast-growing industry aimed at helping people with disabilities like ALS and paralysis regain independence through brain implants. Synchron will also eliminate jobs in New York City and is working to develop a new device, WIRED reported.
The news gives context to a cryptic comment CEO Tom Oxley gave on a conference panel in New York City last week. “There are hundreds of components in our system, and it just takes a delayed one to slow down your submission to the FDA,” said Oxley, flanked by his competitors at Neuralink and Precision Neuroscience. “We had one particular component that we were caught up on.” – O. Rose Broderick
El-Sayed: ‘We’ve created the space for a few grifters to come in and … lie to the public”
Come January, Abdul El-Sayed will be the first epidemiologist in the Senate. His election comes as the U.S. is struggling through a spike in measles cases, a Dengue fever outbreak, and a recent foodborne illness crisis.
STAT’s Nick Florko spoke with the senator-elect about how he hopes to rebuild trust in science, as well as who’s responsible for the current state of affairs. “We didn’t have to get here,” El-Sayed said. “In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information-mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame … our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.” Read the whole meaty interview here.

India has seen a 38% reduction in tuberculosis (TB) mortality since 2015, compared to a global average of 35%, and a 94% treatment success rate among patients with drug-susceptible TB, according to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report 2026.
Last year, the South-East Asia Region recorded the largest number of new TB cases (35%), followed by the Western Pacific Region (27%) and the African Region (25%).
Around 88% of new TB cases occurred in 30 countries. India, Indonesia (10%), the Philippines (6.8%), China (6.5%), Pakistan (6.4%), Nigeria (4.9%), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (3.9%) and Bangladesh (3.7%) accounted for about two-thirds of the global total.
The top five countries made up 55% of the total.
Globally, about 50% of people treated for TB and their households face total costs (direct medical expenditures, non-medical expenditures, and indirect costs such as income losses) that are catastrophic (greater than 20% of total household income).
People with compromised immune systems, such as those living with HIV, undernutrition or diabetes, or people who use tobacco have a higher risk of falling ill. An estimated 9.6 lakh new TB cases were attributable to undernutrition, 9.2 lakh to diabetes, 7.3 lakh to alcohol use disorders, 6.9 lakh to smoking and 5.5 lakh to HIV infection.
The report showed a total of 1.13 million people died from TB in 2025. Globally, TB is the world’s leading cause of death from a single infectious agent. Last year, an estimated 10.6 million people fell ill with TB worldwide, including 5.7 million men, 3.7 million women and 1.2 million children.
Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) remains a public health crisis and a health security threat. Only about two in five people with drug-resistant TB received treatment in 2025. Global efforts to combat TB have saved an estimated 86 million lives since 2000.
Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria that most often affects the lungs. It spreads through the air when people with TB cough, sneeze or spit. TB is preventable and curable.
Between December 7, 2024 and November 8, 2026, the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan achieved significant progress, identifying and bringing over 25 crore individuals within the scope of screening activities.
“India’s reduction in TB mortality has been the result of interventions under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), including proactive case finding including use of AI-enabled X-rays, rapid diagnostics, prompt treatment initiation, differentiated TB care, and nutritional support through the Nikshay Poshan Yojana and Nikshay Mitra initiative. These interventions were supported by AI tools for identification of hotspots, prediction of high-risk TB cases prone for adverse outcomes, Khushi – AI Chatbot & Avatar Videobot, etc.,” the Union Health Ministry statement said.

'They will kill you too': Sonia Gandhi's turbulent journey in Indian politics
- Published
On the morning of 31 October 1984, Sonia Gandhi was a young wife and mother, living in the prime minister's residence in Delhi. She was about to take a bath when she heard shots ring out in the garden.
Her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, India's prime minister, had just left for her office in an adjoining building. Moments later, she would be assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in retaliation for the Indian army's storming of the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Sikhism's holiest shrine, earlier that year.
The sound was like firecrackers, but "different". The children's nanny came pounding on the bathroom door, hysterical, pointing towards the garden.
Sonia ran towards the path. A white Ambassador car was moving slowly towards her. Inside, Indira lay covered in blood, her sari stained, her eyes open, her face wearing what Sonia remembered as a look of surprise.
"Mummy, Mummy," she tried to say. No words came. At the hospital, she waited for hours before a doctor's shake of the head told her what she feared.
The ordeal did not end there. Rajiv Gandhi, her husband and the elder son of Indira Gandhi, summoned from a rally in West Bengal, arrived to tell her that party leaders wanted him to become prime minister.
Sonia's response was fury and terror. "They will kill you; they will kill you, too!" she pleaded. Rajiv replied: "They will kill me anyway." That evening, as Indira's body lay at home, Rajiv was sworn in.
It is one of the most searing passages in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's new memoir: private devastation unfolding alongside the pressures of public life.
The woman who had largely stayed away from politics was now married to India's prime minister, and would eventually find herself at the head of the Congress party, leading it through two general election victories and becoming one of the country's most consequential political figures.
The passage also foreshadows another devastating loss. In 1991, Rajiv himself was assassinated.
For Sonia, the years that followed were marked by retreat.
At 19, a young woman from a small Italian town, she had met Rajiv, an Indian student, in England. Their relationship took her into a new country and family, and a close bond with Indira followed. India became home through her husband and her mother-in-law.
After Rajiv's killing, even the public appearances required by the memorial trusts she headed became an ordeal. Before speeches, she feared tears would overwhelm her.
When the Dalai Lama asked whether she felt vengeful towards her husband's killers, she answered, "No, I don't," and burst into sobs. Slowly, she writes, Rajiv became "a presence within me rather than a piercing absence".
But grief returned at family milestones. At her son Rahul's Cambridge graduation in 1995, she and her children were overcome by the thought of how proud Rajiv would have been.
Politics, meanwhile, was closing in. The Congress party, the political vehicle of her husband's family for generations, was losing cohesion and electoral ground. Senior leaders were defecting, and the calls for Sonia to step in were growing louder.
She initially refused. She writes she had seen politics through Rajiv: its achievements, but also its "ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery". "I'd always disliked politics," she writes. It had taken first her mother-in-law, then "the love of my life, my children's father".
Yet the party's decline began to feel personal. Walking past photographs of Indira and Rajiv, she was seized by "a mixture of pain and guilt". She feared that the forces they had fought to "protect India's pluralistic ethos" were gaining ground: a rising Hindu nationalism that, in her view, threatened the "secular and pluralistic vision" of India they had sought to defend.
Congress leaders argued that without her, the party could splinter, leaving little to resist communal politics. The family name, she believed, carried an appeal beyond religion, caste, language and region. This, she says, was "the most compelling argument".
Her doubts were also about her own credentials. How could an outsider occupy a position held by two formidable figures? At home, Rahul and Priyanka feared losing their mother as they had lost their grandmother and father. Before a New Year holiday, they extracted a promise: "Don't you do anything crazy while we're away."
The "answer", she says, came through the Bhagavad Gita. Though not religious in adult life, Sonia arranged private lessons with a Sanskrit scholar in January 1997. They read the text verse by verse. She writes that its central message – to perform one's dharma, or duty, without attachment to the fruits of one's actions – eventually resolved her inner conflict.
"I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did."
The memoir's most dramatic political scene, however, comes seven years later, after Congress's 2004 election victory. Sonia had led the party's campaign.
Sonia goes with Manmohan Singh to meet India's president at the presidential palace in Delhi and formally stake the Congress-led alliance's claim to form a government. Everyone assumes she will become prime minister. She says nothing.
At home, she tells a senior aide she intends to refuse. Party workers gather at the gates; senior colleagues demand a meeting.
"You fought the election, you led us," says one. "People believed in you. How can you let them down like this? Our workers will revolt. You think they'll accept another leader?"
Alliance leaders arrive to persuade her. They surround her, she recalls, and one insists: "We will not take no for an answer." Overwhelmed, she murmurs "Theek hai" - all right. They take it as consent and begin congratulating her.
Her children are appalled, she writes. Rahul storms in: "You said yes?" Her daughter Priyanka urges her not to be forced into a decision.
Sonia writes she spends a long night arguing with herself, friends and family. The risk is not merely personal. She believes the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would continue to exploit her foreign birth and that accepting office would allow the controversy to "create havoc" and hurt the country. By morning she is clear. "I've made up my mind. I'm going to stick to my stand," she tells Rahul.
She chooses Singh, a trained economist and a party member, instead, describing him as a man "above reproach", with a "deep and consummate understanding of governance".
The book is at its most revealing when it turns from family memory to the India she believes has been lost.
Sonia says that when she entered public life there was "a certain decency and decorum in parliamentary politics".
Political attacks and harsh words were not new, but she sees a sharper appetite among those in power "to belittle and torment those who differ from them, to intimidate those they perceive as opponents". It is, she says, part of a wider international drift towards "a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes".
Her portrait of prime minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP is unusually direct.
The two have had "practically no real contact", she writes, beyond formal greetings at parliamentary gatherings and occasional exchanges - "Theek hain, aap?" ("Are you all right?") - when she returned from hospital. "He tends to look away," she says, "avoiding eye contact."
Modi's idea of India, she writes, was shaped by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and "affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others". His is an India of "hierarchy, order, and control"; hers is "an India against hegemony", standing for "inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice".
There is a striking concession amid the polemic - she says she understood Modi's "discomfort with the ruling elite of our times".
Sonia says she felt uneasy in Delhi's privileged drawing rooms, where political conversation seemed "very far removed from the reality of India".
Modi's origins, she writes, "may not be as humble as his PR team" suggests, but he "had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world". It is a rare acknowledgement of the social distance between the Congress establishment and the electorate Modi came to represent.
The memoir also offers some glimpses of Sonia's encounters with world leaders.
She remembers Vladimir Putin as an "engaging personality" who took her on a boat ride in St Petersburg, pointing out monuments along the way. She says she was impressed by his grasp of geopolitics and his "determination to restore Russia to its former powerful status" - "long before the Ukraine war, a different era".
A more amusing encounter involved France's Nicolas Sarkozy, who arrived in India in 2008 without his then partner Carla Bruni because they were unmarried.
At a state banquet, the Indian vice-president's wife cheerfully grilled him about when he planned to marry her, whether he missed her and whether a date had been fixed. Sarkozy obligingly answered her questions while messaging Bruni on his phone.
Belonging is not a neutral history. The Bofors gun scandal, which badly damaged Rajiv Gandhi's government and dogged the family for decades, gets a relatively brief treatment.
The 502-page memoir is less forthcoming about the less flattering aspects of Congress's own record. Sonia has much to say about political corruption, hypocrisy and the decline of public standards under her opponents, but largely sidesteps the culture of patronage, cronyism and corruption that dogged Congress during its years in power. There is little reckoning, either, with the party's own share of responsibility for the erosion of public trust.
She is at pains to defend the political inheritance of her husband and mother-in-law, even as the party they built has suffered a prolonged decline. The story she tells is as much about the costs of carrying that inheritance as it is about a woman who says she never wanted the life she ended up leading.
That gives the memoir's final pages an unmistakable melancholy. Sonia, 79, is now a member of the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of parliament. Rahul, 55, is a four-term MP and leader of the opposition; Priyanka, 53, is also a member of parliament.
Sonia says the challenge was to remain faithful to "a just and humane society", through pain and loss, victory and defeat, and the manoeuvring that politics demands. But she ends not with triumph, nor even with the assurance that history will vindicate her.
"At this moment it seems to me that, although I tried my best, I didn't succeed in beating back the forces I'd set out to fight."

One of the most eye-opening aspects of last week’s midterms was the new cohort of religious politicians it sent to Congress — many of them part of a wave of Democratic-leaning Christians.
Democrats made shocking gains with religious voters — but not everywhere
Catholics voted Democrat, and evangelicals stayed home. Is this a fluke, or the start of a new reality for both parties?
Another striking feature was the dramatic shift among many religious voters.
For years, American politics has seemed stuck on a partisan track, with religious-identified voters shifting more firmly to the right, and the nonreligious tacking to the left. There are a few exceptions, of course — Jewish voters, Latino Catholics, and Black Protestants, who have stayed firmly Democratic — but the broader tide has flowed clearly one way.
Key takeaways
- This year’s blue tsunami carried voters everywhere to the left; it also scrambled voting trends in America’s religious electorate.
- Catholics shifted hard to the left after Donald Trump won their vote by a double-digit margin in 2024.
- Jewish voters were still strongly Democratic, though there are clear signs of lower support than in previous electoral cycles.
- Other religious groups, mainline Protestants and Muslims, contributed to a diverse Democratic coalition — while evangelicals appeared less enthusiastic to turn out.
The 2026 vote, for the first time in a while, makes that picture look less certain. Based on exit polls, county-level data, and some post-election analysis, we already have a handful of intriguing signs of change. The data is still early and patchy, but it appears that Catholic voters around the country moved left, evangelical Christians stayed home, and some Jewish voters dug in against the anti-Israel rhetoric and moved rightward. And in Utah, generational differences, particularly among Mormons, may be starting to change the political makeup of a rock-ribbed conservative state.
There are caveats: Wave elections, especially when they’re of the historic proportions of last week’s Democratic tsunami, can obscure and cloud these changes. When everyone moves in one direction, it can be hard to distinguish specific storylines. And with religion, as with any single voter attribute, it can be difficult to tease out just how much faith and religious identity influenced vote choice, as opposed to working in combination with race, class, and concerns about issues like affordability and immigration.
And better data is still to come; the gold standard of voter roll-validated studies, like the Pew Research Center’s, won’t be available until next year.
Yet that combination of factors also suggests a new possibility for our politics: that religious voters of all creeds can come to function as swing voters too, cracking up old alliances, like on the religious right, and offering the hint of new winning coalitions, as Catholics and mainline Protestant Christians seem to have done for the Democrats.
The largest shift: Catholic voters swung against the GOP
Catholics play a special role in American politics. They spent much of the last century operating as a solid Democratic bloc, reaching a peak in the 1960s when John F. Kennedy, the first Catholic president, won about 80 percent of their vote. Since then, they’ve gradually become more Republican, due to assimilation of former European Catholic immigrants, the rise of conservative activism over abortion and social issues, and the rise of the religious right.
In the last two decades, Catholics have tended to reflect the views of the median American voter, evenly split in the 2012, 2016, and 2020 presidential elections. But that changed in 2024. Across different polls and surveys, Catholics shifted decisively to the right: backing Trump 59-39 according to exit polls, and 55-43, according to the Pew Research Center.
Now, in a year in which Trump and Republicans frequently clashed with Pope Leo XIV and his bishops — over the Iran war, mass deportations, and immigration policy — Catholic voters again turned into a wild card.
This year, according to exit polls, they swung left, with the margin shifting by more than 20 points. Democrats narrowly won the Catholic vote this time, 50-49. As a subgroup, that put Catholics up there with Asian voters, Latinos, urban and suburban voters, Gen Z and millennials as being the top groups that swung to the left this year.
Other estimates from the religion and politics scholar Ryan Burge show particularly noticeable shifts among white Catholics, swinging about 9 points toward Democrats, even if a majority of them still voted for Republican congressional candidates. In Texas, his analysis showed that counties with higher shares of Latino Catholics were much more likely to support the winning Democratic Senate candidate, James Talarico.
The results were even more dramatic in the most Catholic House districts. Of the 12 districts with the highest share of Catholics, the average swing in the vote was about 15 points, and Democrats won eight of these seats, while gaining in all 12.
Catholics have tended to basically operate like the median voter — swinging in the same direction as the overall popular vote. That makes it harder to pinpoint any unique motivators that caused Catholics to move against the GOP: Trump’s fights with Catholic leaders, the lack of a mobilized anti-abortion movement this year, or the affordability concerns that moved all voters.
One notable exception here are Latino Catholics, who tend to be the most Democratic of the Catholic electorate, and most opposed to Trump’s immigration and deportation policies this cycle. It’s no coincidence that they’re concentrated in the Southwest, including those parts of Texas that swung toward Talarico and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa over both economic stress and anger over immigration enforcement.
Does this all suggest the rise of a new Catholic swing vote? Potentially — combined with the decline in abortion politics in the US, and a more active Vatican. For the first time, the Church has an American pope, one who isn’t afraid to get involved with current affairs and push harder on Catholic social teachings (which align more with the Democratic Party’s views of society and the economy). That could have meaningful repercussions heading into 2028.
Though still very blue, some Jewish voters broke with the Democrats
Jewish Americans, though they only make up about 2 percent of the American population, became a huge focus of political attention this year — in large part because of how central they are to Democratic coalitions (along with Black Americans, they are some of the most loyal Democratic voters), and because Israel became a flashpoint in American politics.
As Democrats made a dramatic shift in the last two years in how they talk about Israel and AIPAC, with increasingly open criticism of the Israeli government’s actions, some Jewish Democrats and Republicans responded with charges of antisemitism — and some Republicans started leaning into overt Islamophobia, particularly in Michigan. In turn, Republicans made bold predictions that Democrats would see a large drop in support this year, especially in Michigan (with an anti-Israel Senate candidate) and New York, where they counted on Jewish voters to rally to the more pro-Israel party.
In the end, there was no mass exodus of Jewish voters — but the exit polls did report a slight shift toward the GOP this year: 68-31, compared to 78-22 in 2024. Other post-election surveys show similar dynamics. (The numbers can vary, in part because different pollsters use different metrics for measuring Jewish support and identity, and also because exit polls can be imprecise.) The Jewish Electorate Institute’s polling from the Mellman Group, for example, shows that while Democrats still held a large, 44-point advantage at the end of the day, (69 percent to the 25 percent that backed the GOP) that was smaller than the margin in 2024, and nearly 20 points smaller than their margin in 2018’s blue wave. That’s an anomaly, given the scale of the tsunami this year.
Even the most Democratic-friendly poll, from GBAO Strategies, had a kind of rightward signal, though a longer-horizon one: It showed nearly identical levels of Democratic support among Jewish voters this year as in 2024 — but both those figures, about 70 percent, are lower than Jewish Democratic support in 2022 (74 percent) and 2020 (77 percent), noted The Forward.
This shift away from Democrats looked especially dramatic in Michigan, where The Forward also noted last week that the winning Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed underperformed other Democratic candidates in precincts with large Jewish populations. In another piece of data, a Michigan exit poll from the NORC-Civic Health and Elections Project, there was a more dramatic result, albeit with a tiny sample size of about 100 people: Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers winning a majority of Jewish voters, 52-47, a much worse result than it found for House Democratic candidates, who won the demographic by more than 30 points. Though small, it adds to other evidence of Democratic underperformance with Jewish voters in the Senate contest.
In surveys about their views, Jewish voters are sending signals that should put both parties on notice. A quarter of Republican Jews in the Mellman Group’s poll reported being concerned their party is “too accepting of antisemitic rhetoric within the Party” while a third said it’s “becoming too much of a home for White nationalists and the far right.”
More than a third of Jewish Democrats, similarly, said they worry the party is becoming “too accepting of antisemitic rhetoric within the Party,” while a quarter think it’s “becoming too much of a home for socialists and the far left.” Given how much larger the Jewish Democratic base is than the Republican one, and how central it is to winning coalitions in battlegrounds, these concerns pose a bigger electoral risk for the Democrats, particularly if the anti-Israel left grows into an even larger and more vocal wing of the party.
Protestants, and evangelicals, showed weaker Republican support
When it comes to evangelical Christians, the data suggests there was a different change afoot in the electorate.
They are perhaps the most important, or at least influential, religious group in American politics, given their strong and stable support for the Republican Party for the last 50 years. That loyalty has delivered them tremendous influence within party politics, while Trump, in particular, seems to have had a unique ability to turn these voters out during presidential elections. And at least in this year’s elections, that level of support for the GOP did not drop: they backed Republicans 82-16, consistent with their support for Trump in 2024.
What they didn’t do in 2026 is show up.
Exit polls suggest they made up a smaller share of the electorate when compared to 2026. That suggests a combination of lower turnout and lower enthusiasm may have contributed to Republican losses — even if those who did vote remained firmly Republican.
Still, the national results obscure one other notable trend that Burge, the religion scholar, noted from the 10 congressional districts with the highest share of evangelical voters — notably concentrated in the South (Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Tennessee). Each of these districts swung left, by an average of 23 points — more than in Catholic or nonevangelical mainline Protestant districts. This suggests stronger turnout and enthusiasm from the non-evangelical portion of these local electorates, which skews more Democratic — and in turn a weaker ability by Republican candidates to turn out evangelical voters in the way that Trump seems like he uniquely can.
In sharp contrast to evangelicals, the oldest but least-healthy strain of American Christianity — the mainline Protestant denominations like Episcopalians, Presbyterians, and Methodists — seems to have delivered a more politically interesting result this year. Many of the House and Senate seats that flipped for the Democrats this year were won by mainline Protestants in Iowa, Kansas, and Texas. They represent what used to be the dominant Christian electorate — which this year demonstrated it could still be a decisive part of a winning Democratic majority.
Heavily mainline districts swung by an average of 15 points toward Democrats, and each of the top eight districts ended up flipping to the Democratic column. The exit polls showed a Democratic gain among Protestants and nonevangelical Christians in general — moving from backing Republicans 63-36 in 2024 to 60-39 this year, a 6-point swing on the margins that can explain these flips.
As these numbers suggest, this is a demographic that seems more ripe for moderate Democratic appeals in the future — though they have been neglected by the establishment left over the last few decades.
We have less data and reliable post-election polling so far on what happened with other parts of the electorate, like Muslim voters, Hindus, and Mormons. What data we do have suggests they all played a part in forming the tidal wave that carried Democrats to their stunning victory last week. But above it all, this year’s results suggest that religious voters can function as swing voters in the post-Trump future, play an influential role in forming winning coalitions, and are not solely the domain of the Republican Party.

My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.
His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.
Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.
Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.
After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.
Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.
In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.
While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.
After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is plotting his return to the AI chipmaking company with his allies, a new report has revealed.
It’s only been a few days since Huang stepped down from the $4 trillion tech firm he founded after he fessed up to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy — and now some say he wants back in.
Huang has had discussions with confidantes about possibly returning as Nvidia’s chief executive, multiple people familiar with the matter told the Financial Times.
One ally said they were convening a “war room” of tech executives to get Huang back at the helm and would try to get support from the White House.
President Donald Trump acted shocked when news broke of Huang’s romantic ties to Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who U.S. intelligence believed was feeding information to Beijing.
“ I view him as a very high quality person. I've known him a long time,” Trump told reporters earlier this week.
The president insisted he had no idea about the U.S. intelligence on Alice Huang when he visited China in May, but the New York Times reported in late October that Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to take action.
Nvidia announced last Sunday, the day that Huang admitted the affair to employees, that it would be conducting an investigation following reporting that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Huang resigned Thursday and was replaced by Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, until a permanent replacement is found.
But it’s not just a couple of allies calling for Huang to return.
An online petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia’s CEO has garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including around 60,000 from shareholders, 6,000 from current Nvidia employees and 1,000 from former employees, according to reports.
Elon Musk, CEO of electric car company Tesla and rocket manufacturer SpaceX, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney were among the tech bros publicly backing the effort.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the Huang ally who spoke to the Financial Times claimed.
But it might not be enough to bring Huang back, especially considering new reports that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.
Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care who reported to him and is also married, five people who worked at the company told The New York Times.
Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter.
“Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offence,” one person involved in the push for Huang’s return admitted when speaking with the Financial Times.

A global outage taking down a wide range of Microsoft 365 services remains ongoing Friday morning.
The outage started midday Thursday, impacting users of Microsoft email, cloud, and AI services. Microsoft has documented the full list of services impacted by the error, while moving early Friday morning to protect customers around the world from losing emails during the extended disruptions.
“Recovery actions are ongoing,” the Microsoft 365 Status account confirmed on X. “To help preserve delayed mail during this event, we’ve extended email timeout to 48 hours.”
Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like “one of the biggest outages of all time,” Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even “worse,” he suggested.
Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC’s report documented various harms, noting that “few public bodies were immune from the outage.” In some cases, doctors couldn’t send patients “important” updates on medication changes or follow-up care.
The financial sector suffered, too, with people blocked from making bank transfers since they couldn’t receive verification codes.
Justice systems were also hobbled. The Supreme Court in the Philippines saw its legal work derailed, NBC reported. And one US sheriff’s office in Colorado reported that the outage made it difficult for people to post bond for prisoners’ immediate release.
It’s unclear how many users were affected, but Microsoft estimated in January that the total number of paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions exceeded 450 million.
Microsoft blames failed server health checks
On a status page, Microsoft said “we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident” and promised to “share a full Post-Incident Report with root cause and defense-in-depth actions after mitigation is complete.”
“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” Microsoft said on X.
But Microsoft’s public statements make clear that the tech giant was blindsided by the outage and struggled for hours to find mitigations that could reliably restore user access.

The government's noose around the online betting scam case, Mahadev app, has tightened further. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) searched 33 locations across six states at the premises of panel operators linked to the illegal betting platform based on disclosures made by Saurabh Chandrakar, one of the platform's principal promoters. Chandrakar was extradited from Oman by the CBI earlier this month. During the searches, the CBI found live betting and gambling panels operating at several locations and dismantled them. The agency also seized digital devices, mobile phones and documents allegedly indicating the use of mule bank accounts and hawala networks. Yesterday, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) arrested Chandrakar under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, with the permission of a special court in Raipur. The court has granted the agency seven days of custody till November 19 for further investigation. After being brought to India on November 1, Chandrakar was arrested by the CBI and remanded to eight days of police custody on November 4. On November 12, a special CBI court sent him to judicial custody till November 19 after the agency did not seek further custodial remand. The ED arrested him the following day in its separate money laundering investigation and secured seven days of custody. Besides, Ravi Uppal, another promoter of the Mahadev betting platform, is also said to have been arrested in the UAE. Indian investigating agencies are reportedly working to secure his extradition to India. Uppal was previously detained in the UAE in 2023, but local investigating agencies subsequently found that he was in Australia. Both Uppal and Chandrakar are also alleged to have obtained passports from Vanuatu. The CBI took over 13 FIRs registered by the Chhattisgarh government in connection with the Mahadev betting app case. The agency is investigating separate cases linked to the alleged betting operations and corruption surrounding the syndicate. The CBI said the platform operates from abroad through a central head office, while its Indian operations are managed by a large network of panel operators. These operators create and manage customer IDs, collect betting money through bank accounts opened or hired in other people's names, and transfer the proceeds overseas through hawala channels. The ED has also searched around 190 premises in connection with the case. It has seized or frozen assets worth approximately ₹2,000 Cr and attached properties valued at around ₹ 3,500 Cr. This includes overseas assets worth around ₹ 1,800 Cr, including 22 immovable properties in Dubai. The agency has filed six prosecution complaints against 116 accused. Chandrakar is the 15th person to be arrested in the case. In its main complaint, filed on October 20, 2023, the ED estimated that the betting syndicate generated around ₹450 Cr in monthly earnings. Its investigation found that the operation was run through a Dubai-based head office, with panel operators spread across India and the UAE. The ED also traced funds allegedly routed through hawala operators and invested in the share market. In September 2023, it identified securities worth around ₹236 Cr held by Dubai-based companies. In July, the ED arrested Vikas Garg, chairman of Ebix Group, alleging that proceeds of crime generated through Mahadev Online Book and another betting platform, Skyexchange, were routed into entities owned or controlled by him. The agency said around ₹940.77 Cr was channelled into these entities and subsequently layered through various transactions to acquire shares, securities and other assets. It also attached properties worth approximately ₹940.77 Cr belonging to Garg, his family members and associated entities. The investigation has also examined alleged links between the betting syndicate and politicians, bureaucrats and other individuals. The ED has alleged that some of the betting proceeds were routed through hawala channels and used to acquire properties overseas. The CBI said its investigation is ongoing and will examine the role of other accused, including those based abroad, panel operators and public servants. The ED, meanwhile, plans to question Chandrakar using statements from his associates, digital evidence and documents related to his foreign entities and alleged money laundering activities.

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.
Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.
“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.
As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.
Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.
“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.
“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.
Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.
The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.
Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.
On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.
A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.
Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.
He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".

  - Published3 November
The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara.
Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories.
"BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said.
"Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law."
On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers.
The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November.

After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
- Published
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."
Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.
The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.
In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.
Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.
CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.
Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."
