The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4 Episode 3, titled “Ain’t That Good News.”
Wedding bells are also ringing for the new Dr. (Jordan Donica) and Mrs. William Kirkland (Denée Benton) in The Gilded Age.
The newlywed couple, who met early on in Season 3 of Julian Fellowes’ period drama series, walked down the aisle and officially sealed the deal on their marriage as of Season 4’s third episode, though not without some road bumps along the way.
Elizabeth Kirkland (Phylicia Rashad) takes particular issue with Peggy’s parents gifting their daughter the broomstick they jumped over for their wedding celebration, because Dorothy Scott (Audra McDonald) could not legally marry Arthur Scott (John Douglas Thompson) due to his enslavement.
Watch on Deadline
“We were on set filming Season 3, and Audra McDonald turned to me and she said, ‘When they get married next season, I want them to jump over the broom because Elizabeth will hate that,’” co-showrunner Sonja Warfield told Deadline. “And so Audra planted that seed, and so that was going to be their core conflict.”
William’s mother, who hasn’t exactly warmed up to Peggy since the journalist and doctor started their courtship, doesn’t want her son and future daughter-in-law to incorporate the tradition because of its roots in slavery, marking commitment for those in bondage whose unions would not be legally recognized.
“We found out historically that it’s kind of inaccurate. Yes, enslaved people were doing that, but in that time post emancipation, they really weren’t, because then they could legally be married and so the tradition came back really in the 20th century,” Warfield continued. “We got to take some poetic license, artistic license and keep it because we were trying some other things, but really it needed to be that because that represents the division between the families,” Warfield said. “Elizabeth does not want to remember anything from enslavement period, while Peggy wants to pay homage to her family, to her dad and her parents. It is completely like diametrically opposed. So that made for great dramatic conflict.”
Another wrinkle in the plans for the nuptials comes in the form of the Fisk Jubilee singers, led by Dorothy and Peggy’s cousin Ava (Adrienne Warren), who attends Peggy’s pre-wedding tea and announces that she’s brought the choir to sing hymns at the ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island. Elizabeth is not fond of this idea either, nor, at first, is her husband (Brian Stokes Mitchell), who ultimately presides over Peggy and William’s ceremony. Much like in the show, this addition was not originally in the plans for Season 4’s third episode.
“I believe Sally [Richardson Whitfield] talked to Dr. [Erica] Dunbar because Sally wanted to add more to the wedding, which I was all for. At first, we had to be budget conscious, but then we got some more budget, so then we were able to add the Fisk Jubilee singers,” Warfield said. “I thought it need[ed] to be important to Peggy in a meaningful way, and so then we get to introduce cousin Ava as one of the singers.”
Warfield described the broom as something “tangible” to be angry about regarding Peggy instead of just saying she doesn’t like her soon-to-be daughter-in-law, giving actress Phylicia Rashad plenty of opportunities to “annihilate just with a look.” Meanwhile, the defensiveness Dorothy feels for her daughter is just one of many emotions on the big day.
RELATED: ‘The Gilded Age’ Cast Throughout The Seasons Of The Period Drama
“Dorothy is more than proud; there’s probably everything in it. There’s pride. There’s relief. There’s joy. There’s a little sadness because she has to let go. She’s got to let go in a way that she hasn’t had to. [Dorothy] probably had more time to cling to [Peggy] because of Peggy’s setting out on her own in the beginning, and so all of that is swirled into one,” McDonald told Deadline. “In some ways she starts to feel a little more nostalgic for and a little more romance toward Arthur again. They feel more like a unit now, given how separated they all were in Seasons 1 and 2. So, to see that bond come back together, she’s feeling that, and Peggy is finally getting the joy that she deserves. She’s emerging into this powerful young modern Black woman. That’s a fulfilling thing to see. Her ancestors are definitely smiling down on her.”
“She’s wearing the crown that her ancestors bought and paid for. So that’s a lot of beautiful things come to fruition. In some ways, it may be why Dorothy is so stringent and so unwilling to back down about the broom,” McDonald continued. “That’s honoring the ancestors. Like ‘Yes, you did buy and pay for this crown, and we are honoring you and saying we see you, we thank you, and we give gratitude to and we remember you. That’s why I think Dorothy’s willing to do a knockdown, hat-pulling, hair-pulling fight to get to this moment. That’s why it’s such a beautiful moment when it happens.”
In an interview paired with McDonald, co-star Cynthia Nixon called Peggy’s wedding “the wedding to end all weddings” and she traced the other ceremonies that have speckled The Gilded Age so far.

“Every one is different. We’ve had Gladys’s wedding with the bride sobbing down the aisle. We’ve had Enid’s and Oscar’s wedding, which is sort of hilarious. We’ve had Ada and Luke’s wedding, which is late in life and full of anguish because you think Agnes isn’t going to come, and it’s more small and modest,” she said. “The wedding of Peggy and Dr. Kirkland, is this fruition of this tremendous love and the most opulent and beautiful, but also heartfelt and full of tradition and singing and the beautiful attire and the stained glass, and it just it is the apex of all the weddings we’ve ever had on the show.”
McDonald shared one last special association with production behind such a major moment in the show.
“The days that we were shooting it, because it took a long time to shoot, it was the night that the Knicks won. So, we literally had to stop shooting for a while to watch those final moments,” the Tony winner said. “Everybody was stationed at phones and Sally Richardson was like, ‘We can’t keep going. Let’s turn on some TVs.’ And we’re all watching, and then screaming our heads off for I don’t know how late it was. And then we went back to finishing the wedding. We did end up watching the sunrise that night, but it was a worthy night. It was kind of magical that it happened on the night of the of the wedding.”

10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes
Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.
For most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live. If you've only used it for basic text, you've probably missed how Apple has added new features to the mix that can solve complex equations, draw graphs, transcribe audio and turn your doodles into images. iOS 27 brought even more, including smarter Siri integration and divider lines, so the app is more capable than ever.
A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended. On the iPhone, that means the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and any iPhone 16 model or later. Those features are flagged along the way, along with anything that requires a specific version of iOS.
1. Math Notes turns Notes into a calculator and graphing tool
The Notes app has a calculator hiding inside it, with the math happening while you're typing. Since iOS 18, when you type an equation and add an equals sign, Math Notes fills in the answer on the spot. It also works with variables, so if you write "dinner = $42" and change that value later, every result that uses it updates automatically. That makes it a surprisingly easy way to split the bill or plan a monthly budget.
Math Notes can do more than give you simple answers. After you type an equation that starts with "y =", tap the equals sign and choose Insert Graph to plot what you've typed right inside the note. If you change the variable, the graph changes automatically to match. It's a neat tool for students to check their homework without a dedicated graphing app.
2. Notes can scan your documents and supports signatures
If you don't have a physical scanner at home, there's no need to download a dedicated scanner app to replace it. Tapping the attachment button in any note shows the Scan Documents option, where Notes will capture a page automatically, including cropping and straightening it for you. The scanner also offers a flash option and image filters if needed.
In Auto mode, you don't even need to tap on the shutter button; the system captures the document once it detects the page's edges and you're holding your iPhone steady. You can scan multiple pages into a single document, which is useful for contracts, lease agreements or anything else that runs longer than a page.
If the document needs a signature, open the scan, tap Markup, then go to Add > Signature. Use a saved signature or draw a new one with your finger, then resize it and drag it into place. It's an easy way to sign and send a form without taking a printout of the pages. Scans are saved to the note as PDFs, which you can annotate.
3. Notes can record and transcribe lectures and meetings
Notes can double as a recorder: choose Record Audio in any note to record and transcribe everything your phone hears. The transcript is searchable, so you can jump into the relevant part of a long lecture instead of scrubbing through the entire session. On iPhone models with Apple Intelligence, Notes can summarize entire recorded lectures or meetings. Phone calls you record also land in Notes inside the Call Recordings folder with a transcript.
The iPhone already has a dedicated recording app in Voice Memos, so it's worth knowing when to use which. Notes is the better pick when the recording is part of something bigger. For a class or a meeting, for example, you can type your own notes, add photos of the whiteboard and keep the recording all in the same note. Everything stays together, so you won't have to switch between multiple apps when you're going through your notes at home. Meanwhile, Voice Memos makes more sense when the audio itself matters most, like an interview you plan to edit or share.
4. Image Wand turns your rough sketches into real images
If you need some help when drawing, sketch something rough with the Markup tools, then pick Image Wand from the same tool palette and circle your sketch. Add a few words describing the image you want, and Apple Intelligence will turn your doodle into a polished image.
You also have the option to circle an empty spot in the note and create a new image based on the text around it. Afterward, fine-tune the image by adding or removing descriptive words. If your note is a packing list for a beach trip, for instance, it will generate a matching seaside illustration to sit at the top.
In iOS 27, Image Playground, which powers this feature in the Notes app, got a new model that can make photorealistic images, not just stylized ones. Since iOS 27.2, most images you generate or edit carry a SynthID watermark, which the SynthID detection website uses to know something was made by AI.
5. Shared notes turn Notes into a family to-do list
Your notes don't have to be only for you; it's possible to share a specific note or an entire folder with your family, friends and coworkers, then everyone can make changes in real time. This is ideal for a household grocery list or a group plan for a trip. The person who creates the shared note remains in control of who can do what.
Just tap the Share button in the note you want to add people to, then choose whether each person can make changes or only view it. Type @ followed by someone's name and they'll get a notification pointing them to the note. If several people are editing the same note, the activity view and highlights show who changed what and when. And in iOS 27, the Shared folder now sits at the top of the folders list with a new icon, so multi-person notes are easier to spot.
6. Apple Intelligence can summarize, reformat and proofread your notes
The Notes app can help with the actual writing you do. Select some text, tap the Apple Intelligence button in the toolbar and pick an option from the Writing Tools menu. This can proofread your text for spelling and grammar mistakes and rewrite it in a friendlier, more professional or more concise tone.
The suite is also useful for reshaping messy notes. It's able to create a summary of a long note or pull out its key points, which is handy after a meeting or before an exam. It will also turn a block of text into a bulleted list or even convert it into a table. If you've jotted down a few phone plans with their prices and data limits, for example, the Table option can organize them into neat rows and columns so they're easier to compare.
Writing Tools isn't limited to just the Notes app; it works almost anywhere you can type on the iPhone, including third-party apps. In iOS 27, Apple Intelligence also suggests ways to improve your writing.
7. Notes can create polished documents
Long notes quickly become messy and hard to organize, but Notes has a few tools to keep them neat. With iOS 18 and newer, you have the option to collapse any heading to minimize sections you're not working on. This means the final version is a bit cleaner to view, while it's also easier to manage everything while writing.
If that's not enough, you can also highlight text in different colors, curating them by sections, information or any other preference. To do so, select the text, tap the Aa format button and pick a color. Notes offers five color options to choose from: pink, purple, orange, mint and blue. iOS 27 also added divider lines, which gives another option to tidy up a mess. Place your cursor where you want a break, open the edit menu and choose Insert Divider Line. If someone views the note on iOS 26 or prior, the divider lines show up as three hyphens(—), so nothing breaks.
iOS 27 also added section links to the mix, letting you link to a specific section of a note where tapping the link jumps straight there. That's particularly useful for a table of contents in a long note. Pasting Markdown now converts it to formatted text automatically, and a new Copy as Markdown option easily brings notes to other apps with the formatting intact.
8. The Notes app doubles as a calligraphy pad with the reed pen
iOS 26 added a reed pen to the Markup tools, which is designed for a traditional calligraphy experience. Like the actual writing instrument, your strokes get thicker or thinner depending on the direction you draw in. It's a unique way to write, especially for special occasions like birthdays and invitations. You'll find the reed pen in the list of Markup tools; tapping it again after selecting it is how you pick a preset.
There are five angle presets to choose from, with the one you pick deciding which stroke direction gives the thickest line. The angle is fixed no matter how you hold your finger, so your strokes stay consistent. Apart from the Notes app, the reed pen also works in Freeform, Journal and Preview — basically anywhere the Markup tools are available.
9. Notes serves as a search resource for your photos and scans
The search bar in the Notes app is smarter than it looks and than how most people casually use it. Beyond your own typed notes, it can search handwriting, objects in images and text in scanned documents. Tap the search button, then type a word from a page or a photo. If you scanned a receipt months ago, searching for the store's name should bring it up. It's an easy way to find snippets from longer notes, especially when you're transcribing lectures or meetings.
This turns your Notes library into a practical place to store paperwork you might need in the future. Consider storing information like warranty cards, appliance manuals, prescriptions and receipts all in Notes, then you can find them by searching for a word on the page instead of scrolling through dozens of scans and navigating file names.
10. Siri can save its answers straight to Notes
Siri and Notes finally work together properly in iOS 27. Siri can create notes with generated content, like information it pulled from the web, instead of only typing what you say. Ask it to put together a packing list for a trip and save it to a new note, and it will comply. This really comes in handy for smaller notes or basic reminders, as well as capturing ideas on the spot when you can't stop to type.
It can also add to an existing note or clean up a list before saving it. If you've got a messy, unformatted list, ask Siri to tidy it up and add it to the right note. Of course, the full power of this requires Siri AI, which launched in English first. iOS 27.2 added French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish. Older iPhone models can also create notes with Siri, but without the AI-generated content, which slightly limits the feature. But the basics are still there to jot down ideas.

Assam to restrict construction in flood-prone areas under proposed zoning law: CM
The state government has prepared the Assam Flood Plain Zoning Bill, 2026, which will be tabled during the winter session of the state assembly next month
The Assam government plans to bring the floodplains of the Brahmaputra and Barak river basins under a legal land-use zoning system to restrict and regulate construction in vulnerable areas, Chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said on Sunday. The move aims to address the risks posed by unregulated development in flood-prone areas.
The state government has prepared the Assam Flood Plain Zoning Bill, 2026, which will be tabled during the winter session of the state assembly next month.
Sarma wrote on X: “Flood management begins with understanding our rivers. The Assam Flood Plain Zoning Bill, 2026, provides for scientific mapping of the Brahmaputra and Barak basins and clearly defined flood zones to protect communities and guide safer development.”
The proposed legislation envisages using LiDAR technology and satellite imagery to map flood-prone areas across the two river basins. Based on this mapping, the government plans to classify land into three categories: prohibited, regulated and unregulated, with different restrictions on construction and development in each zone.
River channels and areas of active flow would fall under the prohibited zone, where construction would not be allowed. Development in regulated zones would be subject to conditions such as elevated plinths and flood-resilient building designs, while normal development would be permitted in unregulated areas outside the identified flood lines.
The proposed zoning system would add a land-use regulation mechanism to the state’s existing flood-control measures, which include embankments, riverbank protection, river-training works and drainage improvements. While these measures seek to protect settlements and infrastructure from floodwaters and erosion, the proposed law aims to regulate construction in areas exposed to flooding.
Floodplain zoning has featured in Assam’s disaster-management planning before. The Assam State Disaster Management Plan, 2022, called for a regulatory framework to demarcate vulnerable areas and manage construction in floodplains. The proposed Bill seeks to give that planning a legal framework.
The draft also envisages setting up Flood Zoning Authorities at different administrative levels to oversee its implementation.
During a review of the draft on November 5, Sarma directed officials to ensure that lawful existing property owners were protected. He also stressed the need to safeguard the interests of Scheduled Tribe and Scheduled Caste communities traditionally residing along riverbanks.
The proposed framework provides for a 60-day period for public hearings and objections, as well as online and physical mechanisms to appeal against zoning decisions. It also includes safeguards for existing property owners.
The need for a broader approach to flood management has been underlined by the scale of this year’s floods. According to the state government’s November 5 review, floods in Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat and Golaghat in July claimed 104 lives.
The government has said the initiative could be financed through externally aided projects and grants, without imposing an additional financial burden on the state. Sarma has also expressed hope of securing central assistance, including through the Union ministry of Jal Shakti.

How to Connect Claude AI to Instagram Edits and Edit Reels on Mac
Before connecting your Instagram Edits app to the MCP server, ensure you have the following pre-requirements:

Part 1: Get Claude Code
Step 1: Open Terminal and type the command: claude –version, and press Return. If you see a version number, it means Claude Code is already installed on your device. You can skip to Part 2 to continue setup.

Next, paste this command into the terminal and press Enter: echo ‘export PATH=”$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH”‘ >> ~/.zshrc

South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed
Analysts had warned that the vote, originally set for December, faced a legitimacy crisis. South Sudan has not held a national election since gaining independence in 2011.
Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, said on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result.
The National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec. 22, would be held on Feb. 11 instead. The country’s information minister, Ateny Wek Ateny, said the postponement would allow more time to register voters and educate them about the process.
South Sudan has never held a national election. Since gaining independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war, it has been ruled by President Salva Kiir, and it has faced seemingly intractable political difficulties.
In 2013, civil war broke out between the government and forces loyal to the main opposition leader, Riek Machar. Under a peace agreement to end the conflict in 2018, Mr. Machar became the vice president in a transitional government.
The upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government.
With Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media.
The election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups.
“The conditions for credible polls are not currently in place,” the International Crisis Group said in a briefing for the U.N. Security Council this week. “Rushed elections could be a decisive final blow to the 2018 framework and would open the door to a return to sustained large-scale violence.”
Mr. Ateny, the information minister, acknowledged that the government could not gain access to “small parts” of the country, but said the election would be credible.
“It’s not always 100 percent, but it can be good for the sovereignty of the country and it’s good for the mandate of the state,” he said in an interview.
In addition to the violence and civil unrest, South Sudanese have been faced with soaring food prices, drought and flooding. Of the country’s roughly 12 million people, more than 8 million are in need of food assistance, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, a globally recognized monitor of hunger.
Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

How do you think you’re going to die?
If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”
In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.
Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover. In almost the same breath, though, he said that if AI continues to develop at “the most rapid trajectory,” humanity is “looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” including a “meaningful risk” of one happening in the next six to 12 months. And even with realistic policy responses slowing things down, the risk remains “exceptionally high,” he said.
From here to there
Unlike some other recent AI doomsday prognosticators who have been a bit vague about the “how” of it all, Cristiano used his lecture to spin a step-by-step tale of escalating AI threats that sounds like it could come from a science-fiction novel. That line of reasoning leans heavily on this summer’s OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident as an example of “roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad were to happen.”

Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra, to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.
Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising.
The winner, who performs under the single name Carmelle, finished on 211 points, 41 clear of the hosts Thailand, with Vietnam third. She received the most votes from both the national juries and the public ballot.
Carmelle, 19, grew up beside the railway tracks in the Bicol region of south-eastern Luzon and has been competing in televised talent contests since she was 12.
Sobra-Sobra mixes pop and rap, is supported by traditional Philippine instruments, the kubing and kulintang, and is sung in Tagalog and English.
After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women”.
“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told the Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”
“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are,” she told the Guardian before the final. “It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas.”
The show opened with a routine celebrating the host country, in which Muay Thai fighters shared the stage with drag performers on street food carts. The 11 acts were then driven on in tuk-tuks, each carrying their national flag.
Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, a star at home for more than 20 years, performed first, among dancers costumed as lotus leaves. Mang x Daou represented Thailand, a duo assembled for the contest in the host country who performed a duet staged like a musical number.
Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai gave one of the most conventionally Eurovision performances of the night with Ananta Maya, a rock ballad staged with fire imagery and a large heart-shaped structure behind him.
He ended it by appealing for support for his country, which he said was “going [through a] very hard situation”. More than 1,500 people were killed and more than 5,000 were reported missing after a rock and ice avalanche near the Chinese border triggered catastrophic flash floods in August.
Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, originally a nine-member a cappella and beatbox group, sang without a single instrument. Three of their members were left out of the final due to a rule capping each act at six performers on stage.
Nyendra from Bhutan sang dressed in the gho, his country’s national dress for men, against a backdrop of Himalayan peaks. Mongolia’s Beck performed in a reinterpreted deel, also a national costume.
Half the result was decided before the show began. The 11 national juries voted at a dress rehearsal on Friday night and put the Philippines top with 93 points, ahead of Vietnam and Malaysia.
The other half came from viewers around the world, who could vote online but not for their own country, and who were given eight free votes each and the option to buy 10 more.
Laos’s entrant, Thinla, was unable to hear her own music during her performance, and her dress rehearsal was aired once all live performances were over. She finished fifth, with the night’s third-highest public score.
Carmelle receives no prize money but a trophy presented by Dara, the Bulgarian singer who won this year’s European contest, and will perform at Eurovision 2027 in Burgas.
Organisers have said the right to stage future editions will not automatically go to the winner, on the grounds that smaller countries lack the infrastructure.
Some of the clearest echoes of Eurovision’s camp traditions came through those who announced the votes.
South Korea’s jury points were read by Jo Kwon, a veteran pop star who has played Adam in the Korean production of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and the title role in Everybody’s Talking About Jamie.
The Philippines’ were read by Vice Ganda, a gay comedian who is one of the biggest stars on Philippine television.
Meanwhile, the guest performer was the Thai singer Jeff Satur, who reached a wider Asian audience through KinnPorsche, a 2022 series in the genre of male same-sex romance dramas that has a large following across Asia.
Organisers intend the Bangkok show to be the first of many regional editions, with the executive producer, Assaf Blecher, saying that 16 or 17 territories had expressed interest in competing next year, among them China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Scientists have assembled a cellular atlas of a crucial brain region called the basal ganglia involved in functions such as movement, decision making, emotions and habit formation — an accomplishment that could help guide new treatments for several devastating diseases.
The researchers mapped the cell types and cellular gene activity in the basal ganglia, an interconnected set of structures deep within the brain, in humans as well as in mice and in macaque and marmoset monkeys. Basal ganglia dysfunction is associated with conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, schizophrenia, Tourette’s syndrome, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder and addiction.
“It is important to understand the structure and function of the basal ganglia in order to develop effective treatments of these diseases,” said neuroscientist Hongkui Zeng, director of brain science at the Allen Institute in Seattle and one of the leaders of the research presented in more than two dozen studies published on Thursday in Cell and related journals.
“It is a major milestone in our journey toward a comprehensive, detailed, multimodal, cross-species aligned cell atlas for the entire human brain,” with a target date sometime in 2028, Zeng added.
The research was conducted as part of the BRAIN Initiative, an effort launched in 2014 to advance the understanding of the brain with the support of the US National Institutes of Health. The work presented on Thursday offers the first comprehensive cross-species cellular roadmap for any brain region.
“Until now, there was no reference describing each cell type in the human basal ganglia together with how it regulates its genes,” said Joseph Ecker, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the Salk Institute in La Jolla, California, another of the research leaders.
“In the near term, the atlas is a reference resource for researchers. We are studying a Parkinson’s gene and can now see which cell types turn that gene on, and which DNA switches are active in those cells. Over the longer term, the atlas can help identify cell-type-specific targets for gene therapy and gene editing,” Ecker said. “It also gives a baseline for comparing diseased tissue with healthy tissue.”
Therapies built on the new work are still years away, Ecker said.
Among other findings, researchers identified a new type of brain cell associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, documented genetic changes in specific cell types that could play a role in autism, and discovered changes in gene activity in certain cells associated with aging.
Cross-species comparisons
Using brain tissue from deceased human donors, the researchers examined the role of 21 million cells in the basal ganglia in people, as well as millions more cells in the three other species.
“Understanding the cellular composition of this brain structure across species will allow for comparative analyses of function as well as connectivity patterns and response to pharmacological interventions,” said Salk Institute neuroscientist and biochemist Margarita Behrens, another of the research leaders.
Many studies for ethical reasons cannot be performed using living human brains. Much of what was previously known about the basal ganglia, and most early testing of new treatments, had come from research involving mice and monkeys.
“We rely on animal models to probe the inner workings of brain cells and circuits in generating brain function and mediating disease effects, and to test the efficacies of therapeutic interventions,” Zeng said.
The structures of the basal ganglia include the striatum, globus pallidus and substantia nigra.
“Together they help select and start movements, and they support habit formation, reward learning, motivation and emotion,” Ecker said.
The atlas combines several layers of data. One shows which genes are switched on in each cell. Another involves the epigenome, a collection of chemical compounds and proteins that attach to the DNA and regulate gene activity. A third layer involves spatial maps showing where each cell type sits in the tissue of the basal ganglia.
“Most of the DNA variants linked to brain disorders lie outside the protein-coding parts of genes. Many of them sit in DNA ‘switches’ that control when and where genes turn on, and those switches are often active only in particular cell types,” Ecker said.
The protein-coding parts of genes carry genetic instructions used to build proteins, the complex molecules that perform most of the critical work inside cells.
An atlas like this one helps trace a disease-risk DNA variant to the specific kind of nerve cell or support cell where it acts.
“That is a first step toward understanding how the variant contributes to disease, and eventually toward treating it,” Ecker said.

Shillong has always had an ear for music. Long before Spotify and YouTube, its musical tastes were shaped by worn-out cassettes, CDs and mixtapes. Hip-hop, R&B, pop and alternative rock gradually found a place in the city’s musical landscape, sharing space with its thriving local rock scene. This November, the Shillong Cherry Blossom Festival will celebrate this musical legacy with a lineup that cuts across generations and genres.
Scheduled for November 20 and 21, the 2026 edition features international acts including American rapper Nelly, pop-rock band Boys Like Girls, singer Khalid, rapper Swae Lee and retro-pop artist Elliot James Reay, alongside Indian singer Darshan Raval. While the lineup offers something for different generations of listeners, it also reflects the city’s taste for global sounds in music.
The festival takes its name from the wild Himalayan cherry trees, which burst into bloom every autumn, painting Shillong’s hills, streets and parks, along with the surrounding Khasi Hills, in shades of pink.
Back to school
Nelly’s early 2000s hits such as ‘Hot in Herre’, ‘Dilemma’ and ‘Ride with Me’ bring back an era when MTV became a core childhood memory; Boys Like Girls, with tracks such as ‘The Great Escape’ and ‘Love Drunk’, recall the pop-rock movement that resonates with young guitar enthusiasts, and for many Gen Zs, Darshan Raval was what Hindi pop sounded like.
Khalid’s ‘Location’, ‘Young Dumb & Broke’, and ‘Better’, along with Swae Lee’s ‘Sunflower’ and ‘Unforgettable’, represent the streaming-platform generation.
For Jason Manners, organiser of the festival says that creating an international-level music festival in Shillong, “is a dream for us, but also a nightmare because we are victims of geography.” He explains, “We are located in a hill station. We don’t have a proper international airport. We are not lucky to be near any big city that makes it easy for an international artist to tour and make the decision to tour. So it is very much organic.”
Jason traces the journey back to 2013, when he travelled to the US to accompany the Maharaja of Tripura Pradyot Bikram Manikya Deb Barma in search of a band for Shillong. His intention was to introduce a fresh musical experience to the city, and the effort eventually led to the booking of an international act. Over the years, he began building relationships within the global music industry. When the Meghalaya government came on board with a similar vision of using music as a means of attracting tourists, the idea of a larger festival began taking shape. “The Government of Meghalaya, especially Chief Minister Conrad K Sangma, has played a pivotal role behind the festival,” says Jason.
Organising a festival of this scale comes with challenges. Recalling an early edition during the COVID years, Jason says, “It got too packed. The audience had to be sent home, and the police had to deploy tear gas, which created a law and order situation. That’s when we also started getting a lot of media attention.”
An experience rooted in culture
Convincing international artists to travel to Shillong also requires considerable effort. “We have to really explain to them what Shillong is and what kind of music culture we have here. And we have to make their journey as comfortable as possible. Some artists have even arrived by helicopter,” says Jason. Despite initial reservations about the journey, he says artists are often impressed by the production and audience. “Most of them actually say that it was the best live show they had in a long time.”
Beyond the music, the festival aims to offer visitors an experience rooted in the food and culture of the Northeast. This year, the food line-up will include traditional Khasi, Jaintia and Garo cuisine, alongside a range of barbecue options, reflecting the region’s love for non-vegetarian fare. Some of the food stalls include The Garo Flavours, Garo Food Hub, Jaintia Indigenous Food, The Pnar’s Kitchen, Al Khasi Stall, and Marshra Khasi, among others. Visitors can also explore merchandise stalls featuring local products, apparel and accessories, as well as games and interactive activities, adding to the festival’s distinctly Shillong and Northeast India-centric experience
The festival is also extending its reach beyond the two days of performances. The Indian International Music Week will be held a day before the festival, bringing together delegates from the music industry. It also works alongside Chief Minister’s Meghalaya’s Grassroots Music Programme, connecting young local musicians with industry experts through workshops, discussions, artist showcases and sessions.
Jason says their growing popularity has also allowed them to support the music economies of other Northeastern States. After helping Sikkim organise its first international music festival last year, called the Orchid Music Festival in Sikkim, the team is now assisting Arunachal Pradesh with artist bookings and logistical planning for Euphonic Voyage.
“For the people of Shillong, the Cherry Blossom Festival is special because it’s truly homegrown - it has grown out of our own soil. It’s bringing artists who have been part of our childhood. Watching these artists live is not just entertainment; it’s emotional healing, and nostalgia,” says Jason.
The Cherry Blossom Festival will be held on November 20 and 21 at the Madan Kurkalang Sports Complex in Bhoirymbong, Shillong. For registration visit www.rockskitickets.com

Anup Gupta is stepping down from his role as a partner at venture capital (VC) firm Nexus Venture Partners after a 16 year-long stint. In a post on LinkedIn, Gupta said that his tenure at the VC firm will come to an end in June 2027. “I am delighted to be passing on the baton in Team Nexus, will be stepping down in June'27. I have been fortunate to contribute to the Indian start-up eco-system right from its early days both as an operator and investor advisor-partner, and excited about new horizons,” said Gupta. The social media post did not elaborate on what he plans to do after exiting Nexus Venture Partners. An alumnus of IIT Kharagpur and IIM Calcutta, Gupta previously served at companies like Booz & Co and WNS. He joined Nexus Venture Partners in 2010 and led the VC firm’s investments in startups like Turtlemint, Uniqus, Kiwi, PaySense, among many others. Founded in 2006 by Naren Gupta, Sandeep Singhal and Suvir Sujan, Nexus Venture Partners primarily invests in early-stage startups. It currently manages $3.2 Bn in assets across eight funds, with its investor base comprising global pension funds, family offices and endowments. The VC firm last closed its eighth fund at $700 Mn in December 2025. Its portfolio comprises listed logistics major Delhivery, IPO-bound Infra.Market, quick commerce startup Zepto, ride-hailing firm Rapido and SaaS unicorn Postman, among others. Overall, it has exited 30 startups, including the likes of Delhivery, Eternal, MapmyIndia, Unicommerce, PaySense and SEDEMAC. It is pertinent to note that this is the second exit of a partner at Nexus VP this year. Previously, SuprDaily cofounder Puneet Kumar exited Nexus as partner in January 2026 to build his own startup. The departure comes amid a broader top-level churn in the Indian VC ecosystem. Earlier this month, Fireside Ventures’ cofounder and partner Vinay Singh left the VC firm. Right after, Prayag Mohanty, principal at Fireside Ventures, also quit the firm. In August, Inc42 reported that Peak XV Partners’ vice president Kriti Gupta was leaving the VC firm after five years. Earlier this year, Ashish Agrawal, Ishaan Mittal and Tejeshwi Sharma also quit Peak XV to float their new VC firm, Mettle Capital. Another former Peak XV Partners MDs Shailesh Lakhani and Harshjit Sethi also quit the VC firm to float Ambition Capital, and are looking to raise $250 Mn for the maiden fund.

The original Blue Yeti microphone was first released in 2009, and it remains the most ubiquitous microphone for home recording 17 years later. Chances are, if you’ve watched a YouTube video, Twitch stream, or listened to a podcast, you’ve heard (and probably seen) this microphone at least once.
Long after absorbing Blue and phasing out the brand name, Logitech has finally released its highly anticipated successor: the Yeti 2. The follow-up maintains the same general shape and look but drastically changes the microphone’s functionality. Instead of simply recording audio, the Yeti 2 has a handful of features to monitor and manipulate the audio passing through it, seamlessly recording production-quality audio with zero delay. While some of the design feels a bit underdeveloped, the Yeti 2 is a deserving sequel to the iconic original model and an easy shoe-in as the best USB microphone you can buy.
Intuitive Interfaces
The Yeti 2's biggest upgrades stares you directly in the face after taking it out of the box. The built-in screen and dial allow for on-the-fly adjustments right on the microphone. No software required. While I was a skeptic at first, I quickly found this little screen to be significantly more convenient than the alternative. It can be used to adjust gain, enable different post-processing settings, and configure the sound profile of the microphone.
More importantly, the screen can quickly provide insights into audio quality at a glance. The main screen shows a graph of the gain-adjusted input volume, which is what the microphone is sending to your computer. It can also display a histogram of volume over time, a pattern to show what direction input is coming from, or … a pixel-art Yeti. This little guy looks confused when you’re quiet, happy when you’re talking at a normal volume, and alarmed when you’re too loud for the microphone to handle. Within the G Hub app, the icons can be swapped out with any of Logi’s other premade avatars (a dragon, flower, frog, or jellyfish), or freely customized with your own images using a simple drag-and-drop menu. This is the least functional feature of the microphone, but it’s an endearing and intuitive way to indicate audio quality at a glance.
The screen also has quite a few adjustable menus for different features, including a de-noise function with four levels, five EQ presets, a pattern customizer with eight default options, and a multitude of toggleable settings to clean up and improve recording quality. While the settings can’t be customized using the screen, the G Hub application provides more in-depth adjustments for how intense each of these settings are, along with explanations of how they work and when to use them.

Samsung and Xiaomi have increased smartphone prices by up to ₹4,000 across 48 variants in India amid rising memory chip prices and subdued consumer demand. Prices for about 30 Samsung phones as well as 19 Xiaomi phones have been increased in a range of ₹1,000-4,000 between November 15-16. Samsung's latest revision covers 14 variants across its Galaxy A07 5G, A17 5G, A36, A37, A56, A57 and F17 5G lineups, with most models becoming costlier by ₹2,000. The Galaxy A57 saw the steepest hike of ₹4,000, taking the 8GB+256GB and 12GB+256GB variants to ₹66,999 and ₹76,499, respectively. Its November 15 revision also raised prices of seven Galaxy M17 5G, M17e and F70e 5G variants by ₹2,000 each. Xiaomi, meanwhile, revised prices across 19 Redmi variants. Hikes ranged from ₹1,000 to ₹4,000, with the Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G seeing the steepest increase. Its 8GB+128GB and 8GB+256GB variants now cost ₹40,999 and ₹43,999, respectively. This adds to an ongoing trend in the smartphone market where higher average selling prices have led to a weaker consumer demand. Damp demand during the recently concluded Diwali sales, one of the major occasions for such purchases in India, is evidence to that. Smartphone sales volumes dipped as much as 20% year-on-year (YoY) during the four-day festive period between November 6-9, as per data from All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA). While overall sales value remained broadly in line with the previous year due to higher average selling prices, the contraction in volumes squeezed retailer margins and store profitability. AIMRA also reported that offline smartphone sales volumes fell nearly 40% in the seven days preceding Dhanteras (November 6), as consumers delayed purchases in anticipation of festive offers. Financing constraints further affected demand, with only 60-70% of logged loan applications receiving approval during the festive period. Against this backdrop, the latest price increases could add to the affordability concerns, particularly in the price-sensitive budget and mid-range segments. AI Data Centre Demand Adds To Memory Chip Supply Constraints The price revisions come amid a broader surge in memory chip prices at the behest of sharper demand from AI infrastructure and data centres. AI infra particularly relies on DRAM, which provides the high-speed memory GPUs needed to process AI workloads, and NAND flash, which enables cost-efficient storage of the massive datasets that enable AI model training. These chips are also essential components in smartphones, laptops, gaming consoles and other consumer electronics. Thus, the rise in AI development globally is now creating tightened supply chains for manufacturers and pushing up procurement costs. The impact extends across consumer electronics, with smartphone, PC and gaming console makers facing higher component costs. This was also highlighted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who recently flagged the growing competition for memory resources during a podcast. He argued that while large amounts of DRAM in personal computers often remain underutilised and could be put to better use in cloud infrastructure. He also pointed to supply constraints in the memory market and said its usual price correction mechanism was not working effectively. Meanwhile, expanding semiconductor manufacturing capacity remains challenging, as setting up new facilities requires significant investment and time.

The electoral officer for All India Football Federation’s (AIFF) December 20 polls, Rajeev Sharma on Sunday published the list of nominations to the electoral college from the state associations, keeping decision pending regarding seven affiliated units.
Sharma said that a decision on seven of the 36 affiliated units would be deferred on the grounds that their elections are either pending or matters relating to them are sub judice. However, no such impediment exists in respect of the remaining 29 affiliated units, as neither their elections are pending nor are any matters concerning them sub judice.
He had called for the nominations -- two members for each unit -- to be submitted by Friday deadline.
Incumbent AIFF president Kalyan Chaubey’s name is not included in the draft electoral college relating to the state units published by Sharma on Sunday.

However under the AIFF Constitution, a person not in the electoral college can still contest for the president’s post if he or she has completed at least one term in the executive committee, according to officials.
Form 2 for the nomination of the presidential candidate does not mention his or her roll number in the electoral college.
Out of the seven affiliated units, the voting right status of Haryana and Tamil Nadu state associations “are to be decided by the Electoral Officer as they are sub-judice before the respective courts”.
He said the voting right status of five state state units -- Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, West Bengal, Pondicherry, Uttarakhand and Jammu and Kashmir -- will be decided “in accordance with Article 4.1 of Schedule 3 of the AIFF Constitution.”
Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu Football Association submitted “new names “ on Saturday, a day after the deadline, “after the conduct of elections.”
The state units of West Bengal, Pondicherry and Uttarakhand have submitted their nominations but their elections are pending. Jammu and Kashmir Football Association elections are also pending and it did not submit any nomination.
Election is scheduled on Sunday (November 15) in the case of Uttarakhand association and on November 27 for Pondicherry. Jammu and Kashmir is scheduled to hold election on November 26.
At least 10 members of the outgoing Executive Committee, including vice president N A Haris (from Karnataka), have been nominated by their respective state associations.
Meanwhile, former AIFF president Praful Patel and Uttar Pradesh state unit chief Arvind Menon could throw their hats into the ring for the top post.
However, no one, including Chaubey, has till now openly expressed an intention to fight for the president’s post.
The four Sportspersons of Merit (SOMs) -- two male and two female -- to be elected on November 23, will also be eligible to cast their votes in the December 20 executive committee elections.
Former India captain Oinam Bembem Devi, former players Shukla Dutta, Bentla D’Coth, Kalpana Das and Sradhanjali Samantaray have filed their nomination papers for the two seats of female SOMs.
For the two seats of male SOMs, Joe Paul Ancheri, U Sharaf Ali, Bruno Coutinho and Mushtaque Ali are in the fray.
They will be elected by an electoral college of 40 former players -- 20 male and 20 female.

How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.
As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.
You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?
Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.
There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.
One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.
We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.
We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.
You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?
Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.
One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.
Can you give an example?
One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.
There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.
The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?
When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.
The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.
So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.
What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?
This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.
Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.
If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?
I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.
I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages
- Published
Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday.
In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions.
Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular."
To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of under-statement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular.
It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations Cup final.
If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment.
The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist?
Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina?
The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half.
Not a backward step was taken.
This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession.
Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted.
But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win.
Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters?
"We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up.
"Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory."
England were in a different class to Spain - yes, you have read that right
Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach.
Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football.
What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them.
England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented.
It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them.
England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right.
From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain.
When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be.
In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge.
Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level".
There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup.
Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them.
Tuchel got his big calls right
If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions.
Yes. And yes.
Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest.
The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here.
But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything.
And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure.
"This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together.
"The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.
"We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup."
England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table.
The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession.
After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice.
England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative.
"I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent.
"I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase."
Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer.
"Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance."
Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

Russell Brand has claimed that he is “not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for” in a message read by his wife on YouTube.
Presenting an episode of their Sunday Service show, Laura Brand delivered some words on behalf of her husband, who is behind bars in Littlehey Prison, a jail for men who have been convicted of sexual offenses. Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Reading from a notepad, Laura Brand said: “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.”
She continued: “The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe.

“The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.
“I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.”
An audibly emotional Laura Brand added: “Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers, your brother in Christ. Russell.”

Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine have arrived in India for a three-day visit
MUMBAI, India -- Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since Catherine was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.
The royal couple will begin in Mumbai city and attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. Founded by William, the environmental initiative awards five winners $1.3 million (£1 million) each to expand solutions addressing climate change.
The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established in 2020, will feature several prominent guests including Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That making its debut performance in India.
“India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country,” William posted on social media.
The couple also will attend events highlighting India’s cricket, fashion and film industries before traveling to New Delhi, where they are scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
The couple met with Modi on their previous trip to India 10 years ago before William, the eldest son of King Charles III, became the heir to the British throne.
The trip marks a significant return to overseas royal engagements for Catherine, who announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for cancer following major abdominal surgery. Kate, as she is commonly known, disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties.
She traveled to Italy without her husband in May, marking her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.

The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has warned of penal action against those failing to comply with the revised prices of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs
The authority, which functions under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, has asked State drug controllers (SDCs) to strictly monitor the prices and submit their action taken reports by November 16, according to an official release on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The revised prices for the 137 anti-cancer drugs came into effect on November 9, 2026, following a gazette order issued on October 17, 2026. The order capped the trade margin on these medicines at 30%.
Based on submissions received from pharmaceutical companies up to November 11, the latest revised price lists have been uploaded on the NPPA website as well as the Pharma Sahi Daam app and portal, the Chemicals and Fertilizers Ministry said.
All manufacturers, stockists, dealers, retailers, hospitals, and medical institutions have been directed to comply with the revised prices and prominently display the updated price lists at their premises and on their websites.
The SDCs have been instructed to strictly monitor compliance across the supply chain and healthcare facilities to ensure that the benefits of the revised maximum retail prices (MRPs) are passed on to patients.
Any violation of the directive may attract overcharging proceedings under the provisions of the DPCO, 2013, the release noted.
Complaints regarding overcharging, shortage, or non-availability of medicines can be reported through the Pharma Sahi Daam app or portal, the NPPA helpline (1800-111-255), or via email at monitoring-nppa@gov.in, it added.

Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.
Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.
Mr. Zelensky said separately in his nightly speech that the Starshield limits hurt Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s jet-powered drones. It is likely, however, that those limits would not affect interceptors in Kyiv, the capital, which is being battered by jet-powered drones but is far from the front lines.
Mr. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment on Friday evening. SpaceX had earlier told Axios that the Ukrainian claim about throttled connectivity was false.

PRAIA, Cape Verde -- PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Cape Verde ’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second five-year term, beating five challengers, including the first woman presidential candidate in the country’s history, provisional results show.
Neves called his reelection as president of the Atlantic island nation off West Africa “a great victory.” The election was dominated by high unemployment and the high cost of living, which has fueled emigration.
Provisional results showed Neves comfortably edged out his opponents, garnering 64% of the vote while Joana Rosa, the main opposition candidate, won 31.4%.
