Scientists race to discover and protect what lives in the ocean
'You wouldn't believe they were of this planet,' says researcher as UN climate summit spotlights marine life
Scientists say not knowing what lives in our oceans is holding back efforts to protect them. Because of that, many are racing to discover and document the wild and diverse species in marine environments that are often hard for humans to access.
Ocean Census, a global collaboration of scientists and non-profit organizations, estimates that scientists have documented less than 10 per cent of some 2.2 million fish, marine mammals, shellfish, plankton, squid, jellyfish and other species that live in our oceans.
"It's very difficult to protect what you don't know," said Michelle Taylor, head of science at Ocean Census.
A sea cucumber with horned appendages, nicknamed Loki, and a bright red-orange coral with fans of slender branches are among 57 new species announced and identified in October from an Ocean Census expedition off Argentina last year.
This new sea cucumber species was nicknamed Loki because of its prominent horned appendages, reminiscent of the god in Norse mythology. It was found in the Mar del Plata submarine canyon off Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
A striking, bright red-orange octocoral was photographed nearly 2,000 metres below the surface of the ocean in Argentina's Mar del Plata canyon. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
A landmark UN biodiversity agreement in 2022 committed to protecting 30 per cent of the world's land, water and marine areas by 2030, but has been falling short on ocean protection, with just 12 per cent of oceans (compared to 27 per cent of lands) set to be protected by 2030.
Canada has so far protected 15.5 per cent of its oceans, according to the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS).
Claire Goodwin, a research scientist at Huntsman Marine Science Centre in St. Andrew's, N.B., said the goal is to protect areas with high biodiversity.
"But if you're not surveying some of your marine life and you don't know what's living there, you can't say which those biodiverse areas are."
A cone jelly captured by the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian off the coast of Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
Sponges that eat meat, provide housing
The problem is that even within Canada, many areas are difficult to explore. Goodwin was part of an expedition in the Saguenay Fjord in Quebec in 2023.
On its steep walls, where only one species of sponge had previously been recorded, her team discovered 20 or 30 sponge species, including some new to science.
Carnivorous sponges were found in Quebec's Saguenay Fjord in 2023. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)
Among them were carnivorous sponges that trap shrimp with glass, velcro-like appendages to engulf and digest slowly, "which was really exciting," said Goodwin, since most sponges are passive filter feeders.
Goodwin says sponges have important roles in the ecosystems — as food for sea stars, homes for some worms and a place to lay eggs for some fish. Sponges in Canadian waters can also grow to half the size of an adult human.
Claire Goodwin collects sponges in the Bay of Fundy off the coast of New Brunswick. (Torben Brydges/Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
The sea slug Dendronotus yrjargul was recorded on a recent expedition led by the Innu Nation. It was the first time the species has been found off the coast of Canada. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC/Innu Nation)
Now Goodwin is working with the Innu Nation in Labrador to survey uncharted waters in their territory. "We literally don't know what the seabed's going to be like, let alone what's going to be living on it."
Climate change impacts and solutions
The race is on to find out as the ocean warms rapidly, and climate change shifts where species are found.
Already, Goodwin says, some species have completely disappeared from regions where they were once common. She points to basket stars, "really cool sea stars that have branching arms," which were once common around St. Andrew's, but haven't been seen there since a rapid warming around 2016.
A basket star, Gorgonocephalus arcticus, is seen in the Saguenay Fjord. The species used to be common in the Bay of Fundy but seems to have disappeared due to climate change. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)
Loïc Jacquemot, a postdoctoral researcher at Université du Québec à Rimouski, said in many areas, we don't even have much of a baseline from which to compare changes.
He's currently surveying Baffin Bay off the coast of Nunavut using a technique called eDNA, which identifies species from DNA shed into the water by organisms' skin, poop and tissues. That way, they can be surveyed without actually seeing or catching them — all you need is a water sample.
Loïc Jacquemot samples water for eDNA in B.C.'s coastal fjords. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)
He said species adapted to colder waters are expected to move into a smaller and smaller area "because, of course, they cannot go much more north," while warmer water species may expand their range.
That can have big impacts on things like the food chain — including fish and shellfish humans eat — and on the way carbon is moved around the ocean by zooplankton species that migrate each day between the depths and the surface.
"It's important for the climate because all these changes impact the way carbon is stored in the ocean," Jacquemot said.
This tiny copepod is one of 20 new species identified by the Ocean Census in October. These organisms are among the zooplankton that move carbon between the surface and depths of the ocean. (The Nippon Foundation-Nekton Ocean Census/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
Photosynthetic algae called diatoms from fjords in Greenland. Diatoms are important for capturing carbon dioxide in the oceans. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)
The carbon stored by the ocean and its species is known as blue carbon. So far it includes 30 per cent of carbon dioxide generated by humans, along with 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by climate change, said a recent UN report, which warned that the ocean's ability to absorb more CO2 and heat is weakening.
Meanwhile, coral reefs, known as biodiversity hotspots with the ability to store huge amounts of carbon, are one of the ecosystems most threatened by climate change.
The impact of the ocean and its species on climate change are at the forefront of this year's UN climate summit, COP31, underway in Antalya, Turkey. Protecting marine ecosystems and "unlocking blue carbon for climate resilience" is one of 10 items on the meeting's "action agenda."
This week at COP31, former U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and groups representing island states pushed for a strong reference to oceans in next year's global "stocktake" of climate policies, supported by the European Union and African countries.
This grenadier fish was observed with parasitic copepods attached to its head during a 2025 Ocean Census expedition off Montagu Island near Antarctica. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
This marine worm, Harmothoe imbricata, was found off Canada's Atlantic coast. (Christy Carr/HMSC)
For the 'biogeochemical functioning of our planet'
Taylor with Ocean Census said marine ecosystems are important for humans — even people who live far from the sea, not just for producing food and medicines, but also on a bigger scale. "You know, it's part of the biogeochemical functioning of our planet. We're very reliant on it, whether we realize it or not."
Taylor, Goodwin and Jacquemot all hope that by sharing with people the amazing diversity of life in the ocean, they can help people appreciate the importance of saving it.
"When we show people pictures and videos of what's underwater, they're always amazed by what we actually have down there," Goodwin said.
Michelle Taylor, head of science for Ocean Census, checks out views from the cameras on the ROV SuBastian during a mission to catalogue deep sea species. (Paul Satchell)
Taylor describes them as an incredible diversity of "wild looking creatures" and says for some of them "you wouldn't believe they were of this planet."
She said she's very worried about coral reefs especially, but "you have to have the attitude that there are solutions to this." In the meantime, she added, "we need to find as many species as we can, so we can understand diversity on this planet before it is lost."
This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia
After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.
Instead, they decided on six.
European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.
In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.
Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations, though, and that many voices must be represented.
“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.
“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president Sunday as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term.
Six candidates are competing, with a runoff scheduled for Nov. 29 if no candidate receives more than half the votes.
Rosa, backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy, is the first woman to run for president since independence from Portugal in 1975. Women have held senior cabinet posts, but Cape Verde has never had a female prime minister or president.
In Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs government policy and holds most executive authority. The president’s role is largely symbolic, although the directly elected head of state can veto legislation.
The Atlantic island nation off West Africa, home to about half a million people, has a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections in a region where that is rare. Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans abroad are registered to vote, almost a fifth of the total electorate.
Many voters feel distant from their leaders and want a president who understands their daily difficulties, while limited economic prospects were driving young people to seek opportunities abroad, said Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde.
Neves, who won in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.
Incumbency gives Neves greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said.
Rosa’s candidacy challenges traditional expectations of women’s roles in a society that remains “very patriarchal,” Évora said.
Rosa has centered her campaign on maintaining a balance of power, arguing that the country needs a counterweight to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, which backs Neves and controls the government and most municipalities.
Known as PAICV, the party won a parliamentary majority in May, ending a decade of government led by the Movement for Democracy. A Rosa victory would again put the presidency and government in rival political camps.
Rosário Luz, a Cape Verde-based writer, said party loyalties mattered more than Rosa’s gender.
“We have a lot of women in politics, but we don’t have the policies for women that we should have,” she said.
Women carry much of the financial responsibility for their households in Cape Verde, but government policies have failed to address that burden, Luz said.

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.
As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.
January 
  
Fourth-hottest January on record
Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia 
  
As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.
February 
  
Fourth-hottest February on record
Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain 
  
The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.
March 
  
Fourth-hottest March on record
Devastating floods across much of the world 
  
In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.
World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly 
  
The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.
April 
  
Second-hottest April on record
Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan 
  
At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.
May 
  
Second-hottest May on record
Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia 
  
At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.
June
  
Second-hottest June on record
Ocean heat enters uncharted territory 
  
Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.
Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth 
  
Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.
West African deluge takes heavy toll 
  
Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.
July
  
Joint-hottest July on record
Fires choke Canada and Europe 
  
Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.
Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup 
  
Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.
At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.
August 
  
Hottest August on record
Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300 
  
Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.
Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown
 
The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.
September
  
Second-hottest September on record
Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia 
  
Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.
October
  
Hottest October on record
Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño 
  
The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.
Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires 
  
Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.
Roads turn to rivers in Chile 
  
After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.
Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest 
  
Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.
November
2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history
Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

In November, right around Veteran's Day, posts online claimed to show former U.S. President Bill Clinton personally helping a homeless veteran outside The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in 1997.
According to the tale, Clinton offered the man, Marcus Williams, his coat, before asking him questions about his service. He then supposedly ordered a Secret Service agent to get Williams food, and personally contacted the Department of Veterans Affairs to help Williams get back on his feet.
The posts began:
"On a freezing December night in 1997, President Bill Clinton was leaving a holiday concert at the Kennedy Center when he noticed a homeless veteran sitting near the entrance. The man wore a thin jacket and was shivering in the cold. In his hands, he held a piece of cardboard with a simple message written on it: "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." What happened next caught the attention of people in the presidential motorcade. Clinton stopped, took off his own coat, placed it around the veteran's shoulders, and sat beside him on the icy concrete.
The veteran, 42 year old Marcus Williams, later told reporters that the President never questioned how he had ended up on the street or lectured him about his choices. Instead, Clinton asked about his military service, the battles he had experienced, and whether anyone had ever properly thanked him for what he had done. According to Secret Service agent Larry Cockell, who later wrote about the encounter, Clinton stayed with Marcus for nearly 25 minutes despite the freezing temperatures. When Marcus admitted that he had not eaten in two days, Clinton sent an agent to a nearby restaurant to get him food. He refused to leave until Marcus had finished his meal.
The posts were accompanied by images supposedly showing the two meeting as well as Williams holding a cardboard sign reading "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether the story and images were real or fake.
We first uploaded the images into Google Lens to perform a reverse image search. Next, we used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo with phrases such as "Bill Clinton Marcus Williams Homeless Veteran" to see whether any reputable news outlets had documented the events. If the scene had occurred and the images were real, we would find evidence in newspapers and media archives like Getty Images. That was not the case. We did not locate any examples of credible outlets publishing the images, nor reporting on the alleged meeting.
We found that neither the story nor the images were real, and that they were generated using artificial intelligence tools. Therefore, we've labeled the claim false.
We uploaded the images accompanying the story into several tools that screen visual media for signs of AI: Sightengine, Hive Moderation, and Google's integrated SynthID detector. The first two found a high likelihood that the images were AI-generated, and the SynthID detector found the invisible watermark indicating Google's AI tools generated the images. We also ran the story through the AI text detection tool Pangram, which also determined that all of the text was written using a large language model such as ChatGPT.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Detecting that the image was fake without using those tools was more difficult, given it was grayscale and grainy, but not impossible. We noticed that the writing on the cardboard sign looked too perfect, the cardboard itself looked unusually bright and the supposedly parallel sidewalk cracks didn't form straight lines or meet at a single vanishing point.
Our searches also uncovered a January article written by the fact-checking organization Lead Stories debunking the exact same story, though featuring a real archival image of Clinton instead of an AI-generated one. That fact-check also noted some factual errors in the text, most prominently that one of Clinton's Secret Service agents wrote about the encounter in a memoir. (No such memoir existed.) Because the exact claim was also previously been fact-checked almost a year ago, we concluded that users posting the claim in October and November were doing so in an attempt to make money.
The fictional story is an example of glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." These types of low-quality posts often use standard or template language, making small tweaks in an attempt to game the social media algorithms. They rely on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories and hope to generate a profit from advertising revenue if the posts go viral.
Snopes previously explained the ongoing trend of politically motivated, AI-generated slop content similar to the claim debunked in this article.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Pat Ahern, 33, who moved from Colorado to Stockholm in 2021. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
When I did a semester abroad in Sweden in 2014, I told myself I wasn't going to get into a relationship. Then I met Evelina.
She was studying law, and we crossed paths at a pub crawl. I was drawn to her compassion, curiosity, sense of humor, and love for nature. We started dating shortly after meeting, and went long-distance when I went back to the US.
In 2015, she got an opportunity to study abroad for about a year in Colorado. The business I'd been trying to start in New York was crashing and burning, so I made a fresh start in Colorado to be with her.
We got to spend more time together over the next few years and wanted to build our life, but as Evelina had a law degree from Sweden, the US didn't seem like a realistic path. Seven years after we met, in 2021, I moved to Sweden, having applied for a residence permit.
Evelina and I got married in 2022. In the grand scheme of things, I think I made a pretty small sacrifice by coming over to Sweden. It would've been a pretty massive sacrifice for her if we chose to live in the US.
How I run my company from Sweden
In order to take my digital marketing agency overseas, I set up a separate business entity in Sweden. I had to pass anti-money-laundering checks to set up a bank account. After seven to eight months, I was legally able to pay myself from the Swedish entity. Thankfully, I'd planned for that and set money aside.
Sweden is eight hours ahead of Colorado, where the majority of my team and clients are based, so I mostly have meetings in the latter half of my day.
At first, I worked into the evening, typically wrapping up around 8 p.m. When I had my son in 2024, I had to make adjustments.
Three days per week, I work until between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. On Tuesdays, I work from the climbing gym I'm a member of near my son's preschool so I can pick him up, spend the evening with him, and put him to bed. I also take Fridays off so we can go on day trips.
Working across time zones has made it more challenging to grab a beer with a friend or go rock climbing after work, but I'm trying to see the positives. I can use the earlier hours of my day to have a more leisurely morning or for deep, focused work. Most weekday mornings, I get my son ready for pre-school and have breakfast with him. Then, I start my day around 10 a.m.
I'm taxed more in Sweden, but it feels worth it
Sweden is exceptional. I pay more taxes than I would in the US, but feel I'm benefiting. When my son was born, the hospital bill was somewhere around $100. In the US, it would have likely cost several thousand dollars. Plus, parents get to share 480 days of parental leave.
The biggest challenge is that Sweden is not a fun place to be in winter. Compared to my experience with Colorado winters, it's colder, windier, and it gets dark far earlier in the day. Traditional Swedish food has grown on me over the years, but I crave good bagels, breakfast burritos, and pizza.
Living in Sweden makes it harder for us to see my friends or family in the US. Thankfully, my wife's friends and their partners in Sweden are now my friends, too, and I've met great people through my climbing gym. Most people I've met here have no issues communicating in English, but I'm still trying to learn Swedish.
Our son is 2 years old. In the future, flipping back and forth between Sweden and the US may be hard, but I'd still love for our family to have a place to call home in both countries someday.

The Telangana State Women’s Commission (TGSCW) has initiated an inquiry into an alleged illegal oocyte donation racket in Hyderabad, issuing notices to eight Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) centres and egg banks over suspected irregularities in their donor records and procurement practices.
The Commission examined representatives of the eight institutions on Friday, November 13, after directing their managements to appear before it. However, TGSCW Chairperson Nerella Sharada expressed dissatisfaction after some centres sent staff members and other representatives instead of senior management, despite being specifically instructed to attend in person. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned after the institutions assured the Commission that their management would appear at the next hearing.
During Friday’s proceedings, the Commission scrutinised reports, records and details of egg donors submitted by the ART centres and egg banks. “Several irregularities and suspicious elements have emerged from the records examined so far,” said Ms. Sharada.
She also questioned claims made by the institutions that nearly 90% of their egg donors came from other States and donated their eggs voluntarily without receiving any remuneration or financial compensation. She said the claims raised several questions and warranted further investigation.
Health Department’s investigation
Commissioner of Health and Family Welfare, Sangeetha Satyanarayana, also attended the inquiry, during which Ms. Sharada sought details about the progress of the department’s investigation into the alleged illegal egg procurement practices. The discussions also covered shortcomings in the existing Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and its implementation, particularly the challenges in regulating and monitoring ART centres and egg banks.
Ms. Sharada said she would soon meet Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha and Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to inform them of the findings and discuss corrective measures, including possible legislative amendments to strengthen regulation of the sector.
More ART centres likely to come under scanner
Ms. Sharada further said that the Commission has also received information indicating the possible involvement of several other ART centres and egg banks in the alleged racket. It plans to issue notices to their management and summon them for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry.
“The Commission will not tolerate illegal practices that compromise women’s health, dignity and rights. We will continue the investigation in coordination with the concerned government departments to identify those responsible and ensure appropriate legal action,” she added.

Border Crossings Have Plummeted. Stephen Miller Isn’t Satisfied.
Mexico has cooperated to significantly slow the flow of migrants. The new White House chief of staff insists it is not enough.
Since President Trump resumed office, the number of illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border has dropped to the lowest point in decades.
For one of Mr. Trump’s top policy advisers, that is not enough.
In conversations with both American and Mexican officials over the last several months, Stephen Miller has insisted that illegal border crossings must be reduced, according to officials in both countries familiar with the private conversations but not authorized to discuss them.
Mr. Miller’s goal, they said, is zero crossings. Mexican officials have said that, with a nearly 2,000-mile border, that is simply not possible.
In his new role as chief of staff, Mr. Miller is expected to continue driving that agenda.
One of the main forums for Mr. Miller’s demands has been his near daily calls with the U.S. ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, some of the officials said. On calls with staff, Mr. Miller, previously the deputy chief of staff, frequently rails about the number of border crossings, despite their low figures, the officials said.
That has been especially true in recent months, they said, as border crossings increased slightly, to the highest point in Mr. Trump’s second term.

On 11 November 2026, terrorists opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down (here, here, and here).
Amid the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows defence expert Wing Commander (Wg Cdr) Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the attack was a false flag operation orchestrated to divert public attention from mounting political pressure on the Narendra Modi government, including Congress protests demanding the Chief Election Commissioner’s resignation and the Arunachal Pradesh controversy. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) stating that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) did not describe the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel as a false flag operation. In the original ANI video, he discussed the security situation in Kulgam, the presence of terrorist sleeper cells, and the need for better intelligence coordination and proactive security measures. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also confirmed on 12 November 2026 that the viral video was digitally altered and falsely attributed remarks to him. AI detection tools, Hive and Hiya, also indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating it.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 11 November 2026, featuring the same footage of Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd), wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, in the original video, he does not describe the Kulgam attack as a false flag operation or link it to the political developments mentioned in the viral clip. Instead, he expresses concern over the incident, noting that Kulgam has witnessed several such attacks in the past. He emphasises the need for a more proactive security approach, better intelligence coordination, and improved intelligence gathering in areas where terrorists operate and maintain sleeper cells. He also highlights the need to investigate how these groups receive logistical support, including accommodation, ammunition, and water.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear that Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) was describing the Kulgam attack as a false-flag operation.
The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also debunked the claim in an X post dated 12 November 2026, stating that the video was digitally manipulated and falsely attributed remarks to Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd). It clarified that he did not make any such comments in the original video and had instead spoken about terrorist organisations and the need for offensive action and better coordination to prevent such attacks.
To sum up, this video of Wg Cdr Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation is digitally manipulated.

Mexican Prosecutor Who Helped C.I.A. Secretly Operate in His State Flees to the U.S.
The prosecutor, who faces arrest in Mexico after allowing C.I.A. officers into Chihuahua state, is under the protection of the U.S. government, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she did not want U.S. forces taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, calling it a breach of sovereignty. Under the Trump administration, meanwhile, the C.I.A. sought to expand its activity in the country, and saw Mr. Zuany as a partner to help it do so quietly.
The C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua was blown when a car crash in April resulted in the deaths of two C.I.A. officers, leading to a national scandal and Mr. Zuany’s resignation. While an investigation determined the crash an accident, the Mexican authorities recently issued a warrant for Mr. Zuany’s arrest on charges related to his involvement with the agency.
Ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury at the C.I.A.’s presence during raids in Chihuahua and denied knowledge of the agency’s activities. On Wednesday, she said in a regular morning news conference that investigations into matter must continue.
“It’s worth finding out who this person is and how he worked with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said of Mr. Zuany.

Abdul El-Sayed will soon become the first epidemiologist in the Senate at a moment that would keep anyone with a public health background up at night. More than 5,000 Americans have been sickened by the measles this year and the United States is expected to lose its formal measles elimination status by the end of the month. Dengue fever is spreading in Florida, respiratory virus season is underway, and the United States just weathered a foodborne illness outbreak that sickened more than 20,000.
In a wide-ranging interview with STAT, the Michigan Democrat emphasized that he is hopeful the United States can fix its growing trust-in-science problem, but he expressed frustration — at Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at drug and insurance companies, and at the field of public health — for leading America down this path.
“We’ve created the space for a few grifters to come in and in effect lie to the public,” El-Sayed said. “To create a level of distrust in science and in public health that has had disastrous consequences.”
Below, El-Sayed speaks about his plan to rebuild trust in science and public health, his intentions toward Kennedy, and how gatekeeping has kept scientific discoveries from the public. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
As the senator-elect from Michigan, how can you help restore trust in health and science? What can you do from Washington to improve these issues?
Well, No. 1, I think you can start taking on greed. Which is why I support “Medicare for All,” because it gets the greed of the insurance industry and the greed of the pharmaceutical industry and the greed of the hospital corporations out of the way so folks can benefit from the incredible things that science creates.
No. 2, I think you have to show the grifters for who they are and how they are, the ways that they use big words that they don’t understand to trick the public, the ways that there’s always a catch at the end where they’re making money off of their grift.
And No. 3, I want to reinvigorate a movement for public health that is willing to stand up to the power of big corporations. … I think we need to be willing to pick a righteous fight in service of the public health.
You’ve mentioned your eagerness to investigate RFK Jr. Are you concerned at all that grilling RFK could serve to further polarize the people that do believe in him?
Well, depending upon how you grill him.
What do you mean?
You can grill a steak and get it to perfect medium rare, or you can grill a steak and it’s well done and inedible, the way the president likes it.
The mistake would be to focus on areas that are polarizing. I wanna understand why he DOGE’d away or he allowed the DOGE’ing away of the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] in ways that left us eating crap lettuce. I want to understand why he hasn’t led the effort to take on the pesticides that are in our food or the additives in our food, why he’s kowtowing to the same corporations he said he was going to stand up to. I want to understand that. Let’s start there.
Why Kennedy supporters should trust him
I’m curious if you have a message to the people that do support Kennedy on why they should trust someone like you on issues of public health.
Well, he told you he’s gonna stand up to the corporations. He hasn’t. I have.
There’s no candidate who’s taken more spending against them in a primary election in their own party than I have, not in history. So at least you know I’m gonna stand up.
I’ve spent my whole career trying to make people healthier, trying to address the greed in our health care system.
There’s all this talk of back and forth: Should RFK Jr. be investigated? Should he be removed? What’s your latest thinking on this?
I think we focus too much on him. I think the bigger question is how do we build the CDC and FDA and NIH [National Institutes of Health] that are worthy of the people that they serve, and that’s gonna always be my focus.
So any investigation that we’re doing is about trying to correct the problems and address the flaws and the faults rather than trying to achieve any sort of retribution.
The people are struggling. They are suffering. They can barely afford groceries, can barely afford gas, can barely see a doctor, are worried about the air they’re breathing, the water they’re drinking, the quality of groceries they’re even buying for an exorbitant price.
My job is to serve them. The personalities involved are secondary to me. My job is to go in and figure out what went wrong, how do we fix it, and how do we hold accountable the people who — if they knowingly broke something — how we do we hold them accountable for it. It’s that simple. It’s less about the personalities. I think we focus too much on that.
Working with RFK Jr.
There’s been this desire among folks within your party to find common ground with RFK on issues. Are there issues that you think you could work with RFK and his team on, or are we kind of past that?
If he actually wants to show up and start doing the things he said he was going to do on pollutants, on additives, sure. I’ll work with anyone. He could be wrong on 95 things, but if he’s right on five, I’ll work with him on those five and hold him accountable for the 95.
Obviously Democrats can’t fix all of these issues. Trust issues started before RFK and I’m sure they’ll go on past RFK. How do you think about how we should judge Democrats’ progress on these issues?
Are we achieving goals that keep people healthy, reduce their costs, empower them. … If we’re doing that, then we’re winning and we’re succeeding. If not, then we’re not. I want people to be able to be their healthiest and their wealthiest. That’s really the bottom line.
It seems like a foregone conclusion, the U.S. will lose its measles elimination status. Do you have thoughts on that?
It’s a travesty. We didn’t have to get here. In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.
Where did we go wrong in making health care so untrustworthy that somebody with such limited cognitive ability and who is so obviously a grifter, where he could step in and change so many minds? That’s on us.
Science is ‘a beautiful, incredible gift’
The belief that the measles vaccine causes autism is going up over time, and it’s been debunked for 20 years. … How do we break through here?
It starts with basic science education. … Too often the way that scientists speak is about speaking to other scientists to make themselves sound smarter rather than speaking to the public, to help the public feel as smart as they really are. By making sure that everybody understands how and why these things work. Science for the public good … that ethos is something that we’ve forgotten. And I really, desperately want us to remember it.
Science is a gift. It’s a beautiful, incredible gift, and we missed the opportunity to communicate it in all of its elegance because too often it is this thing that is sort of held among the scientific community for consumption by the scientific community. And then we allow a lot of our best science to sit behind paywalls people can’t hop over. So there’s a resentment that happens in publicly funded science for the most part, and we’re keeping [it] out of the hands of people who need it most.
These are big structural questions that ought to animate the way we do science for the rest of the 21st century, and I’m hoping that I can use my role as a doctor and a scientist in the Senate to start driving that conversation among the folks in science.
You can focus on RFK Jr. all you want, but he identified a set of weaknesses that those of us who have committed our lives to science and the public’s health that we allowed to exist in the first place.
How hopeful are you that we can solve these trust issues?
I wouldn’t be doing this if I didn’t believe we could. Science always wins. I just hope that it wins quickly. But the beautiful thing about science is that in the end it always finds the right answer.

How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?
- Published
England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.
But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina.
So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look.
Were the situations the same?
First of all the context of the two games was entirely different.
England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players.
Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on.
But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.
Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano.
Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford.
"Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners."
What was different with the subs?
Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it.
In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off.
Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward.
But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend.
However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward.
The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute.
And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance.
However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs.
Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin.
Burn replaced fellow defender White in the 89th minute.
"Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel.
"So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game.
"I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs."
What do the stats tell us?
England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm.
In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53.
Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41.
In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%.
In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia, as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%.
"For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"We defended in a 4-4-1," he continued.
"The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I said it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave."
England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain.
But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy.
What made the difference?
So what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity?
After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle.
"I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side.
"There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side."
Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game.
"Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he said.
Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2.
He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time.
Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers."

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.
Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran. He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night.
In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.”
He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’”
Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK).
He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods.
His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence.
The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption. They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights.
Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.”
According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners.
In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed. In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences.
Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.”
Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.
Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.”
In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”.
He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life.
Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. Hailey never took a breath; she was brain dead.
Her parents sat vigil for two days, waiting for her sister to arrive from overseas so she could say goodbye. When they finally accepted that their daughter had died, the organ donation team took over.
Six months later, our ICU received a letter describing the four lives Hailey had saved. Her kidneys went to two grandparents, each now playing with their grandchildren. Her liver saved a young woman dying of hepatitis who was now snorkeling in a tropical ocean. And her heart was beating inside a young man with a fatal congenital heart condition who was now hiking along the coast.
I’ve never forgotten Hailey or the lives she saved, and I believe deeply in organ donation. But starting Nov. 18, new rules from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network will change how the organ donation process works, allowing organ procurement organizations to approach families about donation before they’ve decided whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment.
The goal is to get more viable organs to the more than 100,000 people in the U.S. waiting for life-saving transplants. But I worry this approach blurs the line between the physicians fighting to save a patient’s life and the teams responsible for organ procurement.
That isn’t fair to families, who expect that our sole concern is their loved one’s well-being. Proposing potential organ donation early opens the door to distrust in their ICU care. We should keep that door shut.
Why it’s so hard to determine death
In 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services reported 73 cases in which organ donation had been authorized, but not completed, where donors showed “neurological signs incompatible with organ donation.” The New York Times reported that some patients may not have been dead at the time organ procurement was initiated, often in rural or small hospitals.
These findings raised troubling questions about whether the motivation for higher transplant numbers had taken precedence over careful assessment of the neurological condition of potential donors.
The Uniform Determination of Death Act, accepted by most states, establishes two definitions of death: irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function, or irreversible loss of function of the entire brain, known as brain death.
To patients’ families, brain death is often harder to grasp than circulatory death. Their loved one appears alive: breathing on a mechanical ventilator, heart still beating steadily on the monitor, skin warm and pink. Yet without mechanical support, if their brain no longer functions, their body will no longer function.
Donation after circulatory death (DCD) involves patients with grave prognoses for whom a decision has been made to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. Many have catastrophic brain injuries, although they do not meet the criteria for brain death. Determining whether a patient is an appropriate candidate for DCD requires a physician’s judgment about the patient’s prognosis, a process that is difficult to standardize.
In contrast, medical standards for determining brain death are uniform and widely practiced in the United States. A diagnosis requires three criteria, as we did for Hailey, rigorously assessed: coma with a known cause, loss of brainstem reflexes, and loss of the ability to breathe spontaneously, tested by a strict protocol known as the apnea test.
No one who has been correctly diagnosed with brain death under these criteria has ever recovered. Not one person.
I’m careful to teach our medical students never to say that we “withdraw care” because even when we stop life-sustaining treatment, we continue to care for our patients. Care for the dying is as critical as care for the living.
These decisions require our full attention and the trust of patients’ families, so it’s imperative that a separate organ donation team work alongside us, remaining independent of the physicians treating the patient.
A safer path to more organ donations
Physicians should be working to increase organ donation while enhancing patient safety.
First, we need to better educate people about what it means to be an organ donor. When someone checks “organ donation” on their driver’s license, they should understand how we define death and what that check mark really means.
Second, we can expand access to neurological expertise in underserved areas, particularly small and rural hospitals that don’t have immediate access to neurologists or neurointensivists. A video consultation with a neurologist or intensive care physician at an academic or comprehensive health care institution can aid in assessing the level of consciousness of patients being considered for DCD, before they’re taken to the operating room for organ recovery.
Another way to increase organ donation is to focus on patients who have been declared brain dead. After brain death, families and health care teams have more time to obtain organs in an orderly fashion, facilitating the best outcome for both donors and recipients.
The ICU clinicians taking care of a patient nearing death are often deep in discussions of the differences (and similarities) between DCD and brain death as they apply to their loved one. The discussions are often confusing and cause conflicted emotions in families facing tragedy.
The new organ procurement organization policy allows donation teams to break into this discussion, often long before family and friends have fully grasped the gravity of the patient’s injury. This interruption can subtly blur the distinction between our caring for the patient and obtaining organs for someone else.
Our first priority must always be the patient before us, and ensuring that the family members making decisions on their behalf understand and trust the care we’re providing.
In the ICU we walk the path of brain death and cardiac death carefully, always remembering that organ donation offers a small piece of biological immortality. Our patients are not yet forever gone.
Tarvez Tucker, M.D., is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University. Her forthcoming book, “The Brain at Twilight: The Neuroscience of Our Last Words and Moments,” will be published in December 2026 by Columbia University Press.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

A Mexican Artist Sang Some of His Hits. Authorities Stopped the Show, Then Arrested Him.
A concert by the singer Gabito Ballesteros was suspended after he sang songs that supposedly glorify cartel culture. The action has renewed a debate over culture and free speech.
A popular Mexican singer’s concert was halted on Friday night because he performed songs considered to be glorifying cartel culture, making him the latest and most high-profile artist to be ensnared in a government crackdown on the genre known as narcocorridos.
He was later arrested by the federal authorities in relation to an unrelated investigation.
Gabito Ballesteros, 27, whose songs have billions of streams, was performing at a fair in Querétaro State in central Mexico when authorities escorted him off the stage.
Before the show, his set list was reviewed and approved by state officials and event organizers, according to a statement issued by the fair. Songs that glorified criminal activities were explicitly excluded, in accordance with state regulations, the fair said.
Last year, the state joined several other states and municipalities throughout Mexico that effectively prohibit the public performance of so-called narcocorridos, a version of traditional Mexican ballads that celebrate drug cartels instead of historic events and everyday life. Violations were punishable with fines or even jail time.
The actions — and the genre itself — have sparked much debate in Mexico, which has been wrestling with both the effects of organized crime, particularly amid pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels, and its identity as defined through popular culture. The discussion also has became a referendum on free speech.
On Friday night, Mr. Ballesteros performed an unauthorized song and local authorities took him offstage to remind him of his prior agreement, the fair said. When he returned, the fair said Mr. Ballesteros started to perform another unauthorized song, “AMG.” The 2022 hit, which references the luxurious lifestyles and fancy cars of cartel members, has nearly one billion streams on Spotify.
