A ₹2,000 traffic challan issued to a motorist for allegedly driving at 101 kmph on the Yamuna Expressway, where the speed limit is 100 kmph, has triggered a debate on social media over speeding rules, cameras and traffic enforcement.
The incident came to light after Anujeet Shivam, who goes by @anujitshivam on X, shared a screenshot of the challan, questioning the fine for exceeding the prescribed speed limit by just 1 kmph.
"1 km/h. That's it," Shivam wrote in his post.
However, the challan screenshot revealed another unusual detail. The speed camera reportedly recorded the location of the alleged violation as 0°N, 0°E, a point in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, rather than an identifiable location on the Yamuna Expressway.
Tagging Noida Traffic Police and UP Traffic Police, Shivam questioned the accuracy of the enforcement mechanism and asked, "Is this really how road safety works?"
Responding to his post, Noida Traffic Police asked him to contact the e-challan helpline at 7065060882.
The incident soon attracted attention, with social media users divided over whether a fine for exceeding the speed limit by 1 kmph was justified. Several also questioned the accuracy and functioning of AI-powered speed cameras.
While some users defended the traffic authorities, arguing that 100 kmph is the maximum permitted speed and not a target for motorists, others questioned the enforcement of such a narrow speed margin.
One user pointed out that allowing a vehicle to exceed the limit by 1 kmph could lead to further questions about where the permissible threshold should end.
"102 is only 1 more than 101. 103 is only 1 more than 102... where should we stop?" the user wrote.
Another argued that motorists should be given a permissible speed tolerance and claimed that a 5% variance should apply. The user also questioned why the speed limit on the expressway was not 120 kmph.
Some users, however, maintained that there was no ambiguity in the rules.
"100 is the limit. Above that, whether 1 or 2 or 50 kmph, it doesn't matter. You will be challaned ₹2,000. That's how the system is programmed," one comment read.
Another user said that the speed limit was the maximum speed a motorist could legally drive at, adding that drivers should ideally maintain a speed slightly below it.
"100 kmph limit is not to go at exactly 100 kmph. That's the maximum limit you can go. It simply means, you should go at 90-95 kmph. AI cameras don't have emotions and logic. They take pictures and the UI isolates based on speed," the user commented.
The debate also shifted to the accuracy of speed detection systems and whether motorists have sufficient grounds to challenge questionable challans.
One user claimed that car speedometers are generally calibrated to show speeds 5-8% higher than the vehicle's actual speed. According to the user, a speed reading of 101 kmph on a speed gun could therefore translate into a higher reading on the vehicle's speedometer.
Another user questioned how motorists could establish their innocence if they received multiple challans despite allegedly staying within the prescribed speed limit.
"There is something wrong. I got 3 challans of ₹2,000 each within 20 minutes on the same expressway. I really do not know how it works, but I did not cross the speed limit of 100. The question is how will I prove?" the user wrote.
Others argued that the controversy was distracting from more serious road safety concerns, including wrong-side driving, trucks parked on roads and vehicles using dazzling headlights.
"Yes, that 1% mistake is a mistake, no doubt. But police are absolutely blind towards wrong-side drivers, truck parking on roads and dazzling lights. Haven't you noticed how much bigger threats those are?" another user commented.

The Italianization of Europe
Over more than a quarter-century, I’ve watched Europe’s politics become more like Italy’s, with all the resulting instability, as the far right came in from the cold.
When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.
At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.
As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.
An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.
Back then, I didn’t see the change around me, but now, more than a quarter-century later, after spending decades reporting on Italian politics and changes across Europe, I have come to understand that I was living in the future.
In the time since, I have seen an Italianization of politics all around the continent, with coalitions of small parties resulting in instability, with fed-up voters desperate for new saviors. But more than anything, I have seen — in Britain, France, Germany — countries following the Italian model by allowing the far right into the political mainstream.

Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans — and cats
Editor's note: Today, November 13, is World Kindness Day!
Kind-minded organizations from various countries came up with the idea and announced it on November 13, 1998. (And the date stuck.) The goal is kinda obvious — do something kind!
It doesn't matter if it's a modest action. One of the founding groups is the Small Kindness Movement of Japan. And no kind deed is too small to acknowledge. One year, the Japanese movement gave an award to a cabbie who pulled over to clear trash bags off the road lest they cause an accident. According to a report in the Christian Science Monitor, the cab driver humbly said it was "no big deal."
So on Friday, November 13, 2026, try a little kindness. To inspire you, we've talked to folks whose lives were changed by kindness — and asked the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, a global network, to submit pictures that capture a kind moment. Animal lovers will be happy to see photos of kindness toward animals as well as an image of a support donkey — a reminder that animals can be kind to us humans, too.
Let's start with a simple yet profound story about a snack.
Back in 2004, Maymunah Yusuf Kadiri, a neuro-psychiatrist and mental health advocate in Nigeria, was a young doctor working in the emergency room at the Lagos State University Teaching hospital. One night sticks in her mind. It was chaos. There were accident victims everywhere. She recalls the blood, the cries and her own exhaustion.
"I hadn't eaten for over 12 hours, and my hands were shaking," says Kadiri, who was 28 at the time. "Then an elderly cleaner, one of those invisible heroes in hospitals, walked up to me with a small nylon bag." Inside was a biscuit and a sachet of water.
"Doctor," she said, "you need small strength to save people."
"It sounds simple, but I'll never forget it. That biscuit tasted like hope. Her kindness reminded me that healing isn't only about medicine, it's about humanity," says Kadiri. "As a psychiatrist, I've seen it over and over: People don't just heal in hospitals, they heal in human connections."
And while one isolated act of kindness may seem random, it can lead to much more.
Huguette Diakabana remembers when she had to drop out of school at age 10 — until a mysterious donor came to her rescue. Her family was planning to emigrate to the U.S. from Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of Congo) and couldn't afford school fees. They figured she'd make up the year later. She had a different idea: "I put on my previous year's uniform and sat outside under the street window of my would-be classroom." One day, the director invited her inside. Diakabana realized someone must have paid her school fees, but who?
Returning to the school years later, Diakabana discovered it was a school guard. She wanted to repay him. "He told me to help others when I could, so I launched a scholarship program," says Diakabana, who now lives in Switzerland and is co-founder of The Luminous Agency, which focuses on digital literacy.
Dr. Junaid Nabi, a physician-scientist who conducts research in health care technology at the RAND School in Washington, D.C. and is a senior fellow at the Aspen Institute, says he's come to realize that kindness isn't actually a trickle in the ocean. An act of kindness is more like dropping a stone that creates expanding ripples, he says.
"There are studies that illustrate how kindness spreads through social networks in measurable ways. When we are kind to someone, they don't just feel better — they become 25% more likely to help others."
One such investigation described how kindness can be contagious. It was sparked by reports of an outbreak of kindness on a cold December morning in 2012. A stranger picked up the tab for the coffee order of the next customer in the drive-through line at a Tim Hortons coffeehouse in Winnipeg, Canada. And that customer picked up the tab of the person behind him. In the end, 226 customers passed on this act of kindness.
The study authors, citing other examples of "pay it forward" kindness at fast food restaurants and their own experiments encouraging subjects to help others, write: "Why, in the absence of external sanctions and opportunities for reciprocation, do people help strangers? One possible explanation is that helping is driven by receiving or observing help. In other words, generosity towards strangers may be socially contagious."
Don't talk yourself out of it
It might sound contradictory, but researchers studying the psychology of altruism, kindness and giving have uncovered this curious paradox: Sometimes, people can be kind-hearted, have a genuine desire to help someone, but in spite of that, not give at all.
Marta Serra-Garcia, a professor of economics and strategy at the Rady School of Management in the University of California, San Diego, is one of the authors of the study Give Enough or Not at all.
"There's a growing body of work in economics and psychology trying to understand altruism. Altruism is a result of a feeling of empathy and the emotion of feeling warm and well when you help others. We know people are altruistic, but we're trying to understand when, why and how," she says.
The study, published in the September Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, revealed that people may prefer to give nothing rather than donate an amount they consider too small — even when those on the receiving end would welcome whatever they can get.
"It seems like an odd thing," Serra-Garcia says in an interview over a video call with NPR. "You're generous, but because you want to do the right thing, you might end up not giving at all, out of concern that your gift would be viewed as inappropriate or might even offend the other person."
In one experiment in the study, givers tended to overestimate the minimum amount recipients would consider acceptable.
"We tend to think there are givers and non-givers," says Serra-Garcia. "The people who give are the generous and kind ones, the non-givers are just not generous." But the study indicates otherwise.
"That perception of appropriateness makes them think, "I'd rather not give at all, although I'm a generous person," says Serra-Garcia.
Nature or nurture?
And where does kindness come from? Are you born with it? Or can you learn to be compassionate and empathetic?
Jeff R. Temple, a professor and psychologist with UTHealth Houston, says kindness is a central thread running through his studies on healthy relationships among adolescents and young adults.
"In our intervention work — including with the Fourth R program and other school-based curricula — we teach adolescents to practice perspective-taking, to express care even during disagreement and recognize the impact of their words and actions. These are essentially the behavioral expressions of kindness."
Such kids are less likely to bully others because they know what healthy relationships are like, he says.
A ripple effect
And let's not forget that kindness can change not only the life of the recipient of the kind deed but of the kind person, says Nabi, who offers this anecdote.
In the 2013 Savar building collapse in Bangladesh, more than 1,000 garment workers died and thousands were injured. Nabi arrived at the disaster site as a Red Cross volunteer, expecting to gain experience in trauma care. Instead, he says, the experience changed his psyche, teaching him about the nature of true kindness.
"In the midst of chaos, with bodies awaiting identification, kindness came down to being present during others' darkest moments," says Nabi. "I performed CPR on workers I knew wouldn't survive and when I couldn't save someone, I stayed by their side, holding their hand."
"Before Savar, I was mechanistic, rushing through clinical work like tasks," he recalls. "The image of workers who had embraced each other as concrete crushed them — that final act of human kindness in the face of death — shattered my callousness completely."
When he returned to the hospital, he listened to patients differently, giving them more of his time. He also urges doctors to volunteer for humanitarian causes to practice compassion.
"Kindness, I learned, is about showing up completely for another person's suffering," Navi reflects, "and letting that experience fundamentally change who you are."
So if you began reading this story with the thought that World Kindness Day is … a gimmick … it is a gimmick imbued with heart and hope.
It's a good reminder to practice kindness more, Dr. Kadiri says. "And here's the beautiful part: When someone receives kindness, they don't just feel better, they become better." They may be inspired to perform their own act of kindness. And that, she says, makes the world a kinder, better place too.

Do the Dems need new leadership?
A Schumer challenger has entered the ring.
Hi readers, happy Friday! Today, we’re saying farewell — for now — to “Democrats in array.” Not quite two weeks after winning the 2026 midterms by a historic margin, the party has a leadership fight on its hands.
On Thursday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, made it official: He’s challenging current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for the title of majority leader next year, promising a bolder and more aggressive agenda for the party.
“It is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen told MS NOW host Jen Psaki when he announced his candidacy on her show. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”
Newly elected Democrats Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), each of whom defeated more leadership-aligned Democrats in their Senate primaries, are backing his bid. But Van Hollen will have an uphill climb to win the job, which is set to be decided in a closed-door vote early next month. Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, starting in 2017, and says he’s confident he will have the votes to be reelected in December.
Searching for “fighters”
The Senate is the only chamber currently dealing with an active leadership fight, but it’s not the only one with some leadership angst. In the House, current Democratic minority leader Hakeem Jeffries is the overwhelming favorite to become the new speaker in January (he currently lacks any Democratic challengers). But not everyone is happy about it, as my colleague Astead Herndon reported on Thursday.
The divide, he argues — both in the Schumer-Van Hollen showdown and frustrations with Jeffries — is not really about progressive versus moderate. Instead, he says, it’s about an energized, angry Democratic base looking for fighters to lead the party into what’s almost certain to be a combative final two years of the Trump administration, and a sense that neither Schumer nor Jeffries are ready to meet the moment.
It’s not just a problem for this cycle, either: Democrats won so widely last week that they’re very likely to hang onto their majorities at least through the 2028 election, Eric Levitz points out.
There’s nothing to say that Democrats will have the same leaders in two years (particularly Schumer, who’s up for reelection in 2028 but may either retire or face a serious primary challenge).
But the intra-party debate that we’re watching play out right now is effectively a preview of the higher-stakes fight to come in 2028, when Democrats could also have control of the presidency — and their freest legislative hand since the 2008 election.
As Eric writes, that will come with some real challenges, not least that Democrats currently appear to be facing an impossible trio of economic promises, one of which they’ll likely need to break. But it will also be a moment of opportunity — if the party’s leaders are ready for it.

Rajasthan United FC claimed its first win of the season with a 2-0 victory over Samaleswari SC in the Indian Football League 2026–27 at the Birsa Munda Athletics Stadium.
After a goalless first half, two second-half goals settled the match, and Thomyo Shimray was involved in both. He opened the scoring in the 51st minute with a shot from a tight angle. In the 87th minute he crossed for Brijesh Giri, who headed in the second goal.
The result lifts Rajasthan to eighth in the table with three points from three matches. Samaleswari remains bottom and is still looking for its first points after three games.
Both sides started brightly, and each went close inside four minutes. In the second minute Alan Thapa met a cross from the left with a powerful header that went just over the bar. Two minutes later Yoihenba Meitei shot from outside the box, and the ball hit the crossbar and came back into play.
The game soon became a stop-start contest for control, with plenty of tactical fouls and neither side able to take charge. The Desert Warriors were the first to find a way through. In the 20th minute, Judah Garcia got into the box and beat goalkeeper Padam Chettri, but his shot went just over. Garcia then sent a direct free-kick off target, and Pranjal Bhumij’s low shot made Padam dive at full stretch before it went wide as Rajasthan started to exert control.
Samaleswari’s best opening came in the 34th minute when Yoihenba’s free-kick was not cleared, and Gope palmed away Mohammed El Jaaouani’s first-time shot.
The first half had started directly, but the second began more cautiously, with both teams keeping men back. It took a moment of invention to break the deadlock. Rajasthan worked a short corner, and Shimray carried the ball into the box from the right. Instead of looking for a team-mate in the middle, he shot from a very tight angle. The ball beat Padam at his near post and went in off the woodwork.
Needing an equaliser, Samaleswari started to be more adventerous, leaving space for Rajasthan to exploit. Four minutes later, Shimray was back in the same position and sent a low cross across the six-yard box, but no one was there to meet it.
Samaleswari kept pushing and in the 61st minute, Jorge Pereyra Diaz worked his way into the box despite close marking and went down as he waited for a chance to shoot. The Argentinian and his team-mates appealed for a penalty, but the referee waved play on. In the 76th minute, Christopher Kamei had time in the final third and went a long-range shot that came back off the crossbar.
Samaleswari put together several promising moves in the closing stages, but Rajasthan dealt with them calmly.
Three minutes from time, Samaleswari lost the ball in its own half. Shimray ran down the left and swung a precise cross to the far post, where Brijesh held off his marker and headed in. Samaleswari pressed until the end, and deep into stoppage time, Veer Arjun Joshi’s lob from the edge of the box found El Jaaouani at the far post, but Amrit Gope made a brilliant save to preserve the clean sheet.

It takes a rare genius to write a satire that is still read 300 years after its publication. Most satire dwells on the peccadilloes of soon-to-be forgotten politicians. And it takes a unique genius to write a satire that is more relevant today than it was in the days of powdered wigs and knee breeches. That is exactly what Jonathan Swift achieved when he published “Gulliver’s Travels Into Remote Regions of the World” on Oct. 28, 1726.
The third part of Swift’s masterpiece focused on “remote regions of the world” under the sway of scientists, technologists and “projectors.” When Swift wrote, these technicians were an isolated species. The Royal Society, the object of his particular wrath, was only founded in 1660 and was powerless compared with the Anglican Church, which provided Swift with his living. But today these scientists, technologists and “projectors” rule the world and control the future, in effect transforming a satire of a slice of 18th-century English society into a dissection of the AI-dominated world that we are busy creating.
The first place Gulliver visits, in his third voyage, is a flying island, Laputa, inhabited by people who would be described, in today’s jargon, as “on the spectrum,” philosophers who are obsessed with abstract thought, particularly about mathematics, astronomy and music, but can’t cope with the practical world. These philosophers are so devoted to abstract reflection that they employ “flappers” to shake them out of their philosophical reveries by slapping them with a blown bladder full of tiny peas or pebbles. Devoted to intellectual purity, they are incapable of dealing with the mundane practicalities of life.

More than three decades before Nvidia became an AI powerhouse worth $3.98 trillion, its founders were busy plotting their business idea over cups of coffee at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley.
What began as informal conversations at a roadside diner eventually laid the foundation for one of the world's most valuable technology companies. Today, Nvidia's chips power some of the most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems, but its journey began at an unlikely place: a restaurant booth.
The story goes back to 1992 and 1993, when Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem started meeting at a Denny's outlet in Silicon Valley. The three engineers had a shared ambition to build a company but needed a place where they could exchange ideas and discuss their plans away from their respective workplaces.
Quick answers to key questions
Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem met at a Denny’s restaurant in Silicon Valley in 1992 and 1993 to discuss their plans for a technology company.
The three engineers held long meetings at the diner, sharing ideas and working through their business plans. Their conversations laid the groundwork for Nvidia, which they co-founded in 1993.
The plaque recognizes the conversations at the restaurant that helped launch Nvidia. Its inscription dedicates the booth to the company and celebrates the idea that began there.
The restaurant temporarily removed the plaque amid an extramarital affairs scandal involving Jensen Huang. Denny’s reinstalled it the next day, saying the shared history deserved to be preserved.
The Silicon Valley restaurant has reinstalled the plaque commemorating the founders’ meetings. It had been presented to Huang in 2023 and briefly taken down before being put back.
At the time, Priem and Malachowsky were working at Sun Microsystems, while Huang was employed at LSI Logic. The Denny's restaurant became their regular meeting spot as they discussed their business plans and the kind of technology company they wanted to build.
The meetings often stretched for several hours, with the three co-founders spending much of their time discussing ideas over coffee.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Malachowsky recalled that they were hardly the ideal customers for the restaurant.
"We were not good customers," Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky said. "We were going to show up for four hours and drink 10 cups of coffee."
Their lengthy meetings eventually led restaurant staff to move them from their booth to a room at the back of the outlet.
Interestingly, the room was also used by San Jose police officers, who would sit nearby and fill out their reports while the three engineers worked on their plans.
"All the cops are writing their reports," Malachowsky said. "We're sitting there with our laptops, trying to figure out whatever we're doing."
Those conversations eventually laid the groundwork for Nvidia, which was co-founded by Huang, Malachowsky and Priem in 1993.
The restaurant also has a personal connection to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who worked at a Denny's outlet in Portland when he was just 15.
Before becoming one of the world's most influential technology executives, Huang worked as a dishwasher, busboy, and waiter at the restaurant.
Denny's is an American diner-style restaurant chain known for its casual dining experience, all-day breakfast menu and affordable meals. Founded in 1953 in Lakewood, California, the chain initially operated as Danny's Donuts before becoming Denny's. Its menu features popular American favourites, including pancakes, burgers, sandwiches, omelettes, steaks and milkshakes. Unlike traditional restaurants that follow fixed breakfast hours, Denny's is particularly known for serving breakfast throughout the day. Over the decades, it has expanded across the United States and international markets, becoming a familiar name in American roadside dining culture.
The Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley recently made headlines after temporarily removing a plaque commemorating the booth where Nvidia's founders discussed their business idea.
The California eatery, however, reinstalled the plaque just a day after taking it down, amid an extramarital affairs scandal involving Huang, NBC News reported.
The plaque was originally presented to Huang on September 26, 2023, by Denny's CEO Kelli Valade. It commemorates the restaurant's role in the early days of Nvidia and the conversations that eventually helped launch the technology giant.
Explaining its decision to reinstall the plaque, Denny's said, “We’re reinstalling the plaque recognizing the conversations at Denny’s that helped launch NVIDIA. Jensen Huang started at Denny’s as a dishwasher. Years later, he and his co-founders gathered in one of our booths to discuss the idea that became NVIDIA. The plaque commemorates that shared history,” as per NBC News.
“America’s Diner has long been a place where people and ideas come together, and that history deserves to be preserved,” the company added.
The plaque's inscription reads: “Denny’s dedicates this booth to Nvidia. The booth that launched a $1 trillion company. Congratulations, Nvidia! Who knew that an idea started here would change the world?”

Among many other things, Downstate, Bruce Norris‘ tricky new play that’s gained considerable acclaim and controversy, is an exercise in cognitive dissonance, a commandingly written and shrewdly directed (by Joe Mantello) work that asks us to confront some of the very things we prize most in ourselves, namely the limits of our compassion and empathy.
Set in a shabby, cheaply furnished middle-class home we’re told is located in downstate Illinois, the play immediately introduces us to the house’s residents: four middle-aged men who bicker over who owes what for the week’s groceries, personal belongings left in common spaces and other petty irritations of daily, group living.
And we’re also introduced to a younger man, maybe in his 30s, who is nervous and uncomfortable. Andy (Thomas Sadoski) has come to confront the most frail of the group home residents: Fred (Francis Guinan), an aging, vaguely confused man in a wheelchair – we learn why he is so confined later – who has something terrible in common with his housemates: He is a convicted sex offender and child predator who has officially served his time in prison but, with no where to go, is living in this group home under strict observation and restrictions.
Watch on Deadline
Fred is a former piano teacher, Andy his former student and you can probably guess the rest. It’s been 30 years since Fred sexually assaulted Andy on two separate occasions, and the former student’s life has been a shambles of shame, depression and struggle ever since. Andy’s wife, Em (Cassie Beck), is by his side for moral support as he attempts to finally face his abuser with a list of the crimes and their impact on his life. Em, too, has a list, its very existence an indication of how abuse spreads well beyond the first victim.
Sharing the home (flawlessly designed by the ever-reliable Scott Pask) with Fred are Dee (K. Todd Freeman), an aging Black gay man and a sort of de facto house mother who does the grocery shopping, makes sure Fred takes his pills and nags Gio (Al’Jaleel McGhee), the youngest of the group, to move his gym equipment out of the common area. Gio, talkative, aggressively friendly and very funny – somehow, Downstate has an improbable amount of genuine humor – holds himself above his housemates, convinced that the relatively advanced age of his victim – she was 17 – bestows on him a moral superiority and a brighter future. It does neither, particularly after he shows up with a new, clueless young friend (Ivy Wolk).
Finally, there’s Felix (Adrian Martinez), the quietest, most antisocial and, frankly, most outwardly pathetic of the bunch, lonely, morosely religious, secretive and resentful at having to live with people he disdains. It’s Felix who seems to draw the most attention and concern from Ivy (The Bear‘s Liza Colón-Zayas), the visiting probation officer who keeps all the men under a watchful eye and whose initial conviviality can’t mask the seriousness with which she takes both her job and the crimes the men in her charge have committed.
Playwright Norris (he wrote the excellent Clybourne Park) builds the tension and momentum of Downstate almost entirely through character interaction – it’s only in retrospect that we realize there hasn’t been much by way of plot, or at least action, in what we’ve just witnessed – and yet the entire play is compelling from beginning to end. We watch as Dee, the most outwardly compassionate and intelligent of the bunch, gradually shows his meaner side, and Gio, for all his lip service to self-improvement and goal-setting, constantly puts himself (and others) in danger. Sad Felix, whose denials of rule-breaking we want to believe, at last gives us no choice but to acknowledge the worst.
And make no doubt, what these characters do, and are capable of, is the worst. Prior to Broadway, Downstate had productions in Washington D.C., Off Broadway, London and at Chicago’s Steppenwolf, drawing some right-wing ire – after a positive review in the Washington Post, Ted Cruz tweeted, “So now the corporate media is praising pedophilia” – but those reactions couldn’t be more wrong-headed. True, Downstate insists that we see and consider the humanity of these men, but that is most certainly not the same as asking us to excuse their crimes. Downstate dares us to forgive the unforgivable, challenging the very concept of grace.
“Praising pedophilia?” Nonsense. If anything, I came away from Downstate entirely convinced that not one of these four characters should live unrestricted among society. Age and infirmity has rendered Fred the former piano teacher somewhat harmless, though his blithe, ostensibly sympathetic demeanor around the still-devastated Andy speaks volumes. Dee, so fiercely protective of Fred, still harbors delusions that excuse his crime, a rationalizing that masks itself as intellectual debate but even that falls to the side when his cruelty and destructiveness surface. The fates of Gio and Felix might be shocking, but not surprising.
Director Mantello guides his excellent cast through Downstate‘s nuances subtly ands unerringly, with the performers creating fully credible characters cursed by – whose to say? – trauma or demons or nature. What Downstate leaves us with, then, is both understanding and the limits of understanding, the frustration of somehow wanting to forgive but knowing that forgiveness can’t provide these victimizers what they crave: A home in the world, a place that isn’t a four-bedroom prison with crummy furniture and an ankle bracelet.

Venue: Broadway’s Booth Theatre
Written By: Bruce Norris
Directed By: Joe Mantello
Cast: K. Todd Freeman, Francis Guinan, Thomas Sadoski, Al’Jaleel McGhee, Cassie Beck, Adrian Martinez, Ivy Wolk, Liza Colón-Zayas
Running Time: 2 hr 20 min (including intermission)
Congrats to the cast and the team. Incredible work. Must see.

Rory McIlroy clinched his eighth Race to Dubai title on Sunday, equalling Colin Montgomerie’s record for the most Order of Merit wins in European Tour history, and dedicated the feat to his father, who is recovering from surgery.
The 37-year-old from Northern Ireland shot a bogey-free 67 to wrap up a fifth successive Race to Dubai crown, finishing ahead of Spain’s Eugenio Chacarra in the season-long standings.
Meanwhile, England’s Tyrrell Hatton won the DP World Tour Championship comfortably, finishing five shots clear.

The latest title added to a strong year for McIlroy, who defended his Masters title at Augusta National in April to claim a second green jacket and strengthen his standing among the sport’s greats.
“I don’t really know what to say. Winning eight Order of Merits was never really in my list of goals when I was growing up,” McIlroy told Sky Sports.
“I remember Monty (Montgomerie) being a stalwart of the European Tour. Going to watch him at the World Match Play at Wentworth over the years, I remember playing with him for the first time at the London Club on the European Tour in 2008.
“To pull up alongside him and win eight of these things, it means the world to me.
“I’m a proud European. I’m a proud European player and I’m proud to be a part of the DP World Tour and I’m very proud of myself right now.”
The milestone carried extra emotional weight for McIlroy, whose father has spent the last two months recovering from major surgery.
“He’s been in the hospital for the last two months. He underwent a huge operation at the end of September, and he’s recovering well, thankfully,” McIlroy said.
“But when I left to come here to the Middle East, I went up to Cleveland to see him before I went. He said to me: ‘Go win the Race to Dubai.’”

South Korea to inspect glasses worn by exam candidates after AI cheating scandal
SEOUL: South Korea will inspect every pair of glasses worn by students taking this week's national college entrance exam to prevent AI-assisted cheating, after cheating in the tax accountant exam shook public confidence in the country's high-stakes testing system.
There have even been calls to postpone the university entrance exam to ensure a fair test after the scandal, although the Education Ministry has ruled out a delay to an exam seen as crucial to success in South Korea's hyper-competitive society.
Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin told a parliamentary hearing on Monday (Nov 16) the ministry would inspect all glasses worn by candidates in every session of the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT). Smart devices were added to the list of banned items in July.
Smart glasses have raised concern globally because they can be used to photograph, film or audio-record confidential material or people without their knowledge.
Notices posted outside every exam room will warn of exam bans and criminal penalties if anyone is found to be cheating, Choi said.
Every exam centre will have at least one member of staff dedicated to monitoring smart devices.
A hotline will link the centres, local education offices and the ministry's control room for any cases that are hard to judge on the spot.
Choi said the ministry would consult specialists on technology such as radio-signal detectors and consider introducing them for next year's test.
Anyone caught wearing or using a smart device during the exams will have that year's results invalidated and will be barred from sitting them the following year.
Choi said the ministry would work with parliament to lengthen the ban from 1 year to between 3 and 10 years. Offenders may also be reported to police for obstructing official duties.
The response follows Sunday's confession by a person who placed first in this year's tax accountant exam after cheating. He admitted photographing exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said on Monday the government would form an emergency team to prepare measures to safeguard the CSAT. She also urged officials to develop AI-based detection technology and called for strengthened penalties for cheating.
The Yonhap News Agency reported on Monday reported that the government will pursue measures, including collecting smart devices and blocking public Wi-Fi, during this week's national college entrance exams.

On Nov. 10, the U.S. House of Representatives voted on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the face of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
The impeachment effort failed in a 211-204 vote, which many Democrats blamed on 11 of their fellow party members who were absent from the voting chamber.
The 11 absent Democrats were Reps. Julia Brownley, Melanie Stansbury, Brittany Pettersen, Laura Gillen, Nancy Pelosi, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland, Frederica Wilson, Jonathan Jackson, Steven Horsford and J. Luis Correa.
Social media users claimed some of those 11 missed the vote because they were attending an event related to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a powerful pro-Israel lobbying group.
The event in question was reportedly hosted by Elect Democrat Women. According to the nonprofit OpenSecrets, the top donor to the Elect Democrat Women-affiliated super PAC, EDW Action Fund, was the United Democracy Project — a super PAC affiliate of AIPAC.
Drop Site News, a nonprofit investigative news outlet, reportedly obtained an RSVP list of the event showing that three of the 11 Democrats who missed the vote were present at the event: Brownley, of California, Stansbury, of New Mexico, and Pettersen, of Colorado. As of this writing, the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal how it sourced the list.
Two of the representatives, Brownley and Pettersen, reportedly acknowledged attending the Elect Democratic Women event. However, none of them had responded to our requests for comment by the time of publication. Until we hear directly from the representatives' offices or primary evidence confirming their attendance emerges, we've left this claim unrated.
On Nov. 11, USA Today reporter Zach Schermele posted that Brownley told him she "left last night's Elect Democratic Women event for the Hegseth vote with plenty of time to spare" and that "when the traffic jam made it clear she might not make it in time, she and other lawmakers started texting each other." He reported that Brownley, 74, then got out of her car and started running, missing the vote by "seconds" (archived).
According to Denver NBC affiliate KUSA, Pettersen acknowledged she attended the event, saying in a statement, "Last night, I was late to the floor and there is no excuse for that. I was at an Electing Democratic Women event."
Stansbury posted a video on Nov. 11 apologizing for her absence, saying, "I know I should've been there at that moment." She blamed rush-hour traffic on Independence Avenue for her absence. She did not mention the EDW event, though her comments were flooded with users accusing her of attending it.
Because the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal where it sourced the list, we are unable to rate this claim. We can, however, break down Drop Site News' findings and any other publicly available information.
The document Drop Site News reportedly obtained also included a "Run of Show" listing the event's schedule, which read:
Run of Show:
- 4:30 pm: Event begins.
  - Mix and mingle
- 5:00 pm: EDW Chairwoman Lois Frankel to give opening remarks.
  - Thank everyone for attending, supporting EDW, and our historic wins.
- 5:10 pm: Acknowledge all new members in attendance and have them answer questions.
- 5:30 pm: Guests resume mingling.
- 6:00 pm: Event ends.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., publicly posted the voting schedule on Nov. 10, which indicated the vote on the impeachment articles he introduced would take place at 5:30 p.m. (archived).
According to Drop Site's reporting, the event took place at Goldfinch Social, a venue in Washington, D.C., about 2 miles from the Capitol.

Iran’s worsening economic crisis is pushing some residents to desperate lengths, with financially distressed people advertising kidneys, corneas, bone marrow and other body parts for sale to pay off debts and cover basic household expenses. An investigation by Iran International has uncovered a growing online market in which Iranians are offering to sell organs and body tissue, with some listings advertising multiple body parts. The findings highlight the financial distress facing ordinary households as the country grapples with mounting economic pressure, international sanctions and the fallout of its confrontation with the United States. The crisis has deepened amid a US naval blockade and uncertainty over when the standoff between Washington and Tehran will ease. US officials have maintained that the economic pressure campaign is taking an increasing toll on Iran. Warnings from the Trump administration suggest that the country's economy could take years to recover, even if the conflict ends. Iran International examined more than 600 advertisements posted on a Telegram channel between late May and late October. Its investigation found that nearly one in three listings offered more than one organ or type of body tissue. The advertisements included offers to sell kidneys, bone marrow, corneas, liver tissue and testicles. Some individuals were reportedly willing to sell multiple body parts to raise money for themselves and their families. The investigation also cited Iran's labour-focused ILNA news agency, which reported that workers were offering kidneys, liver tissue and bone marrow to meet household expenses and avoid losing their homes. The practice is not limited to online platforms. In central Tehran, Farhang Hosseini Street has reportedly acquired the name “Kidney Street”, where people approach potential buyers. Its proximity to a medical facility and a charity supporting kidney patients has made it a known location for such advertisements. The growing number of listings reflects the severe financial pressures facing some Iranian households, as mounting living costs and debt leave people with increasingly desperate options. The advertisements have emerged as Washington continues to tighten economic pressure on Tehran through sanctions and a naval blockade. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has defended the strategy, arguing that Washington does not need to resume combat operations because the economic measures are already having a significant impact. “The economic pain that is being inflicted on Iran right now is extraordinary and it compounds. It's growing every day,” Rubio said, according to Al Jazeera. US President Donald Trump has also warned that Iran faces a prolonged recovery. Last week, he said the country could take 25 years to rebuild from the damage caused by the war, even if hostilities ended immediately. The US Treasury Department has similarly maintained that the economic pressure campaign is achieving its objectives. An official told an outlet that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had informed Trump that the worsening economic situation could further destabilise Iran's leadership and increase pressure on Tehran to reach a deal. According to the report, Iran's currency, the rial, has lost around a quarter of its value since the campaign began in August. Annual inflation reportedly climbed to 90% last month, compared with 35% in early 2025. Iran's oil exports have also come under pressure. The report claimed that the country had been unable to load tankers since late August and had already sold oil that was at sea. The confrontation has also raised security concerns in Washington. Bessent was reportedly moved from his home in Washington DC to a military base following threats from Iran. Citing people familiar with the matter, The New York Times reported that the decision came after officials concluded that plots targeting current and former US officials had advanced to a more serious stage. Bessent's role in “Operation Economic Outcast”, the campaign aimed at intensifying economic pressure on Iran through sanctions and other measures, has reportedly made him a potential target. For ordinary Iranians, however, the consequences of the standoff are increasingly visible in the struggle to afford basic necessities. The growing number of advertisements offering organs and body tissue for sale highlights the human cost of an economic crisis that shows little sign of easing. On a summer day in 1992, a man dumped a cooler full of a fish called yellow perch into Lake Mary Ronan, in northwest Montana.
Why do people keep dumping buckets of fish into Montana’s lakes?
Guerilla ecology is incredibly easy. It also has disastrous consequences.
We know this because two teenagers saw him do it; they wrote down his license plate number and called in a tip to the Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks department (FWP), which immediately dispatched biologists to capture and kill the perch with nets and poison.
The teenagers got a reward of $500 each for their efforts, while the man was charged with illegally introducing non-native fish into the lake, slapped with a small fine, and sent on his way. The law changed soon after: Now, intentionally introducing a non-native, invasive species to Montana’s waters is a felony punishable by as long as two years in prison or a fine of up to $25,000, or both.
Why I wrote about this
I visited Flathead Lake Biological Station in October, and while I was there I heard from a biologist about this strange, totally avoidable, invisible catastrophe in the making. I was absolutely fascinated — as I looked at the lake, I hardly believed it could lose its signature clarity because of a bucketful of fish — and decided I had no choice but to open this can of worms.
But the perch? The yellow perch — at least two of them — survived, multiplied, and quickly went on to wreak havoc. They established dominance in the lake, wiping out its population of a native fish called the Westslope Cutthroat trout and causing other ecosystem disruptions. This hasn’t only happened here: Montana is filled with thousands of beautiful alpine lakes and rivers, nestled in the sort of rugged territory that sold people on the idea of the West. Yet, across the state, without permission, people keep dumping non-native fish into them.
The reason is simple: The introduced fish, according to some anglers, are more fun to fish than the stuff that’s already swimming around in Montana’s waters. But this guerrilla ecology — or “bucket biology” as some call it — risks upending delicate, longstanding ecosystems, harming not only native fish, but also animals that depend on them, like bald eagles, bears, and otters. It could turn Montana’s pristine waters into murky messes that also require millions of dollars in cleanup and additional maintenance every year.
And it’s not just a problem in Montana. Across the country, states are trying to stop people from filling lakes with fish that don’t belong. It’s a high-stakes issue with ramifications that can reach far beyond the underwater neighborhood of a single lake; efforts to stop illegal fish-dumping have now spawned everything from high-dollar bounties and dedicated fish forensics.
“A decision made by one person can affect an entire interconnected ecosystem,” said Craig Barfoot, Fisheries Program Manager for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes (CSKT), which is based on the Flathead Reservation in northwestern Montana and oversees some of the most pristine aquatic habitats in the state. “It’s like an act of arson.”
The power of a bucket
Flathead Lake, about an hour’s drive south of Glacier National Park, is the sort of place postcards were made for. The 27-mile-long lake, half within the Flathead Reservation (and overseen by the tribes) and half managed by the state, is one of the cleanest, clearest lakes in the populated world — a survey last year found that the lake is clear down to about 36 feet — which draws all sorts of creatures to its shore. During a two-day visit in October, I saw a black bear ambling along the shore and a bald eagle sitting in a tree, tearing into a fish it had scooped out of the water.
This massive glacial lake “was ice about 15,000 years ago,” said Tom Bansak, associate director of the Flathead Lake Bio Station, a research station in the lake that’s run by the University of Montana. “Before western contact, there were maybe eight to 10 species of fish in the lake, which is not very many for a lake of its size.”
That changed starting in the late 1800s, when wildlife managers at the federal and state levels decided to start stocking lakes around the country with fish that were raised in hatcheries and released into the water for recreational fishing. For decades, states mostly made stocking decisions based not on local ecologies but rather on the kinds of fish people wanted to catch, filling them with nonnative fish like trout, bass, walleye, and pike. If you live in the United States, there’s a good chance the closest popular fishing spot is filled with stocked fish; at Flathead Lake, wildlife managers introduced around 30 different kinds of non-native fish, of which about a dozen established spawning populations, and today non-native fish outnumber native ones.
Eventually, state wildlife agencies began to realize that this sort of recreation-driven stocking can harm local ecosystems: In the 1970s, for example, Montana decided to stop stocking non-native fish in most of its streams and rivers. It still stocks plenty of fish, though, including a few non-native species, in some of its lakes and reservoirs, as do most other states.
For some people, however, that’s not enough. Some anglers believe the fish native to Montana, like bull trout, cutthroat trout, and sturgeon, just aren’t as fun to catch or as tasty to eat as, say, northern pike and walleye — both of which have been illegally introduced to the state’s waters in recent years.
Enter the bucket biologists. It can take as little as a bucketful of fish to alter the population of an entire lake, which means that if someone is bored of the fishing options at their local lake, they could unilaterally decide to spice things up with little risk of getting caught. Despite nonnative fish introductions now being a felony in Montana (and at least four other states), not a single person has been charged, let alone convicted there; that man the two teens saw at Lake Mary Ronan more than 30 years ago is the only person to have ever even been reported.
“People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.”
— Sam Bourret, FWP Fisheries biologist
But fish and wildlife officials know it’s still happening because they keep finding non-native fish in the state’s waterways, and the most likely way they got there is by someone illegally dumping them in.
”They’re obviously avid anglers, and we probably know them,” said Sam Bourret, a fisheries biologist at FWP based near Flathead Lake. Investigating illegal fish introductions is Bourret’s speciality: The Great Falls Tribune called him the “fish detective” for pioneering a forensic technique that looks at chemical clues inside otoliths, fishes’ stone-like ear bones, to figure out where they might have come from. He’s also used data modeling based on conditions like elevation and fishing pressure to figure out which lakes might be most vulnerable to future fish introductions, which could help steer resources towards them and stop would-be bucket biologists. From his time on the job, which has included many firsthand interactions with anglers, he can tell many of them are irked that they can’t stock the fish they want wherever they want them. “I do think some of these people are spiteful in their desire to move fish around,” Bourret said. “People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.”
Sometimes the culprit is less intentional. Non-native fish that are kept in ponds on private property (which technically require permits to build and stock but often slip by under the radar) can get into nearby rivers or lakes if the pond overflows during a storm, or by being picked up by a bird and then dropped into another waterbody. Earlier this year, FWP biologists on Bourret’s team removed 4,000 goldfish from a pond at a hotel on the edge of Montana’s Thompson River; the pond had been an attraction for families visiting the hotel with small children, who liked to scoop fish out of the water with nets. But goldfish can be disastrous for freshwater ecosystems, and the FWP wanted to be sure they wouldn’t slip into the adjacent river — and from there into a nearby lake.
But they often don’t get so far ahead of a potential problem. “Introduced fish probably go undetected often,” Bourret said. “We usually find out about them through a needle in a haystack catch. Once a population sets up in a lake, it’s already way too late.”
Fish-shaped dominoes
Monitoring species in the underwater realm of rivers, lakes, and streams is vastly more challenging than it is on land. “It’s a lot more obvious when a terrestrial animal doesn’t belong,” says Andrew Gilham, Fisheries Management Bureau Chief at FWP. “If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird. But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.”
And that may even play into the general public’s understanding of just how much impact a few fish can have. “Some of it may just be that they don’t really understand the consequences that can follow illegal introductions,” he said.
Aquatic ecosystems are delicate balances, and in a healthy lake the populations of fish, predators, and small organisms like zooplankton and phytoplankton typically exist in a hard-won equilibrium. To simplify greatly, there are usually enough zooplankton to eat phytoplankton and prevent algal blooms, enough zooplankton-eating fish to prevent the zooplankton from eating all the phytoplankton, and enough predators to keep those zooplankton-eating fish in check — but not so many that the smaller fish get wiped out.
“If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird. But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.”
— Andrew Gilham, Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Bucket biology, especially with voracious carnivores like pike, is a bit like tossing a fish-shaped grenade into the lake. If the newcomers establish a spawning population, they can compete for resources with the native fish or eat them directly, eventually causing something called a trophic cascade: a domino-like series of events that can upend an entire ecosystem.
What happens to fish in a lake can have huge effects on the creatures outside of it, too. In the Yellowstone region, Yellowstone Lake had long been home to a native fish species called the cutthroat trout. These fish would make long, winding spawning migrations through the Yellowstone lake and river system, where some four mammal species and 16 bird species — bears, otters, eagles, and pelicans, among others — would pluck them out of the water for meals. The migrating cutthroat were also important vectors for nutrients, which came from the fish’s poop and were important food sources for plants and algae growing in and along the waterways.
But then, in the 1990s, a non-native species arrived (likely through an illegal introduction): lake trout. Lake trout eat cutthroat, and without any predators of their own, they could feast on the smaller fish without anything to stop them. Once the lake trout appeared in Yellowstone Lake, they decimated cutthroat populations; according to a report from the National Park Service, by 1998, there were some 125,000 lake trout in the lake, and they ate somewhere between 3 and 4 million cutthroat that year.
Zooplankton in the lake, which the cutthroat used to eat, had a population boom, which led to a decline in phytoplankton. And the lake trout just stayed in the lake rather than migrating through the rivers and streams like the cutthroat did, which not only robbed those waters of the additional nutrients they brought, but also took a of a high-impact food source away from bears, otters, and birds. Bear and otter activity alongside the streams declined; while bears are opportunistic feeders and likely found another food source, the otters probably had a harder time finding something to supplement their diets. Bald eagle nests saw a sharp decline in their success rates after cutthroat disappeared, and osprey nest counts fell from 60 in 2001 to 3-5 from 2008-2015.
“We don’t want to just be moving things around willy-nilly,” said Niall Clancy, director of the Fisheries Lab at Salish Kootenai College. “Because one thing we learned is that we are bad at predicting the impacts — and there’s a good chance that something will go wrong that we didn’t think of.”
And, Clancy added, these sorts of introductions can cause financial cascades alongside trophic ones: FWP now spends millions of dollars each year to reduce invasive fish populations in the state’s lakes and boost native fish populations through hatchery programs. This, in turn, diverts money away from other programs.
Can the buckets be stopped?
Stopping illegal fish introductions is a nearly impossible task; catching someone red-handed would require vigilantly monitoring thousands and thousands of miles of shoreline in Montana. Instead, FWP and groups like the CSKT are investing in things like an educational outreach program and signs along popular waterfronts that exhort people not to dump live fish, warning that doing so is a felony.
FWP has also teamed up with groups like Trout Unlimited, a nonprofit that advocates for fish and waterway conservation, to offer massive rewards for information on bucket biologists. In 2017, for example, they offered a reward of over $35,000 for information related to the illegal introduction of walleye in Swan Lake, a lake about eight miles east of Flathead as the crow flies. But even the promise of a big reward hasn’t worked, and nobody has come forward yet. Instead, FWP declared open season on invasive fish like brown trout and walleye, requiring that anyone who catches one of the fish kill it rather than toss it back into the water, and then bring the entire fish into a FWP office so that biologists can study it. Biologists at FWP are also exploring other solutions like following the lead of Washington state in introducing sterile non-native fish to lakes. This would reduce the populations of non-native fish by tricking fertile ones into wasting their mating efforts on fish that will never be able to reproduce.
For the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, the issue goes beyond the science.
“We have stories about the native bull trout and the native West Oak cutthroat going back to before colonization,” said Rich Janssen, head of the CSKT’s department of natural resources. “They’re part of our heritage and our culture, and when they’re gone, they’re gone. It’s like losing our language.”
At Flathead Lake, the lower half of which is in the Flathead Reservation, the fish that were introduced through earlier federal and state stocking programs largely settled into a state of coexistence with the native fish. That doesn’t mean they were completely harmless, however: They competed for resources with the bull trout and cutthroat, which led to a reduction in those fish. Today, the CSKT has placed restrictions on bull trout and cutthroat fishing, banning people from taking those fish except for religious reasons, and has stepped up efforts to proactively monitor for new non-native fish at Flathead Lake. They’ve also removed fishing restrictions for smallmouth bass and northern pike in tribal waters. Both species were illegally introduced to the lake and can not only outcompete the bull trout and cutthroat but eat them outright, so anglers are now welcome to take as many of those non-native fish out of the water as they’d like.
“They’re part of our heritage and our culture, and when they’re gone, they’re gone. It’s like losing our language.”
— Rich Janssen, Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes
When I went for a swim in Flathead Lake this fall, the water was startlingly clear and calm, the surface broken every now and then by ripples from a passing fish or insect. But farther north, where the Flathead River meets the lake, a gauntlet of hungry pike lay in wait for bull trout making their way upriver to spawn. And as cold as the water was — it is a glacial lake, after all — it has also been warming with climate change, creating more pockets of warmer water for smallmouth bass to spawn in and shrinking the cold-water areas that the bull and cutthroat trout like.
I waved at a passing motorboat, which had a fishing pole stuck into a holder on its side. More and more people have been moving to Montana in recent years, attracted by the rugged nature and the allure of the West; new houses and docks have sprung up along Flathead Lake’s shoreline. But much like the pike and bass, their presence has been putting more pressure on the local landscape, and the newcomers could make the problem worse if they decide Montana’s fish aren’t as good as what they have back home. The future of the lake, and many others like it across the country, is murky. What it will look like depends, in large part, on what people decide to do with their buckets.

A video showing people vandalising and fighting inside a restaurant is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows an incident in West Bengal, where RSS workers allegedly created a ruckus and vandalised the restaurant when asked to pay for their food. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS workers vandalising a restaurant in West Bengal after being asked to pay for their food.
Fact: The video shows an incident at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Dhaka, Bangladesh, where a group of people vandalised the premises following a dispute over seating arrangements. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved in the attack. The incident has no connection to RSS workers or West Bengal. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same video. According to these reports, the incident took place at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Mohakhali, Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 13 November 2026. The incident reportedly began with an argument over seating arrangements between a customer and restaurant staff. According to the restaurant owner, a young man took a seat that a family was already waiting for. When a staff member intervened, the young man left but later returned with others and assaulted an employee named Khalil outside the restaurant. The group then vandalised the restaurant, damaging furniture and other items. The incident caused panic among customers and left several people injured. Police visited the spot and said they were examining CCTV footage to identify those involved and take legal action. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved, an allegation that police said they were investigating (here, here, and here).
The restaurant is located in the Mohakhali area of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Photos of the restaurant available on Google Maps match the visuals in the viral video, confirming that the incident took place in Bangladesh and not West Bengal.
To sum up, the video of a ruckus at a restaurant in Bangladesh is being shared as RSS workers’ hooliganism at a restaurant in West Bengal.

Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.
This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions.
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.
As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.
Fighting food insecurity
Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.
Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.
Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.
Forward momentum
Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “Eat Real Food.”
But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.
In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually.
Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.
Food is medicine in our local community
Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.
One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.
For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
What other researchers have found
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security.
Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels. This data supports our own previous findings.
However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.
Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.
Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
Meagen Rosenthal, University of Mississippi and Natalie Minton, University of Mississippi

Man arrested for allegedly posing as decorated combat veteran to steal $80k
David Agtsteribbe, a 58-year-old from Hampton Bays, New York, is accused of funneling money from a local American Legion into his personal bank account
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

A New York man has been arrested for posing as a decorated and wounded combat veteran to steal more than $80,000 from the veterans’ organization where he worked, according to prosecutors.
David Agtsteribbe, a 58-year-old from Hampton Bays on Long Island, is accused of Grand Larceny, Criminal Possession of a Forged Instrument and several other charges for funneling money from a local American Legion into his personal bank account to pay for bills, clothes, travel and Amazon purchases, Suffolk County District Attorney Raymond A. Tierney announced earlier this week.
“Our veterans earned their honors through sacrifice and service. This defendant allegedly exploited those sacrifices for his own selfish gain. It is a shameful abuse of trust, and one that we will prosecute,” Tierney said in a statement.
Agtsteribbe enlisted in the Army in 1986, but a year later, he was court-martialed and pleaded guilty to stealing money from another soldier. He left the Army in 1988 after receiving a bad-conduct discharge.
In 2021, Agtsteribbe became the Hampton Bays American Legion’s finance officer by using fake military credentials, including a wounded-in-combat designation and a Purple Heart award given to soldiers who are injured or killed in action, according to prosecutors.
The American Legion does not allow veterans with a bad-conduct discharge to join, but Agtsteribbe claimed to have been honorably discharged.
From September 2022 to this past August, Agtsteribbe stole nearly $81,800 to pay his personal expenses, according to prosecutors.
Agtsteribbe was arrested Monday and ordered during his arraignment Tuesday to remain in custody as his case plays out. He faces 25 years to life in prison if convicted on the top count of Grand Larceny in the Second Degree.
Agtsteribbe, who had already been in jail twice for grand larceny, pleaded not guilty to the new charges Tuesday, NBC New York reported.
Bill Coderre, Suffolk County’s American Legion commander, said it was “a case of stolen valor” and a “serious breach of our trust” in a statement shared by the outlet.
"It's bad theft. Especially for people who need it, and there’s a lot of people who do need it, especially vets,” veteran Rodney Smith told CBS News New York.
Simone Scotto, who owns Scotto's Pizza in Hampton Bays, told the outlet, "I feel bad for the American Legion of Hampton Bays because they do a lot of things for the community.”
The Independent has reached out to the Hampton Bays American Legion for comment.

The World Health Organisation warned on Friday (November 13, 2026) of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.
“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.
Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza’s population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the “Yellow Line” — a demarcation established under October’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire.
“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where of course the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Ms. Van De Weerdt explained.
The Israeli military told Reuters the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law, and are not intended to harm the civilian population.
“The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs launched the winterisation plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.
Last week COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organisations.
Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.
“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come,” Ms. Van De Weerdt said.
Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.
The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mould and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.
While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.
“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today, so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.“
COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organisations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators, and other equipment have entered Gaza.

In Europe, an Emboldened Iran Contributes to a Sense of Anxiety
Prosecutors and government officials believe Iran or its proxies are behind a series of security breaches and threats in Britain and Europe, unsettling the region.
On Veterans Day this past week, President Trump declared that his decision to go to war with Iran had been a complete success.
“When this conflict is over, and it will be soon,” he said, speaking on a blustery morning from Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington, “the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place.”
That is not how it feels in Europe.
A growing number of attempted terrorist attacks across the continent and in Britain, including a foiled plot against a major American military base, arson attacks on Jewish community sites and cyberattacks that raised temperatures in refrigerators and blood banks are rattling national security officials and unnerving the public. Many have been attributed to Iran or to proxies acting on its behalf.
The sense of global unease was heightened when the U.S. government grounded all air travel for hours on Friday in what officials later said was a technical issue.
European residents had already grown frustrated before the most recent round of turmoil. The economic consequences of the war that Mr. Trump and the Israeli government started against Iran in February have piled up: Gas prices are higher because of disruptions of oil deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz. Groceries cost more. Heating homes in winter has become far less affordable.
And in recent weeks, the effect has grown darker as security officials have accused Iran or its proxies of conducting a series of terrorism-related plots. In September, U.S. prosecutors say, an Iraqi man, an Iranian operative and a senior operative for an Iran proxy group in a New York jail plotted to attack R.A.F. Fairford, an air base in England used by American bombers. They did not succeed, but the effort prompted a major security incident.
