Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a new passport this week.
Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.
Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.
Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.
Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.
On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.
“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.
Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.
Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.
This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.
Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.
Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.
Despite the abuses and oppression that mired her 15 years in power and subsequent conviction for crimes against humanity, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.
Analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.
Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.
“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is based in India.
Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.
Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.
Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

Bangladesh veteran Litton Das praised new batting star Towhid Hridoy after the pair shared a record partnership on the first day of the first Test against South Africa at the Wanderers Stadium on Sunday.
“He batted really well,” Das said in a television interview after Hridoy hit 137 in a Bangladesh total of 327 for six before being dismissed off the last ball of the day.
“He showed he can bat with discipline. The way he batted gave me more confidence,” said Das, who was unbeaten on 92 after the pair added 200 for the sixth wicket - a record for any wicket for Bangladesh against South Africa.
It was also a Bangladesh record total against South Africa, while Hridoy equalled Mahmudul Hasan Joy’s record for a Bangladesh individual score against South Africa.
Bangladesh’s strong position seemed a distant dream after a devastating new ball blitz by Kagiso Rabada had them reeling at 22 for three. Rabada took the first five wickets and finished the day with five for 51. He added his praise for Hridoy.
“He played really well. We threw everything at him, so hat’s off to him.”
Rabada said it was a typical Wanderers pitch, although lacking in real pace. “It’s easy to score boundaries and score at a high rate because the ball comes on. They applied themselves and showed really good discipline. But with the old ball perhaps we could have bowled a bit better.”
Das said the new ball created problems for the batsmen. “They bowled really well with the new ball,” he said. “In these conditions the new ball is really challenging. But with the old ball it is easier to bat.”
Das said a key aspect of the partnership with Hridoy was rotation of the strike and being able to take advantage of bad balls.
With the second new ball only four overs old, Das said there would be a new challenge on Monday against bowlers who will be fresh at the start of the day.
Marco Jansen trapped Hridoy leg before wicket with a swinging full toss after the 25-year-old right-hander had hit 14 fours and a six in 227-ball innings.
Hridoy was playing in his fourth Test. He made 350 not out for Bangladesh A against South Africa A in Potchefstroom in August and returned to South Africa in prime form after making a Bangladesh record 242 not out and 82 in his previous Test against the West Indies in Sylhet last week.

On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.”
New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms.
None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.
According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?
Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.”
Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other.
In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed.
With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia. The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia. Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come.
Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year.
A commercial launch seemed just around the corner. But deadlines kept getting pushed back. As it turned out, engineering a flying autonomous robot was just part of the overall problem. You also needed to design an airspace that they could operate in, train humans to pilot or supervise them, develop an economic framework within which they could earn money, and so on. “It's a very important, safe, careful dance,” says Greg Bowles, Chief Policy Officer at Joby Aviation.
Silicon Valley’s speed has long been in conflict with air travel norms. “Aviation regulation has been conservative and prioritizes reliability, because the consequences of failure are severe,” says Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general in the Department of Transportation. “Certification standards and airworthiness require proof and demonstrated safety, and that usually means incremental rather than radical change.” The FAA was in no rush to let unproven robots go careening around the national airspace.
AI faced another kind of resistance in Europe. In 2017, aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Dassault asked the EASA, the European Union’s version of the FAA, to consider allowing airliners to operate with a single pilot in the cockpit. Traditionally, airliners require multiple pilots to divide the considerable workload of flying a plane and to ensure that if one pilot becomes incapacitated, the other can carry on. In Airbus’ vision, automated systems would shoulder the copilot’s workload and even take over entirely if needed.
That idea horrified pilots. The European Cockpit Association, a union of airline pilots, lodged a strong protest. Such a move “would remove an independent safety professional from the flight deck and give operators greater influence over the safety judgments that a pilot would otherwise make,” the union explained to me in an email. Last year, EASA shelved the plan.
Nevertheless, AI pressed onward. In 2023, the FAA began issuing waivers to allow delivery-drone flights beyond the visual range of operators; by the end of this year it could make the rule change permanent. Some of the biggest players are already pushing ahead aggressively. This past August, Amazon announced that it planned to expand its drone delivery service to 500 locations across the country by the end of the year. Walmart is planning drone delivery from 270 store locations by the end of 2027.
The ultimate goal is far larger. Industry insiders say that in a maximal vision of the technology’s build-out, hundreds of thousands of drones will be servicing most or all of the US population. “In five to 10 years, it’s going to be completely ubiquitous,” Anthony Vittone, chief operating officer of the drone technology company DroneUp, told me in a story for Sherwood News last year. “People are going to be, like, ‘I don’t know how I lived without it.’”
Joby and other eVTOL companies haven’t progressed quite as fast, but they, too, are moving ahead. In April, Joby flew the first-ever point-to-point eVTOL flight within New York City, from John F. Kennedy Airport to three heliports in Manhattan. The company has carried out similar flights in California and Texas, all under the auspices of the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), a federal initiative rolled out by the Trump administration this past March to demonstrate the capabilities of modern drones and eVTOLs.
These demo flights, Bowles says, are just the “front edge” of the Joby S4’s operational rollout. Next will come demonstration flights with nonpaying passengers, demonstration flights with paying passengers, and finally flights that will take passengers from A to B. “All of that is permitted under eIPP, with increasing levels of oversight,” he says.
To start, these flights will have human pilots, but it’s very expensive to pay one human to fly around a handful of paying passengers; for the model to make any economic sense, the aircraft will have to fly themselves. And if self-driving is a tough challenge for cars, it’s all the more so for aircraft, where an unexpected control system failure isn’t just dangerous but likely deadly.
Given the scale of the challenge, the entry point of AI into human passenger flight won’t be as flashy as piloting eVTOLs; it’ll occupy a more modest, behind-the-scenes role. Already, data companies like Palantir and aviation industry stalwarts like Jeppesen and Thales are selling AI-enabled software that lets regulators, airlines, and flight dispatchers sift through masses of data to identify risks and plan aircraft and crew scheduling.
In September, the FAA announced that it deployed software built by the Boston-based data company Air Space Intelligence. The new AI-powered tool is called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” or SMART, and it’s aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” The program isn’t intended to replace controllers, the government says, but to make doing their jobs easier by using predictive AI to head off scheduling snags. “Combining SMART with our ongoing hardware upgrades gives us the tools to cut flight delays, optimize traffic, and keep airspace capacity across the country open—all while maintaining our gold standard of safety,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said in a press release.
The system is supposed to help controllers make decisions, not make those decisions for them. But if the program feeds nonsensical information into the system, will human operators be able to catch the mistake? “This is the Trump/DOGE/Musk effect,” says the recently retired FAA employee, who asked to remain anonymous. “They’re pushing through all this new technology without any understanding of the complexity of the national airspace system.”
Some lawmakers are also concerned about SMART. On October 13, almost two dozen Democratic lawmakers reportedly sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking it to review the program, citing fears that it might “hallucinate safety-critical information.”
Then there’s the question of whether SMART could worsen the chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. The FAA hopes that the technology lessens the shortage by requiring fewer workers; other industries, though, have yet to see AI-generated efficiencies actually materialize. Even if the software doesn’t directly replace humans, the efficiency could be used to justify a workforce reduction. In May, the FAA reduced its staffing target for active air traffic controllers from the 2024 goal of 14,633 down to 12,563, citing “modern staffing models and scheduling tools.”
Some are more optimistic than others. “I think the SMART program is an important improvement,” Schiavo says. “No one wants the current aviation environment with midairs, runway incursions, myriad near misses, delays, groundings, loss of separation, and long taxi or clearance wait times.”
Michael McCormick, a professor of air traffic management at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, also sees advantages to a predictive tool. “When you have the computing capability to look at the entire trajectory of the aircraft, you can see where the conflicts are going to be,” he says. “And the general axiom in air traffic control is that the sooner you know about a potential conflict, the less effort is required to resolve it.”
That sounds great, but building machines that do a good job most of the time is one thing; machines that can function at the level of reliability required by aviation is another. At present, researchers are focusing on so-called deterministic neural networks—models trained offline whose weights are frozen before being deployed in the real world. These can’t hallucinate, but they may harbor other risky failure modes. In a 2021 paper, Darren Cofer, a researcher at Collins Aerospace, pointed out that when such systems find themselves in situations they haven’t encountered before in training, they can generate “unexpected (and potentially dangerous) outputs.”
The stakes will be even higher when AI software starts making real-time air traffic control decisions, which will start in airspace devoted to autonomous aircraft. According to McCormick, that’ll most likely be select corridors near drone hubs and eVTOL vertiports. With swarms of robot aircraft zipping back and forth, things will be too hairy for human pilots and controllers. “The objective is not to use traditional air traffic control,” he says, “because it would overwhelm the national airspace system if it tried to handle that volume and complexity of airframes moving around.”
With two systems working side by side—one with human decisionmakers, the other with AI—we’ll have a real-time basis to compare the performance of both approaches. Any computer-based system can potentially be hacked; any AI system creative enough to ideate novel solutions could also hallucinate crucial details. Without a human in the loop, seemingly obvious mistakes might go unnoticed until it’s too late.

After Democrats in Texas flipped a U.S. Senate seat, won 14 U.S. House seats and the governor's office in the 2026 midterm elections, a claim (archived) circulated that the wins happened only because the party fraudulently "found" 20 million new voters who all voted blue.
For example, an X user wrote, "There's no chance Texas found 20 million new voters who voted exclusively 100% for Democrats. It's fraud!"
The same text also circulated on Facebook (archived) and other social media platforms.
We found no proof that the Democratic Party in Texas fraudulently "found" and registered 20 million new voters to skew races in their favor in the Nov. 3 elections. The claim appeared to conflate a separate, unproven claim about the number of new voters nationwide with the number of new voters in Texas alone.
Therefore, we rate this claim false.
Texas had just over 19 million registered voters by mid-October, according to its secretary of state. Figures from that office showed the number of registered voters had risen by about 2% since the presidential election in 2024. The number of registered voters rose about 5.4% between the 2022 and 2024 elections. An additional 20 million voters would have created a 107.4% increase in registered voters since 2024 or a 113.2% increase since 2022.
The state's unofficial voter turnout figures showed that 9,850,031 people voted in person or by mail in the state's 2026 midterm elections — a little more than half of Texas' registered voters.
Given the figures from the Texas secretary of state, it wasn't possible for Democrats to have fraudulently "found" 20 million people to tip the state's elections, because fewer than half that number voted in the elections at all. A sudden doubling of the number of registered voters would have raised alarm bells with officials. This did not occur.
The origin of the "20 million" figure was unclear, but it may have come from a bar chart that claimed to show that House Democrats gained 20 million voters across the entire U.S. between 2022 and 2026. The fact-checking organization Lead Stories reported on this graph and found no credible source for its projected 2026 voter numbers.
Rather, Lead Stories pointed to the University of Florida's General Election turnout tables, which showed 123,540,000 ballots counted nationwide in the 2026 midterms by Nov. 6. The same source showed 112,030,874 ballots counted in the 2022 midterms, the most recent equivalent race. The bar chart claimed 126 million people had voted in House races in 2026, around 2.5 million more than the University of Florida's estimate.
The university's figures suggested an increase of 11,509,126 ballots counted between the 2022 and 2026 elections, around half of the 20 million figure the unsourced bar chart suggested.
It wasn't possible to determine how many more individual voters had voted for House Democrats in 2026 vs. in 2022 because state officials had not yet certified their election results at the time of this writing and when the graph circulated.
Regardless of the accuracy of the graph or claim, it was true that Democrats picked up a sizable number of votes in their House and Senate races to secure control of both chambers nationwide. Pollsters credited young voters, male voters and Hispanic voters with securing Democratic wins.
At the time of this writing, there were no credible allegations of widespread fraud.
The false claim played into election fraud theories about bad actors "finding" votes in elections. Snopes has previously reported on variations of this claim in the form of noncitizen voting (which rarely happens), duplicate ballots (which are extremely difficult to produce) and vote spikes (which are a natural part of vote counts).

What is happening in Sudan? The civil war the world forgot
The conflict in Sudan has been described as a war on civilians – and the facts are devastating

Since April 2023, Sudan has been in the grip of one of the deadliest civil wars in a generation. As many as 150,000 people are believed to have been killed and millions displaced.
Right now it is the largest humanitarian crisis, the largest displacement crisis and the largest hunger crisis in the world.
The UN has warned that attacks in Darfur bear the “hallmarks of genocide” and the brutality and widespread use of rape as a weapon of war is unprecedented.
There are no signs of an immediate ceasefire or an end to the conflict, which has been described by humanitarians and Sudanese families as a war on civilians.
How did the war start?
Sudan’s war broke out in April 2023. A vicious power struggle between Sudanese army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, or “Hemedti”, head of the powerful paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), exploded into open fighting across the country.
The two generals had once been uneasy allies. They joined forces after the 2019 popular uprising unseated the country’s longterm autocrat Omar al-Bashir, forming a joint government with a civilian prime minister.
At the time there were concerns about a deadly military crackdown on protesters and the involvement of the RSF, that with its precursor the Janjaweed – had already been accused of committing crimes, atrocities, and ethnic cleansing in Darfur, targeting non-Arab communities. (Both sides denied all accusations).
By 2021, the two generals staged a coup. But their power struggle reached breaking point in April 2023, mainly over plans to bring the 100,000-strong RSF under army command.
Fighting first erupted in the capital, Khartoum, and quickly spread across the country, morphing into an international proxy conflict.
Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have said there is mounting evidence that the UAE has bankrolled the RSF in breach of arms embargoes, which the Emirates denies. The RSF in turn accuses the army of being backed by Egypt and Iran.
Where is the fighting now?
The front lines have shifted dramatically. After losing control of Khartoum to the RSF, the army retook the capital in March 2025. But by October 2025, in the west, the RSF had captured El Fasher, the army’s last stronghold in Darfur, after an 18-month siege and slaughter.
This year, a UN independent fact-finding mission for Sudan said the RSF’s ethnically targeted killings, widespread sexual violence and enforced disappearances bore the “hallmarks of genocide”.
The SAF (Sudan Armed Forces) and its affiliated militias have also been accused of atrocities by UN investigators, which the SAF also denies.
Since then, the war’s centre of gravity has moved to the Kordofan region, which links Darfur to central Sudan.
El Obeid: the new front line
El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, is now one of the most important battlegrounds of the war. Its position at a crossroads linking the country’s central and western regions makes it strategic. Until very recently, it was almost completely surrounded by RSF fighters and under partial siege.
The city of around half a million people is also now home to an estimated 100,000 displaced people. But it offers little safety. It has been under intense drone strikes. The UN has warned that the patterns of violence seen in El Fasher are now emerging in El Obeid.
Key facts and figures
- Death toll: There is no official death toll. Conflict monitor Acled says it has verified nearly 60,000 dead, although other estimates say as many as 150,000 have been killed
- Humanitarian crisis: Nearly 34 million people across Sudan need aid, while 21 million lack health services; this has led to Sudan becoming the largest humanitarian crisis in the world, according to the WHO
- Displacement: At least 14 million people have been forced from their homes, a quarter of the population, making it the world’s largest displacement crisis. Neighbouring countries host over 4.4 million Sudanese refugees
- Sexual violence: Conflict-related sexual violence in Sudan is unprecedented in terms of the scale, prevalence and brutality of its widespread use as a weapon of war, according to the UN’s human rights office
- Children: An estimated 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026. Unicef has documented the rape of children as young as one year old
- Famine: Around 20 million people or 40 per cent of the population face high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the IPC, the UN-backed global hunger monitor. Famine was confirmed in El Fasher in 2024 and in Kadugli, South Kordofan, in September 2025. Sudan is also the world’s largest hunger crisis right now.
- Drought: The IPC warned in October that Super El Niño-induced drought is compounding conflict and driving a growing risk of famine in Darfur and Kordofan. It also found that the drought now covers more than half of the country
- Healthcare: The WHO has verified 217 attacks on healthcare since April 2023, resulting in thousands of deaths. In 2026, 37 per cent of health facilities were reported to be non-functional
- Aid: As of 8 October, the UN’s $2.9bn appeal for Sudan is 40 per cent unfunded
- Genocide: In February 2026, a UN fact-finding mission said RSF atrocities in El Fasher bore the “hallmarks of genocide” against non-Arab communities

(Bloomberg) -- The weekend US air traffic outage ranks as the worst in 35 years for flight cancellations caused by a technology issue, surpassing Southwest Airlines Co.’s 2022 systems meltdown, according to travel app Flighty. 
With every US carrier affected by the four-hour nationwide stoppage on Friday, the number of flight cancellations had exceed 17,000 by Sunday, aviation data providers including Flighty and Cirium said. That surpassed the 16,900 scrapped flights caused by Southwest’s tech troubles in the winter holiday of 2022.
Airlines and passengers are still reeling from the days of disruption caused by only the third nationwide ground-stop in history, and the worst since the September 2001 terror attacks. The issue has been traced to the replacement of outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas and a router that started flooding the air-traffic control system with connection attempts. 
Cancellations started to ease on Sunday, with more than 2,220 flights affected as of 11.15 p.m. New York time, according to FlightAware data, though more than 10,100 services were delayed as airlines struggled to get planes and crew back on schedule.
Major airlines including Delta Air Lines Inc. and Alaska Air Group Inc. said they are anticipating a more normal service or vastly reduced cancelations Monday.
So far, American Airlines Group Inc. is the most-impacted airline by total, with more than 5,300 services scrapped since Friday, while financially-troubled JetBlue Airways Corp. was the worst hit as a proportion of flights, according to flight data provider Cirium.
The latest air traffic tech troubles also surpassed major crises like the 2024 global IT failure of CrowdStrike Holdings Inc., which grounded flights and impacted businesses around the world. The CrowdStrike chaos triggered a further crisis for Delta at the time, after its crew-scheduling system failed.

Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.
Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms.
"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.
Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.
In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.
The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.
Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.
Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.
Following widespread complaints about the rising cost of living, he recently said he would work to reduce the cost of fuel but denied that this was a return to the subsidy. For decades, many Nigerians have seen cheap fuel as one of the few perks of living in Africa's largest oil producer.
His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.
Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.
"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.
However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.
"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.
While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.
Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.
"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.
To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.
But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.
Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.
"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."
To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.
"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.

The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.
Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.
He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.
"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.
Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.
"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.
Another huge challenge facing Nigeria is the power sector, which has suffered from years of underinvestment.
The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.
Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.
The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.
"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.
Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.
The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.
For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.
"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.
"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.
Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.
"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.
As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge - building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.
"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.
"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

Tesla's decision to wind down Cybertruck production has Marques Brownlee worried about a different delayed vehicle.
"This doesn't bode well for the Roadster," Brownlee, the YouTube reviewer popularly known as MKBHD, said on a Friday episode of the "WVFRM Podcast."
On November 6, Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced on X that the EV maker would stop building the Cybertruck by mid-2027 to focus on production of the steering wheel-less Cybercab. Earlier this year, Tesla also retired its Model S and Model X, as it shifts more of its attention toward autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots.
That makes the Roadster, Tesla's twice-revealed and long-delayed supercar, a questionable fit in the automaker's lineup, MKBHD said. It's the only vehicle in Tesla's lineup that the automaker isn't trying to make fully autonomous.
MKBHD has followed the Roadster saga particularly closely. He previously held two reservations for the high-flying vehicle, but he said in September 2025 that he had canceled one after waiting nearly a decade for delivery.
And, for the Cybertruck, he said he thinks Tesla missed a golden opportunity.
"If they just made like a good, simple SUV type-thing, like the EV9," he said. "That would have sold a lot. People would have wanted that everywhere."
About MKBHD's hair…
The YouTuber has a big bet with Tesla stans: If Tesla, as it once predicted, sells Cybercabs to US consumers by the end of 2026 under $30,000, he'll shave his head.
Tesla debuted its gold-painted Cybercabs in Austin in September, but the vehicles were used exclusively in Tesla's own ride-hailing service — not sold to individual drivers.
On Friday, he said that Tesla's plan to continue making Cybertrucks until mid-2027 made him more confident in his bet.
"Alright, I'm probably good," MKBHD said on the podcast. "I did just get a haircut."
That bet got a little more complicated late Friday and into Saturday.
Tesla opened early Cybercab orders to select customers and is predicting a December delivery for its first units. The consumer Cybercab has a $29,990 starting price (before a $300-a-month subscription) — and MKBHD was among the initial invitees.
"My hair is safe for several reasons," he wrote, pointing to the car's invite-only sales run and the fact that owners can't use it at first as a ride-hail. "It's a paperweight if I take this thing home."
Musk responded on Saturday: "He's a chicken."

LCA Mk-1A to join IAF within this financial year: Air Chief Marshal Dixit
Operationalising the LCA Mk-1A is an immediate priority for the IAF.
Indian Air Force (IAF) chief Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit on Monday said the delayed light combat aircraft (LCA Mk-1A) will be inducted into service within the financial year 2026-27 as the force takes steps to shore up its fighter fleet.
“We will have LCA Mk-1A joining the IAF within this financial year. We will have a squadron, and then we will continue developing, and we will take it further. Not only LCA Mk-1A, now LCA Mk-2 will roll out maybe next year. We are also working very hard for AMCA (advanced medium combat aircraft),” he said at the ANI National Security Summit 3.0.
After taking over as IAF chief on October 31, Dixit outlined the force’s top priorities, placing the indigenous Tejas LCA Mk-1A, alongside the LCA Mk-2 and AMCA programmes, at the forefront of its modernisation drive.
“Creating indigenous capability in a fully designed, developed, tested and then produced fighter is a challenge and only a handful of countries have been able to achieve it,” Dixit said. Restoring the IAF’s combat strength through a renewed push for indigenisation is his foremost task, as the air force grapples with a critical shortage of fighter aircraft.
Operationalising the LCA Mk-1A is an immediate priority for the IAF. The aircraft is finally nearing induction after missing several deadlines. It will be the first aircraft to enter service under Dixit’s watch.
The LCA Mk-1A will replace the IAF’s workhorse MiG-21s, which retired last year after more than six decades of service. The IAF has placed two orders with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) for 180 Mk-1A fighter jets worth a combined ₹1.1 lakh crore.
The more advanced LCA Mk-2 programme is gathering momentum. HAL has built the structure and coupling is complete – the front, the centre and the rear fuselage sections have been joined, and the airframe is ready. HAL is targeting the first ground run by March next year, with the maiden flight expected later in the year. The IAF will now move a case for the LCA Mk-2 procurement. It will replace the Mirage 2000s, MiG-29s and Jaguars.
Speeding up the AMCA programme is also critical because China has already deployed the J-20 fifth-generation fighters, and is rolling out the J-35 stealth fighters.

Lupus patients struggling with the debilitating disease are lining up to try experimental CAR-T therapies even after the recent deaths of four patients in clinical trials for a variety of autoimmune diseases, according to doctors who treat the life-threatening condition.
The trials remain halted and full details of the deaths — three linked to Novartis and one to Bristol Myers Squibb — have not been released.
Still, patients are willing to take the risk, compelled by accounts of people with advanced disease who were able to stop all medications and reclaim normal lives.
“I have patients that are literally waiting to get in,” said Dr. Anca Askanase, chief of rheumatology at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York, who has enrolled patients in the Bristol Myers CAR-T trials.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, the most common and severe form of lupus, causes agonising joint pain and raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease. Current treatments, which range from steroids to immunosuppressants and targeted biologics, often fail to control the disease. Some 10% to 15% of people with lupus die prematurely.
Brittan Kopittke, 27, who works for the University of North Carolina helping to counsel patients considering CAR-T, was diagnosed with lupus at age 22. SLE, which affects about 300,000 people in the US, typically develops between the ages of 15 and 44.
What began as a rash on her chest rapidly progressed to crippling joint pain, mouth sores and crushing fatigue. Steroids to reduce inflammation and the antimalarial drug hydroxychloroquine to tamp down antibodies attacking her healthy cells and tissues failed.
“My mouth sores were rampant. I was struggling to eat. I was struggling to drink. I was just very, very miserable,” she said.
Despite trying a cocktail of medicines, her disease advanced, attacking her kidneys, heart and lungs.
“I had reached the end of the line with treatments,” she said.
In June 2024, Kopittke went to UNC-Chapel Hill for a trial testing CAR-T, a personalised immunotherapy successfully used to treat blood cancers. It involves removing blood cells called T cells, genetically reengineering them to attack rogue immune cells, and reinfusing them with the aim of growing new, healthy immune cells.
Kopittke developed two dangerous reactions: cytokine release syndrome, which causes systemic inflammation, and a life-threatening, high-grade neurological complication called ICANS that left her unresponsive for three days.
Now, some two years into remission, Kopittke said she does not “sugarcoat” the risks when advising patients. “But I do say that I would do this again.”
150 trials underway
Novartis, Bristol Myers, and other companies with approved CAR-T cancer therapies, such as Johnson & Johnson and Gilead, are currently testing the technology against other hard-to-treat diseases.
There are about 150 trials underway pursuing CAR-T for lupus, as well as many others for myasthenia gravis, scleroderma, myositis, multiple sclerosis and stiff-person syndrome.
“There’s billions and billions of dollars pouring into this space,” said P.J. Utz, a Stanford Medicine autoimmunity researcher.
The risks became clear when Novartis in late August said it halted eight trials of its experimental rap-cel CAR-T therapy in autoimmune and neurological disorders after three patients died from a rare but known hyperinflammatory complication called IEC-HS.
Novartis, in an emailed statement, said it is working with multiple investigators and external academic experts to understand the root cause of the deaths and will share its findings “once the analysis is completed and the results can contribute to furthering patient care.”
Bristol also paused enrollment in its CAR-T autoimmune trials, citing temporary inflammatory events in patients. On October 23, it announced the death of a multiple sclerosis patient in one of the trials but said it had identified the cause of the safety issue and hopes to resume testing in 2027.
Piecing together what happened
The revelation of deaths in the Novartis trials surprised doctors eager to try CAR-T, buoyed by the success of Georg Schett of the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. In 2022, Schett published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine showing five lupus patients achieved remission with CAR-T. Subsequent studies showed lasting remission.
The Novartis deaths have left doctors in the dark, Schett said. The company needs to disclose what diseases the patients had, how well controlled their diseases were and what emergency treatments they received, Schett added.
Without those details, he said, doctors enrolling patients in other trials are left to speculate. “This is very sad for the community.”
Schett said he and CAR-T inventor Carl June of the University of Pennsylvania have tried to piece together what happened in the Novartis trials for an article they have submitted to NEJM.
He attributes the rare hyperinflammatory events in part to Novartis’ compressed manufacturing process, which reduces the time it takes to produce the cells from more than 10 days to fewer than two.
With this process, patients receive cells in an immature form, which Schett suggests is triggering a severe inflammatory response as cells expand in patients’ bodies. “We don’t see that in other programs,” he said.
He and others were less concerned about the more familiar side effects reported by Bristol Myers.
“We have treated high-grade inflammatory events that have been reversible with treatment,” said Kopittke’s doctor, Saira Sheikh, of the University of North Carolina, who chairs a network of nearly 70 lupus clinical trial centres.
Dr. Cuoghi Edens, a rheumatologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, which treats more than 100 paediatric lupus patients, said her hospital has had great success with a CAR-T therapy from Cabaletta Bio, which uses a more traditional manufacturing process.
Cabaletta has started testing its treatment in patients as young as 12. Edens said she walked through the informed consent process with a 15-year-old late last month.
“When the potential long-term impact of your diagnosis is death,” Edens said, “I don’t know if (treatment risks are) going to make that big of a difference to these patients.

Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday
Thousands of travelers are still waiting on airlines to reschedule cancelled flights after Friday's nationwide ground stop.
More than 2,300 flights have been cancelled and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. are delayed as of Sunday evening, according to FlightAware.com. Airports in Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta were experiencing the largest number of delays, with more than 250 flights each.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that "by the end of today, end of tomorrow, I think we will be back to normal."
"What happens when you have a ground stop like what happened on Friday is we have airplanes and air crews that are out of position," Duffy said during an interview with NBC's Meet The Press. "It takes some time for the airlines to re-choreograph all of their crews and aircraft."
Duffy on Saturday blamed faulty maintenance by L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, for the nationwide ground stop.
L3Harris was working on replacing two sections of old copper wire with new fiber-optic cables, Duffy said. At some point, the FAA's legacy equipment became overloaded and disrupted communications.
"The initial investigation indicates that two potential locations as the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas."
L3Harris on Saturday said it takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on the nation "seriously."
"With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3 Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system," the company said in a statement. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."
President Trump on Sunday called on Congress to approve more funding for air traffic control to update its aging systems.
"We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve," Trump said in a post on social media.
In 2025, under Trump, Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control safety system upgrades. But on Friday, Duffy and the White House requested $50 billion in emergency funding.
"We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades," Duffy said on the Sunday news program. "We need to put money into it to make sure that it's still resilient for the future."
But two Democrats, Rep. André Carson of Indiana and Rep. Rick Larsen of Washington state, members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, said billions have been appropriated but only a portion has been spent.
"Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system," Larsen and Carson said in a statement on Saturday. "Fifteen months later, the administration's obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?"
Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told NPR on Sunday that he encourages every effort to understand what led to Friday's ground stop, and ensure that policies, practices and mitigation plans were followed.
But the ultimate credit goes to the air traffic controllers, he said.
"It's one of those moments that nobody can be prepared for, nobody can plan for," Daniels told NPR. But it shows what air traffic controllers can do when an entire national airspace system is shut down while working on unreliable equipment, he said.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.
“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”
US Central Command denied that the radar system had been destroyed and said US forces had intercepted two Iranian drones headed for Bahrain.
Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump said he had asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.
Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
An opinion poll in the UK showed 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was 45%, with 22% opposed.
The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.
Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”
Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.
In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for a review of Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.
The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.
Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely in political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.
The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

The United States has raised the possibility of Ukraine withdrawing from its eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership during recent peace negotiations with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. The question was discussed during the latest round of talks involving US, Ukrainian and Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi. Zelenskyy said this was the first time Washington had explicitly linked Ukraine's potential NATO membership to territorial concessions during the negotiations. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’” Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday. The Ukrainian president described the issue as an extremely difficult one, pointing to Russia's longstanding opposition to Ukraine joining the Western military alliance. Moscow has repeatedly treated NATO's eastward expansion and Kyiv's membership ambitions as security threats, with Russian President Vladimir Putin citing the issue among his justifications for launching the full-scale invasion in February 2022. Zelenskyy has reiterated that Ukraine was not prepared to surrender its territory. He said any possible decision would depend on a comprehensive package of security guarantees, military support and financial assistance, and that he would put such an arrangement to a national referendum. The reported discussion centres on whether Ukraine could withdraw from Donbas as part of a broader settlement that would secure its future membership of NATO. Donbas, an industrial region in eastern Ukraine comprising Donetsk and Luhansk, has been one of the biggest obstacles in negotiations to end the war. Russian forces have occupied large parts of the region, while Moscow has continued to demand that Kyiv withdraw from the remaining areas under Ukrainian control. Putin has previously made Ukraine's withdrawal from Donbas a condition for a peace agreement. In September 2022, Russia declared the annexation of Donetsk and Luhansk, along with Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, following referendums held in occupied territories. Ukraine and most of the international community rejected the votes and the annexations as illegal. Moscow has also maintained its claim over Crimea, which it annexed in 2014. Neither the United States nor the United Nations recognises Russia's annexation claims. The latest remarks from Zelenskyy suggest that Washington may be exploring whether NATO membership could form part of a compromise over territory. However, his account describes a question raised by US negotiators, rather than a confirmed agreement or a formal proposal accepted by either side. Zelenskyy has said Kyiv would need firm security assurances before considering any territorial compromise. He has called for guarantees modelled on Article 5 of the NATO treaty, which states that an armed attack against one member is to be treated as an attack against all members. He said the security package under discussion should include guarantees from NATO and the European Union, an adequately equipped and funded Ukrainian military, sufficient troops and weapons, and financial assistance for reconstruction. Zelenskyy has argued that such assurances would be essential to prevent Russia from launching another attack after a ceasefire or peace agreement. The Ukrainian president has also said that any potential arrangement involving territorial concessions would have to be put before the Ukrainian people in a referendum. His position remains that Kyiv will not voluntarily surrender its territory. Ukraine's ambition to join NATO has been a central source of tension between Moscow and the West for years. NATO's collective-defence clause, Article 5, means that an attack on one member is considered an attack on the entire alliance. Membership would therefore offer Ukraine a far stronger security commitment than a conventional bilateral agreement. Putin has repeatedly opposed Ukraine's NATO ambitions, arguing that the alliance's presence near Russia's borders threatens Moscow's security. Russia has sought assurances that Ukraine will not join the alliance as part of negotiations to end the war. The latest discussions highlight the difficult choices facing Ukraine as diplomatic efforts to end the war continue. Zelenskyy's comments indicate that Ukraine is willing to discuss the terms of a possible settlement, but not to accept territorial concessions without substantial guarantees in return. The proposal also faces a major obstacle: Putin's opposition to Ukrainian NATO membership. Even if Kyiv were to consider withdrawing from Donbas, there is no indication that Moscow would accept Ukraine joining the alliance as compensation. With inputs from Reuters. U.S. Visa Restrictions Threaten African Contestants in Miss Universe
A crackdown on entry by some citizens of African countries by the U.S. immigration officials means that some contestants might not get visas in time to attend the pageant in Puerto Rico this month.
At least two African contestants for Miss Universe said they were in danger of missing the pageant in Puerto Rico this month because they had not secured U.S. visas amid a crackdown by the Trump administration.
One contestant, Miss Zambia, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka, said she would not travel to the annual event on Nov. 24 because she had not received her visa, according to Arm Model Management, which said it was the franchise holder of Miss Zambia 2026.
Her nonattendance is “linked to the United States presidential travel restrictions affecting Zambia and other African nations,” the agency said in a statement on social media. “She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves.”
The contestant from Zimbabwe, Roseanna Hall, said on social media that she, too, had not received a U.S. visa. “I will not give up,” she said. Contestants from South Sudan and the Republic of Congo also faced delays, according to news reports.
The Miss Universe organization did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security also did not respond to a similar request. It was unclear why the contestants had not received visas.
The social media page of the Miss Universe organization listed 20 African countries among its contestants for the pageant to held in the U.S. territory.
The Trump administration has curtailed several avenues to legal migration to the United States as part of a crackdown, including visa bans and restrictions that have hit African countries hard. The administration in January imposed full or partial travel bans and visa restrictions on 36 countries, and 29 of those are in Africa.
In December, the Trump administration widened travel restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while keeping in place full restrictions for citizens of the Republic of Congo and adding them for South Sudan.
Homeland Security has said it was “slamming the door shut on the foreign invaders who have undermined our national security.”
Citizens of African countries have for decades complained of draconian visa rules imposed by the governments of the United States and European countries. Governments say the restrictions aim to control migration and prevent fraud, but many Africans say they impede legitimate professional, business and study opportunities and stop family members from attending occasions such as births, weddings and funerals.
Those restrictions have become more severe since public attitudes in many Western countries have turned against immigration over the past decade.
Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine, but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall.
Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production.
As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.
We are a team of geographers and sustainability scientists who study environmental change, environmental health, conservation, agriculture and land management. Our team wanted to better understand how farmers in South Africa’s wine-producing regions are responding as a range of environmental and economic pressures rise. We talked with growers, conservation practitioners and wine industry experts in the Western Cape and analyzed how 107 vineyards, about 20% of the total, were using sustainable land stewardship practices to adapt.
In many agricultural landscapes, production and conservation goals are frequently viewed as competing priorities. But our research found that many vineyard operators in the Western Cape see long-term stewardship and conservation of soil and wildlife habitat as essential strategies for business success.
Conservation as an investment, not a constraint
The Western Cape is home to the Cape Floral Region, a global biodiversity hot spot. It includes fynbos, a unique biome containing thousands of endemic plant species, including types of proteas, ericas and restios that are found nowhere else on Earth.

The grand ritual of ‘Soorasamharam’ as part of Kanda Sashti festival was enacted at Dhandayuthapaniswamy Temple in Palani on Sunday.
Kanda Sashti festival commenced with the ceremony of tying ‘kappu’ on November 10.
The much-awaited ritual of ‘Soorasamharam’ was conducted on the giriveedhis. Special pujas started at 4 a.m. with Vishwaroopa darshan, followed by “vila puja” at 4.30 a.m. The utchi kala puja was performed at noon and sayaratcha puja by 1. 30 p.m.
In view of ‘Soorasamharam’, devotees were allowed to the hilltop temple only upto 11 a.m.
After the ritual of presiding deity Lord Chinna Kumaraswamy getting the lance or ‘Vel’ from Malaikozhunthu Amman was performed, the temple doors were closed.
A special puja was performed for the Parasakthi vel at Thiruavinankudi Murugan Temple.
Lord Chinna Kumarasamy vanquishing Taragasooran was held on North Giri Veedhi, Banugopan Soorn on East Giri Veedhi, Singamugasooran at East Giri Veedhi and Soorapathman on West Giri Veedhi.
Temple Joint Commissioner, Hariharan, Deputy Commissioner, Venkatesh, MLA, Ravi Manoharan, Revenue Divisional Officer, Priyanka, were among those who were present.
Hundreds of policemen were deployed in the town as devotees from far and near had thronged the temple in large numbers.

Fajardo's 4 scores lead Elks past Alouettes to capture 113th Grey Cup
Edmonton snaps 11-year title drought, winning 15th championship in franchise history
Cody Fajardo earned his Grey Cup redemption.
Fajardo, named Sunday's MVP, threw two TD passes and ran for two more to power the Edmonton Elks past the Montreal Alouettes 37-30.
Fajardo was facing the team he led to the 2023 Grey Cup title before being dealt to Alberta the following season.
Asked about his future in the CFL post-game, Fajarado offered: "I've been so glad to be the starting quarterback for this organization. Win or lose I wasn't going to make an emotional decision. I'm going to talk to my wife, go through the process we always do.
"But gosh, I love being the starting quarterback for this organization ... especially tonight."
After finishing last in the West Division standings last season, Edmonton earned its first Grey Cup since 2015 and 15th in franchise history. The Elks also improved to 9-3 in all-time championship matchups with Montreal.
Montreal, which posted a CFL-best 14-4 regular-season record, suffered a second straight Grey Cup setback since winning in 2023. The Als lost 25-17 to the Saskatchewan Roughriders in last year's title game.
Vincent Blanchard's 42-yard field goal with 2:14 to play put Edmonton ahead 34-27. Montreal took possession at its own 34 with 2:07 remaining but turned the ball over on downs with 1:40 remaining.
That set up Blanchard's game-clinching 43-yard boot at 13:55 before 32,419 spectators at McMahon Stadium, short of a sellout (35,650). The Grey Cup victory is sweet for Edmonton owner Deb Thompson, who took over the franchise following the passing of her husband, Larry Thompson, in September 2025.
Jose Maltos Diaz connected from 50 yards out at 14:59 to trim the deficit to 37-30, but there would be no miracle return for Montreal.
Maltos Diaz pulled Montreal to within 31-27 with a 25-yard field goal at 2:38. The Alouettes took over at their 32 after Isaac Adeyemi-Berglund recovered Brendan O'Leary-Orange's fumble but had to punt.
Before the opening kickoff, the legendary Canadian Forces Snowbirds performed their final public flyover in their CT-114 Tutor jets. The iconic aerial team made three passes over McMahon Stadium, the final one as Canadian musician Sarah McLachlan finished O Canada.
And once play began, it did in brilliant weather. At kickoff, the temperature was a rather balmy 12 C under a setting sun.
Joshua Cephus had Edmonton's other two touchdowns. Blanchard added the converts and three field goals.
Davis Alexander, Caleb Evans and Tyson Philpot — who was named the game's most valuable Canadian — scored Montreal's touchdowns. Maltos-Diaz booted the converts and three field goals.

Montreal opened the second half with Alexander's 10-yard TD run at 3:11 to go ahead 24-21. But Edmonton countered with Fajardo's five-yard touchdown pass to Cephus at 9:37.
Fajardo's 11-yard TD strike to Cephus with 40 seconds left in the second quarter earned Edmonton its 21-17 halftime advantage. Fajardo figured in all three Elks touchdowns, scoring the other two himself.
Montreal led in net offensive yards (195-163) and time of possession (17 minutes 52 seconds) but a huge missed opportunity loomed large.
Trailing 14-10, Evans just overthrew a wide-open Philpot, who'd got behind Edmonton's defence on second and short. Then on the punt, Montrell Washington fumbled but beat Montreal's Tyrice Beverette to the ball at the Edmonton 13-yard line.
Evans' one-yard TD run at 10:58 put Montreal up 17-14. It followed Kabion Ento's interception and was aided by an unnecessary roughness call on Kordell Jackson.

A.I. Weapons Need Data for Their Training. Ukraine Has a Lot to Offer.
The Ukrainian government has opened up a trove of five million battlefield videos to defense companies at home and abroad.
The forest, seen from a drone, appeared as a vast, monotonous landscape of black tree trunks, shadows and patches of snow.
To the human eye, it appeared deserted. But to an artificial intelligence system looking for people, it did not. The system put a red box around a tiny human form, probably a soldier lurking in the trees.
Behind this feat lay vast volumes of data. Just as ChatGPT and other A.I. chatbots must be exposed to how humans write, military A.I. systems must be exposed to how humans fight. In Ukraine, this happens through a huge trove of battlefield videos, audio and text data collected over nearly five years.
The war database is being used by about 30 Ukrainian defense companies to develop A.I. weapons. Ukraine is now opening this repository, which it calls Avenger Labs, to firms in allied countries, hoping to deepen security partnerships.
Ukraine is providing the data at no charge, but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to any software they develop. Under the first agreement to be reached, 12 British defense companies will gain access. Ukraine is in talks with other countries.
While there is no shortage of Western companies developing autonomous weapons, there is a shortage of the data needed to train them. Ukraine can offer more of it than any other potential partner.
