A dramatic Microsoft 365 outage impacting widely used services like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot dragged into a second day on Friday after the company failed overnight to resolve an issue that left institutions and individuals around the world without crucial communication tools. The services did seem to be on a slow path to recovery by midmorning on Friday.
“We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability,” Microsoft said in a statement posted to its status dashboard on Friday morning. The company had said on Thursday evening that its initial attempts to fix the problem were “not taking as expected.”
The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge.
Microsoft has not said yet what caused the outage but has hinted that it was related to cascading server failures inside multiple data centers around the world that shifted too much load onto remaining operational machines.
“We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company wrote in Microsoft 365 Status update on Thursday afternoon. “We’re testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable,” the company added a few minutes later.
An additional update a few minutes after that noted, “We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”
Microsoft emphasized repeatedly in statements that there was no indication of the outage being caused by a cyberattack.
“This is absolutely going to go down as one of the big ones, up there with the Facebook outage of October 2021,” says Doug Madory, director of internet analysis at monitoring firm Kentik. “We don't know the root cause yet, but it is interesting to break down the traffic by source data center. The recovery came in fits and starts and varied greatly by source, probably due to Microsoft's efforts to bring the service back online.”
A prolonged outage of such a critical underlying digital service is not unprecedented, but Microsoft has a special position among cloud providers as an older company that was already ubiquitous in global computing from the PC era. Many organizations integrate Microsoft productivity services at the core of their operations, simply because they have used Windows computers for decades and have longstanding relationships with Microsoft.
“What makes this particularly significant is the criticality of the services affected, especially email and communication systems relied upon by government and other essential organisations,” says Swapneel Patnekar, the CEO of Indian web security firm Shreshta IT Technologies. “The impact goes well beyond the inconvenience of a typical service disruption.”
Many observers pointed out on Thursday and Friday that Microsoft has recently shed staff through attrition, layoffs, and buyout offers. The company’s annual filings say it had 223,000 full-time employees on June 30, down from 228,000 at the same time in 2025. Then in July, the company eliminated 9,000 jobs globally, of which 3,200 were cuts related to an overhaul of its Xbox teams. In October, the company reportedly made buyout offers to 60,000 employees, though apparently this was intended to speed attrition, not cull all of those roles.
Then there’s the AI factor. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in April that as much as 30 percent of the code the company is generating is now written using AI in automated tools.
“Satya's recent comments have a much different look today than they did even a week ago,” says Jake Williams, a faculty member at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy. “I don't think we'll ever be able to say that the staff reductions caused this outage, but you'll never convince me that all the tribal knowledge that walked out the door wouldn't have been invaluable in resolving it.”
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Reports of widespread disruption from the Microsoft outage started appearing during the working day on Friday in countries in Asia and Australasia, spreading across the world as more people logged on.
Schools, retail stores, courts, and medical organizations across Australia said everything from exams to health care appointments were disrupted. “Medical scans have been cancelled due to both myself and the clinic not being able to access referrals via email or fax,” one person told Australian media. Officials in Japan’s government said its own platforms had been disrupted, and staff were using phones and chat tools as they couldn’t access Outlook.
In the UK, multiple police forces have said they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.
Meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported issues with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his company had been brought to a standstill by the outages.
Unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.
“It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”
During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement.
Since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.
Patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, says that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”

'Sandpapergate': Usman Khawaja says being frozen out by Cricket Australia 'a small price to pay' for ball-tampering claims, calls bans 'grotesquely overboard'
Usman Khawaja says bans handed out to David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were "grotesquely overboard" following sandpaper scandal in 2018; Khawaja claims every member of Australia dressing room knew about the plot eight years ago, an allegation vehemently denied by Pat Cummins
Monday 16 November 2026 09:15, UK
Usman Khawaja says being frozen out by Cricket Australia would be a "small price to pay" after his claims about the 2018 ball-tampering affair in South Africa.
Khawaja alleged in his autobiography 'Sabr' that every member of the Australia dressing room was aware of the plot to alter the condition of the ball with sandpaper and not just the players who copped bans in Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.
The 39-year-old's account has been backed up by former team-mates Warner and Chadd Sayers but vehemently denied by current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the bowling group in the series against the Proteas eight years ago.

Khawaja retired from international cricket after Australia's 4-1 Ashes thrashing of England earlier this year but continues to play for Brisbane Heat in the Big Bash League.
'I have stood up for three guys I feel were treated unfairly'
Speaking on an episode of the They Used to Be podcast, which was recorded before Cummins' called Khawaja's claims about 'Sandpapergate' "100 per cent wrong and "utter nonsense", the batter said: "I still have a very good relationship with (Cricket Australia chief executive) Todd Greenberg.
"What happens to that relationship in the future, honestly [I don't know]. If Cricket Australia for some reason doesn't want to, it's a small price to pay in my mind for doing what I did.
"I have stood up for three guys I feel were treated unfairly (Warner, Smith and Bancroft).
"But there are other guys that are still playing in the team right now that there might be some sort of cost. I have tried my best to balance that out.
"There is always a cost in everything you do. There has been a cost to my family, too. But I am also not playing the victim here, because I knew what I was getting into.
"I knew what was coming. I just didn't realise it would be so personal."
Khawaja: 'Sandpapergate' bans were 'grotesquely overboard'
On the podcast, Khawaja spoke of an "awkward" conversation with Smith before the release of his book.
He also called the penalties dished out following the sandpaper storm as "grotesquely overboard" and "over the top" with then-skipper Smith and vice-captain Warner hit with year-long suspensions and Bancroft banned for nine months.
Warner was also told he could not captain again before that sanction was lifted years later.
Khawaja added: "I'm not here to say 'he did this', 'that person did that, or 'he knew this or he knew that'.
"It was more a case of 'we win as a team, we lose as a team, we take chances as a team'. I think if there is an opportunity to do that, we can move forward once and for all.
"But I don't think we've ever done that, and this is why it keeps coming back to us over and over again. Speculation after speculation just keeps rearing its ugly head."

Nikhil Gupta, the alleged Indian smuggler accused of plotting the assassination attempt on Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, has told a US judge that he plotted the operation alone. In a letter to the US district judge Victor Marrero ahead of his sentencing on November 20, Gupta said he regretted the decision.
“I wish I could turn back time to 2023 and undo my mistakes. Now, when I look back, I don't even recognise the man I had become. In early 2023, even though my life looked just fine from the outside, I was a mess. I was not me,” Gupta said in the letter.
Gupta, who was detained in the Czech Republic and later extradited to the US to face trial, said he had contemplated suicide.
“When I first got arrested, I had suicidal thoughts flashing through my mind continuously, and every night I contemplated ending my life so I would not wake up the next morning. But at the same time, I was thinking about my family-my kids, my wife, my mother and my cats and how I had already caused them so much pain. I deeply regretted the suffering I caused them and the people around me,” he said.
In February, Gupta pleaded guilty in a New York federal court to three federal charges related to a foiled plot to assassinate the Sikh separatist leader. He admitted guilt to all three counts brought against him by the U.S. Department of Justice:
Murder-for-hire carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison while conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, which also carries up to 10 years in prison, and conspiracy to commit money laundering carries a maximum of 20 years.
According to Hindustan Times, prosecutors have urged the judge to sentence Gupta to 293 months, or just over 24 years. Gupta's lawyers, on the other hand, are seeking a much shorter term of 144 months, or roughly 12 years.
According to the US Department of Justice, Gupta was recruited in 2023 by an Indian government employee, Vikash Yadav, to arrange the assassination of Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen based in New York. The alleged murder plot was exposed after Gupta attempted to hire a hitman for $100,000, unaware that the contact was an undercover US federal agent. Gupta arranged for an associate to deliver a $15,000 cash advance in Manhattan and shared Pannun's personal details and surveillance photos.

They Left Iran, but Now the Regime Is Seizing Their Assets to Silence Them
The Iranian authorities are pursuing diaspora dissidents and journalists, extending the government’s repressive apparatus far beyond its borders.
The retired couple in Iran first realized that something was wrong when their bank cards stopped working in early May. After inquiring with the authorities, they discovered that their assets had been frozen by order of the country’s intelligence ministry.
The couple learned, eventually, that they were being punished for the actions of their daughter Noushin Najafiragheb, who lived in Europe — specifically, for her social media posts opposing the Iranian government, according to another daughter, Mehrnoush Najafiragheb.
Across Iran, the government has used asset seizures as punishment for actions taken abroad. Homes and businesses have been seized, life savings raided, family heirlooms taken. When those targeted had little inside Iran themselves, the authorities went after their family members back home, interviews show.
As the Najafiragheb family pressed their case with the authorities, Mehrnoush said, they encountered dozens of other people facing the specter of losing their life’s savings as punishment for the actions of their relatives abroad.
“We realized we weren’t alone,” Ms. Najafiragheb recalled her mother telling her. She said her sister Noushin had declined to be interviewed to avoid further government pressure on her family.

BBC Children in Need has raised £38,720,170 during its 2026 annual fundraising appeal, bringing together celebrities, television presenters and young fundraisers for an evening focused on supporting children and young people across the United Kingdom. The live programme was broadcast on Friday, 13 November, on BBC One and BBC iPlayer. This year's campaign, titled Challenge Yourself 2026, encouraged people across the country to take on personal challenges and raise money for the charity. The event featured several celebrity appearances, including Hollywood actors Timothee Chalamet, Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy. The stars of Dune: Part Three also joined the programme for a special prank involving presenter Rylan Clark. The evening also recognised people who had taken on demanding fundraising activities, including BBC Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans, who completed a cycling challenge across the four nations. The charity announced a total of £38,720,170 towards the end of the live broadcast. Donations remained open after the programme, meaning the amount could increase further. The show was presented by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan Clark, Sara Cox and Tyler West from MediaCityUK in Salford. The campaign's theme, Challenge Yourself 2026, invited supporters to create their own fundraising activities. The aim was to encourage people of different ages to participate, whether through individual challenges or group activities. BBC Children in Need supports projects and organisations that work with children and young people facing difficult circumstances. Its funding helps address issues such as poverty, mental health difficulties and challenges within family life. The annual appeal also gives young people an opportunity to share their experiences and explain how charity-funded projects have helped them. Among the celebrity appearances during the programme were Dune: Part Three actors Timothee Chalamet, Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy. The four actors took part in a prank involving Rylan Clark, who believed he was conducting a regular interview with the cast about their upcoming film. However, three children were secretly controlling the conversation by giving the actors instructions through earpieces. This led to several unusual moments during the interview, leaving Clark confused. In one instance, Chalamet was instructed to check his phone and tell the presenter that he was bidding on an air fryer. The other actors also followed instructions from the children, making the interview increasingly difficult for Clark to manage. The segment was one of the entertainment highlights of the evening, with the actors using their appearance to support the charity's annual appeal. Another major contribution came from BBC Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans, who completed a cycling challenge covering almost 400 miles across the four nations. The five-day journey began in Glasgow and took him through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales before ending in Cardiff on Friday, 13 November. His challenge raised £4,760,086 for BBC Children in Need. Evans appeared on the live programme after completing the journey and spoke about the physical demands of the ride. He described it as the hardest challenge of his life, explaining that completing such a long distance had pushed him beyond his comfort zone. The programme also featured performances from the BBC Children in Need Choir and Scottish band Texas, along with a special dance performance involving the presenters and professional dancers from Strictly Come Dancing. The £38.7 million announced during the broadcast marked the amount raised by the end of the television appeal, with the charity continuing to accept donations afterwards. The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.
“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.
The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.
However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

Tearful McIlroy dedicates record-equalling win to ill dad
- Published
DP World Tour Championship final leaderboard

Rory McIlroy wiped away tears as he dedicated his eighth Race to Dubai victory to his ill father, Gerry.
Moments after matching Colin Montgomerie's record of season-long European tour titles on Sunday, the Northern Irishman was asked about the health of his father.
An emotional McIlroy revealed Gerry has been in hospital for two months after "a huge operation" - a double lung transplant - at the end of September.
"He's recovering well, thankfully," McIlroy told the DP World Tour.
"But before I left to come here to the Middle East, I went up to Cleveland to see him. He said to me: 'Go win The Race to Dubai'.
"This one's for him."
It came after a thrilling climax at the traditional season-ending DP World Tour Championship with Tyrrell Hatton securing a commanding victory, while McIlroy pipped Spaniard Eugenio Chacarra to the overall crown.
Hatton's closing six-under-par 66 helped him romp to a five-shot victory on 15 under par but most eyes were on the thrilling battle that went down to the final hole.
It is the fifth successive year that McIlroy has won the award and it has drawn him level with Montgomerie, the Scot who set a mark 21 years ago that few thought would ever be matched.
"Yeah, double digits," smiled McIlroy when asked what would be his final target of Race to Dubai victories.
"I'd love to surpass Monty next year and we'll go from there."
McIlroy's confidence in going along with a target shouted out by the fans surrounding the 18th green at the Earth Course in Dubai on Sunday was refreshing to hear.
But he appears to be playing and talking with a little more freedom in recent years - the sort of freedom that comes as a result of finally completing the career Grand Slam and winning successive Masters titles - and leads to declarations of winning 10, or more.
"Winning eight Order of Merits (Race to Dubai titles) was never in my list of goals growing up," said McIlroy, who closed with a bogey-free 67 to finish on 10 under and must surely now be considered Europe's greatest golfer.
"I remember Monty being a stalwart of the European tour and playing with him at the London Club in 2008, so to pull up alongside him and win eight of these means the world to me."
After Jon Rahm's victory in Abu Dhabi last week, fellow former LIV Golf member Hatton showed his class with a five-shot success at the Earth Course at Jumeirah Golf Estates.
Hatton showed his combustible side earlier in the week but, despite later admitting to being "weirdly nervous" he appeared serene on Sunday.
In the final group and knowing he couldn't win the overall Race to Dubai title, he was detached enough to block out the scramble as he strolled to his ninth DP World Tour victory - even asking an on-course reporter who was going to win as he walked from the 17th green to 18th tee.
It was that head-to-head battle between Chacarra and McIlroy that dominated the tournament, a battle that, after a long hard season, came right down to the wire.
Both players knew victory would win them the title. There were permutations galore for finishing second, third, or below that.
Chacarra and McIlroy went toe-to-toe in and the overall lead in the rankings chopped and changed down an absorbing back nine as neither man backed down.
At one juncture just one-tenth of a point separated the pair.
But a late surge from Northern Ireland's McIlroy allowed him to finish runner-up behind England's Hatton in the tournament and collect enough points to edge out the gutsy Spaniard.
Chacarra, who earned around $15-20m during three years as a LIV player, is in just his second season on the DP World Tour. He is the only three-time winner of this year's campaign and was desperate to add his name to compatriots Rahm and Seve Ballesteros as the third Spanish order of merit winner.
After four early birdies he looked in fine shape. The pressure began to tell as he posted three bogeys in four holes around the turn. But he responded brilliantly with two more birdies to push McIlroy all the way.
Chacarra, the 26-year-old world number 39, finished in a tie for third to end up second in the overall standings and earn a PGA Tour card for next season.
As tough as it was this year for McIlroy to win, mainly due to playing on the PGA Tour for the first half of the season, 2027 will be even harder because there will be some big names flooding in after the collapse of LIV Golf.
Rahm and Hatton are just two high-profile LIV players who are suspended from the PGA Tour for a year following their involvement with the breakaway tour. They will both have a full season on the European circuit that will give them a big advantage over McIlroy.
Along with many other big names such as Sergio Garcia, Joaquin Niemann and Tom McKibbin, there's even the possibility of Bryson DeChambeau, the biggest LIV name of all, applying to join the DP World Tour for next season.
The American is eligible thanks to his 2024 US Open triumph, at McIlroy's painful expense, and had to apply by the end of the Sunday of the DP World Tour Championship.
Is McIlroy Europe's greatest ever golfer?
After this latest addition to McIlroy's glowing CV it's hard to make a case against him being Europe's greatest ever golfer – and as he continues to find new targets to stay motivated one of them is very much to unequivocally nail down that title.
Motivation was a problem in the immediate aftermath of finally ending his long wait to win the Masters in 2025 as he became just the sixth man to win the career Grand Slam.
But a year later he had re-found it as he became just the fourth back-to-back Green Jacket winner with his brilliant defence at Augusta National back in April.
That put him on six major titles, level with England's Sir Nick Faldo and just one behind the great Harry Vardon, whose name adorns the trophy McIlroy has just hoisted for the eighth time.
Still only 37, McIlroy still has plenty of time to overhaul Montgomerie and hold the outright record for the most European number one titles – despite playing on two tours throughout the majority of his career.
Targets have changed – McIlroy is not chasing the world number one spot or winning any old trophy. He's voiced his desire to focus on majors, play more in Europe and around the globe and keep stacking up these order of merit titles.
An Olympic title is perhaps the only honour missing from his trophy cabinet, and he will have the chance to change that in 2028 on a familiar Riviera Country Club Course, which is a regular stop-off on the PGA Tour and where he finished second a this year's Genesis Invitational.
He will be attempting to become the first man to win three Masters in a row next April, before the US Open at Pebble Beach and Open Championship at St Andrews offer great chances at venues McIlroy knows he can thrive on.
McIlroy has won six Ryder Cups as a stalwart for Europe and is just seven points behind all-time leader Sergio Garcia.
But even if the Northern Irishman quit the game right now he's already built a more than compelling argument that he's the greatest player the continent has ever seen.

Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country.
The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday.
It is the British army veteran’s fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.
He spoke at a conference organised by the Superhumans Center, a clinic in Lviv that specialises in care and rehabilitation of those who have fought in the conflict. The prince has previously supported the group, which provides prosthetic limbs to those who have lost them in battle.
He said: “Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success.”
Harry watched wheelchair rugby players who hope to be in Ukraine’s team at next year’s Invictus Games, which will take place in Birmingham. Ukraine is aiming to send about 60 competitors to the event – its largest ever team.
The prince said the games for wounded military veterans, which he set up in 2014, could one day be held in Ukraine. “When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” he promised.
At the rugby match, Harry hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, who took part in the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. The 41-year-old, who uses prosthetic legs, said he was “still an active serviceman”, and the prince expressed surprise he found time to train.
Odainyk said afterwards he had told Harry his involvement in his sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games”.
The prince visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, in September 2025 and in April this year. During the April visit, he called Ukraine “a country bravely and successfully defending Europe’s eastern flank” and said “it matters that we don’t lose sight of the significance of that”.
The 42-year-old spent a decade in the British army and served in Afghanistan, including as a helicopter pilot. He has described those years as the happiest of his life.

Prince and Princess of Wales arrive in India ahead of meeting with Modi
- Published
The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived in India for a three-day visit that will include a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The visit is the first time William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together in four years.
Her cancer treatment has limited the amount of international travel she has undertaken but she will be with her husband for several engagements this week.
Most are related to the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, which awards five £1m prizes for the best solutions to the biggest climate challenges.
"The princess is enormously proud of what the prince has achieved with Earthshot and is really looking forward to being alongside him for what is one of the most important moments in his year," said a spokesperson for the royals.
"She's seen it develop into something truly remarkable and is excited to experience first-hand just how far it has come."
The meeting with Modi was a late addition to the royal schedule after the Indian prime minister confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.
They will fly from Mumbai to Delhi for the meeting on Wednesday.
"For the Prince, it represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage," a Kensington Palace spokesperson said.
"We've seen him increasingly support the UK's diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level."
The couple last met Modi on their official visit to India in 2016.
Arriving in Mumbai earlier on Monday Prince William posted a message about the trip on social media: "India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country."
The royals will carry out a number of engagements in Mumbai related to the environment, cricket, young families and the Bollywood film industry.
At an Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony, five innovations will be announced as winners of the million-pound prizes.
Nominees range from projects to increase the number of electric rickshaws in India to a scheme able to detect wildfires faster than Nasa.
The event will be hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.
Take That will perform and guests will include actor Rami Malek and Australian conservationist and TV presenter Robert Irwin, who joined Prince William when he was a surprise guest on The Graham Norton show last month.
"There is a lot of environmental potential here in Mumbai," said Irwin. "There is also a huge amount of young people who have a passion for environmentalism and I think Earthshot is mobilising that here in India."

The Supreme Court has suspended the life sentences of two convicts in the case of the gangrape of Bilkis Bano and the murder of seven of her family members during the 2002 riots in Gujarat and granted them bail.
Also Read: Bilkis Bano case : Grant of remission ‘classic case’ of using SC order to violate law; verdict
A Bench of Justices MM Sundresh and P.B. Varale noted that Bipin Chandra Joshi and Pradeep Mordhiya had been incarcerated for more than 17 years.
"Having heard the parties, it suffices to state that the appellants have been incarcerated for a period of more than 17 years, and also the fact remains that one of the appellants has a severe handicap. Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law," the apex court said in its October 28 order, which has now been uploaded.
"In view of the above and considering the issues involved in this appeal, we suspend the sentence and grant bail to the appellants on such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the concerned trial court," the bench added.
Also Read | Unlawful remission: On the Bilkis Bano case
Arguing that the two men have been incarcerated for more than 17 years, senior advocate Siddharth Luthra submitted that one of the convicts had not been named in the FIR and was implicated after nearly three years following the 2002 riots.
Additional Solicitor General Raja Thakre vehemently opposed the plea and said the High Court and the trial court have taken into consideration the relevant material brought on record, especially as the offence committed is so serious.
Bilkis Bano was 21 years old and five months pregnant when she was gang-raped while trying to escape the horror of the communal riots that broke out after the Godhra train burning incident in February 2002. Her three-year-old daughter was among the seven family members killed.
The two convicts, Mordhiya and Joshi, are among the 11 whose remission was quashed by the Supreme Court in 2024.
The other convicts in the case are Govind Nai, Ramesh Chandana, Mitesh Bhatt, Bakabhai Vohania, Kesarbhai Vohania, Jaswant Nai, Radheshyam Shah, Rajubhai Soni and Shailesh Bhatt.
Joshi and Mordhiya were convicted by the trial court under Sections 143 (unlawful assembly), 147 (rioting), 302 (murder) read with Sections 376 (rape) of the Indian Penal Code and were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life with fine.
On January 8, 2024, the apex court annulled the remission the Gujarat government granted to the 11 convicts in the high-profile case while slamming the state for being "complicit" with an accused and abusing its discretion.
Slamming the Gujarat government for remitting their sentences, the apex court said it had "usurped" the power of the Maharashtra government to grant remission. The Bilkis Bano case was transferred from a Gujarat court to a court in Mumbai, and the Supreme Court said the Maharashtra government was vested with the power to grant remission.

Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
- Published
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.
Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.
"That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme.
Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) indicated that it was considering steps to capture peak levels of particulate matter (PM), a major pollutant, that exceed the existing monitoring range, after air quality data from several government monitoring stations in Delhi went missing for hours during the pollution spike following Deepavali on Sunday.
The Hindu reported on Monday (November 9, 2026) that the data gaps had led to an artificially lower official air quality index (AQI), making air quality appear better than it actually was, according to experts.
In a statement on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) , the CPCB said PM levels were measured only up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³) for AQI calculations, which explained the missing data on Deepavali night, when actual concentrations exceeded this limit.
“The PM analysers deployed at the time of introduction of the NAQI (National Air Quality Index) [in 2015] were calibrated for a measurement range of 0-1,000 µg/m³. Accordingly, consistent with this, the designed system of automated data validation treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range, and such readings are not used in the computation,” the CPCB statement read.
“During extreme episodes, which are occasional, like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of the relevant pollutant for the concerned station,” the statement added.
Deliberations under way
The CPCB said internal deliberations and consultations on processing data “beyond system design range” were under way.
The CPCB also said spikes in ambient pollutant concentrations, such as those caused by firecrackers bursting, are episodic and short-lived. “The NAQI recognises that prolonged exposure, rather than a momentary reading, is a more relevant indicator of ill effects on human health,” the statement read.
Under the AQI calculation methodology adopted by the CPCB in 2015, the overall index is based on eight parameters and is calculated only if data are available for a minimum of three pollutants, out of which one should necessarily be either PM2.5 or PM10.
“The methodology was formed in 2015 and at that time it was decided that the accuracy was good only up to 1,000 µg/m³ and both PM2.5 and PM10 were capped at it for calculation of AQI. But the equipment got better with time and Delhi’s air quality analysers and instruments were also updated, but the methodology was never updated after that,” an official told The Hindu.
“But now there are discussions of raising this cap so that peak values above 1,000 µg/m³ could be measured,” the official added.
Of the 59 air quality monitoring stations in Delhi, 46 are operated by the Delhi government’s Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), which does not calculate the AQI. The DPCC had recorded PM2.5 and PM10 levels exceeding 1,000 µg/m³ on Deepavali night, though several readings were initially missing.
The CPCB uses data from these 46 stations, along with readings from other monitoring stations, to calculate the AQI.
Air quality improves
Meanwhile, Delhi’s air quality improved to the ‘poor’ category on Tuesday (November 10, 2026), with the 24-hour average AQI recorded at 299, just below the ‘very poor’ threshold of 300.
Experts attributed the improvement to increased wind speeds and said air quality was likely to improve further over the next few days.

Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.
Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.
"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.
"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.
Prabowo accepts Raka's resignation
Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.
Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.
Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.
"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."
Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.
"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.
Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.
Long-running allegations over candidacy lead to court disputes
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.
The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.
Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.
Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.
Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.
Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.
"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

What do Scotland do about 'scunnered' Gannon-Doak?
- Published
Two years ago, when Scotland defeated Croatia in the Nations League, that November night at Hampden was the dawn of Ben Gannon-Doak.
The then-teenager took £77m Manchester City man Josko Gvardiol to the cleaners and fans demanded the national team be built around the winger.
The Tartan Army's love for him has never faded - it arguably peaked when he stole the show in Scotland's World Cup opening win over Haiti - but it is fair to say they are growing frustrated, arguably on the Bournemouth man's behalf.
Under Sebastien Pocognoli, Gannon-Doak - who turned 21 on Wednesday - has been deployed at right wing-back, a role that demands defensive instincts unnatural to the pacy attacker.
It is already clear the new head coach is wedded to his preferred system, but it is one that is stifling one of Scotland's greatest attacking outlets - even though his final product still leaves a lot to be desired.
As his side prepare to visit Nations League Group B1 leaders Switzerland on Monday needing a win to have any chance of a promotion play-off place, Pocognoli has addressed both concerns - citing he is not uneasy about either - but pundits and punters alike cannot seem to shift their suspicions.
Is Gannon-Doak 'scunnered'?
In that 1-0 victory over 10-man Croatia, it was Gannon-Doak's fearlessness in facing one of Europe's most elite and experienced teams that caught the eye.
His electric speed and directness excited a support who had long been crying out for a player with such qualities and the confidence in applying them. A natural winger, if you will.
In Pocognoli's system, though, there is no space for wingers. Something that former Rangers full-back Richard Foster says must "scunner" the wee man.
"When you're a full-back and you get to play wing-back, it's amazing - all of a sudden you are 10-20 yards up the pitch, doing more attacking and you can be a bit more aggressive," he said on BBC Scotland's Sportsound.
"When you ask a winger to do that, most of the time they are absolutely scunnered. They are thinking 'I don't want to go back there'.

"Looking at the squad [against North Macedonia], the three most exciting players we had - Findlay Curtis, Josh McPake and Gannon-Doak - are all wingers and he didn't bring two on.
"You look at the previous game [against Slovenia] and the difference McPake and Curtis made by coming on and taking players on - it gives everyone a lift.
"As a fan, you want to get excited about what you are watching. We are playing in a shape where we have the most exciting talents on the bench and they can't get on unless you adjust things. I just think he has to change the formation."
Foster is far from the only one wishing for a shift in shape - and not just for Gannon-Doak's benefit. Much has been made about the Scots' options in defence, too, and whether they match-up to the method.
However, it is arguable Gannon-Doak is the biggest casualty of them all.
"I don't think we're getting the best out of Ben," former Scotland captain Scott Brown told BBC Scotland.
"You saw him making so many last-ditch headers on Friday. He's having to add things to his game that he probably hasn't done before, like throw-ins, defending one-v-one."
No need to mention that throw-in, Scott. But that wasn't the only instance where Gannon-Doak looked a little lost. Think the 'Confused Travolta' meme.
Pocognoli 'happy' despite Gannon-Doak flaws
While his position is a new worry, his precision with his final product is not.
Almost in a microcosm, Gannon-Doak's play was laid bare when be hurtled to the byeline before winning what turned out to be the match-winning penalty against the North Macedonians on Friday.
"He made a great run for the penalty, but I did think he could have got his shot away a bit earlier and maybe not taken that extra touch," Brown said.
Back in 2024, the wee live-wire was forgiven for not always finding a pal with a pass or choking at crunch time with his final ball.
However, as the years go on and the caps rack up, his shortcomings are still on show. His end product is still largely poor and patience is wearing thin.
"As long as he is high on the pitch and is creating one-v-ones, I am happy," Pocognoli reiterated post his maiden Hampden win.
"With Ben, we know that he is a young age and needs to work on specific things. On Friday night, he had great opportunities.
"We know that he needs to improve on the end product. But he created a penalty and, against Slovenia and North Macedonia away, he created a number of unbelievable one-v-ones. He did that on Friday night as well.
"We know he can be good if we dominate the game and he can get in good positions if we control the ball.
"I am happy with his performance."
So Pocognoli is comfortable for now. Already that appears to be a running theme for the head coach - even if others are not.

Private markets asset manager Oister Global has launched a growth-stage deeptech fund with a target corpus of ₹600 Cr. The firm will target backing Indian startups developing technologies across strategic sectors. The Oister Deep Tech Fund, registered as a SEBI Category II AIF, intends to raise ₹400 Cr, along with a ₹200 Cr greenshoe option to build a concentrated portfolio of 8-10 companies. In a statement, the investment firm shared that it will focus on mature deeptech companies that have developed commercially viable technologies and are looking to scale their operations. Its investment focus will span sectors like spacetech, defence and aerospace, semiconductors and electronics, quantum technologies, advanced mobility, advanced materials and energy storage. The fund will target companies with proprietary intellectual property (IP), including patents in India and international markets, multiple revenue streams and customers across domestic and global markets. "Early-stage investors back the idea, and larger institutions tend to wait until a company is well past its hardest years. The growth stage in between, where technology turns into a business, has had very few committed investors. That is the gap we saw, and it is why we launched the Oister Deep Tech Fund," said Rohit Bhayana, cofounder and co-CEO of Oister Global. Bridging The Growth-Stage Funding Gap The fund launch comes amid a growing investor interest in India's budding deeptech ecosystem. Recent examples include AUM Ventures' ₹750 Cr India Innovation Fund II, Speciale Invest's proposed ₹1,400 Cr growth-stage fund and Celesta Capital's planned ₹2,000 Cr India-focused deeptech fund. Meanwhile, Yali Capital closed its maiden deeptech fund at ₹893 Cr in July 2025. As a result, the overall investment numbers have also been on the up. Indian deeptech startups raised nearly $365 Mn across 66 deals in H1 2026, representing a 17% YoY growth in funding, compared with $310 Mn in H1 2025, according to Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report: H1 2026. Pertinent to note that much of this capital deployment has continued to remain concentrated in the early stage, with not many investors showing the same enthusiasm when it comes to startups operating in the latter stages. Citing this discrepancy, Oister Global said that growth-stage funding can help bridge the gap by providing patient capital to companies that have already de-risked their technology but require larger investments to manufacture products, fulfil orders and expand into international markets. The fund has already identified an initial shortlist of companies across its target sectors, with further investments to be evaluated as capital is deployed. Oister previously backed startups in the country through its growth-stage and secondary investment vehicles. Its portfolio includes companies such as BlackBuck, Servify, M1xchange, Kuku FM and Purplle, among others. In May, it launched its third ACE fund with a ₹500 Cr corpus after the second ACE fund closed with a ₹400 Cr corpus, twice its initial target of ₹200 Cr. The third fund took its total secondaries allotment to ₹1,000 Cr. Besides directly investing in startups, Oister also operates with a fund of funds thesis. Till date, it has turned limited partner for various startup funds for VC firms including Blume Ventures, Speciale Invest and Stride Ventures.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

South Africa's ANC records worst-ever results in local elections
- Published
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".
While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 30.76% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 64.82% 20 years ago.
The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.
The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 9.76%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."
Entering the count centre tonight, South Africa's president and leader of the ANC Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost majority rule in the national elections in 2024 for the first time in its history. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is now known as the GNU, or government of national unity.
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose marginally from 21.83% in 2021, and was below the 26.9% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52.29%, an increase from 45.9% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.
"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC", said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."
The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."
The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Cyril Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
- ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline 
  - Published4 days ago
"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."
The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.
South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.
"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is, "Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together."
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

On Veterans Day, a video (archived) circulated online that social media users claimed authentically showed a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimanding U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his group after someone talked and laughed while taking photos at the monument.
One X user who shared the clip wrote, "Pete Hegseth and his group were loudly reprimanded for laughing while visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier"
Pete Hegseth and his group were loudly reprimanded for laughing while visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier https://t.co/mKZzmTQa0L https://t.co/DZUT7MpTRp
— philip lewis (@Phil_Lewis_) November 11, 2026
Claims about what the clip showed also circulated on Facebook and Instagram (archived, archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the video.
The video was authentic and showed a real event on Nov. 11. CNN posted the video on its YouTube channel. There was no indication the footage had been created or edited using artificial intelligence. Therefore, we rate this claim true.
The Department of Defense's Assistant to the Secretary of War for Public Affairs and Senior Advisor Sean Parnell told Snopes in a written statement:
The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.
In the video, Hegseth and four others posed on the steps in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a monument in Arlington, Virginia, that marks the grave of the unidentified service members from the U.S. who died in wars since World War I.
As Hegseth's group walked up the stairs away from the monument (time code 00:41), someone could be heard talking and laughing. The U.S. Army Sentinel on guard shouted in response, "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
It was not clear who in Hegseth's group talked and laughed, though one woman who posed with Hegseth could be seen gesturing with her hands as the group walked up the stairs before the sentinel's reprimand.
Newsweek reported that the group caught talking and laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown soldier consisted of Hegseth, his wife Jennifer Hegseth, his chief of staff Ricky Buria, his Deputy Chief of Staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
A photo from reputable photo repository Getty Images showed Hegseth's wife was present at the Veterans Day commemoration at Arlington Cemetery on Nov. 11 and wore a dark brown or burgundy dress that was also visible in CNN's coverage.
Because the other three people in the group stood with their backs to the camera, Snopes could not independently verify Newsweek's claim that they were Hegseth's senior staff.
Soldiers have guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington since March 1926. The Arlington National Cemetery wrote on its website that the guards initially "discouraged visitors from climbing or stepping on the Tomb."
The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," has guarded the monument since April 6, 1948. Barbara Starr, CNN's former Pentagon correspondent, told (time code 11:24) the network on Nov. 11 that sentinels will correct any visitors who do not act with "respect and silence" at the tomb.
The incident at Arlington comes at a time when Hegseth is facing immense pressure over the war in Iran, which has been widely understood as a reason midterm voters moved away from the Republican Party in the November midterm elections.
On Nov. 10, the day before the incident at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Republicans in the House blocked an attempt to impeach Hegseth. That same day, U.S. President Donald Trump signaled his continued support for Hegseth on Truth Social, calling the outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, who led the push for Hegseth's impeachment, a "TOTAL LOSER."
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated a number of rumors about Hegseth.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

Jammu- Army troops opened fire after observing suspicious movement in a forest area near the Line of Control in Poonch district of Jammu and Kashmir early Monday, officials said.
Alert troops guarding the border in the Kanari area of the Sawjian sector noticed suspicious activity around 1.30 am, the officials said.

Samsung is discontinuing these useful mobile apps in December
You don’t have long to grab the augmented reality tools for your Galaxy devices.
Samsung is yanking a couple of augmented reality apps that some folks might find handy from the Galaxy Store. If you're interested in snagging Quick Measure or AR Doodle for your Galaxy devices, it's best to do that relatively soon as the company will remove the apps on December 31. However, Samsung suggested it may bring them back in the future.
Quick Measure has an apt name. It's a virtual ruler app that allows you to measure distances and areas in meatspace. As for AR Doodle, that enables you to sketch on and add 3D effects to photos and videos.
Samsung has posted similar notices of termination on each app's store listing. It said that, after December 31, "new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it is already downloaded, but please be aware that some features may not function properly." The company added that they won't get compatibility updates for future versions of its operating system. So, updating your device's OS once we're into 2027 could break Quick Measure or AR Doodle.
"We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause," Samsung added. "We are committed to returning with improved services in the future." The company hasn't shed any light on when Quick Measure or AR Doodle might return, or if it will move their features into other offerings.
As long as you're quick on the draw, you can download Quick Measure and AR Doodle to compatible devices from Samsung's Galaxy Store.

The Telangana Health Department has intensified its investigation into the alleged illegal oocyte (egg) collection racket, with inspections conducted at 27 of the 44 identified Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) facilities across the State. Officials have detected 13 regulatory violations in seven hospitals and issued show-cause notices to their managements.
Health Minister C. Damodar Rajanarasimha has directed the department to conduct a comprehensive investigation into alleged illegal activities being carried out under the guise of oocyte collection and initiate stringent action against institutions and individuals found violating prescribed regulations.
Acting on the Minister’s directions, task force teams have been inspecting IVF centres across the State for the past four days. Inspections at the remaining facilities are continuing.
Aspects of investigation
The department said further action would be initiated after a detailed examination of records seized by the police and information obtained from the National ART and Surrogacy Registry. The investigation also includes examining the involvement of women identified in connection with the case, doctors, IVF centres and intermediaries allegedly facilitating the activities.
As part of the investigation, the Health department officials visited the National ART and Surrogacy Registry in New Delhi on November 6 and sought details of the data submitted by registered ART clinics and ART banks operating in Telangana.
The department has reiterated that oocyte collection must strictly comply with the provisions of the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act and Rules. All ART clinics and ART banks operating in the State are required to obtain mandatory statutory registration and adhere to the prescribed regulatory framework.
The Health Department also cautioned women against falling prey to misleading assurances and financial inducements offered by intermediaries, warning that such arrangements could expose them to unauthorised medical procedures.
