Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden downfall is in a sense shocking, considering his wealth, global fame, and role leading what was until recently the world’s most valuable company.
Why the left and right are both cheering Jensen Huang’s downfall
The deposed Nvidia CEO’s diverse coalition of haters could reshape AI policy.
But Huang’s immense influence in Washington — and particularly in President Donald Trump’s Washington — has long been intensely controversial among a surprisingly diverse cross-section of the political, business, and tech advocacy world. And his ouster not only drives a wedge through Trump’s second-term coalition, it could usher in a major change in how the US steers the AI revolution.
Huang — who resigned this week after allegations he’d had affairs with two Nvidia employees and one Chinese businesswoman who some US officials claim was spying on him for the Chinese government — has been crucial in helping shape the Trump administration’s AI policies. That’s perhaps no surprise, given that Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial to the AI revolution.
His many critics, however, say Huang’s influence has been deeply harmful. Their main objection? They believe the Trump administration hasn’t been doing enough to stop China from getting or accessing advanced AI chips — in part because of Huang’s lobbying and sway with the president.
This coalition of Huang critics spans the political spectrum. It includes right-wing China hawks and the bipartisan foreign policy establishment, who want to win an AI race against China. It includes economic populists in both parties, who resent China’s economic sway. It even includes some leading members of the Trump administration itself — Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have reportedly pushed for tighter chip restrictions.
It also contains some even odder bedfellows. The coalition includes people who want to slow down the AI race, like the tech safety advocates who warn that advanced AI could cause human extinction. Yet it also includes two major US frontier AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, who hope to impede the growth of Chinese competitors by limiting their access to chips.
All of these disparate groups come together around the core idea that the US urgently needs to do more to stop advanced chips from getting to China. Selling AI chips to China is like “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said.
Standing against them all — and often getting his way with Trump — has been Jensen Huang.
Beyond the obvious — Nvidia’s business is selling chips, and Huang wants to be able to sell more chips in more places — Huang is associated with a camp in the AI policy debate that some have dubbed with “let it rip.” Along with former White House AI czar David Sacks, Huang has scoffed at warnings that AI could cause human extinction, calling them “irresponsible” and “doomsday narratives.” He’s also dismissed some national security concerns, saying that being a “China hawk” was a “badge of shame” and said that the bigger risk to American influence over AI would be US companies losing market share around the world.
So Huang’s ouster and the claims of Chinese espionage around it have opened up an opportunity for a shakeup in US policy — and a rare chance for those China hawks to potentially investigate, undermine, and push out their rivals, while seizing the policy reins around chip exports.
Trump administration officials who want tougher restrictions have their knives out for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a frequent ally of Huang’s. There’s a bipartisan push in Congress for new export controls legislation before the end of the year. Congressional Republican committee chairs are demanding Huang and Lutnick come in and testify in the coming weeks, before Democrats take over Congress.
Plus, there are the partisan incentives for Democrats to dig into the question of what Trump knew about all this (he was reportedly briefed on the spy concerns last fall). And there are political incentives for ambitious Republicans to find an issue on which they can distance themselves from an unpopular administration without antagonizing their conservative base.
With so many different forces invested in the outcome, you can bet this topic will continue to dominate headlines for months to come — with unpredictable results for both the new Democratic Congress, the future of the GOP, and the AI boom.
The many critics of Jensen Huang’s influence on the Trump administration
In Washington itself, the most influential faction opposed to Huang is the bipartisan national security establishment, most of whom strongly believe in the necessity of competing with China for global influence.
These “China hawks” were influential in the Biden administration and have historically been dominant in GOP administrations and on GOP-controlled congressional committees. And many of them have been flabbergasted at Trump’s policies toward China and Chips this term.
“I don’t think we should be using any American technology to uplift China’s capabilities in AI given how era-defining this technology will be in national security and in our economy,” Vivek Chilukuri of the Center for a New American Security, a center-left think tank, told me. “A company’s going to argue for this, that’s what companies do. But the interest of any one company should not be trumping the national security of the United States.
Moving further right, there’s a MAGA-aligned faction that is skeptical of foreign wars such as Trump’s conflict in Iran — but even some of them are still quite antagonistic to China.
Take, for instance, Trump’s onetime campaign manager and White House adviser Steve Bannon. He’s been furiously protesting Huang’s influence on the administration for more than a year — in September 2025, he argued that Huang should be arrested for being “an agent of influence of the Chinese Communist Party,” and argued we needed to “shut down” China’s “access to technology, chips, and training.”
Advocates and politicians focused on economic issues and reining in corporate power also have long criticized Nvidia. Oren Cass of the center-right group American Compass wrote an article titled “Break up Nvidia” last year, arguing that “its excessive concentration of power is exactly what antitrust law intends to combat.”
Meanwhile, the left, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), a longtime critic of Big Tech, has frequently suggested Huang was corruptly influencing the Trump administration. At a hearing in June, she mentioned that Huang or his company had donated to Trump’s inauguration and his White House ballroom project. “If it’s not plain old-fashioned bribery, it sure smells like it,” she said.
Many in the AI safety advocacy world have also long criticized — and feared — Nvidia. That’s in part because they hope slowing down sales of AI chips abroad could slow what they view as a dangerous race to superintelligence. Additionally, after AI safety fears hit the mainstream in September due to Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation and viral warnings, Huang took an increasingly public role in dismissing such fears.
Other AI safety advocates cite the company as having a chilling effect on public debate. “For months now, I’ve heard about widespread fear among think tank researchers and policy experts who publish work against Nvidia’s interests,” AI safety researcher Steven Adler wrote last year. “If you speak with people in-the-know at AI companies, fear of retaliation from Nvidia is a major concern when staking out policy positions.”
Indeed, OpenAI and Anthropic are highly dependent on Nvidia for its chips, so open criticism of the company is not common. Yet those big two US AI labs have been at odds with Nvidia in urging the Trump administration to do more to crack down on Chinese access to advanced chips, and to more heavily scrutinize Chinese “open source” AI models.
But to Huang and others in his camp, the growth of Chinese AI is a feature, not a bug. Sacks, for instance, has repeatedly argued that “open weight” or “open source” models — which make their parameters publicly available, in contrast to the proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic — would help avert “an unsafe and dystopian future where advanced AI capabilities are centralized and controlled by only a few hands.” The leading open weight models are currently from Chinese companies.
Huang has also used a more straightforward argument: that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States of America.
“American technology has to win across the world at every single layer,” he said in May. “If we can export chips, we should.”
Now it will be left to Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, to carry that message, instead of a rock-star founder with a global cult following that’s drawn comparisons to Steve Jobs at his peak at Apple. Her first task: taking stock of all the powerful actors across the political, advocacy, and business world rooting for her to fail. Perhaps DeepSeek could help make a list?

Johnny Depp’s return in Paramount’s “Ebenezer” won the global box office this weekend, edging out Indian powerhouse “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” to claim the worldwide crown, while Toho’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” crossed the $100 million milestone.
	Directed by Ti West, “Ebenezer” debuted at No. 1 globally with a worldwide weekend estimate of $42 million. The dark reimagining of Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” opened at the top of the North American chart with $19 million across 3,535 locations, while international audiences delivered a stronger $23 million debut across 63 markets.
Audiences largely embraced Depp’s turn as Ebenezer Scrooge alongside an ensemble cast featuring Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Tramell Tillman and Ian McKellen. Exit polling yielded an “A-” CinemaScore, a 90% Verified Hot Popcornmeter rating on Rotten Tomatoes and 4.5 out of 5 stars on PostTrak (including 85% total positive and 66% definite recommend scores), with 51% of surveyed moviegoers citing Depp as their primary attendance driver.
Overseas, “Ebenezer” topped the charts in several key territories, led by a No. 1 opening in the U.K. with $5.4 million from 633 locations. Other chart-topping debuts included Italy ($2 million from 365 sites), Mexico ($1.7 million from 855 sites), Spain ($1 million from 323 sites), Poland ($900,000 from 208 sites, including paid previews), Belgium ($372,000 from 74 sites, including previews) and Panama/Central America ($340,000 from 125 sites, including previews). Strong runner-up bows came from France ($2.5 million from 505 sites, including previews), Germany ($1.5 million from 512 sites), Brazil ($475,000 from 589 sites), the Netherlands ($416,000 from 103 sites) and Colombia ($262,000 from 204 sites). Elsewhere, Australia opened at No. 3 with $650,000, the U.A.E. placed fourth with $222,000 (part of a $600,000 Middle East regional bow), and Japan opened at No. 6 – ranking as the top MPA release – with $450,000.
Paramount backed the launch with an extensive global marketing push anchored by Depp’s surprise in-character appearance at San Diego Comic-Con (which generated over 152 million social impressions) and a trailer launch that drew more than 225 million views in seven days. International activations ranged from a winter-themed Leicester Square world premiere and London ghost tours to a Day of the Dead marigold installation in Mexico City, an end-credits song by Mylène Farmer in France, and sports integrations across the Premier League, LaLiga, Bundesliga, NFL and NBA.
Hot on “Ebenezer’s” heels, Namit Malhotra’s “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” retained the No. 1 international crown and took second place globally, surging to a $147.5 million worldwide cumulative gross after just 11 days in release – already making it the seventh highest-grossing Indian film of all time. Fueled by stellar word-of-mouth and brisk midweek business, the Nitesh Tiwari-directed epic enjoyed a phenomenal second-weekend hold, dropping just 34% for a $38.1 million global frame, including $32.6 million from international markets.
Presented by Sony Pictures and Prime Focus Studios in association with Monster Mind Creations and DNEG, starring Ranbir Kapoor, Yash and Sai Pallavi, with a score by Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman, “Ramayana” expanded into six new markets this weekend to reach 43 territories overall. Record-breaking openings for an Indian release were notched in Indonesia ($573,000), Cambodia ($286,000) and Mexico. India remained the undisputed powerhouse with a cumulative tally of $97.2 million, buoyed by the highest second weekend in local history at INR223 crore ($23.6 million). Top-performing overseas cumes to date include the U.K. ($5.5 million), the U.A.E. ($4.7 million), Australia ($4.2 million), Thailand ($1.5 million), Malaysia ($1.4 million) and Germany ($1.1 million). The rollout continues on Nov. 19 in Brazil, Italy, Ukraine and Hungary, followed by Poland on Nov. 20 and major Latin American territories plus Czechia on Nov. 26.
Meanwhile, Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” continued its box office rampage, taking fourth place worldwide with a $15.6 million frame and pushing its global cumulative total past the $100 million mark to $104.8 million. Warner Bros.’ “The Cat in the Hat” claimed third place globally with $17 million (bringing its worldwide cume to $55.8 million), while Sony’s “How to Rob a Bank” rounded out the global top five with $10.2 million.
In the large-format sector, local-language titles and alternative content powered Imax to a $13.7 million global weekend. “Godzilla Minus Zero” added $4.8 million across Imax screens in its sophomore frame – comprising $1.6 million in North America and $3.2 million internationally, including $1.4 million in Japan (where its local Imax total hit $6.7 million) – lifting its global Imax cume to $32 million. “Ramayana” contributed another $3 million in its second Imax weekend, with $2.6 million coming from international venues and $1.2 million from India alone (reaching $4.6 million locally), bringing its worldwide Imax tally to $12.4 million.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

Quick Answer
Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 ad mocks Apple’s iPhone Duo at a difficult time. Reports of cracked displays, long delivery delays, and missing features have raised concerns about Apple’s first foldable. With its reputation for hardware excellence at stake, Apple needs more than silence to restore confidence.
Believe it or not, Samsung might finally have landed an ad glove on Apple. While the two brands have been taking digs at each other for years, Apple has kept things subtle, while Samsung has never been shy about being more direct. So when Apple finally decided to join the foldable race with the iPhone Duo, it was hardly surprising to see Samsung going all out against its rival – from Apple’s late arrival to the foldable party, the Duo name, the features, the price, you name it, and Samsung probably has tried to make fun of it. But as in the past, these attempts seemed just that… attempts to ruffle a leading brand on a perceived weakness, and to reassure their own fanbase. But very recently, we think Samsung struck a bit of a serious nerve in the Apple nervous system.
The Samsung Z Fold 8 slices up an apple (no, really!)
Samsung released a 32-second video on Instagram that shows an apple (duh) with a “new” sticker on the open screen of the Galaxy Z Fold8. The phone folds, and the apple gets sliced. This slice rolls down the floor, through all the old versions of the Z Fold in the past to show how many foldables Samsung launched before Apple made its first.
The video also boasts about the Z Fold 8 being thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, all while comparing it to a slice of apple. This is not the most clever or cinematic Apple attack we have ever seen, but it is entertaining and thankfully is not over the top (unlike some others). What it also is, is a direct jab at something that Apple rarely has had to face – a perceived hardware problem with the iPhone.
iPhone Duo: from potential elixir to possible albatross
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, we thought it would be just the thing the foldables needed. Foldables have been a regular part of tech news and product portfolios since pre-COVID times (the first Galaxy Z Fold came in 2019), but even after years of iterations and multiple devices from multiple brands, the foldable segment was actually running out of steam.
So, when Apple launched the iPhone Duo, we thought that foldables would finally get some serious momentum. After all, once Apple launches something (even if it has been in the market for some time), it usually becomes more desirable and eminently “inspirational” for the competition: we have seen new features, specs, and design get picked up by the competition from Apple products, and become mainstream. From accepting touch to rejecting 3.5 mm audio jacks, it has all happened. So you could hardly blame many for thinking that Apple would launch a foldable phone, and voila! All foldable phones would start selling like hotcakes.
That scenario, however, does not seem to be playing out.
When Apple launched the iPhone Duo, the tech world went abuzz, which is business as usual when a new iPhone launches. But when the iPhone Duo became available for purchase, all the news that came in was not good. In many markets, due to supply and production issues, consumers had to wait for two months or more to get a device even after paying an advance. The brand’s decision to limit sales to two devices per person was also not well-received in some markets. It would have been understandable in the case of a new brand launching its first product, but from the first trillion-dollar company in the world, it just seemed unusually odd. The fact that it came with a super premium price tag did not help matters.
All those who have got their hands on Apple’s first foldable phone have not been thoroughly impressed with it either. There has been talk of users missing the speed and convenience of Face ID, the lack of app optimization, the new placement of the status bar, and more. And as if that were not enough, there was news that landed Apple in perhaps the hottest soup it has been in a very long time – reports have started coming in of the internal display cracking at the hinge, and a line of dead pixels appearing on it.
Often coming late to the party and rocking it…but perhaps not this time!
Once again, such problems from a new brand’s first product might have been treated with more patience. But imagine spending Rs. 2,99,900 and getting a device whose display has hardware issues. Imagine also being a person who has booked the device and is waiting for their unit, which is two months away. While Apple has acknowledged the issue, insisted that the issues exist in a small number of devices, and has assured users that all devices facing the issue will be replaced, a lot of damage has been done.
Apple’s reputation has, in some ways, worked against it. With Apple, the tech world has become accustomed to waiting for features, functions, and form factors that were seen on other devices. Android users have mocked Apple fans for getting the features that were on Android after years. But while Apple has delayed the addition of a feature or an entry into a segment, it has generally delivered an excellent performance. And that has been the defense of many Apple fans – Apple might not be the first to make a certain kind of device or bring a certain feature, but its implementation (whether it was capacitive touchscreens, Touch ID, App Store, and more) has been excellent and often an industry benchmark.
With Duo, that belief is being rocked. The brand has stepped into the foldable zone almost seven years after others, and launched a device with what seems to be a hardware flaw– not a software bug that can be fixed with an update, but a problem that can only be fixed with replacement.
Is silence golden for the communication wizard?
Apple’s handling of the issue so far has been a little unusual. The brand has found itself in trouble in the past as well with issues such as Antennagate and Bendgate, both of which generated a storm of criticism. But Apple officially addressed those issues publicly – Steve Jobs himself came out with an explanation in the case of the iPhone 4 when its stainless steel band interfered with the phone’s cellular performance, and the company also issued a very detailed statement on BendGate, famously pointing out that the issue had occurred with only nine users.
While there has not been radio silence from Apple with regard to Duo’s screen, no major management figure has come out to explain the issue or build back confidence – even in his first earnings call, new Apple CEO John Ternus limited himself to saying that while the issue existed, it affected a very small percentage of units. This relative silence could be (mis)interpreted by many in the public. To many, it does not seem as if the brand is working out solutions, as it has actually been launching devices left, right, and center since the Duo was launched.
To see management showcasing new products and talking of record earnings, even while complaints trickle in about a high-profile flagship does not make for great optics. We hope that changes soon, or alternatively, Apple comes out with a strong defense of its first foldable – it needs it. The longer it keeps silent, the more space it gives to its competitors to score points off its perceived weakness. And Apple cannot really afford to let cracks develop not just on the Duo, but in its own reputation for hardware excellence. As Samsung has shown, its competitors will not hang back in taking potshots at it. And unless credibly explained, these shots will start to hurt.
Given its potential and the hype around it, the Duo could still prove to be the elixir the foldable sector needs, but Apple needs to address the issues around it swiftly and effectively. This is a challenge unlike any other the brand has faced in recent times. Even the relative failure of the Vision Pro was more about a product being too futuristic (almost a prototype of sorts for an elite audience). The Duo, however, is supposed to redefine how we use foldables in particular and even smartphones in general. Many have even called it Apple’s most radical iPhone since the OG iPhone. How John Ternus tackles the issues surrounding the Duo could well define the tone of his tenure.

Go Public
WestJet denied family's cancelled flight was actually cancelled, claiming passenger rights didn't apply
Airline reversed course after Go Public got involved
Dustin and Shania Klause's family vacation to Hawaii was thrown into jeopardy after WestJet scrapped their return flight a few months before departure and refused to rebook them on another flight for the same day.
The airline justified its refusal by claiming the flight hadn't been cancelled but, rather, rescheduled — even though it was completely removed from the family's itinerary.
"It's purely a flight cancellation," said a frustrated Dustin, who lives with Shania in Stony Plain, Alta., near Edmonton. "I feel like we were just kind of left in the dust."
The couple had planned the November trip to Kona, Hawaii, with six family members to spend time together following the death of Shania's mother from ovarian cancer.
"It's just really important to our family to do this together," said Shania. "We had finally had it all worked out."
The family, five adults and three children, planned the November trip to Kona, Hawaii, to spend time together following the death of Shania's mother. From left to right: Shania's sister-in-law and brother, Tenise and Chad Verbeek; Shania's late mom, Robin Verbeek; Shania's dad, Dale Verbeek; Shania and Dustin Klause. (Submitted by Dustin Klause)
However, in August, WestJet sent an updated itinerary omitting the Kona-to-Vancouver segment of their Nov. 24 return flight to Edmonton — leaving the family without a way home. When Dustin called to complain, the airline offered a replacement return flight departing two days later, which conflicted with several family members' work schedules.
So Dustin, who had researched his rights, insisted WestJet rebook them on another airline for their original travel date — a requirement under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations (APPR) for cancellations within an airline's control.
WestJet refused. Multiple customer service agents told Dustin — in calls he recorded — that the regulations didn't apply because the flight disruption was a schedule change.
"If it was a cancellation then, yes, we would be obligated to put you on any carrier we could get you on, but in this case, this is a schedule change," said an agent.
- Got a story you want investigated? Contact Sophia and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca
After Dustin argued repeatedly that his flight had, in fact, been cancelled, the agent replied, "It is considered a schedule-change cancellation. There's a difference."
Not so, according to the Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA). Its online guidance states that passenger protection rules apply regardless of how an airline labels a flight disruption.
"A schedule change is effectively a cancellation," said Zohair Khan, co-founder of Airfairness, which, for a fee, helps passengers claim flight disruption compensation.
"The flight that you were booked on is gone, and now you're on a different flight."
WestJet reverses course
Airlines have repeatedly flouted Canada's rebooking rules for flight cancellations, resulting in forfeited trips or passengers paying out-of-pocket to salvage their vacations.
WestJet suggested as an option that Dustin accept a refund for the return flight. However, because airfares had increased, Go Public confirmed it would cost the family thousands extra to buy tickets for the same date on another airline.
"We should not have to pay any more money," said Dustin. "At this point, our hands are so tied that we probably have to cancel."
After hearing from Go Public, WestJet reversed course and rebooked the family on their original departure date with partner airline Delta.
"They should have done that from the beginning," said Shania.
WestJet didn't comment directly on Dustin's case except to say that it would offer the family an apology.
The airline also didn't explain why its email notifying the family of the scrapped return flight included refund options under U.S. regulations, but omitted rebooking rights under Canadian regulations.
"Those APPR regulations should be front and centre," said Khan.
$755,000 in fines for rebooking violations
Under the APPR for flight cancellations, major airlines must offer passengers a choice between a refund or rebooking on the next available flight operated by them or a partner airline. But if the replacement fight delays travel by more than nine hours — or 48 hours for cancellations outside the airline's control — the carrier must rebook the passenger on any available airline.
Since 2025, the CTA has fined major airlines WestJet, Air Canada, Air Transat, and JetBlue Airways a combined $755,000 for 199 violations of rebooking rules.
Air Canada is challenging its $426,000 penalty for 71 violations last year, arguing the airline was affected by a labour dispute.
Zohair Khan, co-founder of Airfairness, says a schedule change is the same as a flight cancellation. (Prasanjeet Choudhury/CBC)
Khan suggests airlines often violate the requirement to rebook on other airlines to cut costs.
"That is the cheapest option, for you to stay on one of their flights," he said. "Unfortunately, most people will accept that."
Under the APPR, passengers are also entitled to up to $1,000 in compensation if an airline cancels a flight for reasons within its control 14 days or less before departure. According to the CTA, airlines have frequently violated this rule as well.
Bigger fines?
To improve compliance with Canada's rebooking rules, Khan supports the federal government's proposal to increase maximum penalties for repeat APPR violations from $25,000 to $1 million.
"I hope no airline has to pay it, but the fact that it exists itself should be a deterrent," said Khan.
However, it's still up in the air whether the new fine limit will be approved, let alone when it would take effect.
Shania and Dustin Klause, far right, are currently enjoying their vacation in Hawaii with family. (Submitted by Dustin Klause)
Meanwhile, Dustin and his family are in Hawaii, relieved that WestJet finally secured them a flight home on their original departure date.
"I'm happy that they actually followed their passenger protection regulations," he said.

Anand Mahindra had one word for a wall-mounted gym built by four IIT Delhi graduates. “Bravo!” the industrialist wrote on social media. He praised how Aroleap X combines mechanics and principles from physical therapy. Mahindra saw potential for the product beyond India. He pointed to small flats and business hotel rooms as places where it could fit. “...a clever convergence of mechanics & physical therapy principles to design a product that has global potential. In small apartments & even in Business Hotel rooms!” he wrote. This is the story of Aroleap X. The idea started with a problem the founders faced themselves. They wanted to maintain their strength training without long trips to the gym. Bulky racks, dumbbells and iron plates would take up space in a small flat. Founders Anurag Dani and Rohit Patel shared an interest in fitness and mechanics. They and their co-founders turned to robotics to rethink how gym equipment provides resistance. The team worked from their hometowns during the COVID-19 pandemic. They put roughly ₹25 lakh of their own savings into research and development. They incorporated Aroleap Fitness Private Limited in 2020. The founders built nearly 15 physical prototypes and refined their manufacturing setup in Bengaluru. They then launched Aroleap X commercially. The device uses a motor to generate resistance without a stack of weights. Users can select loads from 2 kg to 75 kg in half-kilo steps. The motor responds in under 10 milliseconds. The unit stands five feet tall and is two feet wide. It folds to a depth of six inches against a wall. When stored, the machine leaves the floor free for other uses at home. Users need about 24 square feet of clear space while training. A companion app connects through Bluetooth and runs on Android and iOS. The app uses a phone or tablet as the screen during a workout. Coach Aro tracks repetitions and can automatically select the resistance. A digital spotter reduces the load if someone struggles to finish a lift. Another mode lets users set a heavier load for the lowering phase of an exercise. Burnout mode can adjust the resistance between repetitions as the user gets tired. The machine has adjustable arms and cables that extend to 1.5 metres. The arms can lock at four angles to change the direction of pull. It comes with a straight bar, handles, a rope attachment and ankle straps. The unit runs on standard Indian household power. The startup raised seed funding from angel investors and venture backers. It later secured deals after pitching on Shark Tank India Season 3. Its equipment has reached homes, physiotherapy clinics and corporate spaces. The Karnataka government has recently issued a joint circular, with multiple concerned departments on board, on measures to ensure the well-being of students across all schools, colleges, hostels, residential schools, and training institutions in the State.
These measures include conducting mandatory check-ups for all girls in schools by a gynaecologist, the provision of sex education, and the creation of awareness among children regarding child rights, issues concerning teenage pregnancies, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, child marriage, and the Child Helpline (1098). Furthermore, the installation of CCTV cameras has been made mandatory in all schools and colleges.
A warning has also been issued stating that failure to prevent — or negligence in addressing — cases of child marriage, teenage pregnancy, and incidents falling under the POCSO Act, 2012, will result in both legal action and disciplinary proceedings against the officials concerned.
The circular is a culmination of a series of measures initiated in June 2025 over concerns about rising cases of child marriage and teenage pregnancy in the State.
Child Protection Committee
Among the measures prescribed is the formation of Child Protection Committees in educational institutions across the State. The committee, comprising parents, children, and teachers, must meet once every three months, and the proceedings of these meetings should be duly recorded, the circular noted.
Schools and residential schools must install complaint boxes and take measures to address the grievances of girl students. It has been mandated that experienced and qualified counsellors be appointed in schools and Pre-University (PU) colleges to address the mental health and other challenges faced by adolescent students. Teachers must persuade parents to re-enrol girls who have dropped out of school and ensure that they continue their education until the age of 18. They must also take measures to prevent school-going children from being subjected to child labour.
Children should be provided with appropriate education to help them understand and identify issues such as crimes against children, child labour, child trafficking, sexual abuse, and child marriage through both formal and informal educational curricula. They should also be taught to recognise any form of abuse, violence, discrimination, or exploitation directed against them, whether within educational institutions or elsewhere, the circular said.
“If a girl student in a school or residential school remains absent for more than three days without providing any notification, the principal must inform the gram panchayat and the child helpline (1098) in writing. The Health Department has stated that appropriate legal action must be taken against shops selling abortion pills without a doctor’s prescription, as well as against doctors and members of the public involved in unauthorised abortion activities,” the circular said.
Substance abuse
Additionally, the guidelines emphasise the need to raise awareness among children about the dangers of substance abuse and drug addiction, alongside conducting regular screenings for such issues. They stipulate that such awareness should also be integrated into the school curriculum.

More than half of households that left ComCare assistance in 2022 returned within 3 years: MSF
Households with stable employment were less likely to return to ComCare assistance, while caregiving responsibilities and health issues remained barriers to financial independence.
SINGAPORE: More than half of households that stopped receiving short-to-medium-term assistance (SMTA) under ComCare in 2022 returned to the scheme within three years, a report released by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) on Monday (Nov 16) showed.
The return rate rose to 54 per cent for the 2022 cohort, up from 49 per cent the previous year, according to the supporting lower-income households trends report.
ComCare's SMTA scheme supports households with temporary financial assistance to meet a family’s basic living expenses.
The increase likely reflects a shift back towards pre-COVID-19 patterns, MSF said. During the pandemic, the ministry had “exercised flexibility to support more households that experienced temporary shocks to their financial circumstances”.
Some households that stopped receiving assistance in 2021 may therefore have needed support only during the pandemic, making them less likely to return.
Despite the increase, the proportion of households returning within three years remained below the 63 per cent recorded among those that left the scheme in 2019, before the pandemic.
The increase was also seen over shorter periods.
Half of the households that stopped receiving assistance in 2022 returned within two years, compared with 46 per cent of the 2021 cohort. The proportion returning within a year also rose, from 38 per cent to 43 per cent.
The report found that most households that returned to ComCare within three years did so in the first year after leaving the scheme. This suggests that households are most vulnerable to changes in their financial circumstances during this period, MSF said.
Responding to queries from CNA, MSF said achieving sustained financial stability can take time, particularly for households facing multiple and sometimes overlapping challenges. 
“A household returning to SMTA could have been ready to exit assistance earlier but had a change in circumstances later, for example due to changes in employment, health or caregiving responsibilities,” it said. 
“ComCare therefore remains available as a social safety net when families need support.”
STABLE EMPLOYMENT LINKED TO LOWER RETURN RATES
The report also found that households with stronger employment outcomes after exiting SMTA were more likely to stay off ComCare assistance.
Among households that stopped receiving the assistance in 2022, 46 per cent of those that did not return within three years had at least one member in stable employment in 2023.
The figure was lower, at 35 per cent, among households that returned to the scheme.
Stable employment is defined as working for at least six consecutive months in a year.
Households that did not return also had a higher median number of months worked over the three years after leaving the scheme – 17 months, compared with 11 months among those who returned.
“Employment support can help household members build skills, confidence, and job readiness,” said MSF.
“Social service offices therefore work with other government agencies, family service centres and community partners to coordinate support and help households stabilise their circumstances as they work towards greater self-reliance.”
However, caregiving responsibilities and health issues remained barriers to securing and sustaining employment.
Among households that returned to SMTA within three years, 23 per cent had at least one child beneficiary aged six or younger when they left the scheme, compared with 16 per cent of those that did not return.
Households that returned to assistance were also more likely to have primary applicants who were medically unfit for work at the time of assessment – 18 per cent, compared with 13 per cent among those that stayed off assistance.
“These findings point to the importance of addressing practical barriers, such as caregiving and health-related needs, alongside employment support,” MSF said.
FEWER HOUSEHOLDS ON COMCARE, BUT PAYOUTS RISE
While return rates increased, the overall number of households receiving ComCare assistance continued to fall.
The number of households receiving SMTA declined to 19,473 last year, from 20,825 in 2024, according to the report.
But the total amount disbursed rose to S$95.8 million (US$75 million) in 2025, from S$94 million in 2024.
A similar trend was seen under ComCare’s long-term assistance, which supports people who are permanently unable to work due to old age, illness or disability and have little or no family support. 
The number of households receiving this form of assistance fell to 2,997 last year, from 3,240 in 2024. The amount disbursed increased to S$22.4 million, from S$21.4 million. 
MSF attributed the higher disbursements to enhancements to assistance rates in 2025 to help households better meet their basic living needs.
MORE COMLINK+ FAMILIES MAKE PROGRESS
Separately, the report found improvements in employment and preschool education outcomes among lower-income families supported by ComLink+. 
The initiative provides support to lower-income families through family coaches, social service agencies and community partners, with the aim of helping them achieve stability, self-reliance and social mobility.
As at December 2025, 11,006 families had agreed to join ComLink+, up from 10,219 a year earlier.
The report tracks the progress of ComLink+ families across six domains: income security, children’s development and education, housing, family functioning, financial resilience and health.
The proportion of ComLink+ families that had achieved stability increased to 49 per cent in 2025 from 44 per cent in 2024, said the report. This meant they met all the relevant stability indicators, including having stable employment, access to housing and children enrolled in school.
ACHIEVING SELF-RELIANCE
For Ms Syafawani Yazid, balancing work and caregiving responsibilities has been a challenge as she raises her two-year-old daughter in a one-room rental flat.
With support from ComLink+, the 28-year-old is working to clear her S$15,000 debt by March 2027, using an Excel spreadsheet to track her expenses and identify areas where she can cut back.
In September, the single mother moved to a more flexible job as a food and beverage service crew member, allowing her to take her daughter to and from preschool regularly. She believes this has helped her daughter become more confident and develop her social skills.
Ms Syafawani also hopes to own a home where her daughter can have a bedroom of her own.
"I just want her to have her own space growing up because that's what I had when I grew up," she said.
Ms Syafawani’s family coach, Mr Zulhakim Mustar, has seen her grow more confident and independent since they began working together last year.
"One thing I like about her is that she continues to stay positive despite her situation," Mr Mustar, who is the manager for ComLink Regional Services at the Social Service Office in Jalan Besar, said.
He encouraged families facing similar challenges to seek guidance from family coaches, who can help them identify suitable support.
“Having a family coach doesn't mean we will solve the problem, but I think it's more about guiding you to address the challenges that you have,” he said. 
FINANCIAL RESILIENCE REMAINS A CONCERN
Income security was one of the domains that saw an improvement. 
The proportion of ComLink+ families achieving social mobility in this domain rose from 28 per cent in 2024 to 36 per cent in 2025, said the report. This meant that they had stable employment, were no longer receiving major forms of financial assistance and had real income growth over time.
But part of the improvement in employment outcomes was due to the inclusion of platform work income in CPF records from 2025, which allowed more families to meet the income criteria.
The report also found that the median real household income of ComLink+ families also increased by 31 per cent in 2025 compared with 2024.
“This reflects their efforts to strengthen their financial circumstances and build a better future for themselves and their children,” the ministry said.
Yet some households continued to face difficulties securing and sustaining stable employment.
Among families that joined ComLink+ in 2023, 21 per cent had no member in stable employment with regular income from 2023 to 2025.
“These families were more likely to face multiple and interrelated barriers, such as poor health, caregiving responsibilities, family functioning concerns, lower educational qualifications, or difficulties finding jobs that matched their circumstances and skills,” said MSF.
Financial resilience also remained a concern.
An MSF longitudinal survey launched in 2022 found that only one in six ComLink+ families had sufficient savings to cover at least three months of household expenses.
“Some families face challenges such as irregular income, caregiving responsibilities, health issues and debts that make it harder to build savings consistently,” said the ministry.  
“Families whose expenses outstrip their income may also face difficulties in accumulating savings. These families are also more likely to have fewer working members or include members with medical conditions.”
MORE FAMILIES MEET PRESCHOOL MILESTONES
In the children's development and education domain, the MSF report found improvements in preschool education outcomes among ComLink+ families.
The proportion of families with preschool-aged children achieving self-reliance in this domain increased to 31 per cent last year, from 28 per cent in 2024. This meant all preschool-aged Singaporean children in these families were enrolled in preschool, had completed mandatory vaccinations and were attending preschool regularly.
MSF told CNA that barriers to regular preschool attendance can include children's health issues, parents juggling work and caregiving responsibilities, and difficulties establishing consistent routines, such as managing separation anxiety.
“Some families may also prefer alternative caregiving arrangements or have other immediate priorities, such as employment, caregiving for other family members, or changes in family circumstances,” the ministry said. 
It added that family coaches and case workers from family service centres work with families to understand these barriers and provide practical support.
The report also showed that the share of families whose enrolled preschool children attended regularly rose from 38 per cent to 44 per cent.
But the proportion of families whose preschool-aged children were enrolled in preschool fell slightly from 89 per cent to 87 per cent.
Senior Parliamentary Secretary for Social and Family Development and Law Eric Chua said that progress takes time and it looks different for every family.
“We’ll continue to help families build more stable lives and hopefully become more self-reliant over time,” he said. 
“When life is a little bit more settled, parents have more room to plan ahead and give their children more choices as they grow up.”
Separately, among ComLink+ families with school-going children, 72 per cent achieved self-reliance in education in 2025, compared with 71 per cent a year earlier.
OUTCOMES IN OTHER DOMAINS
Outcomes in the other four domains remained largely stable.
In the housing domain, the proportion of families living in public rental housing who moved into purchased homes remained at 2 per cent. 
MSF said moving from renting to owning a home is a significant milestone for ComLink+ families. 
“Home ownership is a major and long-term financial commitment, and families have different starting points and circumstances. Meaningful and sustained progress takes time,” it added. 
For the health domain, 88 per cent of families achieved stability, similar to 2024. 
This meant that no family members had been hospitalised or visited an emergency department in the previous 12 months, and children had completed their mandatory vaccinations by age three.
Meanwhile, 88 per cent of families achieved stability in the family functioning domain, down slightly from 89 per cent in 2024.
The remaining 12 per cent had cases involving domestic violence, child protection or other protection concerns, according to the report.

Rest assured this week that while Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft services were flatlining, the company’s billing operations were still firing on all cylinders. Copilot can’t run on air alone, after all. It needs cash.
The silver lining to the week is that, in the light of our global recovery from one of the most debilitating tech outages in recent memory, Microsoft now owes you compensation. And depending on the size of your operation and the degree to which you rely on Microsoft products, the payout could be substantial.
If you have a business relationship with Microsoft—a subscription to a Microsoft 365 Business plan, email hosted on Microsoft Exchange, or perhaps a Teams Premium tier—that relationship is governed by reams of documentation, among them being a Service Level Agreement.
Service Level Agreements, or SLAs, are old hat to large enterprises who use them to hold accountable service providers like web hosts and email services, ensuring they stay online and operational—and they are often in the realm of demanding 99.99 percent reliability or higher, as is the default promise with Microsoft Azure. If a provider fails to hit the promised availability level, the customer is due a refund (or credit towards next month’s bill, at least).
But SLAs don’t only apply to the Fortune 500. If you have a business account with Microsoft, no matter how small it is, your service is also governed by these promises. And now, Microsoft owes you compensation.
“Business account” is the key phrase in the above, mind you. If you have a Microsoft 365 Family plan or any other individual or personal plan, you are basically out of luck. Outlook could go offline for a month, and you wouldn’t be entitled to anything aside from a series of pointed Facebook posts.
The consumer Microsoft Services Agreement states that individual users can get refunds or credits at Microsoft’s “sole discretion,” but it doesn’t even mention SLAs and promises nothing in the way of uptime. In other words, if your email system wasn’t working for you on November 12, you can ask for money back, but your odds of receiving anything are low.
The Fine Print Is in Your Favor for Once
Business users are in a much more advantageous position, though Microsoft doesn’t exactly go out of its way to guide you through the refund process. SLA refunds are not automatic. You have to request them for each incident, and the process is hardly straightforward.
To figure out what you’re owed, start by taking a look at the SLA for Microsoft’s Online Services. (This is different than the above consumer Microsoft Services Agreement.) It’s more than 53,000 words long, and quite repetitive, but I’ll digest the important facts for you here.
While many of the promised service levels are identical, start by double-checking the specific Microsoft products you use, as the SLA is broken down by product. A search for “Exchange Online” reveals everything you need to know, in surprisingly plain English.
Downtime is defined as “Any period of time when users are unable to send or receive email with Outlook Web Access.”
Uptime Percentage is calculated by a simple formula: Subtract the minutes of downtime from your total User Minutes, then divide the result by your total User Minutes. Take that result and multiply it by 100.
“Downtime is measured in user-minutes; that is, for each Applicable Period, Downtime is the sum of the length (in minutes) of each Incident that occurs during that Applicable Period multiplied by the number of users impacted by that Incident.”
User Minutes is the total number of minutes in the billing cycle; typically 30 days.
If the calculated Uptime Percentage falls below 99.9 percent, you are entitled to credit (not a cash refund) under the following terms:
| Uptime Percentage | Service Credit | 
|---|---|
| < 99.9% | 25% | 
| < 99.5% | 50% | 
| < 95% | 100% | 
If we assume the outage lasted about 18 hours for you, that equates to a 2.5 percent Downtime Percentage or a 97.5 percent Uptime Percentage for a 30-day billing cycle. And that puts you squarely in 50 percent Service Credit territory.
How to File for Compensation
While Microsoft is transparent about what you are owed, it has less to say about what you have to do to receive it.
The SLA simply states that “In order for Microsoft to consider a claim, you must submit the claim to customer support at Microsoft Corporation including all information necessary for Microsoft to validate the claim.” You are also directed to supply the following:
That’s a lot of information, but Microsoft likely does not need much in the way of (i) , (ii), or (v) to validate this global incident. You will need to supply the name or your “affected resource” and how many users were impacted. For the sake of completeness, include in your message the codes for outages for Exchange (EX1550543), Outlook (MO1550821), and Teams (TM1550488) as relevant to your business.
I also did the math on what my various Microsoft subscriptions cost. I only have two, Exchange Online and Microsoft 365 Business Standard, both of which were impacted by the outage. Total price of my last bill: $24.88. Thus, total credit due: $12.44. That may barely be beer money for me, but a company of 100 people will likely be owed over $1,000. If you don’t have these numbers handy, you’ll find them under Billing > Bills & Payments in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center.
With that information collected, then what? Microsoft simply directs you to file a claim with customer service, so that’s exactly what I did. In the same Admin Center, the method to file an email service request is a little tricky. It’s not in the left-hand navigation but rather can be found on the bottom right of the screen. Click the headset icon which expands to reveal “Help & support.” This will default you to Microsoft’s AI chatbot. Within this page, click the headset icon at the top of the screen, which will take you to a “Contact support” page. Choose Email from this screen, and fill in the form with the information you’ve collected.
Your submission should garner a quick response that includes a case number tracking ID. I filed for compensation on Friday and haven’t received any other response yet than a confirmation of receipt, but considering that 12 principal-filled dollars are on the line, you can bet I’ll be tracking it closely.
As a final note: Be aware that claims must be submitted by the end of the month following the outage. So you have until December 31, 2026 to file your claim for the November 12 incident.
I reached out to Microsoft for comment on this story and a PR rep said she would “let me know if the company has anything to share” while offering the same statement you have probably seen too many times already: “We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously.”
Now we’ll see how seriously it takes the refund process.

As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday’s global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It’s not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point.
It’s not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus—one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever.
Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn’t starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, “they will be squeezed to death,” he wrote.
Plenty of scholars objected at the time, dismissing von Foerster’s conclusion as “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd.” The global population did not keep accelerating at an exponential rate; the baby boom petered out just a few years after von Foerster published his paper.
“He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right,” mathematical biologist Joel Cohen of Rockefeller University and Columbia University recently told Popular Science. “The all-time peak happened in the early 1960s.” Nor did von Foerster foresee the impacts of longer life expectancy and the sharp decline in child mortality rates.

A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
A fire has burned through a building in southern Thailand and killed 11 people
BANGKOK -- A fire burned through a building in southern Thailand early Monday, killing 11 people, authorities said.
The fire started around 2 a.m. in the building in Phuket that has a motorcycle rental shop on the ground floor and residences on the upper floors, officials of the local government said. It took firefighters about an hour to bring the fire under control.
There were 17 other people who were slightly injured.
Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but initial investigations found an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started.
Phuket Gov. Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tires. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.
He said the victims appeared to try to escape the fire to the higher floors. One body was found on the third floor and 10 others were found on the fifth floor.
Phuket is on an island in southern Thailand and a popular tourist destination.

Edtech unicorn upGrad has launched upGrad Next, an enterprise advisory practice that will help companies restructure their organisations and prepare their employees for AI adoption. The new vertical will advise senior executives on organisational structure, hiring, employee compensation, and workforce development. upGrad’s existing enterprise business, which the company said worked with more than 700 organisations in FY26, will help put these recommendations into practice through employee reskilling, leadership development, and hiring. The new vertical will be led by four managing directors – former Deloitte partners Anandorup Ghose and Krishna Chaitanya Malladi, former EY partner Hrishikesh Godbole and former Deloitte executive Dinkar Pawan. They will advise companies on organisational restructuring and workforce transformation, with more senior leaders expected to join in the coming weeks. The launch comes as businesses adopt AI and look to restructure their operations and workforce. While companies have invested in digital transformation over the past decade, preparing employees for AI-led changes remains a challenge. In a LinkedIn post announcing the launch, upGrad cofounder and chairperson Ronnie Screwvala said the next decade would focus on reshaping workforces to help companies manage and realise returns from their digital transformation investments. Screwvala said companies would need advice on how to organise their teams, hire, pay, and train employees, along with help implementing these changes. He added that upGrad Next would move away from the traditional consulting model, where fees depend on the number of consultants deployed and their billing rates. “Not a myriad of consultants, not the traditional headcount-times-billing-rate model, but real, strong experience, sharpened with the power of AI and accountable for outcomes,” Screwvala said. upGrad’s Unacademy Buyout The launch comes two months after upGrad closed its acquisition of rival edtech platform Unacademy in September 2026 in a deal valued at just over $200 Mn. The transaction followed months of negotiations and regulatory clearances. Unacademy cofounder Gaurav Munjal announced the deal’s closure and acknowledged that the startup had sold for a fraction of its peak valuation of $3.5 Bn in 2021. Following the acquisition, Munjal announced his decision to step down as Unacademy's CEO and transition to the role of executive chairman. On the financial front, upGrad reported a 52% decline in net loss to ₹130 Cr in FY26 from ₹274 Cr in FY25, while gross revenue rose 7% to ₹2,070 Cr. The company attributed the improvement to AI-led efficiencies, which helped lower its marketing and technology costs even as revenue increased.

Jensen Huang’s midlife-crisis makeover hasn’t helped the Nvidia CEO’s image this week. In a matter of days, Huang’s questionable sartorial leanings have shifted wildly from wannabe cool Harley dad to low-down leather Lothario. Fashion moves fast, but even in the style world, this is a breakneck volte-face.
As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.
This is where WIRED comes to the rescue, aided by Vogue, GQ and a celebrity stylist, no less. We’ve charted the menacing glow-up of tech bros before, but merely observing the worrying trend back in 2025 is clearly no longer enough. It’s time to roll up our Armani sleeves and help.
“Tech bros were total nerds before," says Karen Clarkson, a professional stylist whose clients have included Nike, Google, Apple, Calvin Klein, and Vivienne Westwood. "Fashion didn’t touch their lives at all. They didn’t have style.” Pictures of Huang’s pre-biker fashion-vacuum days certainly bear this out. “Then, like [Jeff] Bezos, they all stepped up. And there’s a rivalry that’s come with that, whether it’s the fashion makeover, the grooming, the skin treatments, or gym regimen. Now we have Mark Zuckerberg in the front row at Prada.”
As a man clearly in dress distress, where better to start than with Murray Clark, head of editorial at British GQ. Controversially, Clark has a radical notion that Huang should keep clothing matters as they are. “I’d argue that Jensen Huang stays exactly how he is because this is who he is—a coiffed, leather-jacket wearing, mistake-making middle-aged man for all the world to see.”
Before publicly admitting on Sunday to having an affair with a businesswoman who US intelligence says is also a Chinese spy, in 2024, Huang confessed onstage that his wife, Lori, suggested and chose his biker outfits for him because he found most other fabrics “itchy.”
If Jensen keeps his jackets (he apparently owns 30 to 40), Clarkson thinks that Huang might even find himself on the catwalk. “If he wants to go down that route, then for sure Demna [Gucci’s creative director] would have him walking in his next show in Milan,” she says. “But he’s very Arnold Schwarzenegger and the Terminator with his black leathers, which is a bit close to the bone, really, with AI and that humanity is potentially doomed. I don’t know if he’s wise to lean into Arnie too heavily.”
Let’s get some sage advice, then, from Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial at British Vogue. “If I were styling Jensen Huang, I’d advise him to cleanse the palate entirely, ditch the rock and roll shrunken leather jackets for something more somber,” Nnadi says. “A collared Oxford shirt and a navy or gray crewneck jumper would do the trick and wouldn’t read as aggressively corporate as a traditional suit. The message needs to be ‘I’m a serious person, and I’m leaving that tragic try-hard boomer dad wardrobe behind along with my despicable behavior.’”
Clarkson agrees, saying that while the term “unapologetic” is often used in fashion, in this instance, Huang needs a more apologetic dress code, moving away from anything too flashy. So out go the overtly sexual Tom Ford leathers—which Jensen can handily sell off for $1 million a pop to his Huang-boys to offset any alimony outlays that may, or may not, be coming his way—and in come understated and neutral tones.
“He could take a leaf out of Harry Styles’ dress down codes and check The Row for minimal looks,” Clarkson says. “A Lemaire workwear jacket is also a good vibe. It shows he’s willing to put in the work to win back his family. Also, since he’s spoken about feeling itchy, maybe he should repent a bit and wear lambswool instead of cashmere.”
Asking Clarkson to step away from her celebrity clients for a moment to perform a hasty hypothetical make under (or glow down?) for Huang, she has very kindly put together three outfits that I think we can all agree give off considerably fewer bad-egg biker vibes with pieces from Paul Smith, The Row, Lemaire, Giorgio Armani, Brunello Cucinelli, and more. If you’re lucky enough to have a budget to match Huang's, we’ve added links to the individual pieces in the captions under each “look.”
“There’s been a lot of tight-fitted leather jackets that just about cover his biceps, which always feels like he’s looking to lure his next lover or like he’s just whizzed off on his Ducati to have a quick lunchtime visit with his mistress,” says Clarkson. “That’s not the vibe you want to go before Congress with.” For the Hill, she suggests Huang go for a Nehru collar that “feels a bit more buttoned up.”
However, because Huang’s existing look is so strong, Clarkson advises that changing it too quickly will not only draw an enormous amount of commentary but even more memes. “Little steps, not a full overnight makeover. That’s why he should perhaps keep the leather jacket, something like a suede blouson instead of the biker,” she says, adding that the black jeans should be ditched in favor of proper pants.
“He could do a tie as well—a bit more apologetic, a bit more formal, a bit more respectful. So a brown leather jacket with a tie and a shirt—so then it’s a segue into a new direction,” Clarkson says, citing Giorgio Armani’s June Milan collection as ideal inspiration.
However, Clarkson says credit must ultimately go to Lori Huang, Jensen’s wife of 41 years. “She did a brilliant job. If anyone comes out of this as a winner, it’s her. She could rebrand as a Hollywood stylist at this point because she’s done a great job of creating an identity for her husband. Almost too good because it’s attracted too many women. Still, she could step away with a really great divorce settlement and a whole new career.”
