Uttarakhand MLA loses temper, vandalises stage after he was denied chance to speak at event; booked
The chief minister lashed out at the Congress, saying it has lost its ground which is causing its members to “lose their mental balance”.
Congress MLA Harish Dhami was on Sunday booked for allegedly vandalising a stage after he was "denied" an opportunity to speak in the presence of Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, even as a war of words erupted between the BJP and the Congress over the incident at a prominent fair.
The chief minister lashed out at the Congress, saying it has lost its ground which is causing its members to "lose their mental balance", while MLA Harish Dhami called the CM "darpok (coward)", accusing him of suppressing people's voice, and challenged the BJP leader to contest against him.
The Congress said it stands strongly with its MLA "in the fight for the respect of its public representatives and the rights of the people". Insult to the opposition representatives through the administration will not be tolerated at any cost, state Congress president Ganesh Godiyal said.
On Saturday, MLA Harish Dhami allegedly threw microphones and chairs on the stage after the chief minister left the venue and alleged that his mic was switched off as he was speaking.
An FIR under relevant sections of the BNS was lodged against the Dharchula MLA and five others for vandalising the inauguration stage of Jauljibi Fair on Saturday following a complaint by Harendra Singh Negi, an officer at the Jauljibi police station.
The FIR has been filed under BNS sections 121 (voluntarily causing hurt ), 132 (assault to deter public servant from discharge of duty), 191(2) (rioting), 324(2) (property damage), and 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace), according to Negi.
Reacting to the incident, Dhami said, "Congress has crossed all boundaries of anarchy in every sphere, so this episode is also an example of the fact that in the coming days, public is going to reject them completely.
"The Congress party has lost its ground, causing its members to lose their mental balance."
"A behaviour that we would not even expect from a child is being displayed by Congress leaders, which is unheard of in a democracy... the same approach is followed by their leaders in Delhi.... Public is watching everything...," the CM told reporters in Dehradun.
Hitting back, the Congress MLA said, "Till now people had heard that the CM is dhadak Dhami, but he is darpok Dhami."
In a social media post on Saturday, MLA Harish Dhami said that he wanted to raise two issues with the government: the death of an eight-year-old girl in the region two days before, and concerns regarding road connectivity in Kanar.
He added that it is "deeply unfortunate that an elected representative was denied the opportunity to present the grievances" of their own constituents on the stage at the Jauljibi Fair.
"Suppressing voices does not make questions disappear, and switching off a microphone cannot silence the voice of the people! Raising issues -- such as the Kanhar road, basic infrastructure in the region, and long-pending development projects -- before the Chief Minister is my duty, not a crime," said MLA Dhami.
He added that the BJP government must understand that in a democracy, "asking questions is not an act of opposition; it is the right of the people".
The Congress MLA said that he made mistakes on the stage and apologised to the residents of his constituency.
"I have neither learnt to be afraid nor to bow down. If I am wrong, then I will admit it… which is why I challenge the chief minister to contest elections from Dharchula in 2027, and, if my party allows, then I will contest from any constituency where the CM contests from," said the Congress MLA.
"While pressure from those in power may stifle voices temporarily, it cannot halt our struggle for issues that serve the public interest. We will neither be intimidated, nor bow down, nor remain silent. Our fight for the rights, dignity, and entitlements of the people of Dharchula will continue with full strength on every platform."
Answer the people's questions. Do not attempt to suppress their voice, he added.
On Sunday, BJP workers protested against Harish Dhami in Dharchula, burning his effigy and shouting slogans against him.
BJP state spokesperson Mathura Dutt Joshi launched a scathing attack on the Congress and said, "The true tactics, character, and face of the Congress have once again been exposed before the public."
"Even if the MLA harboured any grievances or complaints, there is no place for such indecent language and improper conduct in public life. The BJP firmly demands that the Congress party issue an immediate public apology for this disgraceful behaviour by its MLA."
Joshi alleged that such actions reflect the unruly and anarchic culture of the Congress, adding that the vigilant people of 'Devbhoomi' will never forgive "such inappropriate attitude and arrogance" from their elected representatives.
Meanwhile, state Congress president Godiyal justified the anger of party MLA Harish Dhami.
"The undemocratic attitude has been shown by Chief Minister Dhami ji. Not giving an opportunity to an elected local public representative to speak from the stage in a historic programme of his own assembly constituency and getting his mic switched off is a completely undemocratic and condemnable act," said Godiyal.
He said that violating the protocol is an insult to the MLA and is also an insult to the people there.
"Protocol has been openly ignored in the Jauljibi fair. Opposition MLAs and public representatives are not being given due respect by the government and administration, which is against healthy democratic traditions. Efforts to suppress the voice of the public are a threat to democracy," said Godiyal.
The state Congress president added that MLA Harish Dhami wanted to present the "burning problems of the area" and the demands of the local people before the chief minister.

TVK adopting anti-God image: Annamalai attacks Vijay govt on Karthigai Deepam
We The Leaders chief K Annamalai has accused the Vijay-led TVK government of taking an anti-God stance in the Karthigai Deepam dispute, drawing parallels with its predecessor, the DMK. The Vijay government's opposition to a fresh plea in the Supreme Court has drawn BJP's criticism too.
The Karthigai Deepam dispute at Tamil Nadu's Thiruparankundram hill has once again become the flashpoint in the state's political battle, with former BJP state president K Annamalai accusing the Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay-led TVK government of adopting an "anti-God image" similar to that of its predecessor, the DMK.
Speaking to journalists on November 16, Annamalai criticised the TVK government for continuing to oppose the lighting of the traditional lamp at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar atop the hill in Madurai. The founder of We The Leaders political movement said the practice was rooted in religious faith and heritage and accused the government of prolonging the dispute despite orders from the Madras High Court.
Annamalai's remarks came amid a fresh legal confrontation over the Karthigai Deepam issue. The Tamil Nadu government, in an affidavit filed before the Supreme Court on November 12, opposed a plea seeking Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) control over the temple and the hill, as well as demands for a permanent lamp at the Deepathoon and lighting the entire hill during the festival.
The Vijay-led government's position on the issue has drawn criticism also from the BJP, which argued that the state was refusing to implement judicial directions permitting the lamp to be lit at the stone pillar.
BJP chief spokesperson Narayan Tirupati accused the TVK administration of following the DMK's approach to the controversy. The matter is scheduled to come up before the Supreme Court on Tuesday (November 17).
The Karthigai Deepam festival in 2026 is on November 24.
ANNAMALAI'S APPEAL TO TVK VIJAY-LED GOVERNMENT
Annamalai accused the TVK government of continuing what he called the DMK's attempt to project an anti-God image.
"Lighting the Karthigai lamp on the lamp pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill is a long-standing religious tradition. Halting this practice, which is tied to people's religious faith and heritage, for political reasons is unacceptable in every way," he said.
The IPS officer-turned-politician argued that the government should implement the Madras High Court's directions rather than prolong the matter through appeals and administrative delays.
Questioning the need for restrictions, Annamalai said devotees visit the hill once a year to light the lamp peacefully and asked what problem the practice could cause.
He also appealed to CM Vijay's government to respect the High Court's order and resolve the dispute through the legal process, warning that government actions should not create unnecessary controversy at a place where people of different faiths have traditionally lived together.
WHAT IS THE KARTHIGAI DEEPAM CONTROVERSY?
The dispute centres on where the Karthigai Deepam, a sacred lamp lit during the Tamil festival of lights, should be placed at Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai.
The Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple, regarded as one of the six sacred abodes of Lord Murugan, has traditionally lit the festival lamp at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple.
However, Hindu groups have sought permission to light it at the Deepathoon, an ancient stone pillar on a higher portion of the hill, approximately 50 metres from the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah.
The issue also has a long legal history. In 1996, the Madras High Court upheld the position that the temple administration traditionally lit the lamp at the Deepa Mandapam and that any change would require the necessary approval.
The dispute resurfaced in 2025 when devotees approached the court seeking permission to light the lamp at the Deepathoon.
On December 1, 2025, Justice GR Swaminathan directed the temple administration to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon in addition to the usual locations. The order also stated that the practice would not interfere with the rights of the Dargah.
The state authorities, then led by the DMK under MK Stalin's leadership, challenged the direction. However, on January 6, 2026, a Division Bench of the Madras High Court, comprising Justices G Jaylachandran and KK Ramakrishnan, upheld the order. It directed the temple administration to light the lamp at Deepathoon, subject to ASI preservation restrictions and security arrangements.
WHAT IS VIJAY GOVERNMENT'S POSITION ON KARTHIGAI DEEPAM?
The Vijay government has defended its position on the issue by arguing that the traditional location for lighting the Karthigai Deepam has been the Deepa Mandapam for more than 150 years.
In its counter-affidavit filed before the Supreme Court on November 12, the state said there was no established custom or historical evidence to show that the festival lamp had traditionally been lit at the summit of the hill or at the Deepathoon.
The affidavit, filed by Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Commissioner TG Vinay, argued that the temple administration alone had the authority to decide the manner and location of religious rituals, in accordance with the Agamas and established customs.
The government also raised concerns about public order, arguing that attempts to introduce competing locations for lighting the lamp could create tensions at a site shared by devotees of different faiths.
It further opposed handing over the temple and the entire hill to the ASI, maintaining that the agency's responsibility was limited to protecting monuments and archaeological features, not administering a functioning temple.
The state cited historical instances from 1862 and 1912, when attempts to light a lamp near the summit were reportedly resisted on the grounds that the practice was not customary and could disturb public peace.
The affidavit also challenged the demand for a permanent, 24/7 lamp at the Deepathoon and the proposal to illuminate the entire hill during the festival.
HOW DID THE KARTHIGAI DEEPAM ISSUE BECOME A POLITICAL FLASHPOINT?
The controversy took on a political dimension because of the competing positions of the BJP, DMK and now the TVK government on religious practices and temple administration.
The BJP has accused successive governments of using administrative and law-and-order arguments to restrict Hindu religious practices. Narayan Tirupati, the BJP's chief spokesperson in Tamil Nadu, alleged that the TVK government was repeating the DMK's approach by opposing the latest plea and questioning the role of the ASI.
He argued that the Madras High Court had already recognised the temple's rights over the Deepathoon area and directed the lighting of the lamp, subject to ASI preservation guidelines.
However, the TVK government maintains that its latest affidavit concerns a separate petition seeking wider relief, including ASI control of the temple and hill, a permanent lamp and illumination of the entire hill. It has defended the existing religious custom and the authority of the temple administration.
The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear the matter on November 17. The Karthigai Deepam festival at Thiruparankundram began on Monday with the flag-hoisting ceremony. The Maha Deepam is scheduled for November 24, making the coming days particularly significant for the temple administration and the devotees.

The headlines may be dominated by artificial intelligence and electoral politics, but beneath it all, another debate constantly simmers, forever threatening to erupt.
Men weren’t always “bad at friendship”
History has a solution for the male loneliness crisis.
I write, of course, of the great male friendship debate.
On one side: writers, journalists, and academics who fret over rising male loneliness, the emotional impact of friendless men on their partners, and the threat to society posed by atomized and isolated fellas. On the other: those who defend male friendships built around shared activities rather than heart-to-hearts.
These arguments often talk past each other. But the historian Tiffany Watt Smith offered me a way to think differently about both: that the gender roles undergirding the conversation are not nearly as fixed as they seem.
“I can definitely tell you that men in the past had much more intimate and romantic and involved friendships than we see today, for sure,” said Smith, who has published a number of books on the histories of friendship and emotions. “The idea that women are the kind of great experts in friendship is a really modern idea.”
I talked with Smith about Aristotle’s idea of the “perfect” friendship (it has to be between two dudes), how gendered notions of friendship inverted in the 19th century, and what men seeking deeper emotional connection from their buddies can learn from the past. You can hear that conversation and and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Smith, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
How do male friendships today compare to those of the past?
For thousands of years, it was really men who were considered the great experts in knowing how to form the highest kinds of friendships and the most intimate kind of bonds. And their friendships were considered the most meaningful and enduring and deep kind of friendships.
If you look back at David and Jonathan in the Bible or Achilles and Patroclus in the Iliad, you see these very dynamic, committed male friendships. When we look at the writings of Aristotle in the fourth-century BC, he’s talking about the deepest kind of friendship. He calls it the perfect friendship.
And this is between two men who he sees as soulmates. And he does say that there are other kinds of friendship, which are lesser friendships. He says you might make friends because it’s kind of convenient or because you enjoy doing the same kinds of things, or maybe you’re trying to help each other out. There’s a kind of quid pro quo-type of friendship. So he does see these kinds of friendship all around him. And he says women do those kinds of friendships.
One of the most famous pieces of writing about friendship ever is Michel de Montaigne’s essay “On Friendship.” Montaigne was a 16th-century essayist and lawyer, and he had this very, very close and committed friendship with another writer called La Boétie. And then after La Boétie died very unexpectedly, Montaigne wrote about their friendship and he said they had this kind of ideal friendship, the kind that Aristotle wrote about, this meeting of souls, and that this was rare and extraordinary.
And he was very explicit. He said, “Men can have these kinds of friendships.” But he very explicitly said, “Women are just incapable of having this kind of perfect friendship. They don’t have the kind of emotional stamina. They’re not clever enough. They’re not educated enough. Their souls aren’t strong enough, essentially, to withstand the complexities and difficulties of friendship.” So it’s a complete inversion from what we see today.
You used this word when you started: romantic. What did you mean by that? Was the Aristotelian conception of a perfect male friendship, was there a kind of romantic element in the way that we use the word romance?
Historians call this style of friendship “romantic friendship.” It doesn’t necessarily mean that they were having a physically active relationship or that they were having sex. They did see themselves as a partnership, and some of these male friends talked about themselves as married. This was a marriage of soul.
“Friendship is something that we have to negotiate on an individual basis. Each friendship is completely singular and we have to work out its rules.”
There’s a very important tombstone in Christ’s College in Cambridge, which commemorates these two doctors in the 16th century who basically lived their whole lives together. They traveled together, they did their research together and so on. And when they died, they were buried together. And the tomb does look like a conventional tomb between a husband and wife.
Now, we don’t know anything about their relationship in practice. I mean, the thing that really matters is the fact that this friendship, because it was commemorated as a friendship, the fact that it could be commemorated so vividly and publicly in such an extravagant way shows us that this is a culture that accepts and idealizes this kind of male friendship.
So how do we get from there to here?
Beginning in the 18th century and certainly by the 19th century, there’s a series of things that happen. One is that we get a distinction between the public space of the workplaces, cities are expanding, offices start to exist. The male sphere is fashioned as one of being in public, being a more rational sphere, and the female sphere starts to be connected with the home and intimacy and emotion.
Those ideas have been kind of floating around for a while, but they start to get really consolidated in the 19th century. And at the same time, a new ideal of femininity starts to emerge and it becomes a real sort of middle-class aspirational goal for women that they have very close friendships, almost as evidence that they can do all of these things.
Young girls in this era are taught a very particular style of friendship, which is, again, it’s very romantic. There’s lots of kissing and declarations of love and so on, but also it’s shown to be very committed. It’s very thoughtful, it’s very caring. And this is seen to be a kind of training ground for motherhood and for marriage.
At the end of the 19th century, we start to portray male friendships as kind of blundering and superficial and lacking in intimacy. And then of course, men carry on having close friendships, but by the beginning of the 20th century, another nail in the coffin, as it were, happens, which is that there’s a rise in understanding of homosexuality across Europe and America, and gay culture becomes much more visible.
In that moment, men become really anxious about having intimate and close relationships with other men. They’re worried about what that looks like and how that might be read. And that, in addition, leads to these anxieties about close male friendships.
If some guy is hearing this and is interested in having more fulfilling friendships, but he doesn’t know how to get there, where might he start?
The thing about history is that it shows us how much things have changed, but it also reminds us that things keep changing and can change again.
We’ve had this amazing history of these very romantic, intense, effusive male friendships. I think a lot of men probably would find that kind of overwhelming and unappealing as a model of friendship, but is there something in between? And one of the things I think that is important to remember is that we can make these changes and these shifts in style and these shifts in the patterns and our approaches to friendships.
One thing that I think it’s really worth listeners remembering is that since friendship has changed in the past, it can change again. There’s nothing biologically innate about the inability to make friends.
Which is freeing, the fact that friendship is not a fixed category for men or for women and that things can be what you want them to be. You’re not held back by some innate aspect of our biology.
I think that’s absolutely true. We get this notion that, well, men are sort of naturally worse at making friends or something, or they naturally have less kind of desire to connect with other people. That’s completely not true. The history of male friendships shows us that that is completely not true. So we can be released from that idea.
There isn’t an obvious, perfect, one-size-fits-all version of friendship. Friendship is something that we have to negotiate on an individual basis. Each friendship is completely singular and we have to work out its rules. What is my style of friendship? What is your style of friendship? How can we find something in the between so that we understand how to communicate and how not to hurt each other and how to build trust between each other?

The Military College of Electronics and Mechanical Engineering (MCEME), Secunderabad, organised a seminar on ‘Space as a Military Domain’ on Saturday, bringing together senior military officers, academicians and representatives of the private sector to deliberate on the growing importance of space in modern warfare and the need to strengthen India’s indigenous military space capabilities.
Lt. Gen. I.S. Rathore, MCEME Commandant, stressed the need to develop resilient space capabilities and achieve technological self-reliance through greater collaboration among the Armed Forces, scientific institutions and industry. He said the seminar provided an important platform for exchanging ideas and building partnerships to advance indigenous military space capabilities, in line with the Indian Army’s Decade of Transformation and the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
The first session, on ‘Space as a Warfighting Domain’, was moderated by Lt. Gen. K. Surendra Nath (retired) and examined geopolitical competition, deterrence, military power, space situational awareness and emerging threats.
The second session focused on ‘Indigenous Military Space Capabilities in India’ and featured a fireside discussion involving representatives of the Telangana government, space-sector companies Skyroot and Sanyark, and start-ups GalaxEye and VyomIC. The third session, ‘Emerging Space Technologies for Military Operations’, explored the use of quantum technology to secure space communications, satellite-based imagery for surveillance, and the development of indigenous satellites and their military applications.

Study Hard, Get a Career, Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
From India to France, the implicit meritocratic bargain that underwrote stable societies by providing advancement to new generations is breaking down.
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.
In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.
In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.
In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.
It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.
The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

On the intervening night of November 8 and 9, over 250 PM2.5 data points from Delhi were missing on the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) website, according to an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Scientist and air quality analyst Manoj Kumar tweeted the statistics in the early hours of November 9. According to him, out of the 59 monitoring stations, as seen on the official website of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
Missing hourly PM2.5 data raises concerns over Delhi’s air quality assessment.
Since midnight on 8 November until 5 am on 9 November, 227 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
A key concern is that many missing readings occurred when concentrations approached the monitoring instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³. These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification.
Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
There is also an unusual pattern at some stations. IGNOU Maidan Garhi, Cantonment Area, Siri Fort and Tikri Kalan recorded PM2.5 concentrations below 30 µg/m³ (Cleanest) during parts of this episode. Given the pollution levels elsewhere, these readings warrant verification for possible instrument or data-quality issues before being used in final averages or AQI calculations.
Reliable air-quality assessment during pollution episodes requires both complete data and transparent treatment of readings that exceed instrument measurement limits.
— Dr. Manoj Kumar (@manoj_kumar_nr) November 9, 2026
Air Quality Index, or AQI, turns air quality data for eight pollutants into one number and one name, providing an easy-to-understand picture of air quality. According to the All India AQI Dashboard, the pollutants are PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, Pb, and NH3. (Lead is not monitored at every station.)
Delhi’s average AQI on the night of Diwali was as follows, according to the CPCB.
However, between 1 am and 3 am on the Diwali night, over 30 monitoring stations were not showing any PM2.5 data. Over the course of the night, more stations failed.
A day after, as the mystery of missing data caused an outrage, the hourly air quality readings missing from the CPCB website became available on the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) website, which showed that the PM2.5 concentration went up to a staggering 3500 micrograms per cubic metre and beyond, which is around 60 times its standard value.
Below is the reading from Mundka station:
Below is the reading from JNU station:
Why does the Missing Data Matter?
India’s air quality figures come from monitoring stations run by state pollution control boards and committees, such as DPCC in Delhi. Stations send their readings to CPCB every 15 minutes. CPCB calculates each station’s AQI by finding a sub-index for every pollutant and taking the highest one. It then publishes the results on its portal, the SAMEER app and its daily bulletin.
A sub-index is the AQI score for a single pollutant on its own. Each pollutant is measured in different units and has a different “safe” range. For example, PM2.5 is in micrograms per cubic metre, and CO is in milligrams per cubic metre. So CPCB converts each pollutant’s reading to the same 0-500 scale, and that converted number is its sub-index.
If the PM2.5 has a sub-index of 75, SO2 has 63, and NO2 has 38, the station’s overall AQI is the highest of these, so here it is 75, driven by PM2.5. One bad pollutant is enough to push the AQI into a worse category, even if the others are fine.
If one looks carefully at the above screenshot from 12 midnight on November 9 from the Anand Vihar monitoring station, one would see that the 24-hour average of the PM2.5 pollutant is the 24-hour average AQI for that particular monitoring station. One would also note that the highest average sub-index determines the AQI.
Now, if PM2.5, which gives a measure of fine particulate matter in the air and is also highest during Diwali due to the bursting of firecrackers, goes missing, the average AQI reading underestimates the pollution in the air to a great extent. According to a Hindustan Times report, if one considers the released readings, Delhi’s AQI for 24 hours until 9 am on November 9 was 384 on a 500 scale against the 370 figure published by CPCB.
Why did the Data Go Missing?
According to Kumar’s post on X (shared when the missing data had not been released), Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
Interestingly, the highest reading also came from Mundka at 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on November 9. JNU was at 3,023 at 4 am the same night and NSUT’s West Campus at 3,008 at 5 am. Eleven of DPCC’s stations went past 2,000 micrograms per cubic metre.
The CPCB released an official statement on November 10 addressing the data gaps, saying that particulate analysers like PM2.5 were calibrated for 0-1,000 µg/m³. Under the automated validation, hourly readings beyond that range are treated as “outside range” and left out of the computation. CPCB conceded this “may appear as a data gap” during extreme episodes like Diwali firecracker bursting. Those hours don’t count towards the 24-hour average for that station. It also stated that the methodology for processing data beyond the system’s design range is “under review”, with internal deliberations underway.
On November 11, Kumar posted on X, if the 255 missing PM2.5 data points were replaced with 1,000 µg/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB, the average showed a 49% increase, from 269 to 400 µg/m³.
Alt News spoke to Kumar, who also told us that while the DPCC continued to record data above 1000 micrograms per cubic metre, it was the CPCB, the body ultimately entrusted with calculating and releasing AQI findings, that did not register it. “DPCC had measured and displayed PM 2.5 concentration above 1000 on that day. But it was not reflected on the CPCB website.”
Explaining the process and the gaps, Kumar said, “Let’s say that the instrument’s operating range is between 0 and 1000. But if it is going above 1000, there will be some uncertainty, but uncertainty can be estimated.”
Even in his November 9 post, Kumar made the point that the readings had gone missing as the concentration readings approached 1000. “These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification,” he wrote.
Furthermore, to calculate AQI, one would need to have at least 16 hours in a day, if not all 24 hours of data. So missing out on important data points during peak pollution periods underrepresents the AQI value.
It’s also worth noting that aur quality monitoring is not cheap: A 2018 Hindustan Times report put the cost of a conventional station at up to Rs 5 crore.

The National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP), under the Union Ministry of Health, has proposed a comprehensive regulatory framework for the registration of allied and healthcare professionals, with pathways for skill upgradation, competency assessment, and transition to regular registration.
Also read | What new rules mean for allied health
The broad categories of allied and healthcare professions governed by the NCAHP include clinical laboratories, surgical and emergency technology, physiotherapy, nutrition, ophthalmology, occupational therapy, community and behavioural health, medical imaging, physician associates, and health informatics.
The proposed framework aims for uniformity, transparency and accountability in professional registration. Practitioners can enhance their competencies in keeping with prescribed standards, a release issued by the Ministry said.
The NCAHP has invited public and stakeholder comments on the Draft Provisional Registration of Allied and Healthcare Professionals Regulations, 2026 framed under the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021.
Key features of the proposed regulations include the establishment of a standardised mechanism for provisional registration in accordance with the NCAHP Act, 2021.
“Importantly, the proposed Regulations also provide opportunities for eligible provisionally registered professionals to undertake prescribed bridge courses for skill enhancement, supervised clinical training and minimum qualifying examinations, wherever applicable, to meet the requirements for regular registration,’’ the Healthy Ministry’s statement said.
This competency-based approach seeks to facilitate professional development and career progression, and improve the quality of allied and healthcare services.
“The proposed framework places emphasis on skill development, professional competence and regulatory accountability,’’ a senior Health Ministry official said.
By linking progression to regular registration with prescribed requirements, the regulations seek to ensure allied and healthcare professionals possess the necessary knowledge and clinical competencies to deliver quality healthcare services.
An integrated online registration system for submitting applications, verifying credentials, assess eligibility, and issue provisional registration certificates is also proposed.
Eligible professionals granted provisional registration will receive a Provisional Registration Unique Identification Number (PR UID). The digital platform will simply procedures, improve access, and promote uniform efficiency across States and Union Territories.
The key features of the proposed regulations include standardised criteria and procedures for provisional registration; online application, verification and issuance of registration certificates with unique identification numbers; provisions for validity, extension, termination and appeals relating to provisional registration; bridge courses for skill enhancement, competency assessments and qualifying exams; supervised clinical training and institutional requirements for professional skill development; and transition to regular registration in the appropriate Central or State Register.
The NCAHP has now invited comments from allied and healthcare professionals, professional associations, educational institutions, State Allied and Healthcare Councils, healthcare institutions, experts, and the general public by December 4, 2026.

The U.S.-Israel Relationship Is Broken. Here’s How Eisenkot Could Fix It.
Former Israeli and U.S. ambassadors, lawmakers and analysts largely agree on steps Gadi Eisenkot could take if he becomes prime minister. But they are risky.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form Israel’s new governing coalition and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is by no means assured of success.
But if he does take power, another hugely daunting challenge would immediately confront him: how to undo the vast damage done to Israel’s relationship with the United States, its closest and most important ally.
It’s hard to imagine things getting much worse.
Many Americans have turned against Israel over its devastating military campaign in Gaza, and even more so over its role in pressing for war with Iran, which led to soaring gas prices.
President Trump announced this month that he would cut off billions of dollars in annual U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year and blamed Israel in part for Republican losses in the midterm elections. Democratic control of Congress could quickly lead to sanctions on violent Israeli settlers and on new settlement construction in the occupied West Bank, as well as to new conditions on arms sales.
In the past, Israel could always turn to Congress for support in clashes with the White House, said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to Washington and deputy prime minister under Mr. Netanyahu. But no longer.
“For the first time in the history of our relationship with the United States, we have no recourse,” he said. “We have to start from scratch. We have a lot of fence mending to do and with no guarantee of success. Zero.”

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.
On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.
Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.
The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.
He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine. “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine. Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine,” Michal said.
The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying: “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”
Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.
It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence firm that authorities have attributed to Russia, following an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.
In September, Kapo said it was confident that incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”. The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.
At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.
Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks against defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries on messaging platforms online to carry out acts of sabotage.
Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.

As Gaza floods overwhelm displacement sites, municipal teams in Al Maghazi refugee camp face a difficult trade-off: Pumping floodwaters out of shelters means taking away fuel needed to supply residents with drinkable water.
“The diesel we use for these pumps comes from the allocation for the wells that are supposed to pump water,” says municipal engineer Imad Abdel Jawad, and this is at a time when their supply is already insufficient.
Rainstorms swept through Gaza over the weekend of November 7 and 8, overwhelming damaged sewage networks and makeshift shelters. In some tents in Al Maghazi, the water was well over a foot deep, Jawad says.
For Hanan Saied, 46, the storm soaked the bedding and clothing she shares with her seven children. She lives in a shelter in Al Maghazi with mud walls, cracks, and plastic sheeting covering the roof, which WIRED Middle East visited.
“The house flooded, and stones and mud fell on us,” Saied says. “The bedding was soaked, and the children’s clothes were soaked.”
Her children used buckets to move water away while her eldest son tried to repair the shelter. Saied spent the night holding her daughter, Sara, who she says has asthma, trying to keep her warm.
Gaza’s Government Media Office has said at least 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians had flooded within 12 hours.
On 8 November, the Israel account on X, run by Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, posted, “Contrary to popular belief, Israel does not control the weather.” The post did not explicitly mention Gaza floods.
The flooding comes after widespread destruction of Gaza’s housing. An April assessment by the European Union, United Nations, and World Bank found that more than 371,888 housing units had been damaged or destroyed and around 1.9 million people internally displaced, often repeatedly.
By 8 November, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that 1.4 million people—65 percent of Gaza’s population—were living in tents or shelters. Humanitarian partners had received appeals from more than 26,000 households whose shelters or belongings had been damaged.
In Al Maghazi, Jawad describes five displacement sites across the camp’s western and northern areas. Parts sit on low ground where rainwater accumulates without an outlet.
His teams used pumps to move water outside the displacement sites. But the problems extend beneath the streets.
Israeli bombardment has damaged sewage manhole covers in Al Maghazi, Jawad says. Other covers have been stolen or deteriorated over time. The resulting openings allow rainwater to pour into sewage networks unable to accommodate the extra volume, causing wastewater to overflow.
“The sewage networks become unable to accommodate the quantities of sewage in addition to the rainwater that leaks into the manholes because the covers are missing,” he says.
Replacement covers are unavailable locally, while materials needed to fabricate alternatives are scarce and expensive. The municipality cannot afford all the work required. Keeping the water supply running takes priority.
“I consider spending money on maintaining wells or maintaining generators to operate water wells a higher priority than allocating some of that money to maintaining sewage manhole covers,” Jawad says.
These shortages extend across Gaza. In its November 5 report, OCHA said Israeli authorities continued to impose particularly tight restrictions on engine oil, lubricants, spare parts, and new generators. Systems for pumping floodwater and sewage were already failing.
Restoring more sustainable power supplies, the agency added, depended on Israeli permission to import solar panels, reconnect the electricity grid, and restart Gaza’s power plant.
The Israel Defense Forces did not respond to WIRED Middle East’s request for comment on restrictions affecting the entry of equipment and supplies needed for flood prevention and infrastructure repairs.
Jawad says trucks and earth-moving machinery are needed to bring material to displacement sites where water collects on muddy ground, improving conditions beneath and around tents.
The consequences also reach clinics. Dr Asma Saleh, a general practitioner at the Al Maghazi clinic of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), reports an increase in children presenting with respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses as the rainy season begins.
Saleh says the clinic sees around 120 children daily, including approximately 22 with influenza-like illness diagnosed from symptoms and 13 with gastroenteritis.
“The inhumane living conditions, collapse of infrastructure, the flowing streets contaminated with sewage, and the shortage of medical supplies are all factors that profoundly impact the health care system in Gaza,” she says.
For Saied, the immediate concern is getting Sara through the next storm. Her daughter has more frequent asthma attacks during winter, she says, and the family has neither a nebuliser nor electricity to operate one.
“My older son spent hours repairing our worn shelter using simple tools, but I don’t know what to do during upcoming storms."
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede the development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, in a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often discovered after it has already spread.
For decades, efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.
“We asked a fundamentally different question: What if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” study leader Rajan Gogna of the Hoag Family Cancer Institute in Newport Beach, California, said in a statement. Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes.
The precancerous lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC). The new study found that women with this precursor condition have elevated blood levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma.
When researchers measured Tu-Stroma in blood, they detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women. In women with genetic risk factors for ovarian cancer, approximately 72% of positive results would be accurate, while negative results would be correct nearly 100% of the time, they reported. “For women at high risk, this could transform how we approach prevention,” co-author Esha Madan, also of Hoag, said in a statement.
Many such women face difficult decisions about preventive surgery to remove their fallopian tubes and ovaries. “Today, decisions about preventive surgery are largely guided by inherited risk, without knowing whether precancerous lesions are actually present,” Madan said. “Our discovery could eventually provide that missing biological information.”

The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines, starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea, where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.
Global pivots towards Asia
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas. Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore.
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration. Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

I open with this caveat: I haven’t had a ton of time to digest the surprise Armand Hammer record that dropped this week. Billy Woods and Elucid rarely miss, though, and my initial reaction is that Snakes & Ladders ranks among their best. It doesn’t have the seamless throughline production-wise that their collabs with Alchemist (Haram and Mercy) do, but it’s still clearly the singular vision of the two men at its center.
Listen to this: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders

Listen to this: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders
Armand Hammer’s latest album is among their best.
Ominous noises dance in the background, blasts of noise add dashes of industrial rage, bass lines throb, and saxophone bleats call out to the sky. Woods and Elucid have always had excellent taste in production, but here they seem to have brought out the best in collaborators like clipping, Kenny Segal, and Child Actor. They’ve also successfully rallied them around a specific sound palette that keeps the record from actually sounding like it has beats from 11 different producers.
Of course, what makes Armand Hammer stand out from many of their contemporaries is their unique and verbose flows. Their lyrical mastery even makes guest rappers like $ilkmoney, who you can practically hear stalking around the mic as he seethes on “Risk,” up their game.
On songs like “Gravity,” Billy Woods navigates burgeoning romance with shocking directness, while also acknowledging obliquely how hard it can be to say what you mean.
Get it off your chest or put it to the side
As a preface, all due respect, I suggest
‘Cause it’s nothing more precious than time
On “Vespers,” he references Siouxsie and the Banshees and says “My nightcap three fingers of Fernet,” which is probably the first time I’ve ever heard Fernet Branca get a shoutout in a rap song.
“Graveside” is another highlight where it’s Elucid’s turn to get vulnerable:
I see you in the grave, I see you in the dirt
Shouts and hollers every which way, hurting
Darkness chase light
Steel shut close curtain
In some ways, this record feels like a culmination of what Billy Woods and Elucid have been working towards on their non-Alchemist-produced Armand Hammer records like We Buy Diabetic Test Strips, but also their recent solo records like Golliwog and Revelator.

Anna Sawai has opened up about her experience of working on How To Rob A Bank and what drew her to the film. While the title suggests a conventional heist thriller, Sawai revealed that the story offered more than she initially anticipated. She said the emotional depth of the characters was one of the aspects that stood out to her during her association with the project.
Anna Sawai opens up about her role in How To Rob A Bank; says, “She keeps things organized and grounded”
Speaking about her first impression of the film, Sawai admitted that she expected it to revolve primarily around a bank robbery. However, as she explored the story further, she discovered an emotional layer that made the project more interesting for her.
“I expected it to be just a bank robbery film,” she says candidly. “But what I really loved was that there’s so much heart in it. I really felt for all the characters.”
The actor also discussed her character, Emi, and her role within the group. Describing Emi as someone who brings a sense of clarity to the team's decisions, Sawai explained how her character approaches situations differently from the others. While the men tend to act on their emotions, Emi takes a more measured approach and helps keep things organised.
“I think she’s actually the brain of the group. She’s able to step back and look at things objectively while the guys are rushing ahead emotionally. She keeps things organized and grounded.”

8 injured after portion of under-construction building collapses in Delhi’s Paharganj
According to Delhi Fire Services, a call regarding the incident was received at 4:40 pm, following which the injured were rushed to a nearby hospital.
At least eight people suffered injuries after a portion of a two-storey building collapsed on the workers in central Delhi’s Paharganj area on Sunday evening. The Delhi Police said the building was under construction and the victims were laying the roof for the second floor when the incident took place.
Police said all victims were rescued within an hour and nobody was in critical condition.
According to the Delhi Fire Service, a call was received around 4:40 pm from the Sangatrashan area in Paharganj about a house collapse opposite a government girls’ school.
The Delhi Fire Service said that three fire tenders were rushed to the spot. “Around 5:25 pm, the team sent a message that the roof slab had collapsed and five persons were taken out by the public and PCR before the DFS team arrived. The DFS teams are still removing debris to look for any more injured persons, if any,” said an official.

Police said around eight persons were working at the under-construction hotel site in Paharganj. The victims were identified as Sheikh Saddam (37), Sheikh Raja (20), Mohd Suhail (50), Sanjud Khan (40), Gautam Yadav (28), Varun Yadav (36), Raja (36) and Mantu (40).
“At the time of the incident, the roof slab of the second floor was being laid when a portion of the building collapsed. On receipt of the information, police staff immediately reached the spot and initiated necessary response measures. During preliminary inspection, the supporting columns were found to be wet, and the building appeared to have tilted,” said DCP (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh.
“We helped rescue all the workers, who have been shifted to Lady Hardinge Medical College and Hospital for treatment. They are stable. Some suffered fractures, others had minor injuries. We will take strict legal action after ascertaining facts in the case,” he added.
MCD incident report on the collapse
Reacting to the incident, an MCD spokesperson said that a portion of the lintel/shuttering collapsed at Property number 3992–3993, Kaseruwalan, Paharganj and the building was being constructed after obtaining prior permission in the form of a sanctioned building plan number 20010602.
“During the removal of shuttering by labourers at the ground floor, a portion of the recently constructed lintel suddenly collapsed, resulting in injuries to some labourers. At the time of inspection, the construction at the subject property was found to have been carried out up to the basement, stilt floor and part of the upper ground floor. No unauthorised construction was noticed at the subject property at the time of inspection,” the MCD spokesperson said.
Around 10 days back, another major case of building collapse was reported in Delhi’s Chawri Bazaar, where a three-storey under-construction building collapsed, killing seven people.
The rescue operation went on from November 5 till November 8 as several persons were trapped under heavy debris.
Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta had announced ex-gratia assistance of ₹10 lakhs for each of the families of the deceased. The Delhi Police had arrested the building owner, Samula, along with three building contractors. The probe had revealed that the structure was unauthorised and no safety norms were being followed. The rescue operation also went on slow due to the narrow and congested lanes.

ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.
Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.
“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”
The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the UN “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.
“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”
Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to Government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.
By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.
New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.
Questions over funding and management
Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.
One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.
Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.
Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for.
“A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” said the humanitarian organisation Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF.
Children face high death rates
Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say.
Most children affected by the disease have not received specialised care, contributing to high death rates.
According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through November 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died.
Conflict and attacks hamper response
Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices.
Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack.
The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict.
Fighting between Government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians.
The virus's rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
Nvidia's CEO resigns after alleged spy scandal. What's next for the company?
A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.
Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.
"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told Morning Edition.
He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.
"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.
Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.
Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.
He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.
"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.
