Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.
Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.
A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.
Untangling humans from the weather
Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.
Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.
Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.
The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.
Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.
A natural experiment in staying home
An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.
Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”
The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.
In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.
The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.
Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.
The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.
Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”
Not every fire went quiet
In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.
There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.
One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.
Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.
When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.
This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.
Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.
Understanding the human Impact
Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.
Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance.
Apple’s new study looks to improve the effectiveness of AI health tools
The study will be conducted through a new app where participants can ask health questions and rate the responses.
The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.
Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence.
During enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models. The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

Srinagar- The Jammu and Kashmir Congress on Monday accused the BJP of indulging in “cheap and petty politics” over the killing of two SPOs in Kishtwar, and demanded that agencies probe all angles of the incident so that clarity is brought forward.
Defending the Jammu and Kashmir Pradesh Congress Committee (JKPCC) president Tariq Karra’s comments that there were claims that the SPOs may have been shot by security personnel who mistook them for militants, party leader Suhail Bukhari said the party condemns the incident, but different stories are emerging about it.
“A thorough investigation into the entire matter so that the exact sequence of events is brought to light,” Bukhari said, addressing a press conference here.
He said the security agencies, the Jammu and Kashmir Police, or even the administration have not yet placed a clear-cut sequence of events formally on record.
“Has the police given any official information about the exact sequence of events so far? To my knowledge, no,” he added.
In such a situation, the Congress leader said, when no official sequence of events has been released, and different versions are circulating locally, as a responsible political leader and head of a responsible political party, Karra, the JKPCC chief is simply saying: investigate all angles and tell us the truth.
“Because knowing what exactly happened there is the right of the families of those martyrs who lost their loved ones. Instead of doing that, it is deeply unfortunate, instead of acting on Karra’s demand for an impartial investigation probing all angles so that the truth reaches the families of those martyrs, heals their wounds, and delivers justice, which they deserve, to know the circumstances in which their loved ones were martyred, look at what the BJP has done,” he said.
Pointing that the security, and law and order, is the responsibility of the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha, Bukhari said that instead of acknowledging that these families deserve to know how their loved ones were killed, the BJP “has indulged in very cheap and petty politics”.
“They do not want it to be clearly known under what circumstances these young men lost their lives,” he added.
The Congress leader said what Karra remarked is not the Congress’ story, but the JKPCC chief has merely stated one among the stories that have emerged so far and “which the people are talking about there”.
“In a situation where an incident has occurred, and the authorities have not once issued a clear statement confirming a specific sequence of events, in that vacuum, many things surface locally. This is not the Congress’s story. Karra merely stated that among the stories that have emerged, one story is also this, which people are talking about there.
“It could be speculation; there could be an alternative truth or fact that has to come out from the investigation. If this were the Congress’s story, we would have asserted that this is what happened. Instead, what did Karra say? That we want an investigation, and all angles should be looked into,” Bukhari said.
He also referred to the row over the transportation of the mortal remains of the slain SPOs, and asked: “What greater injustice, what greater insult could be inflicted upon the memory of those young men, their sacrifice, and their families?”
“This responsibility lies directly with the BJP, because they oversee the Home Ministry and the security apparatus here,” he said.
Bukhari claimed that the BJP is “rattled”, and that their local MLAs and Leader of the Opposition, Sunil Sharma, know that they “keep beating the drum claiming they have fixed the situation here, yet the state of security is such that people are still being killed, whether in Kulgam or in Kishtwar”.
“People are making sacrifices, and questions will be asked of them because the apparatus is under their control. So, to avoid being questioned and held accountable, they are trying to divert and deflect the issue,” the Congress leader added.
Referring to the alleged use of derogatory terms like ‘nalayak’ (useless) and ‘naehli’ (incompetence) against police officers during a heated exchange with security officers by Leader of Opposition Sunil Sharma, Bukhari accused the BJP of shamelessly “humiliating” the security institutions and J&K Police for the sake of politics.
“What greater insult could there be to our security agencies and brave jawans, when members of a force are laying down their lives and the BJP, just to wash its hands of responsibility, labels them worthless and incompetent? It is a matter of utter shame,” he added.
Demanding accountability, Bukhari said Sharma cannot hide behind “fabricated stories”.
“You will have to answer these questions: under what circumstances did those two jawans go there for duty? Who issued the order? Bring clarity: who approved those operational SOPs? And this matter goes all the way from the bottom to the top, where Home Minister Amit Shah himself will be held responsible for all of this,” Bukhari said.
The Congress leader added that the party that has “repeatedly insulted our soldiers and heroes” should not lecture us on how to respect security forces.
“You keep repeating like a parrot that ‘we have improved the situation’. Issue a White Paper and tell us whether the situation has improved or deteriorated. You cannot say both things at once. Issue a White Paper and explain why the security situation in Jammu and Kashmir is like this, or accept that you have failed and that you are incompetent.
On the remarks of the local MLA Shagun Parihar that announcements were made from mosques about killing Hindus, Bukhari said the party demands an inquiry to establish the facts.
“The Congress party will not let them cover it up. The local MLA there has made a very inflammatory statement. That area is extremely sensitive. You know that this party constantly does politics in the name of Hindu-Muslim and on the blood of people.
“She made a statement claiming that announcements were made from local mosques. We demand, and we also urge the administration, to immediately establish an inquiry. Ask her what proof she has to make such a claim. And if she does not have proof, not only must she and her party apologise, but strict action must also be taken against her,” the Congress leader said.

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.
Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.
Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.
A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

This week's "Saturday Night Live" cold open was a who's-who of the AI revolution.
Comedian John Mulaney kicked off the episode by playing a CIA officer conducting national security training for tech billionaires. Specifically, how to identify a spy.
Mulaney's character is joined by Palantir cofounder Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes), and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane).
"America needs you to learn the difference between a woman who actually wants to have sex with you, and a woman who is clearly a spy," Mulaney said. "You all saw how former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned this week after he was caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy."
Last Sunday, Nvidia's board of directors said it would investigate whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort" on the same day he admitted to an extramarital affair in a memo to staff. Huang resigned from his position days later.
On "Saturday Night Live," Mulaney's character empathized with the tech billionaires.
"Look, I can't imagine how disorienting this has been for you. To go from these bug-eyed little weirdos to being gods," Mulaney said. "Never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you, A: survived, and B: been given all the world's wealth and power."
Mulaney asked the tech executives why someone "very beautiful" would be interested in them.
"Because I have a good personality and normal, human mannerisms?" Marshall's Altman said.
Zuckerberg, played by Dismukes, guessed it's because "she's comforted by my Meta glasses recording her at all times."
Wickline's Amodei theorized it's because "she's using me... for my body."
Mulaney then asked the group to pretend an attractive woman approached them at the bar and asked, "What are you working on?" Amodei and Zuckerberg weighed in.
"I would say, Madam, what a pleasure to see you this evening. May I interest you in an industry secret?" Amodei said. Zuckerberg said he would "assume that she wanted to sleep with the man who created the Metaverse, as all women do."
Near the end, former 'SNL' cast member Bowen Yang returned as Huang. "It's me. Jensen 'hide your wife' Huang," Yang says as he joins the other tech billionaires. "Ladies, when you invite Jensen over, you know what's about to go down. The S&P 500."
He added, "That's right. I'm into BDSM: Breakin' da stock market." Nvidia lost more than $500 billion in market value over the last week.
Yang's Huang cautioned his fellow tech executives against being like him. "Remember, women don't like guys like us. That's how we became guys like us," he said.
In real life, some Nvidia loyalists are hoping the board will reinstate Huang. Nvidia's board of directors said it's considering internal and external candidates for the permanent CEO position.

Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”

The Hindu on Tuesday carried a standalone image of thick smog enveloping Rashtrapati Bhavan on Monday morning with the caption ‘Pollution unlimited’. On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”

Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
- Published
Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.
The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.
The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.
Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.
The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.
It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.
The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.
Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.
This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association.
The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people - which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

Diabetes management is moving beyond periodic finger-prick tests and clinic visits, with technologies such as continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), insulin pumps and mobile applications providing more detailed information on glucose levels and helping patients make day-to-day decisions about their care.
CGMs use a sensor placed on the arm or abdomen to measure glucose levels at regular intervals, offering a picture of fluctuations through the day and night. Insulin pumps deliver insulin continuously, while automated insulin delivery systems combine CGM readings with algorithms to adjust insulin delivery. Mobile applications can bring together information on glucose levels, food intake, physical activity and medication.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kunal Bahl, the 43-year-old cofounder of the Indian digital commerce holding company AceVector Limited and investment firm Titan Capital. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Entrepreneurship was always on the cards for me. An H-1B rejection just fast-tracked it.
I grew up in New Delhi, and then I went to the University of Pennsylvania in the US for a program that blended an engineering and business degree.
While I was in college, a bunch of big things happened in the tech sphere: Google went public, and Facebook became viral. By 2006, which is when I graduated, it was all the rage.
The internet economy was taking off. I had a lot of business ideas, but it became clear that I could not start a company because of my visa status. I was on an F-1 visa, and I first needed to find an employer who could sponsor my H-1B, then lay out a pathway into Silicon Valley. From there, I'd try to start my own company.
I interned at Microsoft during my junior year and returned in October 2006 in a full-time role after graduating.
Then my H-1B visa petition was rejected
While waiting for my H-1B visa selection, I was counting down the days until my Optional Practical Training, a temporary yearlong work authorization after graduation, would expire.
I remember vividly that, in June or July of 2007, I got an email that said my H-1B petition had been rejected.
For a moment, I didn't understand. It was unfathomable to me that, if I worked at a company like Microsoft, my H-1B visa would not be approved.
I checked with the Microsoft team. Looking at their faces, I gathered that there was a finality to the rejection.
The company was very nice about the situation, suggesting that I work in the Microsoft India office and try again for the H-1B after a year.
At no point had I considered moving back to India. But I gathered myself up and decided that if I go back to my country, I'd work for myself, not for Microsoft.
No time wasted starting my company
I no longer had the baggage of having to figure out this H-1B situation. I felt liberated because I didn't have to worry about visas or green cards.
So I called up my best friend from high school, Rohit Bansal, who was working in a financial institution at the time. We used to sit next to each other in class and talk about starting a business together. I asked if he wanted to do something together.
He said, "Great, let's do it."
Our company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before I touched down in India.
Building a startup in India in 2007 was a challenge
India has a hot startup ecosystem now. That cannot be said of the India of 2007.
The country had very few internet users and smartphones, and digital payments were few and far between. Things were pretty dull, to be honest. I was not returning to the promised land or a burgeoning startup ecosystem.
Even launching a startup was frowned upon. People would ask, "You guys have a good education, so why didn't you get a job? Does nobody want to hire you?"
We started as a physical coupon book business, because Indians love a good value. But getting funding was a challenge. Angel investors weren't common then.
We had both saved up a bit from our year working corporate jobs and pooled our savings — about $60,000 in total. That became our seed capital.
We stayed with our families for food and accommodation, and worked out of a small office in the basement of a residential building in Delhi's furniture market. We had neighbors complain about people going in and out of the building late, because Rohit and I would work 20 hours a day to get our business off the ground.
Our company pivoted from being an online couponing platform like Groupon to one of India's first e-commerce platforms, called Snapdeal. Now we have two publicly listed companies that we spun off from the original coupon book business.
We wanted to give back to the startup ecosystem in India, as well. In 2011, once we had built up some capital, we started investing in early-stage startups and formed Titan Capital.
Over the last 15 years, we've invested in more than 320 startups, many of which have gone public. I'm now also a judge on Shark Tank India.
The India of today is full of opportunity
In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous, though it hurt at the time. It was part of a larger plan: I had to return to India and help the next generation of founders.
It was easy for me to pack up my bags and come back because I wasn't married and didn't have children. And I know it's far more difficult for those who have dependents living with them in the US, like children or parents.
So I do empathize with workers facing immigration struggles in the US.
That said, India has changed drastically since the time we started our company.
India now has a billion internet users. There's ubiquitous smartphone penetration. There are so many coworking spaces for startup founders. There is a high talent density.
There is a robust funding ecosystem. The startup tech scene is front of mind for the government.
There is no better time to come back to India.

Canada Letter
Games behind paywalls and exorbitant costs forcing a drop in attendance — even to watch Connor McDavid in Edmonton — have only compounded the loss of a Saturday night ritual.
The National Hockey League season is less than two months old, and much of the focus in Canada has been on how expensive it is to attend games, and how costly and cumbersome it has become to watch them on television.
Attendance has fallen in several markets, including Edmonton, where Connor McDavid has an astonishing 49 points in 20 games and is on pace to challenge Wayne Gretzky’s single-season scoring record of 215 points.
This week, The Globe and Mail reported that three TV providers had filed a complaint with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission asking Rogers Sportsnet to reverse its decision to put more than 50 Monday night N.H.L. games behind a paywall on its streaming service for an extra $13 a month.
Further increasing the cost and complexity of watching hockey, Wednesday night games are on Prime Video. TSN broadcasts some regional games with blackouts, and a subscription to NHL Centre Ice is needed to watch out-of-market games.
Until this season, the N.H.L. could be found for free.
In June, the CBC and Rogers Sportsnet announced that the national broadcaster would no longer air N.H.L. games on Saturday nights, a first in 75 years, ending the cultural institution “Hockey Night in Canada.” Last month, the CBC announced it would begin airing Professional Women’s Hockey League games when its season begins in December.

What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stop since 9/11
- Published
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.
The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.
What about international flights?
All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.
There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.
Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.
Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.
When will normal service resume?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.
"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.
Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations.
American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning.
What caused the ground stop?
Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.
"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.
He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag.
"It's going to continue to fail," he said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.
He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.
Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.
Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.
When was the last ground stop?
It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.
"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.
Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.
"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.
The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.
But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

Punjab woman, accomplice held in Rajasthan train track blast; police suspect ISI's 'romance' strategy to recruit women
Police said the woman is a resident of Gurdaspur and is separated from her husband who is lodged in jail in Punjab in a drug trafficking case.
A day after a woman and her male accomplice were arrested from Gurdaspur in Punjab in connection with the November 3 railway track blast in Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan, police on Sunday said that the accused had links with Pakistan-based handlers and had made two unsuccessful attempts to blow up the railway line before carrying out the explosion earlier this month.
The 21-year-old woman and her 23-year-old male accomplice were arrested on Saturday in a joint operation by the Rajasthan Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), Sri Ganganagar Police and Punjab Police.
Investigators recovered two foreign-made pistols, 46 live cartridges and ₹30,000 allegedly received for carrying out the blast, police said.
Alleged Pak handlers linked to ISI
ATS Additional Director General of Police Dinesh MN said preliminary investigations revealed that the duo was in contact with two Pakistan-based handlers, identified as Shah and Chacha, the latter suspected of having links with Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI).
"The woman was in contact with Pakistani handler Shah and carried out the blast with the assistance of her accomplice. They were acting on instructions from Shah and another person known as Chacha in Pakistan, who is suspected to be associated with the ISI," Dinesh said.
Police said the woman is a resident of Dostpur village in Gurdaspur and is separated from her husband who is lodged in jail in Punjab in a drug trafficking case. Investigators suspect she subsequently established contact with Pakistan-based handlers. She had allegedly been in contact with the handlers for nearly 15 months and had been communicating with them primarily through WhatsApp.
Police said the accused initially planned to target the railway track in the Ramsinghpur police station area on October 6, but the attempt could not proceed because explosives were unavailable. On October 12 or 13, they allegedly planted a timer bomb supplied by Shah, but it failed to explode due to a technical malfunction. The third attempt, on November 3, resulted in the explosion around 9.45 pm.
Investigators believe the prime suspect was chosen for the operation because her presence near the railway track was less likely to create suspicion.
How the arrests were carried out
The arrests followed technical surveillance, examination of social media accounts and intelligence inputs from central agencies. A team led by IPS officer Nitin Chaudhary and ATS Bikaner unit in-charge Surendra Kumar coordinated with Punjab Counter Intelligence and Gurdaspur SSP Aditya to apprehend the suspects. Dinesh MN said he was also present during the operation in Punjab.

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.
Two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.
“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.
“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.
“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.
In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has done so in the past.
He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.
During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.
“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.
On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
Turning a Windows defense against itself
The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.
By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links, the attacker causes Defender to open the CLFS container in the security context of the antimalware engine. If an associated authentication file is missing, CLFS creates it using Defender’s System privileges. Because CLFS assigns the newly created file the Discretionary Access Control List of the original file, the attacker may gain access to a file created with System privileges, allowing the file-creation operation to be abused as part of a privilege-escalation attack.
Ironically, the vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to prevent attackers from exploiting other vulnerabilities in CLFS.
“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges,” Nightmare Eclipse wrote. “Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.”

You forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.
That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.
You might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention. Kim’s goal was to bring a similar experience to physical objects in our lives. “We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,” she tells WIRED. While folks have encouraged Kim to sell OAT kits online, she hasn't decided whether to pursue it as a business opportunity.
Kim says everyone spends all day staring at mobile devices, and AI agents—even if they're designed to handle tasks on your behalf—still demand attention from your smartphone screen. OATs were a way to bring those interactions out into the real world.
Giving AI a physical body isn't new, as companies rush to create “the next smartphone,” whether that's failed attempts like the Humane Ai Pin, OpenAI's upcoming hardware created in collaboration with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, or Meta's Muse Charm. The pocket-sized gadget houses Meta's popular Muse AI agent and is expected to launch in December. Increasingly, though, companies have leaned on “cuteness” in their strategy for widespread adoption.
OATs have an E Ink display connected to internal and external sensors that can track things like moisture, temperature, humidity, light, occupancy, and motion. (The hardware is relatively cheap, around $20 for the main module.) The sprites are created with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image-generation service, creating a suite of emotions for various states based on the sensor data. You can set all of this up through a web portal, where you can name your OAT and choose which sensors to use for the object you're attaching it to.
The web app will generate “Positive” and “Negative” behaviors based on your object's name and description. So if the OAT is attached to a plant, positive triggers could be “consistent air temperature readings” and “low humidity levels” if the plant of choice prefers dry environments. However, you can customize these behaviors to suit your specific plant type.
It can be used for very simple things. Want to use your skateboard more often? Attach the OAT to your board, and if it hasn't detected motion for a few days, the avatar will look sad and lonely. You don't want that, do you? As Kim says, “These kinds of inanimate objects can be more expressive.” When you hop on the board, the OAT avatar will be happy, with fun faces.
The catch is that the system's battery life is really short, showing why this is more of a proof of concept than anything else. OATs last around three to four days, but paired with the sound-level sensor, they'll only last a day. It has a USB-C port for charging the lithium-ion polymer battery.
Kim says she distributed OATs to many people and found that they used them in three different ways. One is, “Am I being used?” Like when you attach an OAT to a coffee machine and have the avatar get excited when the machine starts grinding beans. The second is for warning people near an object. For example, 3D printers release toxic fumes during use, and attaching an OAT to one can warn people that the device is operational. And the third is to track their own behaviors. Someone attached an OAT to a dumbbell to track how often they lifted weights, encouraging themselves to exercise regularly so they wouldn't disappoint the AI pet.
The demo at the symposium was popular, and Kim turned it into a competition to see who could come up with the most interesting ideas about what objects to pair with the OATs. Kim's website features a gallery with sprites people made, from an animated conference badge to a panda avatar for an Owala water bottle.
But the demo also ignited a huge discussion about anthropomorphizing artificial intelligence, and whether it’s proper to give these sprites humanlike traits and emotions to make people feel connected with them.
It's already a topic in play within the AI industry. Companies often refer to their chatbot behaviors in human terms, like when they “hallucinate.” Anthropic announced a “dreaming” feature this summer where its AI agent cleaned up its local memory as a background process. These anthropomorphized terms can distort moral judgments about AI and cause people to overly trust the tools.
Kim says that's why OATs have very limited interactions, restricted to expressive emotions and the E Ink display.
“Anthropomorphism can be very useful in certain ways, like helping people to change their behaviors,” Kim says. “People name their car, and they name their bike. I rarely see people who name their iPhone. I feel like in the future of computing we will have more of a relationship with AI, but we should definitely be careful not to abuse this."
